events.text: The Leeward Isle drifts a day behind the others, and its people fly kites to tell the fleet they are still there. {npc}, who has made the kites for nine hundred years, has dropped one over the edge. It is caught on a cloud-pine growing sideways from the isle's underside, flapping like a hand waving goodbye.
events.arc: The Kite-Maker of the Leeward Isle

choices.text: Climb down the roots of the isle for it

effects.log: You go down hand over hand with the whole sky under your feet. The kite is torn but whole. {npc} holds it like a returned child.

choices.text: Call it up with a thread of qi

effects.log: The kite comes up on a breath of yours, slow and dignified. {npc} watches the thread of qi more than the kite.

choices.text: Tell {npc} a kite is only paper

effects.log: {npc} looks at you for a long moment and goes inside. The isle flies one kite fewer that year.

events.text: Every year now {npc} sends you a small kite by the evening wind, paper thin as a breath, with a word painted on it. This year the word is "late". The Leeward Isle has fallen two days behind, and the fleet has not looked back.
events.arc: The Kite-Maker of the Leeward Isle

choices.text: Fly to the fleet and tell them

effects.log: The lead isle's steersman had not noticed. Nobody had. The fleet slows half a day, grudgingly, and {npc} sends you a kite with "thank you" on it.

choices.text: Help {npc} make kites big enough to be seen

effects.log: You spend a season gluing silk the size of sails. When it rises, the whole fleet sees it, and the isles at the back fly kites back.

events.text: A storm of the high winds tears through the fleet. When it clears, the Leeward Isle is gone from the sky. Then you see the kite: one small paper kite, very far off, still flying. Someone is still holding the string.
events.arc: The Kite-Maker of the Leeward Isle

choices.text: Follow the string through the storm's tail

ok.log: You find the isle snagged in a cloud-reef, {npc} on the edge with the string in both hands, nine hundred years of patience in the grip. You tow them home.

fail.log: The tail of the storm throws you back twice. By the time you reach the isle, the fleet's steersmen have found it by the same kite.

choices.text: Tell the steersmen where the kite is

effects.log: You point. The fleet turns. The Leeward Isle comes home on a towline, and {npc} does not let go of the string until it is moored.

events.text: {npc} has made a last kite, wide as a hall, painted with every isle of the fleet. "I am tired of being the one at the back," {he} says. "Fly it for me, from the front, and the back will know someone is looking."
events.arc: The Kite-Maker of the Leeward Isle

choices.text: Fly it from the lead isle every year

effects.log: It flies from the bow of the fleet every spring from then on. The isles at the back fly theirs in answer, and none of them falls behind again.

choices.text: Teach the young of the isle to make them instead

effects.log: The Leeward Isle has twelve kite-makers by the next century. {npc} says it is the noisiest place in the sky, and has never looked happier.

events.text: Snow above the clouds falls upward. Every winter it rises from the cloud sea in slow white columns and settles on the undersides of the isles, so that for a season the world hangs from a white ceiling. Children of the isles lie on their backs at the edge to watch it come up.

choices.text: Lie down at the edge and watch

effects.log: You watch the snow rise for a whole afternoon. Something in your breathing slows to match it.

choices.text: Catch a flake and study it

effects.log: It has seven points and turns slowly in your palm, against the wind. You think about that for a month.

events.text: At the cloud market a weigher sells clouds by the bolt: cumulus for bedding, mist for a hall's ceiling, one small thundercloud in a jade jar, labelled "not for beginners". The weigher catches you looking at the jar.

choices.text: Buy the thundercloud (2 Low-Grade Spirit Stones)

effects.log: It grumbles in its jar on your shelf for a decade. When you finally let it out in seclusion, the storm teaches your meridians something new.

choices.text: Ask how anyone weighs a cloud

effects.log: "By the shadow," says the weigher, and shows you. You will never look at a shadow the same way again.

events.text: {npc} runs the cloud-skiff between the Lantern Isle and the Low Reef, and in four centuries {he} has never once tied up at either end. Passengers hop on and off while the skiff slows to a crawl. Today {he} nods at you: "Ride along. I will not stop, but I will slow."
events.arc: The Ferryman Who Never Docked

effects.log: The skiff sways under you. {npc} grins, someone who has made one crossing a million times and still likes it.
"Docking is how you get stuck," {npc} says, and says nothing more for an hour.
The skiff glides by with a courteous dip of the pole. You watch it go.

events.text: Halfway over the cloud sea, {npc} shows you a small sealed box under the thwart. "Letters between the two isles. Neither postmaster speaks to the other, so I carry what they cannot say." One letter has a corner torn from the damp.
events.arc: The Ferryman Who Never Docked

effects.log: You press the corner back with a thread of warmth. {npc} says nothing, and tucks the box a little deeper.

choices.text: Ask what the quarrel is about

effects.log: {npc} laughs. "Neither remembers. It began about a goat, two hundred years back."

choices.text: Keep your eyes on the clouds

effects.log: You pretend not to see the box. {npc} approves of that, quietly.

events.text: The skiff stops. For the first time in four centuries {npc} has run aground on a cloud-reef, and the two postmasters are shouting across the water. {npc} looks at you: "Say a word. Either one will do."
events.arc: The Ferryman Who Never Docked

choices.text: Read the mended letter aloud to both

effects.log: The goat is in the first line. Both postmasters go quiet, then one laughs, and the other cannot help it either.

choices.text: Push the skiff free and say nothing

effects.log: You shove until the reef lets go. The postmasters keep shouting, but at a distance, which is how they like it.

events.text: The two postmasters now send their letters together, in the same box, with a ribbon around them. {npc} still does not dock. "But I slow," {he} says, "a little longer each time, and one day I may find the ground has a nice feeling."
events.arc: The Ferryman Who Never Docked

effects.log: It becomes your small ritual: one crossing, no stopping, a pot of tea going cold between you.
You send a bolt of cloud-silk for the sail instead. It shows up on the skiff the next season.

events.text: {npc} gave up the pole at last, and the skiff now belongs to a girl from the Low Reef who docks every time. {npc} sits on the Lantern Isle quay, watching the water, and when you pass {he} raises a hand: "Slow enough?"
events.arc: The Ferryman Who Never Docked

effects.log: You share a long evening of not much. It is the best crossing you ever made.
{npc} nods, satisfied, and looks back at the sea.

events.text: The Isle of Slow Tilt leans one finger-width to the east each decade, so its teahouse has legs of different lengths. {npc}, the keeper, tops the wedge under the third leg each morning and sighs. "Tea poured here runs uphill by noon," {he} says. "Try a cup."
events.arc: The Teahouse at the Leaning Edge

effects.log: The tea pours slantwise into your mouth and is, you admit, the best you have had.
You spend a week shimming legs. The floor is flat, and the teahouse loses what made it strange.

choices.text: Order a plain cup of cold water

effects.log: {npc} sniffs, but serves it, and the water runs uphill too.

events.text: A storm-front comes in and the isle tilts hard. The whole teahouse slides a hand-span. {npc} calmly holds the kettle level and says, "Quick, the pot," as if the room were not moving.
events.arc: The Teahouse at the Leaning Edge

effects.log: You catch it with two fingers. {npc} nods as if this were the whole point of tea.

choices.text: Steady the isle with a thread of qi

effects.log: The tilt eases for a breath, long enough for the kettle to settle. {npc} gives you a look of warm suspicion.
The whole room laughs with you. It is the first time {npc} has laughed in a century.

events.text: {npc} tells you a secret: the isle is leaning toward a place. "Something calls it," {he} says, "and every cup I pour is a guess at what." A sailor of the Low Reef asks if you would chart the lean.
events.arc: The Teahouse at the Leaning Edge

choices.text: Take the chart and follow the lean

effects.log: You plot the tilt for years. It points to a quiet reef where nothing happens, and you settle there for a time.

choices.text: Keep the secret and drink the tea

effects.log: Some leans are best left to wonder. {npc} slides you a free cup.

events.text: The isle reaches the place it was leaning toward: a still pool of cloud with a single peach tree on a floating stone. {npc} stands under it and weeps without noise. "Tea," {he} says. "Of course. Tea."
events.arc: The Teahouse at the Leaning Edge

effects.log: You pour as slowly as the isle moves. {npc} drinks, and the tree drops one peach into the cup.
You step away. Some arrivals are private.

events.text: The Isle of Slow Tilt never gets anywhere in your lifetime, and {npc} keeps pouring. You visit once a year. The tea runs uphill, the floor stays crooked, and it is the only place in the Heavens that has ever felt like home.
events.arc: The Teahouse at the Leaning Edge

choices.text: Raise a cup to the wedge under the leg

effects.log: The wedge gets a new name. The teahouse gets a regular.
It hangs by the door for centuries.

events.text: At the Ministry of Fog, junior clerk {npc} has lost a bolt of morning mist, the very bolt due at the Jade Court at noon. {He} stands at your desk twisting a sleeve. "You knew where the stores were. Please. They will take my post."
events.arc: The Ministry of Fog Mislays a Bolt

effects.log: You find it folded inside a coat of the previous Director, who left three hundred years ago and is still not forgiven.

choices.text: Make a bolt of mist from scratch

effects.log: You gather what you can from the damp of the stairwell. It is thin, but it is mist.
{npc} blanches. "That is worse." But {he} goes.

events.text: The Jade Court receives the mist, and the Marshal of Ceremony lifts a thin eyebrow. "This fog is slightly damp." {npc} stands very straight. "It is the damp of the dawn," {he} says. "That is the whole value of it."
events.arc: The Ministry of Fog Mislays a Bolt

choices.text: Back {him} up with a quiet word

effects.log: The Marshal blinks, and accepts the damp. {npc} will remember who stood next to {him}.
The Marshal looks at you for a long moment and says the fog is acceptable. {npc} looks at you with different eyes.

events.text: {npc} is promoted to Under-Clerk of Mists, which is a title with no extra pay but a longer desk. {He} sends a gift: a tiny jar of fog that stays cold forever. "In case you ever need to disappear," the card says.
events.arc: The Ministry of Fog Mislays a Bolt

effects.log: Years later you will open it at exactly the right wrong moment.

choices.text: Send {him} a bolt of silk for the new desk

effects.log: The desk gets a cloth. The clerk gets a story to tell.

events.text: The Ministry of Fog is audited. {npc} is on the list of clerks to be questioned about the missing bolt of the old days. {He} looks at you from across the hall, and does not say a word.
events.arc: The Ministry of Fog Mislays a Bolt

effects.log: You tell the auditors the bolt was yours to lose. You pay in standing, and {npc} pays you in loyalty.
{npc} tells the story whole, laughing at the whole affair. The auditors write it down, and move on.

events.text: {npc} runs a stall at the foot of the Stair of Ten Thousand Steps, selling pastries seasoned with qi instead of salt. The mild ones taste of snow; the strong ones of lightning. "Pick your weather," {he} says, and holds up a tray.
events.arc: The Pastry-Cook Who Seasons with Qi

effects.log: It cracks on your tongue and makes your teeth hum for an hour. You love it.
It is cold and quiet and tastes like the winter you almost remember.
{npc} lets you stand by the oven. It is warm and smells of burnt sugar.

events.text: A rival cook opens across the stair, selling pastries seasoned with grudges. They taste, people say, exactly like being right. Queues grow. {npc} watches the line and eats a plain bun in silence.
events.arc: The Pastry-Cook Who Seasons with Qi

choices.text: Buy the rival's pastry and see

effects.log: It tastes like winning an argument. Ten minutes later it tastes of nothing at all.
{npc} accepts it and, somewhat to your surprise, begins to talk about the old days at court.
You eat neither, and feel unusually light.

events.text: The Dowager of the Third Isle sends for a pastry for the day of that birth, and wants it to taste of the rain that fell eight hundred years ago. {npc} is stuck. "I can't make a rain I did not taste."
events.arc: The Pastry-Cook Who Seasons with Qi

effects.log: You tell {him} of a rain you remember. {npc} cooks it, and the Dowager weeps into the cup.

choices.text: Ask the Dowager for a sip of the memory

effects.log: The Dowager grumbles, then speaks of a cold green morning. {npc} bakes that.

events.text: The stall is now three stalls and a pavilion. {npc} insists on keeping the original tray, which has a chip in the corner. "That is where the first one fell," {he} says. "I would not trade the chip."
events.arc: The Pastry-Cook Who Seasons with Qi

choices.text: Offer to open the pavilion with a blessing

effects.log: You say a few words. The queue cheers, and {npc} pretends not to care.

choices.text: Buy a plain bun like the old days

effects.log: It is plain, and still the best you have had.

events.text: The stall was never more than a stall, and that was the point. {npc} still bakes at dawn. Every spring you bring a pot of tea and buy the same pastry. The seasoning never changes: a little lightning, a little patience.
events.arc: The Pastry-Cook Who Seasons with Qi

effects.log: There are worse rituals for a long life.

choices.text: Send a student in your place

effects.log: The student comes back with a pastry and a scolding.

events.text: In the Archive of Unfiled Slips, {npc} sorts jade not by title or author but by the feeling it leaves in the hand: hope, regret, mild embarrassment. "Titles lie," {he} says. "A slip never lies about how it feels." {He} offers you a slip face down.
events.arc: The Archivist Who Indexes by Feeling

choices.text: Take the slip and read it

effects.log: It is a poem about a lost umbrella. It leaves you with a slow, sweet sadness.
It feels like a door you have forgotten you left open.
{npc} files it under "polite refusals" and smiles.

events.text: A cataloguer from the Ministry of Precedence arrives to reorganise the archive by rank of author. {npc} stands in the doorway with arms folded. "Over my dead isle," {he} says, which at that age is a real threat.
events.arc: The Archivist Who Indexes by Feeling

effects.log: You present a case in the cataloguer's own language: that the reader's time is the true scarce thing. The cataloguer retreats to think.

choices.text: Hide the best slips in your sleeve

effects.log: It is a petty, cheerful, useful crime. The cataloguer finds nothing worth ranking.
The argument ends in a draw. You are told it was your fault anyway.

events.text: {npc} falls ill from pure staleness, as archivists of a thousand years can. The slips on the shelves begin to feel flat. One by one they lose their moods. "I need a new reader," {he} whispers. "Someone who feels things badly."
events.arc: The Archivist Who Indexes by Feeling

effects.log: You read badly, with feeling. The slips on the shelves rustle and perk up.
The cataloguer arrives reluctantly and, to everyone's astonishment, cries over a slip about a lost umbrella.

events.text: {npc} is better. The archive is orderly in the way a happy mess is orderly. A new slip arrives anonymously one morning, face down, and {he} hands it to you. It is a short note of thanks, in your own hand, from some years you do not remember writing it.
events.arc: The Archivist Who Indexes by Feeling

effects.log: You place it in your sleeve. It leaves you with a feeling that has no name.
{npc} laughs hard enough to shake the shelves.

events.text: The archive closes for an inventory one winter and never fully opens again. {npc} stays on as night guard of a place that has no readers. You visit and read badly aloud to the dark shelves, which seem to listen.
events.arc: The Archivist Who Indexes by Feeling

effects.log: The dark shelves rustle in the cold. You hear them after you leave.
{npc} thanks you and leaves it unlit, out of respect for the shelves.

events.text: Winds above have names and moods, and Old Nim is a stubborn east wind that blows through the Quill Isle every autumn and tears the washing from the lines. {npc}, the isle's launderer, has been feuding with it for six hundred years. "Talk to it," {he} says. "It listens to strangers."
events.arc: The Wind Called Old Nim

effects.log: "Old Nim," you say. The wind drops, curious. You tell it about the washing.
You raise a screen of bamboo and silk. Old Nim flaps against it, offended.
Old Nim takes your hat, and returns it a week later, full of snow.

events.text: Old Nim has come early and brought news from below: the ache of a mortal prayer in a language you used to speak. It blows past the lines, quieter than in other years, and {npc} lets the washing flap.
events.arc: The Wind Called Old Nim

choices.text: Listen to what the wind carries

effects.log: It is only a child asking whether the dead can see the stars. You do not tell the wind your answer.

choices.text: Tell {npc} to bring the washing in

effects.log: {npc} refuses. "Old Nim has earned a flap," {he} says, and winks.

events.text: A storm-front blows in from the south, and Old Nim vanishes. For weeks the isle is windless, washing hangs slack, and {npc} grows worried. "Old Nim has gone off to fight, I know it. Winds do."
events.arc: The Wind Called Old Nim

effects.log: You fly out to the storm's edge. Old Nim is caught in a knot of cross-currents, sulking.
You sit with {him} until the first small gust arrives, shy and rather proud.

events.text: Old Nim comes home and sweeps the whole isle in one wide gust, a long fond embrace, and goes on with the autumn. {npc} laughs aloud. "Well," {he} says. "It remembers."
events.arc: The Wind Called Old Nim

choices.text: Hang a bell for the wind

effects.log: A bell now hangs on the quay. Old Nim sets it ringing each autumn, and the isle sleeps well.

choices.text: Hang your own washing out too

effects.log: It flies away. You wave goodbye to a shirt.

events.text: Old Nim never quite returns, and the isle's autumn washing is always dry and calm. {npc} still checks the line each dawn. "Old Nim will come," {he} says, "when there is something to say."
events.arc: The Wind Called Old Nim

effects.log: You never hear it, but one year a gust lifts your sleeve and drops a feather in your hand.

choices.text: Leave a hat on the line

effects.log: It stays there for a century.

events.text: At the Bridge Market, factions get the shaded stalls and rogues get the sunny ones. {npc}, the steward of stall allotments, looks you up and down. "No seal," {he} says. "Double the fee, and the sunny corner by the drain." Two stones, written in a polite hand.
events.arc: The Stall Without a Seal

choices.text: Pay the double fee (2 Low-Grade Spirit Stones)

effects.log: You pay. {npc} gives a thin smile and a stool of the wrong height.

choices.text: Argue that the fee is against the market charter

effects.log: Your reading of the charter surprises {him}. The fee drops by half, and the stool gets better.
The next bridge is smaller and cheaper, and the crowds are sparse but kind.

events.text: A sealed merchant of the Nine Clouds Palace sets up next to you and sells the same thing at three times the price. People buy from the merchant anyway. The seal, it seems, is the product.
events.arc: The Stall Without a Seal

effects.log: The queue turns your way. {npc} sees it, and does not like it.

choices.text: Sell something no seal could sell

effects.log: You offer stories with each purchase. The crowd lingers, and talks.

choices.text: Share a pot of tea with the neighbour

effects.log: Rivals can still be civil. The neighbour seems surprised.

events.text: {npc} comes to your stall, in plain robes, at the end of a day. "The Steward has fined you for noise," {he} says. "I wrote the fine myself. I would like to know why I did."
events.arc: The Stall Without a Seal

choices.text: Tell {him} the truth about the fee

effects.log: {npc} listens, then tears the fine slip in half. "I will think about the charter," {he} says.
{npc} sits at the odd stool and drinks. Nothing is resolved, but something loosens.

events.text: The market charter is rewritten that decade. A rogue now pays the same fee as a seal, a small change in a very long law. {npc} sends a note: "The sunny corner is yours for free. The drain, regrettably, remains."
events.arc: The Stall Without a Seal

effects.log: The stall becomes a landmark. People call it the Stall Without a Seal.

choices.text: Give the corner to a newer rogue

effects.log: You hand over the stool. The new rogue starts with a better stall than you did.

events.text: Nothing changes in the market, and you stop expecting it to. But a regular, one of the sealed, begins to buy from you in the early hours, before the queue forms. You do not ask why. The tea is shared, and the prices stay fair.
events.arc: The Stall Without a Seal

choices.text: Keep the early hour just for them

effects.log: It becomes a quiet friendship across a gulf. Neither of you names it.

choices.text: Close the stall and move on

effects.log: You take the stool with you. It is still the wrong height.

events.text: {npc}, born on the Pearl Isle fifteen years ago, has never seen dust. Never seen mud, either, or a thing that rots. "Is it true," {he} asks you, "that things below go brown and soft?" {He} has been practising the word "mould".
events.arc: The Heaven-Born Who Had Never Seen Dust

effects.log: {npc} listens with huge eyes. "And people live in it?" "Some do." "How brave."

choices.text: Bring a jar of soil from below

effects.log: {npc} turns the jar, sniffs, and puts a finger in it. The finger comes out brown. {He} stares.

choices.text: Say it is not worth wondering about

effects.log: {npc} nods politely, and wonders anyway.

events.text: {npc} plants a peach pit in the jar of soil and waits. Nothing happens. {He} waits harder. "It must be the wrong kind of waiting," {he} says to you, crestfallen.
events.arc: The Heaven-Born Who Had Never Seen Dust

choices.text: Teach {him} patience of the soil kind

effects.log: You sit with {him} and say nothing for a month. A green thread breaks the surface.

choices.text: Tell {him} sometimes it simply does not grow

effects.log: {npc} nods gravely. "Even so," {he} says. "I will wait."

events.text: The seedling grows fast and strange, with leaves like thumbs. {npc} brings it to the Jade Court for a prize, where it is declared "an irregularity". The room goes cold. {He} grips the pot and does not cry.
events.arc: The Heaven-Born Who Had Never Seen Dust

effects.log: You say the irregularity is the point. The court is unmoved, but a few clerks nod.
You walk {him} out into the evening, and say that irregularities are what trees are for.

events.text: {npc} is grown now, and the seedling is a small tree on the Pearl Isle that bears fruit in odd seasons. "Taste it," {he} says. It is bitter and sweet and tastes of dust, which {he} has finally learned to love.
events.arc: The Heaven-Born Who Had Never Seen Dust

effects.log: The taste lingers: a green dry afternoon you never lived. It is a gift.
You plant it far from the Pearl Isle. It does not grow, but you keep the jar.

events.text: The seedling dies. {npc} buries it in the jar of soil, solemnly, and tells you that rot is the thing the word "mould" meant. "It is not as terrible as I feared," {he} says. "It is just slow."
events.arc: The Heaven-Born Who Had Never Seen Dust

effects.log: You carve a stone. {npc} thanks you and means it.
There is not much to say about death above. You say it badly, and kindly.

events.text: A cloud carp, soft as a pillow and large as a shield, has followed you home from the Low Reef market. It swims in the air beside you, bumping your shoulder. {npc}, the stall-keeper, runs after you. "That one chose you," {he} says, "and I have been trying to sell it for forty years."
events.arc: The Cloud Carp That Followed You Home

effects.log: It nudges your sleeve in satisfaction and refuses to be left on any chair.
"Rumours," says {npc}. "Mostly the dull ones." The carp looks pleased.
The carp follows you for three streets before giving up. {npc} looks relieved and sad.

events.text: The carp has taken to eating every rumour in your hall. It grows round and gleaming. When a visitor starts a piece of gossip, it drifts across and swallows it whole, leaving only silence and a slightly guilty bubble.
events.arc: The Cloud Carp That Followed You Home

choices.text: Feed it better rumours on purpose

effects.log: You test it: rumours that are dull, rumours that are lies. It eats them all and glows a little brighter.

choices.text: Let it eat what it likes

effects.log: The hall grows quiet and strangely honest. Guests speak plainly or not at all.

events.text: The carp stops eating. It drifts against the window, pale. {npc} arrives with a bowl of broth. "It has swallowed a true one," {he} says, "and cannot digest it. A rumour that did not want to be a rumour."
events.arc: The Cloud Carp That Followed You Home

choices.text: Find the truth it has swallowed

effects.log: You trace the rumour to a clerk who needs to speak and cannot. You help the clerk, and the carp coughs up a pearl.

choices.text: Sit with the carp through the night

effects.log: Its breath eases at dawn. It is a good carp.

events.text: The carp is old, even for a carp. It swims in a slower ring each season. One morning it hangs in the window and does not move, a soft pale shape in the light. {npc} comes and puts a hand on the glass.
events.arc: The Cloud Carp That Followed You Home

choices.text: Bury it in the cloud sea

effects.log: You lower it gently. The clouds close around it, and it is gone.
You leave it there for a long time. Visitors speak quietly.

events.text: The carp lives for centuries and eats the gossip of three regimes. When it finally drifts off, it takes with it every dull rumour you ever heard, and the hall is a calm place afterwards. You never learn what it knew.
events.arc: The Cloud Carp That Followed You Home

choices.text: Raise a cup to the carp

effects.log: It is a small tribute, but a sincere one.
None comes, but you leave the window open.

events.text: The thousand-year peaches on the Third Terrace ripen once every thousand years, and the gardener, {npc}, is in the third year of waiting. "A watched peach never ripens," {he} says, "so I have taken up knitting to look away." The scarf is already four paces long.
events.arc: The Peach-Gardener of the Third Terrace

effects.log: You take shifts. Nothing happens, quietly, for months.
You drop a stitch. Then another. {npc} fixes them patiently and says nothing.

choices.text: Admire the peach trees from the path

effects.log: They are beautiful, heavy with something to come.

events.text: A fruit-thief, a heaven-born child with sticky fingers, climbs the trees at night. {npc} catches a glimpse and tilts the lantern. "Let the child be," {he} says to you, "these are not ripe, and the child knows it. It is the climbing that is loved."
events.arc: The Peach-Gardener of the Third Terrace

choices.text: Tell the child what the trees forgive

effects.log: You say the trees do not forgive greed. The child nods, wide-eyed, and spends the night counting leaves.

choices.text: Warn the Marshal of the Terrace

effects.log: The Marshal posts a guard. The trees feel it, and some pits stay closed.
You keep an eye on the child from a distance. It is a good eye.

events.text: The first peach ripens at dawn, a single globe the colour of an evening. {npc} holds the knife over it and cannot cut. "A thousand years," {he} says. "And I have no idea what to do with it."
events.arc: The Peach-Gardener of the Third Terrace

choices.text: Suggest sharing it with the isle

effects.log: A hundred slivers, each the size of a petal. The isle eats in silence and cannot speak of it after.

choices.text: Suggest keeping it whole for the next gardener

effects.log: It sits on a stand, glowing, until the next gardener arrives.

events.text: {npc} retires. The scarf is now twenty paces long and wound around the trunk of the oldest tree. The new gardener is the heaven-born child, grown up and a good deal less sticky. "The trees are not ripe," the child says. "But it is the climbing I love."
events.arc: The Peach-Gardener of the Third Terrace

choices.text: Climb the tree with the new gardener

effects.log: You climb. The view over the Third Terrace is like a held breath.

choices.text: Bring them tea in the evening

effects.log: It is the least you can do, and the most they want.

events.text: The scarf is finished at last. {npc} wraps the trunk of the oldest peach tree with it, and says: "In a thousand years someone will unwind it, and wonder." The gardener sits down under the tree and does not get up for an hour.
events.arc: The Peach-Gardener of the Third Terrace

choices.text: Sit with {him} until it is dark

effects.log: The tree rustles above you. The peaches are not ripe, and nobody minds.

choices.text: Leave a stone of thanks at the roots

effects.log: It is a small gesture, and the tree seems to accept it.

events.text: {npc}, an old gardener of the Rainy Reach, petitions the Ministry of Weather for a single soft rain, to fall on one plot on one morning. The clerk says it needs seven seals and a year. "The rain does not wait for seals," {npc} says to you, "but the Ministry does."
events.arc: The Petition for One Soft Rain

effects.log: You walk it through six offices. The seventh clerk is on holiday.

choices.text: Call in a favour from a friend in the Ministry

effects.log: A warm word, a cup of wine, and the petition moves to the front.

choices.text: Advise {him} to plant something that likes the sun

effects.log: {npc} snorts. "I plant what I love."

events.text: The seventh seal arrives, along with a bill for the rain: a modest number of stones, itemised in a very small hand. {npc} stares at it and then at the plot, which has gone brown at the edges.
events.arc: The Petition for One Soft Rain

choices.text: Pay the bill (3 Low-Grade Spirit Stones)

effects.log: You pay. {npc} says nothing, but squeezes your arm like someone holding a rope.

choices.text: Petition the Ministry for a waiver

effects.log: You write a short, shameless, true letter. The waiver comes in a month, with a sniff.

choices.text: Offer to carry water in the meantime

effects.log: It is a long, patient week. The plot lives.

events.text: The rain falls on the plot one soft morning, exactly where petitioned and not a hand-span beyond. Neighbours on the Rainy Reach glare from the dry edge. {npc} stands in the downpour with a face like a held breath.
events.arc: The Petition for One Soft Rain

effects.log: It is a very quiet rain. You both come in wet, and happy.

choices.text: Explain the rain to the neighbours

effects.log: You say it was a favour owed to an old gardener. The neighbours grumble and then bring bowls.

events.text: The waiver rain falls late, weak and slightly off-target. {npc} takes it with grace. "A rain is a rain," {he} says. "Even a late one is a thing to be grateful for."
events.arc: The Petition for One Soft Rain

choices.text: Plant a row of something that likes shade

effects.log: The row takes. It takes better, in fact, than anything in the sunlit plot.

choices.text: Share a cup of tea in the damp

effects.log: It is a damp, good cup.

events.text: At the Starlit Stalls, {npc} sells jars of fallen starlight, each labelled with an hour and an isle. "This one is the dusk over the Quill Isle," {he} says, "four centuries ago. The light is old, but it keeps." A jar hums in your hand.
events.arc: The Collector of Jarred Starlight

choices.text: Buy a jar (2 Low-Grade Spirit Stones)

effects.log: It glows in your cupboard, and sometimes hums in the night.

choices.text: Ask where the starlight came from

effects.log: {npc} grins. "Fallen on nets I hung from the Pavilion roof, every night for three hundred years." {He} is proud, and a little mad.
There are hundreds. Each one is a particular night.

events.text: {npc} has a rival, a collector of shadows from the same stars. They stand side by side at the Stalls and do not speak. Customers are told to choose: the light or the dark. Most choose both.
events.arc: The Collector of Jarred Starlight

effects.log: The light and shadow of one dusk fit together like halves of a coin.
You bring them tea, and both pretend not to notice. A week later they share a stall.
Sides are fun. You pick a side and keep it.

events.text: A great star falls, close, in the night. The collectors rush out with nets, but it is too bright, too large, and it burns every net to nothing. {npc} comes back with a charred sleeve and the look of someone who has seen too much.
events.arc: The Collector of Jarred Starlight

effects.log: You gather the cold embers into a jar. {npc} stares at it for a long time.
There is a lot to be said for darkness after bright light. You say very little.

events.text: The jar of the Great Fall sits on a high shelf at the Stalls, unlabelled. {npc} will not sell it. "This one is not mine," {he} says. "It belongs to whoever sees it next."
events.arc: The Collector of Jarred Starlight

effects.log: You hold it. For a moment you see the night in which it fell, whole.
It glows there for centuries. Passers-by stop and stare.

events.text: {npc} retires from the Stalls and hands the nets to a child. The light and the dark lie side by side in one jar, labelled with both names. "It took us three hundred years," {he} says, "to be friends."
events.arc: The Collector of Jarred Starlight

choices.text: Raise a toast to the pair of them

effects.log: The jar glows warm. You raise a cup to a good long friendship.
It sits next to your bed. It hums in your sleep.

events.text: Every dawn, {npc} sweeps the Jade Void stairs from the top to the bottom, and every dusk from the bottom to the top. The stairs are long. A younger disciple jokes {he} must be doing penance. {npc} merely smiles. "I am doing the stairs."
events.arc: The Sweeper of the Jade Void Stairs

effects.log: You feel the broom and the step and nothing else for an hour. It is a lesson of sorts.
"The step I am on," says {npc}. It is a good answer, and annoying.
The stairs shine behind {him}. You walk up them without looking down.

events.text: The Sect Elder announces a Grand Inspection, and every step must be perfect by noon. Disciples panic and trample the clean stairs. {npc} sweeps on, one step at a time, with the broom in rhythm.
events.arc: The Sweeper of the Jade Void Stairs

choices.text: Hold the line against the crowd

effects.log: You stand at the top and ask for slow feet. The disciples listen, abashed.

choices.text: Help sweep the worst of it

effects.log: Six hands, one broom. The stairs are done by noon, barely.
The inspection passes. The stairs pass too.

events.text: The Elder pauses at the step you swept and says: "Who did this?" {npc} stays silent, eyes down. The Elder looks from the step to you, and waits.
events.arc: The Sweeper of the Jade Void Stairs

effects.log: The Elder nods. {npc} is promoted to the keeping of the gate. {He} does not seem to mind, nor to want it.
The Elder smiles faintly. "So the stairs are shared work," the Elder says, and walks on.

events.text: {npc} has moved to the Gate, and the stairs are swept by another now, a quick careless hand. But on certain dawns you find a single leaf placed carefully on the top step. It is a message, and you know whose.
events.arc: The Sweeper of the Jade Void Stairs

effects.log: You do it every morning for a year. The leaf returns.
It stays for days, then blows away.

events.text: You keep sweeping the stairs together on the rainy days, for decades, saying very little. Neither of you is promoted. It is the best work you did.
events.arc: The Sweeper of the Jade Void Stairs

choices.text: Keep the ritual for another century

effects.log: The stairs are the cleanest in the Heavens.

choices.text: Hand the broom to the next disciple

effects.log: It passes on. The stairs go on being swept.

events.text: The Long Bridge between the Quill Isle and the Marsh Isle has nine hundred lamps, lit each dusk by {npc} with a taper of old starlight. It takes {him} till midnight. "Every lamp has a mood," {he} says. "Number three hundred twelve has not wanted to light since the flood."
events.arc: The Lamplighter of the Long Bridge

effects.log: You speak to it for a long minute. It flickers, then flares, as if embarrassed.
You learn each lamp's name. Some of the names are rude.
You walk in the light of their work and do not notice.

events.text: A fog rolls onto the bridge, thick as wool, and the lamps cannot cut it. A caravan of cloud-mules is on the planks, blind. {npc} runs along the rail calling out the lamp numbers, one by one, like beads.
events.arc: The Lamplighter of the Long Bridge

choices.text: Light the lamps ahead by hand

effects.log: You race the length of the bridge, lighting each with a thread of qi. The mules come through in a wobbly line.
Two voices are better than one. The mules follow the sound.

choices.text: Wait for the fog to lift

effects.log: You stand still at a lamp and let the caravan find its own way.

events.text: The Ministry of Precedence offers {npc} a post: Lord Warden of Lamps, a title, a robe, and an end to the evening walks. "I have never worn a robe," {he} says, turning the paper over. "Does it have pockets?"
events.arc: The Lamplighter of the Long Bridge

choices.text: Say take it, and the pockets

effects.log: You tell {him} a robe never hurt anyone. {npc} accepts, and hangs the taper on the hook.
You say nothing is better than the evening walk. {npc} smiles, and refuses.

events.text: The robed Lord Warden of Lamps walks the bridge no more. The lamps burn out one by one, unnoticed, over a decade. When {npc} finally looks, half the bridge is dark. "I should have kept my pockets empty," {he} says.
events.arc: The Lamplighter of the Long Bridge

effects.log: You relight the bridge. It takes a month. {npc} walks it with you, in a robe too long.
{npc} brightens, a little.

events.text: {npc} walks the bridge until the end of a long life, lamp by lamp. The taper passes to a girl from the Marsh Isle who learns the lamps' names and adds a few ruder ones. The bridge has never been brighter.
events.arc: The Lamplighter of the Long Bridge

choices.text: Walk the bridge once a year

effects.log: It becomes your small ritual. The lamps greet you.

choices.text: Light number three hundred twelve again

effects.log: It flares at once, proud.

events.text: At the border post of the Demon Realm, {npc} serves a stew that is eaten by both sides. The Heavenly Court officers eat it with their helmets on, ashamed. The Demon Realm guards eat it without. "It is the same stew," {npc} says, "and I will not rename it."
events.arc: The Cook at the Demon Realm Border

choices.text: Eat at the demon table, openly

effects.log: The stew is good. A Court officer glares from across the yard. You raise your spoon.
You carry the stew back to your quarters. Nobody sees, and nobody asks.
The stew steams. It smells honest.

events.text: A Court inspector arrives to shut the stall for "consorting". {npc} lays out two bowls without comment. The inspector stares at them. "Which is the permitted stew?" "Both," says {npc}. "They are the same."
events.arc: The Cook at the Demon Realm Border

effects.log: The inspector eats. The inspector, to the astonishment of all, asks for seconds.

choices.text: Slip the inspector a note of etiquette

effects.log: You remind them that guest-right is older than the border. They pause.
The inspector eats in silence and leaves in silence. Nobody is sure what happened.

events.text: {npc} is invited to cook at a banquet of the Jade Court, a first for anyone from the border. "They want the stew," {he} says, wary. "But will they eat it with their helmets off?"
events.arc: The Cook at the Demon Realm Border

effects.log: You walk in together. The court eats, then falls silent, then asks for more.
{npc} refuses, politely, in front of the whole court. It is a very quiet scandal.

events.text: The Court never serves the stew again, but the officers of the border post eat it without helmets now. Nobody mentions it. {npc} nods across the yard at you each time you pass, a small respectful tilt of the ladle.
events.arc: The Cook at the Demon Realm Border

effects.log: It becomes a ritual between the two of you. It means: the stew is the same.

choices.text: Eat a bowl for old times

effects.log: It tastes the same as ever.

events.text: The border moves as borders do, slow and unannounced. {npc} stays where the stew is. One morning the stall is on the other side, and neither side minds. "Same stew," {he} says. "Different soil."
events.arc: The Cook at the Demon Realm Border

effects.log: You carry them with grace. The stew survives the move.
The stall stands across the line. You wave, and {he} waves back.

events.text: The long noon has come: for a whole week the sun sits still above the isles and no shadow moves. People sleep under it with their faces covered, and the Ministry of Weather posts a notice that nothing at all is wrong. Everything feels, very slightly, like a held note.

choices.text: Sleep through it in the shade

effects.log: You wake a week later, rested in a way that seems illegal.

choices.text: Walk the length of a shadow that does not move

effects.log: You walk until you reach the end of it, and look back at the beginning. It is only a pace away.

events.text: Two old immortals haggle over the price of a single bowl at the Bridge Market. By the account of the stall-keepers, they have been haggling over it for six hundred years. Today they appear to be near a price. The crowd gathers, in hope or in dread.

effects.log: The price is agreed, a copper short of both of their asks. They look horrified, then relieved.

choices.text: Buy the bowl yourself (2 Low-Grade Spirit Stones)

effects.log: The two haggle-masters bow to you in grief at losing their only game. You feel you did harm.

events.text: A kitchen where the stove is a small captive cloud, fed on spirit-grass, lets out steam in the shapes of dishes not yet cooked. The cook swears it is never wrong. Today the steam shows a bowl you have never heard of, and a face you almost know.

choices.text: Ask the cook to make it

effects.log: The bowl arrives, plain and strange, and tastes of a memory that does not belong to you.
The cook shrugs. "The steam is not that kind. It shows what is coming."

events.text: The Mirror Lake of the Quill Isle shows not your face but the face you wore at some moment you have forgotten: a younger one, a sadder one, a more hopeful. People line up to be surprised. You take your turn.

choices.text: Study the face in the lake

effects.log: You see yourself at a gate, at a loss. You wish you could tell that face something.
The face smiles and the surface ripples. You feel obscurely forgiven.

events.text: A grove of cloud-bamboo sings in the wind, each stalk a note. A retired court musician sits among them with a flute, trying to play along and failing. "They are always a half-tone off," the musician complains. "I have loved them for eight hundred years."

choices.text: Sit and listen to the grove

effects.log: The half-tone off is the best part. You tell the musician so.
You thread a little qi through one. It rings true, and the grove goes quiet in offence.

events.text: On the Stair of Ten Thousand Steps, two clerks stop on the same landing to gossip, and the whole stair stops with them. A line of climbers waits behind, politely, in the knowledge that someone will leak what was said.

effects.log: It is nothing; a missing ledger and a cousin's wedding. You come away strangely moved.
You climb past in a rush. The clerks fall silent and then resume.

events.text: The Festival of Drifting Lanterns: each isle launches a lantern into the sky, and the lanterns drift for a year and return to the isle that launched them, scorched and wise. Nobody knows how they find their way. A child asks you what you wish for yours.

effects.log: The lantern rises, small and golden. The child nods approvingly.
You send it up blank. It comes back, a year later, with a single character written on it in a hand you do not know.

events.text: A sky whale passes beside the Lantern Isle, slow as a mountain, its flanks scarred with old lightning. The whole isle falls silent, then waves. The whale does not wave back, but one great eye turns toward the isle, and then away.

effects.log: Something huge and gentle takes note of you. It is enough.

choices.text: Watch until it is out of sight

effects.log: It takes an hour. Your breath slows to match its long unhurried swim.

events.text: A mist hound has been loose on the Bridge Isle for three nights, and the night-guards have lost its track. It is not dangerous, just friendly, a grey, loping, shapeless thing. A child reports it asleep under the market stairs, snoring like a kettle.

choices.text: Coax it out with a bone

effects.log: The hound drifts out, wags its fog, and follows you home. The guards write it off as a rumour.

choices.text: Tell the guards where it is

effects.log: They come with a net and a bun. The hound takes the bun and ignores the net.

events.text: The nearest neighbour of your isle lives a day's sail away, and sends a message every dawn by a sparrow: "Is it still there?" Your answer has always been yes. Today the sparrow returns with a different message: "I cannot see you. The fog is thick. Say something."

effects.log: The sparrow carries it into the fog. A faint reply arrives at dusk, off-key and glad.

choices.text: Light a lamp on the quay

effects.log: A neighbour's answering lamp blinks, once, far off.

events.text: You find a table set for two at the edge of the isle, with tea still warm. No one is there. A card under the pot says "For the first person who has time." You sit.

choices.text: Pour for yourself and the empty chair

effects.log: The empty chair is an excellent listener. You come away lighter.
No one comes. You leave a note: "Thank you for the tea."

events.text: It is the quietest week of a quiet century, and you realise you cannot name a single thing that happened in it. You feel, oddly, not bored but full. A kind of weather settles in your chest.

effects.log: It does not demand anything. It goes on being quiet.

choices.text: Go out and find someone to tell

effects.log: They listen, then admit they felt the same.

events.text: Two ministers of the Jade Court arrive at a door at the same instant and neither will go first. The queue behind them lengthens down the hall. The Marshal of Ceremony hesitates; precedence has no rule for two equals. It has been an hour.

choices.text: Suggest they step through together, sideways

effects.log: They do, wedged, outraged, and make history.

choices.text: Offer to go first yourself and break the deadlock

effects.log: You do. The ministers glare at your back for a decade.

events.text: The season of the isles drifting apart begins. Your isle slips out of the fleet's line, and the neighbours wave from farther and farther off. It is gentle, and a little sad, like a long goodbye said slowly across a year.

choices.text: Write letters to send by sparrow

effects.log: The sparrow is busy all season. The replies are warm.

choices.text: Enjoy the quiet while it lasts

effects.log: You do. The fleet comes back in spring, a little closer.

events.text: A tribulation cloud drifts by the isle like some other person's storm: dark, huge, flickering with purpose, entirely uninterested in you. It passes on toward the Cold Reef. In the distance, someone is about to have a very long day.

effects.log: The cloud rumbles on. Somewhere, a distant lightning bolt makes an unexpected choice.
It is spectacular, and you learn something of how it turns.

events.text: A broken staircase from the war of the immortals still hangs off the side of the Ash Isle, ending in nothing. Children dare each other to the last step. A scholar sits at the bottom, sketching the cracks.

effects.log: You stand at the edge of a stair that goes nowhere. The wind is very fresh.
The scholar tells you the stair held a banquet once. You almost hear it.

events.text: A door in the cliff-face of the Quiet Isle is sealed with a lock of cold starlight. A sign by it says: "Do not disturb the sleeper." Nobody knows who put it there, or whether the sleeper minds being visited.

choices.text: Leave a bowl of tea at the door

effects.log: You set it down and walk away. In the morning the bowl is gone, washed, set neatly back.
The door hums. You decide that was an answer.

events.text: A cloud-reef that appears on no chart lies off the Pearl Isle. Fishermen say it is a trick of the light. You see it clearly: a ridge of pale fluff, with something moving along its flank, small and shy.

effects.log: The reef is real. A reef-crab, large as a table, waves a claw at you and goes back to sleep.

choices.text: Mark it on a new chart

effects.log: You send the chart to the Ministry of Maps. They return it with a note: "No."

events.text: You are given a peach pit that remembers its tree. Hold it close, and it hums with the shape of a garden that burned twelve hundred years ago. The giver says it was found in a drawer, wrapped in a child's sock.

effects.log: You dream of the garden. It was orderly and loved.
It does not take. But the soil keeps something of its hum.

events.text: The cloud-gardens bloom once a decade, and the petals rise instead of falling. For a day the sky above the Garden Isle is full of slow pink, drifting toward the stars. People lie under it and are very still.

effects.log: One lands on your chest and does not move. You carry it home.
The tea has the taste of an unnamed spring.

events.text: Thunder sparrows nest on the cliffs of the Edge Isle, and each spring the young learn to fly by being pushed. The parents stand at the lip, looking stern. A child beside you is asking whether it hurts. "Always," says a clerk. "Then they fly."

effects.log: It tumbles, spins, and rises on a gust. The parents pretend not to be proud.
The child wraps up and watches the sky for hours.

events.text: A starfall crater near the Cold Reef is warm to the touch, even a century after the star came down. A family has set up a picnic at the rim: bread, wine, the world's oldest stove. They invite you to sit.

effects.log: The stove is very good. The conversation is better.
It has fine glass in it, with a pattern like a hand. You do not tell anyone.

events.text: Steersman {npc} guides the Heron Isle at the tail of the fleet, and has opinions about the pace. "Too fast," {he} says, "always too fast. An isle should drift like a thought, not run like a rumour." {He} asks if you would carry a petition to the lead steersman.
events.arc: The Steersman Who Argued with the Fleet

effects.log: The lead steersman reads it twice and laughs. It is, you suspect, the thousandth such petition.

choices.text: Ask {him} to teach you the drift

effects.log: {npc} shows you how to read a current by the taste of the air. It is subtle and a little salty.

choices.text: Say the pace suits you fine

effects.log: {npc} sighs and returns to the helm.

events.text: A cloud-reef rises ahead in the dusk. The fleet swerves hard, and the Heron Isle, slow by design, falls to the back, scraping the reef's edge. {npc} wrestles the great sweep alone while the isle groans.
events.arc: The Steersman Who Argued with the Fleet

choices.text: Add your strength to the sweep

effects.log: Together you turn the isle by a hair. It scrapes, shudders, and slides clear.

choices.text: Call the other steersmen for help

effects.log: Three isles send ropes. The Heron comes free on a tow, embarrassed and intact.

choices.text: Hold on and pray to the wind

effects.log: The wind, for once, listens.

events.text: The fleet pauses for a council on the pace. {npc} is invited to speak. {He} stands, forgets every word, and says only: "Slow down a little." The room is quiet for a long time. Then someone says, "Fair."
events.arc: The Steersman Who Argued with the Fleet

effects.log: Your voice carries. The council votes to slow by a hand-span, and {npc} sits down trembling.
The old steersman drinks in silence and then, unexpectedly, sings.

events.text: The fleet drifts a hand-span slower, and the Heron Isle is no longer last. {npc} marks the day with a small flag at the helm, and every year after, the whole tail of the fleet flies one too.
events.arc: The Steersman Who Argued with the Fleet

effects.log: It flutters in the wind of a hundred isles. You are part of a slow, quiet movement.
You raise your tea to it. It tastes unhurried.

events.text: {npc} retires the helm to a young steersman and takes up a seat on the Heron's prow, watching the clouds go by. "It was never the pace," {he} says. "It was wanting someone to ask me what I thought."
events.arc: The Steersman Who Argued with the Fleet

effects.log: You ask. {npc} talks until the lamps are lit, and you listen, and nobody else does.

choices.text: Leave a flag on the rail

effects.log: It stays there for years.

events.text: {npc} brews cloud-wine in an iron pot on the Vintner's Isle, from fog gathered at dawn. Each bottle remembers the morning it was gathered, and tastes of it. "Pick a year," {he} says. "I will tell you what mood it was in."
events.arc: The Brewer of Cloud-Wine Who Forgot the Year

choices.text: Pick the year you arrived above

effects.log: The wine tastes of a bright, nervous morning. You almost cry.
It is a quiet sad one, with a taste of rain on slate. {npc} nods. "That was a good year for brooding."
{npc} puts the bottle away without a word, kindly.

events.text: {npc} has lost the label of a bottle laid down eight hundred years ago. It sits dusty in the cellar, unmarked. "I cannot remember the year," {he} says, wretched. "The wine will not tell me. It is shy."
events.arc: The Brewer of Cloud-Wine Who Forgot the Year

effects.log: You pour two cups. It tastes of a festival, a long table, someone laughing. {npc} goes very still.

choices.text: Suggest it be left to age

effects.log: The bottle returns to the dark. {npc} nods, relieved to be spared the grief.
{npc} gives a thin smile. It is not fine, but it is kind.

events.text: The wine is a wedding. {npc} remembers at last: the wedding of {his} teacher's daughter, the year before the war, where {he} danced badly and was happy. There is no one left to tell. {He} sets out two cups.
events.arc: The Brewer of Cloud-Wine Who Forgot the Year

choices.text: Raise a cup with {him} to the dancers

effects.log: You raise your tea to the badly danced years. {npc} laughs through tears.

choices.text: Ask {him} to teach you the dance

effects.log: It is a dreadful dance, full of elbows. You learn it anyway.

events.text: The unmarked bottle ages another century. When it is finally opened at a feast, it is a plain, honest wine of no great year, and everyone says so, politely. {npc} says it is exactly the wine it wanted to be.
events.arc: The Brewer of Cloud-Wine Who Forgot the Year

choices.text: Raise a cup to unlabelled things

effects.log: The table drinks. It is a pleasant, unremarkable evening, which is the best sort.
It sits on your shelf, a little dusty.

events.text: The Ministry of Precedence must seat the Jade Banquet, and {npc} the Under-Marshal holds the chart. Two ministers cannot sit within three places of each other. A third cannot sit facing the door. A fourth was insulted by the last banquet. {He} stares at the page. "It has no solution," {he} says.
events.arc: The Seating Chart of the Jade Banquet

choices.text: Take a look at the chart

effects.log: You find a pattern: seat the quarrel next to a deaf cousin. {npc} stares at you as at a prophet.
"Round has no head," says {npc}. "That is the problem and the cure." {He} tries it.
{npc} sighs and returns to the chart.

events.text: The banquet is a success. The quarrelling ministers sit apart yet content, and the fourth, who was insulted, finds the seat by the window entirely to taste. The Chancellor pauses by {npc}, and says: "Who made this?"
events.arc: The Seating Chart of the Jade Banquet

effects.log: {npc} is named Marshal of Banquets. The cost is a longer desk and a shorter temper.
The Chancellor nods at you with approval. {npc} glances at you, then away.

events.text: The new Marshal of Banquets writes you a letter. Beneath the formal opening, in a smaller hand: "Come to the next one. I have saved you a seat. It has no rank at all, and a very good view."
events.arc: The Seating Chart of the Jade Banquet

effects.log: The seat is at the end, by the draught, with a view of everyone. It is a splendid vantage.

choices.text: Send regrets with a gift of wine

effects.log: The Marshal writes back: "Next time."

events.text: A younger minister takes {npc}'s post by cunning, and the old seating chart is thrown in a fire. {npc} watches the pages curl. "It never had a solution," {he} says. "I made one anyway. That is all anyone does."
events.arc: The Seating Chart of the Jade Banquet

choices.text: Sit with {him} at the unranked seat

effects.log: The two of you watch the banquet from the draught. It is a good banquet.
{npc} thanks you and looks, for once, entirely at peace.

events.text: The Marshal of Banquets never mentions it, and you never ask. But on the night of every Jade Banquet, a cup of tea sits quietly by your elbow, untouched by any hand you see.
events.arc: The Seating Chart of the Jade Banquet

effects.log: It is perfectly warm. You say nothing, and nod to the room.

choices.text: Leave it for the next guest

effects.log: It stays warm all evening.

events.text: Star-moths live in the lamp-room of the Observatory Isle, wings dusted with real starlight, and {npc} has kept them for seven hundred years. They flutter to the brightest lamp, which is why the Observatory has so few. "Open the window," {he} says. "They want the night."
events.arc: The Keeper of the Star-Moths

effects.log: The moths stream out like a spill of sparks, and return before dawn, each a little brighter.

choices.text: Keep the window shut and watch

effects.log: They beat at the glass until dawn. {npc} says nothing, but watches you.
Their wings glow like handfuls of far-off light.

events.text: A moth is missing. {npc} counts and counts again. "That one flew too far. They do, in autumn. The wind off the Edge." {He} sits down on the stair, small. "I have named every one of them."
events.arc: The Keeper of the Star-Moths

choices.text: Go out on the night wind to find the lost moth

effects.log: You search the cold edge of the sky. A faint spark answers you, tangled in a lantern-string on the Ash Isle.
You hold a lamp up in the dark. At midnight a small light returns, bruised.

events.text: The Observatory Master wants the moths for a lantern-feast, a thousand of them in a glass hall. {npc} listens, horrified. "They would burn themselves out in a night," {he} says. "It is a beautiful idea. It would be a cruelty."
events.arc: The Keeper of the Star-Moths

effects.log: You write to the Master. The feast is held with paper moths instead. {npc} looks at you as at a long-lost relative.

choices.text: Suggest a smaller feast of twelve moths

effects.log: Twelve, to be returned by dawn. The compromise is accepted, and the guests whisper at their beauty.

events.text: {npc} grows old and the moths grow old and the Observatory is dark more and more. One night every moth comes to your window and rests there, a hundred small lights, and goes. You know what it means.
events.arc: The Keeper of the Star-Moths

choices.text: Keep the window open from then on

effects.log: Every autumn a few return. You never learn how they found you.
They send a mourner and a wreath of paper moths.

events.text: The moths are loosed on a kind autumn night, by {npc} and by you, and they fly into the dark in a long river of light. {npc} watches them go. "Now they are free," {he} says. "And I am no one's keeper."
events.arc: The Keeper of the Star-Moths

effects.log: You walk in the dark together, and nobody speaks. It is the best silence you have had.

choices.text: Light a single lamp on the stair

effects.log: One moth returns. Just one.

events.text: At the cloud-silk stall, {npc} names a price to the sealed customers and a higher one to you. "Rogue price," {he} says without shame. "You may leave. You will not find a better bolt." It is, annoyingly, true.
events.arc: The Cloud-Silk Merchant Who Charged Rogues Extra

choices.text: Pay the rogue price (3 Low-Grade Spirit Stones)

effects.log: You pay. The silk is excellent, and your pride has a small hole in it.
You haggle with all your patience. {npc} lowers the price a copper, and respects you a little more.
You walk. A bolt follows you with its eyes.

events.text: A sealed customer buys the same silk at half the price and brags about it. {npc} smiles at the boast. You realise the rogue price is not a price, it is a message.
events.arc: The Cloud-Silk Merchant Who Charged Rogues Extra

choices.text: Say it aloud in the market

effects.log: Heads turn. {npc} goes pink. A few merchants nearby shift their own price boards.
You find a rogue weaver two bridges down. Their silk is thicker and kinder.
You carry the silk home. It is warm.

events.text: {npc} comes to your door with a bolt of silk, red-faced. "I was told by my guild to charge the rogue price," {he} says. "I did not like it, and I did it for years. Here. For nothing." You are not sure whether to accept.
events.arc: The Cloud-Silk Merchant Who Charged Rogues Extra

choices.text: Accept it, with a polite word

effects.log: You thank {him} and mean it. {npc} nods, relieved, and goes.

choices.text: Decline, and offer to pay the fair price

effects.log: You press the fair price into {his} palm. It is a strange peace, hard won.

events.text: The guild drops the rogue price, grudgingly. {npc} posts a single price board with a single price on it and looks, for the first time in years, easy. "You made me braver than I like," {he} tells you.
events.arc: The Cloud-Silk Merchant Who Charged Rogues Extra

choices.text: Buy a bolt at the new price

effects.log: It is the same silk, and costs less. It feels much better.
{npc} nods back.

events.text: The rogue weaver two bridges down becomes known as the silk-seller for those without a seal. You buy from {npc} for centuries. The prices are fair, the silk thick, and the stall has a good view of the bridge.
events.arc: The Cloud-Silk Merchant Who Charged Rogues Extra

choices.text: Recommend {him} to every rogue you meet

effects.log: The stall grows. The weaver names a bolt of silk after you.
The weaver is fine either way.

events.text: Once a decade a mortal prayer-paper lifts on a thermal from below and arrives, battered, at the Post Isle. {npc}, the clerk of stray letters, tries to read the address. This one is for a person who left the mortal world six hundred years ago, whose name is yours.
events.arc: The Letter That Came Up on the Wind

effects.log: It is a child asking for a place to put a grave-flower. The child has been dead for centuries now.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to return it to the wind

effects.log: {npc} nods and lets it go. It rises, folded, into the high clouds.

choices.text: Say it was not for you

effects.log: {npc} marks it "undeliverable" and files it away.

events.text: You cannot stop thinking about the letter. {npc} invites you to the stray-letter room, shelves of them, faded, waiting. "These never find their people," {he} says. "I read them aloud, in the evening, so someone has heard."
events.arc: The Letter That Came Up on the Wind

effects.log: You read ten. One is a joke, one is a quarrel, one is a love-letter so simple it makes you ache.

choices.text: Offer to help find their people

effects.log: You trace three to isles still sailing. It is slow, fond work.

choices.text: Sit in the room a while

effects.log: The paper smells of old rain and distance.

events.text: A cloud-skiff with a bundle of stray letters arrives from the Edge. One letter is addressed to {npc}, in a hand that {he} has not seen in nine hundred years. {He} holds it and cannot open it.
events.arc: The Letter That Came Up on the Wind

effects.log: {npc} nods. It is short: a thanks, a regret, a pressed flower. {He} weeps, quietly, and thanks you.
{npc} reads it alone, and afterwards says only: "A good life." You do not ask who.

events.text: The stray-letter room is full of readers on winter evenings now, a small gathering, a lamp, a kettle. {npc} bows to you at the door. "It was you," {he} says. "You came back."
events.arc: The Letter That Came Up on the Wind

choices.text: Take a turn at the reading desk

effects.log: You read a letter in your best voice. The room listens, and a stranger laughs and cries.
The tea goes round. The evening is soft.

events.text: You trace three letters to their isles. Two are received with joy. The third is returned with a note: "The person you seek has moved on. Thank you." You file it under the sort of silence the room is full of.
events.arc: The Letter That Came Up on the Wind

effects.log: It sits on your shelf, a small proof that someone tried.
Some letters wait a long time for their people.

events.text: On the Whistling Hill, every heaven-born child learns to whistle up the wind, and the two best are rivals, {npc} and a cousin. Today they stand at the crest, sizing each other up. {npc} turns to you: "You judge. You are old enough to be fair."
events.arc: The Heaven-Born Twins and the Whistling Hill

effects.log: You sit on a rock. The wind rises in two directions at once, with a rather comic result.
"Oh," says {npc}. "I thought you were braver." The wind drops.
The wind rises in a spiral. Neither of them will admit it was lovely.

events.text: The wind of the cousin is cleaner, but the wind of {npc} is stranger. It carries a smell of faraway rain. You are asked to choose. Both children watch your face as if it held a verdict from heaven.
events.arc: The Heaven-Born Twins and the Whistling Hill

effects.log: The cousin whoops. {npc} goes white, then very still. You feel you have taken something.
{npc} whoops. The cousin goes still. You feel you have given something.

choices.text: Call it a draw and share a bun

effects.log: Both children stare at you, outraged, then take a bun each.

events.text: Years pass. {npc} comes back from a journey with a wind in a bottle and an offer to the cousin: "Whistle it up with me, the two of us." The old rivalry has turned into something rarer, and a little stranger.
events.arc: The Heaven-Born Twins and the Whistling Hill

effects.log: The wind inside is a tiny gale with the voice of both children, laughing. It spills into the sky.
They walk up the hill together, in step.

events.text: {npc} bears a grudge for a lifetime, lightly, as heaven-born do. One day the cousin's child comes to you with a question about whistling, and you answer, and a chain of small kindnesses begins that outlasts the grudge.
events.arc: The Heaven-Born Twins and the Whistling Hill

effects.log: The child whistles up a weak wind, and a very large smile.
{npc} receives the child gruffly, and stays up half the night teaching.

events.text: {npc} and the cousin whistle at the crest every spring, two old rivals in the same gale. The hill whistles back. Visitors say it is the oldest tune in the sky, and the two of them say it is only a good wind.
events.arc: The Heaven-Born Twins and the Whistling Hill

effects.log: The tune is simple and strange. You stay till dark.
It carries on the breeze.

events.text: Under the cloud-bamboo of the Quiet Isle, two old friends have played one game of stones for a thousand years, a move each decade. {npc} is the one whose turn it is. {He} has been thinking for three years. Your arrival, {he} says, is an interruption of the best kind.
events.arc: The Game of a Thousand Years

effects.log: You study the stones. It is a very strange position, and beautiful.
"Nobody," says {npc}. "That is the point. The one who wins ends the game."
The two old players drink together. It is the best interruption in some years.

events.text: {npc}'s friend falls ill. The game sits half-played, and {npc} cannot decide whether to move. "If I move, the game goes on," {he} says. "If I do not, it stops, and that is a kind of ending." The stones wait.
events.arc: The Game of a Thousand Years

effects.log: A quiet move. The game goes on, and the friend, on the pillow, smiles at the news of it.

choices.text: Suggest {he} leave the stones as they are

effects.log: {npc} nods slowly. The game stays still, a held breath.

events.text: The friend recovers, and the game restarts with a new tempo. A move every year now, then a move a month, then every evening. The two old players are, for the first time in centuries, in a hurry. It is a joy to watch.
events.arc: The Game of a Thousand Years

effects.log: The game ends in a draw, a thousand years of tension released in a laugh.

choices.text: Place a stone yourself, by invitation

effects.log: You place it carefully. The two old players stare at it for a long time.

events.text: The game is over, and the two friends sit with nothing to play. "What now?" asks {npc}. You propose a new game, a small one, no more than a century. They glare at you, then grin. The stones are laid.
events.arc: The Game of a Thousand Years

choices.text: Play a quick round with them

effects.log: You lose, comprehensively. They are delighted.
They are already at it, old hands over a new board.

events.text: The game never restarts. {npc}'s friend does not recover, and {npc} sits alone under the bamboo for a decade, then another. One evening a student comes to ask about the stones. {npc} begins to explain, slowly, and stays up all night.
events.arc: The Game of a Thousand Years

effects.log: The stones teach better than any word. You are not the only student.
It is gone by morning.

events.text: {npc} keeps a pot of stock that has simmered over a captive flame for a thousand years, never emptied, never quite full. Each bowl served is topped up with a ladle of water and a handful of qi. "It is the same soup," {he} says, "and different every night."
events.arc: The Soup with a Thousand-Year Stock

effects.log: It tastes like everyone who ever ate it. You have never had such company in a bowl.
"A bone from every feast," says {npc}. "And a leaf from every friend."
It is blackened with age and shines in the firelight.

events.text: The flame under the pot flickers. It is old, and tired, and the stock is beginning to sour. {npc} fans it frantically. "If it dies, the soup dies," {he} says, "and a thousand years of the same pot go out with it."
events.arc: The Soup with a Thousand-Year Stock

choices.text: Feed the flame a thread of your qi

effects.log: It brightens, and the stock sweetens again. {npc} stares at you as at a stranger who has done a kind thing.

choices.text: Fetch a new coal from the Hearth Isle

effects.log: It takes a day of travel and a bribe of pastries. The new coal sits in the old fire, and takes.
You do what you can. The flame steadies by itself.

events.text: A critic of the Ministry of Banquets arrives and tastes the soup. The critic eats the whole bowl, slowly. Then the critic says: "It tastes of nothing in particular." {npc} goes quiet and white.
events.arc: The Soup with a Thousand-Year Stock

effects.log: You tell the critic that nothing in particular is exactly what a thousand years tastes like. The critic ponders.
The critic accepts, and slowly begins to cry. It is a good soup after all.

events.text: The soup is named a treasure of the Heavens. {npc} refuses the title. "It is just supper," {he} says. But the line outside grows, and a leaf from every visitor goes into the pot. It will outlast all of us.
events.arc: The Soup with a Thousand-Year Stock

effects.log: It sinks into the stock. You feel, obscurely, that you are part of something.

choices.text: Eat in the queue with the others

effects.log: The soup is shared, plain, and deeply good.

events.text: The pot is passed to a young cook, who stirs it with a long wooden spoon and a very straight back. {npc} sits at the corner table, a retired guest, and tastes. "Same soup," {he} says, with tears in {his} eyes. "Different cook."
events.arc: The Soup with a Thousand-Year Stock

effects.log: The young cook turns red and ladles you extra.

choices.text: Say nothing and finish the bowl

effects.log: You eat in a long contented silence.

events.text: In the gardens of the Nine Clouds Palace, {npc} tends nine terraces of plum, and each terrace flowers on a different cloud. The palace's ladies come for the blossom and never once ask the gardener's name. "It is better that way," {he} says. "They look at the trees."
events.arc: The Gardener of the Nine Clouds Palace

choices.text: Ask {his} name anyway, and say it aloud

effects.log: {npc} blushes to the roots. "No one has said it in a long time."
Under {his} hand the plum trees shape like quiet dancers. You learn something of patience.

choices.text: Admire the blossom with the ladies

effects.log: The blossom is lovely. The ladies are lovelier. You keep your eyes on the trees.

events.text: A Grand Lady of the Palace orders a terrace pulled up for a dance floor. {npc} stands by the plum and says nothing. The workers wait with their hammers, looking at the ground. The Lady looks at you.
events.arc: The Gardener of the Nine Clouds Palace

effects.log: You suggest the dance floor be built over the lower terrace instead. The Lady frowns, then agrees. {npc} breathes out.

choices.text: Say the Lady is right and step aside

effects.log: The trees come down. {npc} is silent for a month. You do not forget.

choices.text: Ask for a day to consider

effects.log: The Lady shrugs. The day buys the trees a week.

events.text: The terrace is saved, and the plums bloom a month early in thanks. {npc} sends you a branch of blossom with a note: "For the one who looked at the trees." You hang it in your window and it blooms every spring.
events.arc: The Gardener of the Nine Clouds Palace

effects.log: The cutting takes in poor soil and blooms white. The gardener visits it.
The petals fall. The Ladies come. You keep the gardener company.

events.text: {npc} is made Keeper of the Nine Terraces, with an official seal and a name carved on a board. It is read aloud at the opening of spring. {He} stands there, hands folded, listening to {his} own name carried by the Ladies like a fan.
events.arc: The Gardener of the Nine Clouds Palace

effects.log: You hold the end of the scroll. {npc} does not look up, but {his} shoulders drop.

choices.text: Leave a plum branch at the board

effects.log: It stays there as long as the blossom.

events.text: At the Star Sea Pavilion, {npc} charts the drift of a hundred named stars on a table of black jade. It is exacting, ancient work, and {he} is bad at tea. "Never turn your back on a star," {he} tells you, "they notice. They remember who looked."
events.arc: The Navigator of the Star Sea Pavilion

choices.text: Take a chart and learn a star

effects.log: You choose a faint one and follow it for a season. It does not seem to mind.
You make a better cup than {he} does. {npc} accepts it with grim dignity.
The stars look back. It is, you decide, a little rude of you.

events.text: {npc} has made an error: a star on the chart is a hair off, and a ship of the Star Sea has been steered by it for forty years. The ship's captain is due for a visit. {npc} is white and rigid. "It cannot be undone," {he} says.
events.arc: The Navigator of the Star Sea Pavilion

choices.text: Help {him} re-chart and send word to the ship

effects.log: You work through two nights. The new chart goes out with a courier. The ship corrects without incident.
The Master is sharp, then silent. {npc} is demoted, but not dismissed. The error is corrected.
The ship, by luck, was never off course.

events.text: The ship returns after forty years, with a barnacle-coated captain who wants to meet whoever corrected the chart. {npc} is hiding behind the star-table. The captain looks at you, then at {npc}, and bows.
events.arc: The Navigator of the Star Sea Pavilion

effects.log: The captain bows deeper. {npc} comes out slowly, and a thin, heartfelt silence follows.
The captain thanks you with great warmth. {npc} watches, quiet and cut.

events.text: {npc} charts a star that has not been seen before, by the faintest hair, and names it with the name of the captain. It is a small, honest tribute. You are given a seat at the first viewing.
events.arc: The Navigator of the Star Sea Pavilion

effects.log: It is pale and patient, a small bright thing at the edge of the black. You feel looked at.
{npc} downs the tea and admits it is not bad.

events.text: A jade qilin calf, no bigger than a goat, has taken up residence on the back stair of the Pearl Isle kitchens. {npc}, the scullion, feeds it scraps. "It will not leave," {he} says, "and I am not sure it is ours to keep. A qilin is a kind of omen."
events.arc: The Jade Qilin Calf on the Back Stair

choices.text: Offer it a bowl of milk

effects.log: It laps with great ceremony. The kitchen goes quiet. A small chime sounds somewhere.
A clerk arrives in two weeks with a form and a net. {npc} meets them at the door with a ladle.
The calf curls up under the stair and sleeps.

events.text: The calf grows. Wherever it walks, small things go right: a dropped plate lands whole, a late guest arrives on time. The scullions fight over who feeds it. {npc} defends it, calling it "ours, for now".
events.arc: The Jade Qilin Calf on the Back Stair

choices.text: Help {npc} build it a proper stall

effects.log: You nail boards in the evenings. The calf watches with unreadable gold eyes.

choices.text: Take it for a walk on the cloud-bridge

effects.log: It treads the planks as if they were solid rock. Passers-by bow to it, uncertain why.

events.text: A rich collector offers a mountain of stones for the calf. {npc} refuses without a word, then comes to you at night. "I do not want to be rich," {he} says. "I want to be right." The calf sleeps in the next room, breathing like a small wind.
events.arc: The Jade Qilin Calf on the Back Stair

effects.log: You say the calf chose the stair. {npc} nods, a long slow nod, and goes to bed.

choices.text: Advise {him} to let the calf go to the hills

effects.log: It is hard. The calf is led to the hills at dawn, and looks back once.

events.text: The calf grows into a full jade qilin that carries the scullion about the Isle on its back, scattering luck like petals. The kitchens have never been so well run, and the stair has a small shrine of milk bowls.
