events.arc: The Jade Qilin Calf on the Back Stair

choices.text: Leave a bowl at the shrine

effects.log: The bowl is empty by morning. The qilin's eye follows you as you leave.
It is the pleasantest stair in the Heavens.

events.text: The qilin returns to the hills, and the scullion visits it on rest days, bringing scraps. Years later it brings a small calf of its own to the back stair, and leaves it there. {npc} laughs until {he} has to sit down.
events.arc: The Jade Qilin Calf on the Back Stair

choices.text: Offer the new calf a bowl of milk

effects.log: It laps. Somewhere a chime sounds.

choices.text: Raise a toast to the stair

effects.log: It has earned one.

events.text: Each year the Isle of Hollow Pines holds the Rising Snow Festival, when the flakes lift off the cloud-sea. {npc} has organised it for four hundred years and is on the edge of tears. The sled-race, the soup, the hot stones: all must be ready by tonight. "Help," {he} says, flatly.
events.arc: The Organiser of the Rising Snow Festival

effects.log: You stir a cauldron for six hours. It is the best soup you ever made, mostly by accident.
You mark the course with lanterns and a rope. Fifty children line up, shrieking.
{npc} gives a tight smile.

events.text: Night falls and the snow does not rise. The festival crowd waits, shivering, on the cold quay. A warm spell has held the snow down. {npc} stands in front of them, white, wordless. The children begin to murmur.
events.arc: The Organiser of the Rising Snow Festival

choices.text: Call up a thread of qi to lift the first flake

effects.log: A single flake rises. Then ten. Then a slow soft river of them. The children cheer.

choices.text: Tell a story to pass the time

effects.log: You tell the oldest tale you know. The crowd settles, then dozes, and the snow rises while they sleep.

events.text: The festival is declared the best in a century. {npc} is lifted on shoulders, mortified. Afterward {he} finds you by the soup and says, low: "I would like you to run it next year. I am tired." It is a very large favour to ask.
events.arc: The Organiser of the Rising Snow Festival

effects.log: You accept the whistle and the list. It is a heavier thing than it looks.
You agree to split it. {npc} lets out a breath held for four hundred years.
{npc} nods, tired, and goes on.

events.text: You run the festival and it is a calamity: too much soup, too little snow, a child lost for an hour. In the grey dawn {npc} sits on the quay with you, wrapped in a quilt. "It is the best one yet," {he} says. "It was ours."
events.arc: The Organiser of the Rising Snow Festival

effects.log: You sit under it together as the first flake of the new day lifts.
The plans are already worse than this year's.

events.text: You and {npc} run the festival together for a century. It is never the best, never the worst, always warm. The crowd comes back every year, bringing their own soup and their own opinions.
events.arc: The Organiser of the Rising Snow Festival

effects.log: You do. The snow rises, and the quay is full.

choices.text: Hand it to the next generation

effects.log: It goes on, loudly.

events.text: Your nearest neighbour is the keeper of the Lantern Isle, a day's sail off. {npc} shouts across the gap every evening, at the hour of tea, since sound carries oddly in the high air. "Is it still there?" {he} calls. "Yes!" you shout back. The ritual is four hundred years old.
events.arc: The Neighbour Who Shouted Across the Gap

effects.log: You shout. The sound carries, flattened, over the sea. A faint cheer answers.
A faint lamp winks back across the gap. It becomes the signal.
The shout dies on the wind. You feel obscurely unkind.

events.text: One evening there is no shout. The quiet is large and cold. {npc}'s isle is just visible, a dim shape, no lamp. You wait an hour. Another. The tea goes cold in your hand.
events.arc: The Neighbour Who Shouted Across the Gap

effects.log: You find {npc} on the quay with a cold, unwell and quite embarrassed. "I lost my voice," {he} croaks.

choices.text: Send a sparrow with a note

effects.log: The sparrow returns at dawn with a scrawled reply: "Throat. Fine. Shouting tomorrow."
Nothing answers, but you feel better.

events.text: {npc} recovers and takes up a new fashion: a signal horn made from a giant shell. It is magnificent and shatters your teacups. "Is it still there?" it bellows, to the entire fleet. The fleet answers, with some rudeness.
events.arc: The Neighbour Who Shouted Across the Gap

choices.text: Answer with a conch of your own

effects.log: The two horns trade notes across the gap, for hours, to the despair of everyone for ten leagues.

choices.text: Leave the horn to the Lantern Isle

effects.log: You stay with the shout. It has worked for four hundred years.

events.text: The gap between your isles widens in the season of drift, and the shouting becomes a signal and then a memory. {npc} sends a last message by sparrow: "Still there?" You send back: "Still here." The sparrow flies for days.
events.arc: The Neighbour Who Shouted Across the Gap

effects.log: The ritual shifts but does not stop. There is something steady in it.
You meet {npc} halfway on a skiff, over a pot of tea, and shout in each other's faces.

events.text: Each morning {npc} sculpts a figure from a cloud on the edge of the Garden Isle: a cat, a bridge, a scholar with a long beard. By noon it is gone. "It is not for keeping," {he} says. "It is for the doing." You have watched {him} for a week.
events.arc: The Sculptor Who Worked Only in Cloud

effects.log: You make a lopsided duck. {npc} calls it "committed".

choices.text: Sit and watch the figures dissolve

effects.log: There is a long soft sadness to it, and a delight. You see why {he} does it.

choices.text: Admire a cat before it goes

effects.log: The cat yawns, stretches, and thins into mist.

events.text: A patron of the Jade Court commissions a permanent cloud-statue, made to last, with a fixing powder from the Ministry of Weather. {npc} refuses at first. "It would stop being a cloud," {he} says, and stares at the sky.
events.arc: The Sculptor Who Worked Only in Cloud

effects.log: You say a cloud that stays is still a cloud. {npc} sighs, takes the commission, and goes quiet.
You say the doing is the point. {npc} writes a polite refusal, with a drawing of a cat.

events.text: The permanent statue is finished. It is a magnificent cloud-scholar, rigid and chalk-white, unmoving in the sun. People gasp. {npc} stands before it, small and grey. "It is perfect," {he} says. "It is dead."
events.arc: The Sculptor Who Worked Only in Cloud

choices.text: Break the fixing and let it go

effects.log: You loosen the powder with a breath. The statue sighs, softens, and drifts away over the isle.

choices.text: Keep the statue and praise it

effects.log: The patron is delighted. {npc} says nothing for a year.

events.text: {npc} begins again, a new cloud each morning, and the people of the Garden Isle gather to watch. Some mornings the figure is a cat. Some mornings it is you. You smile at yourself in the mist and wave.
events.arc: The Sculptor Who Worked Only in Cloud

choices.text: Wave back to your cloud self

effects.log: It waves, and thins, and is gone. It is a very good likeness.

choices.text: Bring a cup for the sculptor

effects.log: The cup is warm. The morning is soft.

events.text: The cloud-sculptor sculpts only in the evenings now, and {npc} makes you a small cat of cloud and lets it sleep on your sill. It lasts the night. In the morning there is a smudge of damp and a look in your eye.
events.arc: The Sculptor Who Worked Only in Cloud

choices.text: Ask for a cat each year

effects.log: It becomes your small ritual. The cats are always different, and always asleep.

choices.text: Thank {him} with a pot of tea

effects.log: The pot is empty by dusk.

events.text: At the Ministry of Prayers, {npc} sorts the prayers that rise from below into trays: urgent, polite, tedious, and "for someone else". It is a dim job and {he} does it with enormous tenderness. A tray labelled "unaddressed" is heaped to the ceiling. "No one reads these," {he} says. "I do."
events.arc: The Clerk of the Ministry of Prayers

effects.log: You read ten. They are simple and strange: a wish for rain, a wish for a thin pig, a wish for one more year.
"They go to the sea," says {npc}. "Where they dissolve. Politely."
It is a mountain of small hopes. You look at it for a while.

events.text: The Ministry announces a reform: unaddressed prayers shall no longer be kept. They will be burned at midday. {npc} reads the order twice and goes to sit in the tray room. The evening lamps are not lit.
events.arc: The Clerk of the Ministry of Prayers

effects.log: You write a petition, sealed in the Ministry's own ink. It is read, discussed, and not rejected.

choices.text: Help {him} copy the best ones out

effects.log: You copy by lamplight for a month. A hundred prayers are saved to a new ledger.
You do not talk. The lamps stay out.

events.text: The reform is amended: unaddressed prayers shall be read aloud at the monthly meeting and sent to whoever raises a hand. {npc} is named the Reader of Unaddressed Prayers, with a lectern, and stands up for the first time in a century.
events.arc: The Clerk of the Ministry of Prayers

choices.text: Raise your hand for the first prayer

effects.log: It is a small wish for a good harvest of some tiny seed. You send a rain. It is the best rain you ever made.
The applause is thin and sincere.

events.text: The copied ledger sits in the tray room, a hundred prayers, bound in plain cloth. When the Ministry is old, they say, it will be the only thing left. {npc} reads from it at night, to the dark, in a low voice.
events.arc: The Clerk of the Ministry of Prayers

effects.log: Each prayer feels like a small door opening. You stay till midnight.
The clerk finds it, and understands.

events.text: A star-rain falls over the Marsh Isle: tiny sparks, cold and pretty, that vanish on the water. Children run out with bowls. The old ones stay in, saying they have seen it three hundred times. Then, one by one, they come out too.

effects.log: Eleven sparks collect and die. You carry the bowl in carefully, as if it held water.
A spark lands on your cheek and goes out. It was cold, and it was a kiss.

events.text: A tribulation cloud settles over the Cold Reef and an immortal inside is having a terrible time. The neighbours sell tea to the onlookers. An old gossip near you comments on each bolt: "Too early. Too weak. Oh, that one stings." You admit the gossip knows lightning.

choices.text: Buy tea and take a seat

effects.log: The tea is hot and thin. The bolts are loud. It is a splendid afternoon.

choices.text: Ask the gossip what to make of the immortal inside

effects.log: "They will live," the gossip says. "But they will not enjoy it."

events.text: A new wind has been born over the Pearl Isle and nobody has named it yet. It is small, fresh, and rather rude, flipping skirts and snatching hats. A committee of three old scholars is deadlocked on the name. A child shouts "Scamp", and the wind seems to approve.

effects.log: "Scamp" is entered into the Ministry's book of winds.

choices.text: Suggest a longer name for dignity

effects.log: The committee approves. The wind sulks for a decade.

events.text: At the Starlit Stalls, a vendor sells starlight by the jar and a customer insists it is last season's. They haggle in the high style, with long, formal accusations. The crowd watches with joy, placing no stakes, but taking sides.

effects.log: The vendor wins by an inch and bows to you in thanks.
The customer wins a better jar. The vendor mutters about you for a month.

events.text: A mist-porridge is served every morning at the Kettle Isle, grey, slow, and without flavour. A new cook adds one pinch of something and everyone looks up, startled. "What is that?" "A thing you forgot," says the cook. Nobody can say what.

effects.log: It tastes of a summer you lived once. You eat it slowly.

choices.text: Ask the cook to say what it is

effects.log: The cook smiles and says nothing.

events.text: A shelf in the Archive of Moving Slips has drifted a step to the left each century, and today it has reached the window. A clerk stands before it, upset. "It will be outside soon," the clerk says. "The slips have never seen the sky."

choices.text: Help carry the slips to a new wall

effects.log: You carry them one by one. The shelf, relieved, stops moving.

choices.text: Open the window and let the slips see

effects.log: The slips shiver in the light. Some of them, you are sure, sigh.

events.text: A pool of cloud-lotus opens only at the end of the hour of twilight, for exactly as long as a person takes to say a prayer. An old watcher waits at its edge every evening. This evening the watcher asks you to say it, as the voice is gone.

choices.text: Say the prayer for the watcher

effects.log: You say what you can. The lotus open, and the old watcher weeps, and thanks you with both hands.

choices.text: Wait beside the watcher in silence

effects.log: The lotus open, and close. The two of you sit till dark.

events.text: A toll-keeper on the Rope Bridge charges one copper per crossing and refuses to say what the copper is for. Travellers pay and shrug. You pay, and ask. "It is for the bridge," says the keeper. "It holds better when it is paid."

choices.text: Pay again on the way back

effects.log: The bridge feels, for a moment, stronger under your feet.
There are only two entries, a century apart. You do not press.

events.text: You climb the Spire Isle at the hour before dawn, and a dozen others are there, no one speaking. The sun rises through a gap in the clouds, and for one minute the whole fleet is gold. Then someone coughs, and the spell breaks, gently.

effects.log: The same sun rises from a different cloud. It is a gentler one.

choices.text: Share a flask of tea with a stranger

effects.log: The stranger says nothing, and you are close.

events.text: At the Edge of Heaven, a gift stall sells postcards of the void. They are quite blank, with a single dot of light in the corner. The stall-keeper swears each one is different. You buy one and find, on the back, a message in your own hand.

effects.log: It says only "Not yet." You are not sure whether to be sad or relieved.
The friend writes back: "Received. What does it mean?" Neither of you knows.

events.text: On the green hills of the Meadow Isle, a family of heaven-born is picnicking beside a sleeping mist hound. The youngest child feeds it. The eldest pretends to disapprove. The middle one stares at you and asks: "What is it like, being old?"

effects.log: It is like being full of rooms. The child considers this and nods.

choices.text: Say it is like being young, with better tea

effects.log: The family laughs. The hound opens one eye.

events.text: A whale-song drifts up from the deep cloud, so low it is felt in the bones before heard. The whole Trade Isle stops in its work. Clerks put down pens. Cooks stop stirring. When it ends, everyone resumes without a word, and everything is a little different.

effects.log: The echo takes a full minute. You feel it in your teeth.
Your hum is a small thing against the song. It feels right anyway.

events.text: In the hot springs of the Steaming Isle, three old immortals soak and gossip about people you have never met. They draw you in with a nod. "You look like someone with a story," one says. "Share it. We are out of ours."

effects.log: They listen with the intense attention of bath-dwellers. You come out pink and happier.
They know. They love it.

events.text: It is the season of the thunder sparrows, when the fledglings practise their first small bolts over the Orchard Isle. Orchardists hold up copper rods and cheer. Every sparkle, every hair standing up, is an occasion. A sparrow lands on your shoulder, hums, and sparks.

choices.text: Hold still and let it sit

effects.log: It sits for a minute, charged and proud, then flies off with a tiny crack.

choices.text: Wave a copper rod and cheer with the rest

effects.log: The orchardists clap you on the back, and a sparrow sparks at your boot.

events.text: In the ruins of the old Banquet Hall, you find a single unbroken cup, gold and cold. Etched on its base: "To the future, whoever you are." It is thick with centuries of dust. You drink from nothing, and the cup rings.

effects.log: It sits on your shelf and rings when you speak a kind word.
It rings once, as you go, and is quiet.

events.text: A grotto at the underside of the Hush Isle hums when you walk past. The hum has a pattern, nearly a tune. A priest of the Ministry of Quiet posted a notice: "Do not hum back." You hum back. Something in the stone pauses, then hums a bar of something older.

effects.log: The stone answers again. It is a duet of sorts.
The hum fades, content.

events.text: On the underside of an isle, among the roots and cloud-pines, someone has hung a tiny teahouse from the branches. There is a note: "Open at dusk. Bring your own cup." At dusk, a lantern comes on. It is the smallest, kindest place you have ever seen.

choices.text: Come back at dusk with a cup

effects.log: A teapot has been left on a branch for you. You drink alone, in a grove of roots and calm.

choices.text: Leave a cup on the branch for another traveller

effects.log: Someone will find it. You hope they stay a while.

events.text: An ancient plum tree on the Ash Isle blooms once in eight hundred years, and this is the week. Elders with canes have come from three isles to see it. They sit under it in silence. A petal lands on the nearest, who says only: "Ah. There you are."

effects.log: You sit. The petals fall. You feel yourself being included in something old.

choices.text: Bring a flask of wine for the tree

effects.log: You pour a little at the root. A petal lands in your cup.

events.text: The Ledger of Blooms is kept by a clerk who records every flower in the Heavens, one per line. Today the clerk is at the line "rose, one, first of the season". The clerk looks at it, then at you, and says: "I forgot to look at the flower."

choices.text: Walk the clerk to the rose

effects.log: The clerk looks for a long time. The rose is red, patient, and entirely unrecorded.

choices.text: Offer to keep the ledger for an hour

effects.log: The clerk goes out and sits in the garden. You write "rose, one" and it feels like a promise.

events.text: A watch-post on the Cliff Isle has been staffed by one retired marshal for six hundred years. Nothing has ever been seen. The marshal logs each day: "Sky: present. Cliffs: present. Self: present." Today the marshal asks you to sign the log.

effects.log: Your name sits under the marshal's lines. "Visitor: present," it says.

choices.text: Add a line of your own

effects.log: "Tea: appreciated." The marshal laughs for the first time in a decade.

events.text: Something pale and pretty grows in the rim of an old starfall crater, a flower with no leaf. It opens at night and gives off a very faint hum. A gardener of the Third Terrace has been trying to graft it, with no success. The flower seems amused.

choices.text: Sit in the crater and listen

effects.log: The hum is the sound of a star finishing its last note.
The graft fails. The gardener laughs, and the flower hums on.

events.text: Once a century the whole fleet assembles in the Great Basin: ten thousand isles in a single ring, lanterns lit, ferries crossing in the dusk. Nobody speaks of why. It is the only time everyone is in the same sky. A stranger beside you says, "I came for the lanterns."

choices.text: Say you came for the neighbours

effects.log: The stranger nods. "That is the real reason."
They weave like small stars. The night is warm.

events.text: You fall asleep in the sun on a bench at the Tea Isle, and wake to find a blanket laid over you, a cup of tea at your side, and no one in sight. The cup is still warm. A card reads only: "You looked tired."

effects.log: It is exactly the right strength. You feel cared for by a stranger.

choices.text: Leave a card of your own

effects.log: "Thank you." It is gone by evening.

events.text: Every century the Reed Lake holds a race of cloud-skiffs, and {npc} has come last for ninety-nine of them. "One more," {he} says, hauling a patched sail. "I have a feeling about this one." The skiff is named Nearly. {He} asks if you will crew.
events.arc: The Skiff Race of the Reed Lake

effects.log: The skiff is leaky and light, and you are suddenly part of something.

choices.text: Offer to patch the sail first

effects.log: You spend a week with needle and silk. The sail looks like a quilt but holds the wind.
{npc} waves, undeterred, and pushes off.

events.text: The race begins in a squall. Skiffs spin and collide. Nearly, being small, slips between two fat rivals and finds itself in third place. {npc} lets out a whoop that echoes off the reeds. The crowd, startled, begins to cheer.
events.arc: The Skiff Race of the Reed Lake

choices.text: Trim the sail for the final stretch

effects.log: You lean on the boom and feel the skiff leap. Second place, then first, for a breath.
The skiff swerves, loses a place, and clears the shoal. A rival strikes it and sinks into the reeds.
Your shout is mostly joy.

events.text: Nearly crosses the line first by a hair, and nobody believes it. The judges check the lines, the sail, the sky. {npc} sits in the bottom of the skiff, shaking. "Is it real?" {he} whispers. "Tell me it is real."
events.arc: The Skiff Race of the Reed Lake

choices.text: Tell {him} it is real, and laugh

effects.log: The judges confirm. The lake roars. {npc} cries into the sail.

choices.text: Fetch the old judge to say it

effects.log: The old judge says it solemnly. It is the most beautiful sentence {npc} has ever heard.

events.text: The next race, {npc} comes last again, and is perfectly happy. "I have won once," {he} says. "Now I can lose properly." The skiff Nearly hangs in the rafters of the Reed Lake inn, with a plaque, and a small pot of tea beneath it.
events.arc: The Skiff Race of the Reed Lake

choices.text: Raise a cup under the skiff

effects.log: The inn raises with you. Nearly sways slightly overhead.
{npc} eats it like a champion.

events.text: {npc} gives up racing and builds skiffs for the young. The first is named Nearly Two. It wins nothing, and sails beautifully. The race goes on, and the Reed Lake is richer for every last place that took it seriously.
events.arc: The Skiff Race of the Reed Lake

effects.log: Your name goes on the bow, small and proud.

choices.text: Watch the next race from the shore

effects.log: You watch. It is long, and happy.

events.text: Tea has gone missing from the pavilion on the Dusk Isle: a pinch here, a leaf there. The master of the house is furious. You find {npc}, the youngest apprentice, behind the kettle with a tin of stolen leaves. {He} goes red to the ears. "I only wanted to learn the blend."
events.arc: The Apprentice Who Stole Only Tea

choices.text: Say nothing and share a cup

effects.log: You drink together in the steam. {npc} breathes out for the first time in weeks.
The master is stern, then curious, then tasting. {npc} is given a month of the kettle.
{npc} does, shaking, and you say nothing to anyone.

events.text: {npc} learns the blend and improves it. A pinch of snow-mint where a leaf of dusk-rose used to go. The guests praise the tea and no one knows why. The master sniffs, sips, and asks the young apprentice to explain.
events.arc: The Apprentice Who Stole Only Tea

effects.log: {npc} stammers, then speaks. The master listens.
The apprentice fumbles, then finds words. It is a poor start, and a fair finish.

events.text: The master retires and names {npc} as heir to the kettle, overlooking three older, better connected apprentices. They grumble. A rumour starts that the choice was bought. {npc} comes to you, shaking.
events.arc: The Apprentice Who Stole Only Tea

effects.log: You speak plainly of the blend. The grumblers go quiet, then sulk, then drink.

choices.text: Advise {him} to make the grumblers a pot

effects.log: It is the best pot of {his} life. The grumblers, grudgingly, are won.

events.text: {npc} runs the Dusk Isle pavilion for a century, and the blend is famous across the fleet. Every year {he} sets aside a tin of the stolen kind and leaves it on the back step. No one is ever sure whom it is for. You suspect.
events.arc: The Apprentice Who Stole Only Tea

effects.log: It is the best tea of the year, and tastes of a dare.

choices.text: Leave it for the next apprentice

effects.log: It is gone in the morning.

events.text: The apprentice quits the kettle and sets up a stall on a cloud-bridge, selling a blend of {his} own. It never competes with the pavilion, and the master sends customers. "Different tea," {npc} says. "Same leaves."
events.arc: The Apprentice Who Stole Only Tea

choices.text: Buy a tin from the stall

effects.log: It tastes faintly of snow and rebellion.

choices.text: Send {him} a bolt of silk for the awning

effects.log: The awning is bright. The stall gets a following.

events.text: The Minister of Weather, {npc}, has been quarrelling with a single cloud for a century. It drifts over the Ministry roof every noon and drops a cold drizzle on the Minister's desk. "It does it on purpose," {he} says, glaring skyward. "I have a witness." The witness is a clerk, who looks at the floor.
events.arc: The Minister Who Sulked at a Cloud

choices.text: Offer to talk to the cloud

effects.log: You speak to it in the polite way. It drips a little warmer.
"A roof is surrender," says {npc}, but {he} buys one.
{npc} stares at you as at a madman.

events.text: The cloud has gone from the Ministry roof, and {npc} cannot sleep. The drizzle is missed. A week of dry noons, and the Minister paces the corridors. "It left because I was rude," {he} mutters. "A cloud has feelings."
events.arc: The Minister Who Sulked at a Cloud

effects.log: You find it over the Orchard Isle, drizzling happily on a patch of pears. {npc} stands at the edge, awkward.

choices.text: Tell {him} to apologise to the sky

effects.log: {npc} stands on the roof and mutters an apology to a blue and empty sky. Then another, louder.
It does not, that week.

events.text: {npc} learns the cloud's name from a pear-grower: Dribble. The Minister speaks it once, shyly, to the sky. Dribble comes, hovers, drops a gentle cold drop on {his} nose, and drifts away. {npc} smiles for the first time in a hundred years.
events.arc: The Minister Who Sulked at a Cloud

effects.log: You drink. The sky is grey and kind.

choices.text: Send the Minister a small umbrella

effects.log: It is a joke, and a gift. {npc} keeps it on the desk.

events.text: The Minister posts an official notice: "The cloud called Dribble is hereby granted free passage over all Ministry property." The notice is read aloud. A drizzle starts at once, delighted, over the clerks. Nobody minds.
events.arc: The Minister Who Sulked at a Cloud

effects.log: The drizzle falls. The clerks laugh and get wet.

choices.text: Notice it on the Ministry board

effects.log: It stays there for centuries.

events.text: Between the reefs and the isles run a hundred bridges of woven cloud-reed, and {npc} mends them, alone, on a long circuit that takes a decade. "By the time I finish the last," {he} says, "the first needs mending." {He} says it with satisfaction, not sorrow.
events.arc: The Mender of Reef-Bridges

choices.text: Walk part of the circuit with {him}

effects.log: You carry the reed and hold the lines. The view from the underside of the bridges is dizzy and astonishing.

choices.text: Ask if {he} ever tires of it

effects.log: "Never," says {npc}. "A bridge is a promise that someone will come." The words stay with you.

choices.text: Cross the nearest bridge and say thanks

effects.log: {npc} nods from below, reed in hand.

events.text: A bridge snaps in the night, a long one, between the Pearl Isle and a market reef. A caravan is stranded on the far side, with a sick child. {npc} is a week away on the circuit. The market sends for you, knowing you walked with the mender.
events.arc: The Mender of Reef-Bridges

choices.text: Mend the bridge with what you learned

ok.log: You work through the night, reed by reed, and the bridge holds. The caravan crosses at dawn.

fail.log: The bridge holds one crossing, then sways badly. The caravan makes it over, scraped and cross.

effects.log: You find the mender in time. {npc} says nothing, climbs aboard, and mends it in an hour.

events.text: {npc} hears about the night's work and comes to find you. "You did it badly," {he} says, "and you did it." {He} hands you a reed knife, worn smooth by hands you will never meet. "Take a stretch of the circuit. I am old."
events.arc: The Mender of Reef-Bridges

choices.text: Accept the knife and a stretch

effects.log: You take the circuit near the Pearl Isle. It is the beginning of a quiet, good habit.

choices.text: Accept the thanks, decline the knife

effects.log: {npc} nods. "Bridges find their menders."

events.text: The circuit grows lighter with more hands. The great bridge is rewoven in a season. {npc} sits at its centre with a bowl of soup, supervising. "In my day," {he} begins, and the whole crew shouts, "It took ten years!"
events.arc: The Mender of Reef-Bridges

effects.log: It is a good soup, the best on a bridge.
It holds. It sways a little, in a friendly way.

events.text: In the Archive of Seldom Wishes, {npc} copies old jade slips by hand, because the carvings fade after two thousand years and someone must keep them. Nobody has asked for the slips in a thousand years. "Somebody will," {he} says, carving. "The day I stop, they will."
events.arc: The Copyist of Slips Nobody Reads

effects.log: You read a slip on the keeping of bees in the high winds. It is absurd and charming.

choices.text: Offer to carve a slip yourself

effects.log: You carve a line and spoil it. {npc} fixes it with one cut. "Practise," {he} says.
It smells of cold stone and attention.

events.text: A young scholar from the Jade Void Sect arrives asking for a slip on bees. {npc} nearly drops the knife. It has been a thousand years. The scholar is rude and in a hurry, and does not realise what a miracle {he} has just been shown.
events.arc: The Copyist of Slips Nobody Reads

choices.text: Lead the scholar to the slip

effects.log: You bring it. The scholar glances at it, grunts, and leaves. {npc} shakes, delighted and furious.

choices.text: Ask the scholar to stay for tea

effects.log: The scholar relents. Over tea, the scholar becomes an ally and a friend.

events.text: The scholar sends a hundred students to the archive, and the little room fills with the scratch of styluses. {npc} stands in the doorway, astonished at being needed. "I never wanted this," {he} says. "I only wanted to keep them."
events.arc: The Copyist of Slips Nobody Reads

effects.log: You set up a rota and a system of reading. The room hums with study.

choices.text: Suggest {he} take only a few, and stay quiet

effects.log: {npc} chooses six students. The archive stays calm, and the slips are loved.

events.text: The archive is still quiet, six students deep. {npc} copies a slip on bees, then a slip on rain, then one on kites. The students read them aloud to each other over tea. It is the happiest the archive has been in a thousand years.
events.arc: The Copyist of Slips Nobody Reads

effects.log: You read a slip on kites. It is oddly stirring.

choices.text: Leave a stack of fresh jade

effects.log: The jade is gone in the morning, carved.

events.text: The archive swells to a hundred students and a small ministry, and {npc} is made Keeper with a title and an assistant. {He} is polite about it and silent about it, and carves in the evenings in a closet.
events.arc: The Copyist of Slips Nobody Reads

effects.log: You find {him} carving a slip on how to keep a thing small. It is the best you have read.

choices.text: Send the assistant on an errand

effects.log: The assistant goes. {npc} carves in peace.

events.text: The Pearl Library lends only to members of the five factions. At the door a doorkeeper, {npc}, glances at your empty sleeve. "No seal," {he} says. "No lending. Read at the bench by the draught, if you like." The bench is cold. The library is warm. A slip you need sits on the third shelf.
events.arc: The Rogue Denied the Pearl Library

effects.log: You read for three days at the draught-bench. You come away with a sore back and a very good idea.
You argue well. {npc} listens, unimpressed, and then, grudgingly, brings the slip to the bench.

choices.text: Pay a reading fee (2 Low-Grade Spirit Stones)

effects.log: The doorkeeper takes the stones without comment and seats you under the lamps.

events.text: A sealed reader at the next table sneers at your coat. Then sees the slip you are reading, and goes quiet. It is the one they have wanted for years. They sit uncomfortably still. Finally they say: "Could I see that?"
events.arc: The Rogue Denied the Pearl Library

effects.log: The reader copies a line and bows. The bow is stiff, but it is a bow.
They ask nicely. It takes a minute. You let them copy.
You carry the idea out of the library, whole.

events.text: {npc} slips you a lending token one evening, a thin copper thing with no seal on it. "It is not a seal," {he} says. "It is a favour. Do not tell anyone." The token opens a side door to the stacks.
events.arc: The Rogue Denied the Pearl Library

effects.log: You borrow three slips and return them within the week. The library does not notice.
The doorkeeper looks at you with something close to respect, and puts it away.

events.text: The library opens a single shelf for the unsealed. It is a low one, near the draught, and half the books are about bees. But it is a shelf, and the doorkeeper stocks it, and the first rogue to borrow from it is you.
events.arc: The Rogue Denied the Pearl Library

effects.log: It is on the keeping of bees. You read it twice and laugh.

choices.text: Leave the shelf to the next reader

effects.log: They find it, and sit down at once.

events.text: You read at the bench for decades. The draught becomes familiar. {npc} brings you a lap-rug one winter and says nothing. It is, by a long chalk, the warmest thing the library has ever done.
events.arc: The Rogue Denied the Pearl Library

choices.text: Wrap the rug around your knees

effects.log: You read until the lamps are lit.
{npc} grunts, which is high praise.

events.text: Every heaven-born child flies by the age of ten. {npc} is twelve and has not left the ground. {He} sits on the lip of the Cliff Isle and watches the others loop and shout. "I am not afraid," {he} says to you. "I just think it is unnecessary."
events.arc: The Heaven-Born Who Would Not Fly

choices.text: Sit beside {him} and watch the sky

effects.log: You watch for an hour. {npc} counts the swifts aloud, and you count with {him}.

choices.text: Offer to fly with {him}, hand in hand

effects.log: {npc} looks at your hand for a long time, and does not take it.
{npc} brightens. "Thank you. Nobody ever says that."

events.text: {npc} learns to climb instead. The cliff-face of the isle, a hundred hand-holds from top to bottom, becomes a sort of cathedral. By thirteen {he} knows every crack. {He} climbs with a calm that frightens the fliers.
events.arc: The Heaven-Born Who Would Not Fly

effects.log: It is slow and glorious. At the bottom, you hang over empty sky and nothing is unnecessary.

choices.text: Tell the other children to leave {him} be

effects.log: The fliers grumble, then watch. A few start climbing too.

events.text: A swift-storm tears through the Cliff Isle and a young flier is caught on a ledge below the underside. They cannot fly out in the wind. Only a climber can reach them. {npc} is looking down at the child with the whole of {his} body.
events.arc: The Heaven-Born Who Would Not Fly

effects.log: {npc} climbs. It is the best climb of {his} life. The child is brought up safe.
The two of you reach the ledge together. {npc} does the real work.

events.text: {npc} never flies. {He} becomes the isle's keeper of the cliff-ways, a hero in a rope, with a hundred fliers who owe {him} breath. "Unnecessary," {he} still says, with a smile, "but very nice to have been needed."
events.arc: The Heaven-Born Who Would Not Fly

choices.text: Raise a cup to the climber

effects.log: The tavern roars. The climber laughs, and holds on to the rail.
It is long, and steep, and the view at the top is entire.

events.text: One evening, years on, {npc} steps off the ledge and flies, simply, for the pleasure of it, not for need. It is a short, wobbly flight. {He} lands in a cloud-bush and laughs till {he} cries.
events.arc: The Heaven-Born Who Would Not Fly

effects.log: The whole isle hears. The applause rolls like thunder.
You fall in beside {him}. It is soft and ridiculous.

events.text: Each dawn, {npc} walks to the Heron Lake with a bowl of rice-cloud and feeds the cranes. For six hundred years {he} did it with a companion, a slow tall figure always at the elbow. This dawn {he} walks alone, and the cranes crowd round, confused.
events.arc: The Two Who Fed the Cranes

effects.log: You say nothing. The cranes take the rice, and the lake is wide and still.
"Gone to the Edge," says {npc}. "Before me. By choice." The cranes pick at the rice.
{npc} nods. The cranes call.

events.text: {npc} still sets two bowls out. One is for the cranes, one is for nothing. The cranes, after a while, eat from both. "They understand," {he} says. "It is better than people. People ask."
events.arc: The Two Who Fed the Cranes

choices.text: Feed the cranes from the second bowl

effects.log: A crane takes a bite from your hand. {npc} watches, with a very small smile.
You respect the empty space. The cranes do not. They eat it all.

events.text: A traveller arrives at the lake, asking after the companion. They carry a letter, thirty years old, from the Edge. {npc} reads it standing, and then sits down on the shore. "The letter says there was no fear," {he} says. "Neither am I."
events.arc: The Two Who Fed the Cranes

choices.text: Sit with {him} until the cranes settle

effects.log: The cranes drift back. The lake is pearly in the dusk.
You walk home through the reeds, softly.

events.text: {npc} walks the lake each dawn, a little slower, and the cranes follow like an honour guard. One morning the bowl is empty, and the cranes stand in a ring at the water's edge, facing the sunrise. You feed them for the rest of your visit.
events.arc: The Two Who Fed the Cranes

effects.log: You come every dawn for a year. It is a quiet duty, and a good one.

choices.text: Leave a bowl at the shore

effects.log: The cranes eat from it for years.

events.text: On the black-glass shore of the Star Sea Pavilion, {npc} fishes with a line of spider-silk and no bait. "The stars bite," {he} says, "if you do not want them." {He} has caught three in a thousand years, and put every one back.
events.arc: The Angler of the Star Sea

effects.log: You cast. Nothing happens, quietly, for a long time. It is very restful.
You talk of nothing. A star glints and vanishes. {npc} grins.

choices.text: Watch the line from a distance

effects.log: It hangs in the dark like a thought.

events.text: Your line tugs. A star, small and cold, has taken it. {npc} puts a finger to {his} lips. "Do not want it," {he} whispers. "That is the trick." The star hangs on the end of your line, dimming, brightening, waiting.
events.arc: The Angler of the Star Sea

choices.text: Let it go without wanting it

effects.log: It slips off in a spark and vanishes into the dark. {npc} nods with deep satisfaction.

choices.text: Pull it in and look closely

effects.log: It is a pebble of cold light, warm as a coin in the hand. You hold it briefly, then return it.

events.text: {npc} falls ill from the cold of the shore, and asks you to keep the line while {he} recovers. You sit through the nights at the black glass, wanting nothing. By the end of the week, you have not caught a thing, and you are rested.
events.arc: The Angler of the Star Sea

effects.log: It becomes a habit. You catch nothing and gain a great deal.
{npc} drinks and looks at the dark sea with love.

events.text: {npc} retires the line and hands it to you. "It has caught four in a thousand years," {he} says. "Five, if you count the one you caught." You do not want the line. You take it. It is lighter than it looks.
events.arc: The Angler of the Star Sea

choices.text: Fish the star sea for a century

effects.log: You fish, and the line hangs in the dark, and the stars come when they please.

choices.text: Hang the line on the pavilion wall

effects.log: It hangs beside a lantern, a small thing of silk.

events.text: {npc}, a hound-keeper of the Gorse Isle, trains mist hounds to track lost travellers across the fogs. The newest pup, Wisp, will not track. It sits, wags its fog, and watches clouds go by. "It is a failure," {he} says, hopeless. "I have never seen a failure so cheerful."
events.arc: The Mist Hound Pup Who Would Not Track

choices.text: Take a turn with the pup

effects.log: Wisp follows you for an hour, then loses interest and rolls in the gorse. It is the happiest dog in the sky.

choices.text: Ask what the pup is interested in

effects.log: "Birds," says {npc}. "And butterflies. And a very particular patch of grass."

choices.text: Pat the pup and move on

effects.log: Wisp grins. {npc} sighs.

events.text: A child is lost on the Gorse Isle in the fog. The best hounds are away on a long hunt. {npc} paces. Wisp sits at the door, ears forward. {He} looks at you: "It is not trained," {he} says. "But it is the only one here."
events.arc: The Mist Hound Pup Who Would Not Track

effects.log: Wisp trots, doubtful, then stiffens at a patch of grass. Beyond it, the child, huddled in a bush. The pup licks the child's face.
Wisp leads {npc} to the child. You wait, anxious, at the door, and cheer when they return.

events.text: Wisp is a hero, and does not care. The pup lies in the sun and watches clouds. {npc} confesses: "I trained them for tracking. I should have trained them for caring. That one needed no training." The other hounds are given patches of grass.
events.arc: The Mist Hound Pup Who Would Not Track

effects.log: You spend a season teaching hounds to care about small things. They learn faster than expected.
Wisp wags its fog until the bone is a memory.

events.text: The hounds of the Gorse Isle are the best in the fleet, and the kindest. Wisp, now old, sleeps on the doorstep. Visitors step over it with great care. "It tracks everything," says {npc}, "if you give it time."
events.arc: The Mist Hound Pup Who Would Not Track

choices.text: Sit with Wisp on the step

effects.log: Wisp leans on your shin. It is warm and full of fog.

choices.text: Raise a cup to the pup

effects.log: It deserves more than one.

events.text: Wisp tracks nothing else, ever, and needs not. {npc} takes the pup everywhere. They are known, the two of them, from isle to isle, a keeper and a hound watching clouds go by. It is the shortest and best hunt of the age.
events.arc: The Mist Hound Pup Who Would Not Track

choices.text: Walk with them for a day

effects.log: The cloud goes by. The grass is a good patch.

choices.text: Send them a bone each spring

effects.log: They send back a leaf.

events.text: For the Festival of Lantern Boats, every household on the Tidemark Isle builds a paper boat to float on the cloud-sea. {npc}, the oldest boatwright, builds nine hundred every year for those who cannot. "One boat per person," {he} says, "and not a word about the seams."
events.arc: The Boatwright of the Lantern Festival

effects.log: You fold for a week. Your fingers hurt, and the boats are crooked, and {npc} says they are perfect.

choices.text: Ask who the boats are for

effects.log: "For the dead and the not-yet-born," says {npc}. "Mostly for those in the middle."

choices.text: Buy a boat and float it

effects.log: It drifts, small and white, until you lose it in the dusk.

events.text: On the eve of the festival, a gale strips the Tidemark Isle of its paper. Nine hundred boats are drenched. {npc} stands among the pulp with empty hands. "I cannot make nine hundred in a night," {he} says. "But I will not make none."
events.arc: The Boatwright of the Lantern Festival

choices.text: Rally the isle to fold through the night

effects.log: Neighbours bring paper, tea and stubbornness. By dawn there are nine hundred boats, mostly crooked.

choices.text: Offer your own robes as paper

effects.log: You tear a sleeve. The robe is cloud-silk and takes the ink like a sail.
Your lamp lasts the night.

events.text: The festival dawns grey and glorious, nine hundred crooked boats on a silver sea. As each is launched, the boatwright names the person it was made for: a girl, a lamplighter, a baker who is gone. {He} comes at last to a boat unlaunched. "This one is mine," {he} says.
events.arc: The Boatwright of the Lantern Festival

effects.log: You push it out with a long reed. It drifts, small and lit, past the last of the isle's lamps.

choices.text: Watch from the quay in silence

effects.log: The boat floats out of sight. The quay is very quiet.

events.text: The Tidemark Isle holds the festival every year after, and you are given a boat each time, folded by someone you have not met. Yours is always crooked. It always floats.
events.arc: The Boatwright of the Lantern Festival

choices.text: Fold a boat for a stranger in return

effects.log: You fold carefully. It is your best, and still crooked.
It carries your wave a little way.

events.text: Two isles, the Plum and the Pear, brew cloud-wine and have quarrelled over which is better for four hundred years. {npc} of the Plum Isle appoints you taster. "Be fair," {he} says. "Be strict. And do not say anything nice about their pear."
events.arc: The Vintners of Two Isles

effects.log: The Plum is sweet and the Pear is dry. You cannot choose, and say so.
{npc} claps you on the back. The Pear vintners glare for a decade.
{npc} sniffs and finds another taster. The quarrel continues.

events.text: Both isles invite you to a banquet on the same night. You cannot attend both. You send regrets to one by mistake, and the offended isle sends a letter in a thin, dangerous hand. The quarrel has found a new object.
events.arc: The Vintners of Two Isles

choices.text: Throw a banquet of your own for both

effects.log: Both isles arrive in bad humour. The wine, shared, is better than either.

choices.text: Apologise by letter and a gift of fruit

effects.log: The Pear Isle accepts with a stiff note. The Plum Isle sulks into winter.

choices.text: Skip them both and go fishing

effects.log: The fish are polite.

events.text: At the shared banquet, a plum-and-pear cloud-wine appears, a blend, quite by accident. It is the best wine anyone present has tasted. Nobody wants to admit it. {npc} sets down the cup with enormous care and says: "That is a disgrace."
events.arc: The Vintners of Two Isles

effects.log: The room breaks into laughter. The blend is called, forever, "The Disgrace".

choices.text: Propose that both isles brew it together

effects.log: There is a long silence. Then, grudgingly, a toast.

events.text: You stay out of the quarrel for good. It rolls on, ten more centuries, with banners and verses. You visit both, taste neither, and are loved by each in the way one loves a neutral country.
events.arc: The Vintners of Two Isles

effects.log: You carry notes between them under the table. They never know.
They are very good verses.

events.text: The Ministry of Precedence has been asked to rule on a cloud that straddles the border of two isles. The Quill Isle says it is theirs; the Marsh Isle says the same. {npc}, the arbiter, cannot decide, and the cloud, meanwhile, rains on both. "You have an eye for these," {he} says to you. "Come and look."
events.arc: The Dispute over a Cloud Boundary

effects.log: You find a seam in the cloud, almost invisible, running exactly along the gap. It is two clouds, long since merged.
The cloud is cut with ceremony. It sulks, and rains very little for a year.

choices.text: Say it is a matter for the Jade Court

effects.log: {npc} sighs and files it up. It will take a century.

events.text: The Quill Isle and the Marsh Isle each send a delegation to hear the ruling. They glare across the hall. The arbiter clears a thin throat. "The cloud," {he} begins, and then looks to you for help.
events.arc: The Dispute over a Cloud Boundary

choices.text: Read the finding aloud: two clouds, merged

effects.log: Both delegations are astonished. The Quill Isle laughs. The Marsh Isle weeps. The cloud, overhead, drizzles.

choices.text: Whisper the finding to the arbiter

effects.log: {npc} reads it with trembling dignity. Both delegations bow to the Ministry.

events.text: The two isles share the cloud by rota, a week each, and the rain falls on schedule. The arbiter is thanked in two languages, and {he} sends you a note: "We have made a small peace. It will not last, but it will last long enough."
events.arc: The Dispute over a Cloud Boundary

effects.log: It hangs in your hall. It is the most honest ruling you have seen.

choices.text: Send the arbiter a barrel of cloud-wine

effects.log: It arrives with the cork already loosened.

events.text: The split cloud is rainless for a year, and then it is two clouds, one over each isle, each rained on by the other. The isles blame the Ministry, which blames the cloud. {npc} is quietly reassigned to the Ministry of Fog.
events.arc: The Dispute over a Cloud Boundary

effects.log: {npc} is surprisingly cheerful. "Fog does not argue," {he} says.
{npc} frames it.

events.text: A thunder sparrow has taken to perching on your sill and repeating, in a tiny crackling voice, whatever it hears elsewhere. It has been in the Court kitchens, the market, the archive. {npc}, the keeper of the Aviary Isle, arrives out of breath. "That one is a menace," {he} says. "And mine."
events.arc: The Sparrow That Carried Gossip

choices.text: Ask the sparrow what it knows

effects.log: It tells you a minister's secret, three rumours, and a recipe. {npc} puts a hand over its beak.

choices.text: Offer to return the sparrow quietly

effects.log: {npc} takes it with gratitude. It spits a final gossip as it goes.
It flies in a circle and settles again.

events.text: The sparrow, escaped again, has repeated something that should not be repeated: a quarrel between two old ministers, loud in the Hall of Precedence. Both ministers come hunting. {npc} comes first, white. "I will pay any fine," {he} says. "Please do not take the bird."
events.arc: The Sparrow That Carried Gossip

choices.text: Speak for the bird to the ministers

effects.log: You say a sparrow is a sparrow. The ministers, smarting, reluctantly forgive.

choices.text: Hide the bird in your sleeve

effects.log: The ministers search the Aviary Isle. You walk out with a lump in your sleeve.
The ministers fume at the door, then leave.

events.text: The sparrow is given a post: Official Repeater of the Ministry of Notices. It is a dignified pen with a small perch. It repeats only what it is paid to. {npc} is relieved, and a little jealous. "It never listened to me," {he} says.
events.arc: The Sparrow That Carried Gossip

choices.text: Visit the bird at its post

effects.log: It greets you in a crackling whisper. It repeats your last words from a year ago, word for word.
It repeats "thank you" at an alarming rate.

events.text: The sparrow lives on your sill for a century, repeating the world, and sometimes, to your surprise, repeating you. Visitors stop to listen. Some of what it says is true. Some of it is exactly what you needed to hear.
events.arc: The Sparrow That Carried Gossip

effects.log: It tells you the day, and you hear the shape of your own thoughts.
It does, with relish.

events.text: At the cloud market, a trader of the Demon Realm, {npc}, stands in front of a stall and is ignored by every stallholder. {He} has been waiting an hour. The clerks look through {him}. You step up and ask the stallholder for the bolt in {his} hand.
events.arc: The Buyer from the Demon Realm Market

effects.log: {npc} bows, stiff with surprise. The stallholder sighs and wraps the bolt.

choices.text: Ask the stallholder to serve {him} first

effects.log: The stallholder mutters, and serves. A line of other customers murmurs, but waits.
The trader waits. The hour goes by.

events.text: {npc} insists on thanks. A dinner is arranged in a quiet room above a noodle shop. {He} brings a dish of the Demon Realm: dark, smoky, delicate. It tastes of long winters and fierce, tender warmth. "My mother's," {he} says. "I do not cook it for just anyone."
events.arc: The Buyer from the Demon Realm Market

effects.log: {npc} watches you eat, and sits very straight. It is a quiet success.
{npc} writes it on a napkin, with solemn care. The napkin is a treasure.
{npc} thanks you gravely.

events.text: The Heavenly Court issues a notice: no dealings with the Demon Realm at the cloud market. {npc} stops coming. You hear nothing for a decade. Then a package arrives with a hand-painted jar of the smoky sauce and a note: "Still here. Still cooking."
events.arc: The Buyer from the Demon Realm Market

choices.text: Reply with a bolt of cloud-silk

effects.log: The reply is slow to arrive. It says: "It fits."

choices.text: Ignore the notice and visit the border

effects.log: You find {npc} at a border stall, older, greyer, and delighted.

events.text: The notice lapses, quietly, as such notices do. {npc} returns to the market, and the stallholders look away, and then look back, and then give a small, awkward nod. It is not a welcome. It is a start.
events.arc: The Buyer from the Demon Realm Market

effects.log: The market notices. The nod grows, a little, across the aisle.

choices.text: Buy a bolt for old times

effects.log: It is the same bolt, you could swear.

events.text: You and {npc} eat the smoky dish on the border every spring for a hundred years. The napkin recipe goes on the wall of a noodle shop. The cooks of the Heavens begin to ask for it, and the Court pretends not to notice.
events.arc: The Buyer from the Demon Realm Market

choices.text: Add a line of your own to the recipe

effects.log: A pinch of snow-mint, a trace of dusk-rose. The cooks approve.

choices.text: Eat in silence and let it be

effects.log: It is the best way.

events.text: Every autumn the families of the Reed Isle pitch tents of cloud-silk on the open edge, to watch the star-rain. {npc} mends them, one by one, with a needle of bone and a thread of dusk. The tents are older than the families. "A tent is a promise," {he} says, "that the sky will not mind."
events.arc: The Mender of Cloud-Silk Tents

effects.log: You hold. The needle flashes, and a tear becomes a seam.
{npc} shows you a stitch that vanishes as you make it. You practise for a month.
They glow faintly in the dusk. It is an effect of the old thread.

events.text: A gale tears the biggest tent, the one that has covered the Reed Isle's whole night-watch for a thousand years, from end to end. The tear is longer than {npc} can mend in a night. The star-rain begins in an hour.
events.arc: The Mender of Cloud-Silk Tents

effects.log: Two needles, one tear. By the first spark the tent is whole, and you are exhausted.
You run to the market and back with a bolt. The patch is not the same colour, but it holds.

events.text: The star-rain comes, and the whole isle watches from beneath the tent. The mended seam glows brighter than the rest. {npc} lies on the ground with a cup of tea and looks up. "Well sewn," {he} says to nobody in particular.
events.arc: The Mender of Cloud-Silk Tents

effects.log: The sparks fall silent. The seam glows. You are very still.

choices.text: Pour the tea for the others

effects.log: The tent is full of cups.

events.text: The patched tent hangs on the edge year after year, mismatched and beloved. The patch is named "Fetch", after you, and the children climb on it. {npc} says: "The best seams are the ones that fail first and teach most."
events.arc: The Mender of Cloud-Silk Tents

effects.log: You do. The tent grows a history.

choices.text: Tell the children the patch's story

effects.log: They listen, round-eyed.

events.text: It hails upward for an afternoon, small clear pellets rising from the cloud sea like beads on a string. They hum faintly as they pass. A child catches one in a bowl and it sings a long rising note until it melts. The whole isle holds out bowls.

effects.log: Your bowl hums for an hour with a ghost of the afternoon.
It is a major chord, and then a minor, and then both.

events.text: A tribulation cloud has settled over a distant peak, and half the Trade Isle has climbed up to watch with telescopes and snacks. A vendor sells paper fans labelled "Survive!". Most of the crowd is rooting for the immortal inside. A few are placing little, silent hopes on the cloud.

choices.text: Buy a fan and wave it

effects.log: The cloud flashes. You feel complicit in something enormous and gentle.
The immortal inside is brave, ridiculous, and magnificent.

events.text: A peddler sells wind in a bottle: spring breeze, autumn gust, the last of a summer afternoon. "Open it when you miss the time," the peddler says. A bottle labelled "unlabelled" catches your eye, humming softly.

choices.text: Buy the unlabelled bottle (2 Low-Grade Spirit Stones)

effects.log: You open it on a quiet evening. It smells of a place you once lived and have forgotten.

choices.text: Sniff a sample and move on

effects.log: A light spring breeze lifts your sleeve.

events.text: A merchant at the cloud market sells jars of noon, bottled at the exact moment the sun stands still on the Long Isle. The jar is warm and bright. The merchant says it is good for despair, long winters and bad meetings. You hold one and feel entirely awake.

choices.text: Buy a jar (2 Low-Grade Spirit Stones)

effects.log: You open it in a dark week. Noon fills the room, and you remember what clear is.
The merchant says "with a very still net", and smiles, and will say no more.

events.text: In a kitchen on the Brine Isle, a pickle-master turns a barrel of cloud-turnips that has been fermenting for nine hundred years. It smells fantastic and ghastly. A line of connoisseurs waits for a thimbleful, eyes closed, as for a sacrament.

effects.log: It is sour, deep and sweet as an old regret. You see why the line is long.
The pickle-master, offended, offers you a smaller thimbleful. You take it.

events.text: A clerk in the Archive of Receipts has fallen asleep on the desk, a stylus still in hand, snoring gently into a ledger. Nobody wakes the clerk, as it has been the same clerk for eight hundred years, and a nap seems fair. Someone drapes a coat over the shoulders.

effects.log: The clerk sighs and nestles in. The archive is a little warmer.

choices.text: Read the ledger the clerk was working on

effects.log: It is a list of every kindness the archive ever recorded. It is long.

events.text: A flute made of cloud-bamboo has been left on a bench in the grove, with a note: "Play me badly." You pick it up. It plays only the note you are thinking of, which is an uncomfortable discovery. You play for a short, honest while.

effects.log: The flute whistles back your own mood. The grove sways, politely.

choices.text: Leave it for the next person

effects.log: You set it on the bench. Someone else will find it.

events.text: Halfway up the Stair of Ten Thousand Steps, there is a landing with a bench, and the bench has an old immortal asleep on it, feet in the air. A sign says: "Do not wake. Step over." Dozens of climbers have. You step over, softly, and feel your own age.

effects.log: The stair resumes. The sleeper snores on.

choices.text: Sit on the other end of the bench

effects.log: You rest your feet beside the sleeper's. It is oddly companionable.

events.text: The night ferries cross between the isles with lanterns at the prow, little dots of gold strung across the sea. A ferryman waves as one passes. The passengers sing, badly, a song about missing the last boat. The whole cloud-sea hums.

effects.log: They wave back, and the song swells.

choices.text: Board the next one and sing along

effects.log: The song is bad and warm. You arrive late and happy.

events.text: A sky-whale calf has lost its mother and drifts along the underside of the Anchor Isle, bumping the roots. The isle-folk throw it fish, which is a poor idea, and cloud-bread, which is a good one. The calf nuzzles the isle with enormous tenderness.

effects.log: It opens a huge mouth and takes it. You feel like a god, briefly.
It stills, listening, then calls once, very small, and floats away toward a distant song.

events.text: Once a year the reef-crabs of the cloud-reefs march across a bridge in a long slow line, claws raised, to nobody knows where. The isle-folk close the bridge and put out lanterns to light the way. A small crab at the back stops and looks at you.

choices.text: Offer the small crab a crumb

effects.log: It takes the crumb, bows its claws, and joins the line.

choices.text: Hold the lantern for the stragglers

effects.log: The last crab passes at dawn. The line is gone.

events.text: The Meadow Isle holds a gentle hunt each spring: not to catch the dawn-deer but to follow them. Hundreds walk after the herd at first light, holding lanterns, saying nothing. The deer know and do not mind. By noon the walkers are lost, tired, and entirely happy.

effects.log: The deer let you walk among them. You come home with dew on your sleeves.

choices.text: Sit at the edge and watch them go

effects.log: It is just as good.

events.text: The shattered gate of the old Sky Citadel stands in the clouds, two pillars with nothing between them. Guides lead tourists through it and say: "The gate stood against ten thousand, and fell. Mind the step." A child asks: "Who won?" The guide has no answer.

effects.log: The guide shrugs. "No one," says the guide. "That is the lesson."
The air on the other side is a little colder.

events.text: Behind the kitchen of a small inn on the Quiet Isle is a well that returns your thoughts. Drop a pebble in, and you hear it fall, and then, softly, you hear what you were thinking when you dropped it. It is useful and discourteous.

effects.log: You were thinking of tea. The well agrees.
A sign goes up: "Think kindly."

events.text: Under a cloud-pine on the Ash Isle is a door the size of a child, overgrown with moss. A sign says nothing. A small bell is tied to the handle. You ring it, and a distant voice calls: "Not today, thank you, but how kind."

choices.text: Leave a gift at the door

effects.log: In the morning the gift is gone, and a leaf lies in its place.
"Still not today," says the voice, very warmly.

events.text: A great jade chime hangs from the tallest cloud-pine of the Old Isle, rung only by the wind. It was cast in the time before the isles drifted, and its note, they say, calls everything back. This evening it rings once, and the whole isle turns its head.

effects.log: It fills you like water fills a cup. You feel called, and not afraid.

choices.text: Note which way the wind came from

effects.log: It came from home. You decide that means something.

events.text: The Teahouse of Opening Petals serves a flower in a clear pot: it unfolds as the tea steeps, and the unfolding is the point. The server places the pot before you without a word. The flower rises, and you remember to breathe.

effects.log: It opens in ten minutes. You feel ten minutes older, and better.

choices.text: Ask the server what the flower is

effects.log: "A different one each time," says the server. "It is never the same."

events.text: Pilgrims carve letters in the face of the Cliff Isle: a name, a wish, a short poem. The oldest are a mile deep in moss. A guide tells you to add your own, in the lowest corner, where the carving is still soft. You carve one word.

effects.log: It will be a little blurred in a century. You are glad.
Most say "I was here". A few say "Why".

events.text: A small market sets up on the rim of a starfall crater once a month: lamp-sellers, fortune-tellers, a woman who sells only spoons. The crater is warm underfoot and the lamps never gutter. Everyone lingers longer than planned.

effects.log: It is a very good spoon. You use it for centuries.
The fortune says "More tea." You find this unfalsifiable.

events.text: It is the name-day of a neighbour on the next isle, and the whole fleet within a day's sail has sent a lantern. A thousand lanterns rise, tied together, in a long glowing string. The neighbour, on the quay, tries not to weep.

effects.log: Your light joins the string, one among a thousand.
The neighbour reads it aloud on the quay, in a shaky voice.

events.text: It rains all afternoon on the Quiet Isle, the soft sort that falls straight down. You sit at a window with a book you do not read and a cup you do not finish. At dusk you realise it has been, without any reason at all, a perfect day.

effects.log: The rain thins at dusk. You feel entirely well.
You write: "Rain. Nothing. Fine."

events.text: On the high peak of the Spire Isle, a small shrine is swept clean each dawn by someone who is never seen. A single flower stands in a cup of snow. You find a broom leaning on the wall, still damp. You sweep a little, then leave it as you found it.

effects.log: The steps shine. A flower appears beside the first.
The shrine accepts it. You walk down feeling accompanied.

events.text: The plaque on the quay of a small isle has weathered to a blank, and nobody remembers what the isle was called. {npc}, who has lived there longest, has always just said "here". The ferry steersmen are cross. "Cannot moor at Here," they grumble. {npc} asks if you will help find a name.
events.arc: The Isle That Lost Its Name

effects.log: You collect eleven names, each sworn certain, and no two alike. The quay is loud with it.

choices.text: Look in the Archive of Moorings

effects.log: You find a ledger with a blot where the name should be. Someone spilled tea three hundred years ago.
{npc} grins. "I rather like it," {he} says. The steersmen sigh.

events.text: The eleven names go to a vote on the quay. The winning name, Pearly, is disliked by half the isle. The ledger-blot, meanwhile, has a faint tea-ring that someone swears reads "Opal". A quarrel brews over breakfast, and {npc} stands between the camps with a ladle.
events.arc: The Isle That Lost Its Name

effects.log: "Opaly-Pearl". The quay groans, then laughs. It is a dreadful name and an agreement.
You back "Here". The quay sulks, then yields.

choices.text: Stay out of it and eat porridge

effects.log: The porridge is good. The quarrel eats itself.

events.text: The new plaque is carved and hung with ceremony. {npc} reads the name aloud and stops. "No," {he} says softly. "That is not it. I remember now." {He} tells you the real name, a small old word, and no one else is near enough to hear.
events.arc: The Isle That Lost Its Name

effects.log: You nod. The plaque keeps the vote; the name keeps the isle.

choices.text: Carve it small on the underside of the plaque

effects.log: No one sees it. {npc} does, and weeps, and thanks you.

events.text: The isle is moored, and ferries call, and the steersmen are content. {npc} still calls it "here". You do too, in the quiet, and the word has begun to sound like the best name for a place that ever was.
events.arc: The Isle That Lost Its Name

effects.log: {npc} answers "here" in turn. It is a very small ritual and a large one.

choices.text: Send a plaque of your own for the quay

effects.log: It says one word. It is hung.

events.text: The isle is Here, formally, by an act of the Ministry of Moorings. The steersmen grumble, then adapt. "Moor at Here" becomes a phrase for arriving anywhere that is good enough. {npc} is quietly famous.
events.arc: The Isle That Lost Its Name

effects.log: You raise your cup to Here. The quay raises its cups with you.
The ferry waves back.

events.text: The Jade Void Sect eats in silence. The refectory is vast and echoing, and the cook, {npc}, has been serving rice-cloud to a thousand disciples for four centuries without hearing a single word of thanks. "They are meditating," {he} says. "I suppose that includes the soup."
events.arc: The Cook of the Jade Void Refectory

choices.text: Say thanks aloud, in the silence

effects.log: The words ring in the hall. A hundred disciples look up. {npc} turns pink and drops a ladle.

choices.text: Leave a note of thanks on the tray

effects.log: {npc} finds it, reads it five times, and pins it above the stove.

choices.text: Eat in silence like the rest

effects.log: The soup is excellent. You say so, in your head.

events.text: The Sect Elder orders the refectory to be plain: no spice, no garnish, only grey rice. Discipline, says the order, is a bland dish. {npc} reads the notice and stares at the shelves of herbs, which have been tended for a hundred years.
events.arc: The Cook of the Jade Void Refectory

effects.log: You argue, quietly, that a spice is not a distraction but a prayer. The Elder, to everyone's surprise, allows one.

choices.text: Help {npc} hide the herbs in the rice

effects.log: The rice is grey, but tastes of dawn. Nobody says a word. Everyone has seconds.
The rice is grey. The disciples eat it, and are quiet in a different way.

events.text: A visiting master of the Nine Clouds Palace tastes the sect's grey rice and asks who cooked it. The refectory goes still. {npc} comes out of the kitchen, wiping hands. "I did," {he} says. The visitor bows to the cook, deeply, in front of a thousand disciples.
events.arc: The Cook of the Jade Void Refectory

effects.log: A single clap. Then a second. Then the hall. {npc} flees to the kitchen, mortified.
You bow back. The hall watches. {npc} stands very straight.

events.text: The Jade Void refectory still eats in silence, but now the silence has a flavour. Every disciple, at the end of the meal, bows to the kitchen door. {npc} stands behind it, listening, and has never been so happy.
events.arc: The Cook of the Jade Void Refectory

effects.log: Your bow joins theirs. The kitchen door is very still.

choices.text: Leave a flower on the sill

effects.log: It stays there, cheerful.

events.text: The herbs stay in the rice, secretly, for a century. Every disciple knows and no Elder asks. The refectory is the best-fed in the Heavens, and the cook has a very small, very satisfied smile that appears only when the rice is passed.
events.arc: The Cook of the Jade Void Refectory

choices.text: Pass the rice with a nod

effects.log: You nod. {npc} nods. A century of conspiracy.

choices.text: Add a herb of your own

effects.log: It is a small rebellion, and delicious.

events.text: At a stall on the Bridge Market, {npc} trims the beards of immortals who have not changed their style in two thousand years. Ministers, marshals, hermits, all sit on the same stool. They talk as the scissors snip, and {npc} says nothing, ever, to anyone. "I hear it all," {he} says, "and I keep it as a barber keeps hair. Swept up and gone."
events.arc: The Barber Who Heard Everything

effects.log: The scissors are quick and cool. {npc} asks nothing and, after a while, you tell {him} a good deal.

choices.text: Ask what the strangest thing {he} ever heard was

effects.log: {npc} chuckles. "A marshal confessed to a love of knitting. Then, the next day, an Elder did. They have never found out about each other."
They are old, silver, and sharp as dawn.

events.text: A Minister of the Jade Court sits in the stool and, in the course of a trim, lets slip a plan that will ruin a rival, a clerk with a family. {npc} clips on, steady. After the Minister leaves, {he} looks at you, pale. "I heard that," {he} says. "I wish I had not."
events.arc: The Barber Who Heard Everything

effects.log: It is a breach of the barber's code, and you both know it. {npc} thinks for a day. Then goes.
{npc} nods slowly. The plan goes ahead. The clerk is ruined. You carry it with you.
A cut hair left on the clerk's desk, with a single word: "Careful." It does the trick.

events.text: The clerk, warned, lays a trap of paper and the Minister walks into it. A scandal flares through the Jade Court. {npc} cuts hair as usual, and hums. A new customer says, dryly: "I hear the barber has a conscience." {npc} says: "Only on Tuesdays."
events.arc: The Barber Who Heard Everything

choices.text: Raise a cup at the stall

effects.log: {npc} accepts it. The customers around you grin and nod.

choices.text: Get a trim and keep quiet

effects.log: It is a good trim.

events.text: {npc} retires the stall and goes to live on a quiet isle, saying nothing about what {he} heard. The scissors are given to an apprentice, who snips, and listens, and says nothing as well. The tradition outlives every beard.
events.arc: The Barber Who Heard Everything

effects.log: You find {him} in the sun with a bowl of tea and no trimmings. "I have no secrets left," {he} says, delighted.

choices.text: Sit for a trim with the apprentice

effects.log: The apprentice is silent, and good.

events.text: Nine hundred years ago you borrowed an umbrella from a neighbour in a rainstorm, and never returned it. Today it falls out of a chest with a clatter. It is a cloud-paper umbrella, still sound. You remember the neighbour: {npc}, a kind woman... or was it a man... of the Reed Isle. {He} lent it with a grin.
events.arc: The Umbrella Borrowed Nine Centuries Ago

choices.text: Take it to the Reed Isle

effects.log: You sail over, a day's journey. The isle has changed. {npc} is not on the quay.
The sparrow returns a week later with no umbrella and no note. It looks smug.

choices.text: Put it back in the chest

effects.log: It will still be there tomorrow, and in nine centuries.

events.text: {npc} is found in a pavilion on the far side of the Reed Isle, a good deal older, with a tin of tea and a very long memory. {He} looks at the umbrella, then at you, then at the sky. "Late," {he} says. "But dry."
events.arc: The Umbrella Borrowed Nine Centuries Ago

effects.log: {npc} waves a hand. "I would have been more upset about the goat."

choices.text: Offer to pay the late fee

effects.log: You press stones into {his} palm. {npc} stares at them. "That was never the point," {he} says.

choices.text: Say it rained a lot that year

effects.log: {npc} laughs. "It did."

events.text: {npc} insists you keep the umbrella, in exchange for tea and company. You stay a week. The two of you speak of rain and neighbours and the people who lent things and never asked. At the end, {npc} says: "Come back in nine hundred years. Bring something to lend."
events.arc: The Umbrella Borrowed Nine Centuries Ago

effects.log: It is a long promise. You mean it.
You leave a small cloud-paper fan. It is the start of another long loan.

events.text: You return the umbrella ten times, to ten different neighbours, over the next few centuries. Each time it is lent right back. It becomes known, across the isles, as the Umbrella That Is Always Somewhere Else.
events.arc: The Umbrella Borrowed Nine Centuries Ago

effects.log: The stranger is bemused and grateful. The umbrella rides on.
It leaves your hand with a small, damp sigh.

events.text: {npc} comes to you in the dusk with a roll of old verses. "My master was the greatest poet of the Heavens," {he} says. "Nobody reads {him} now. I am the last student." The roll smells of old jasmine. {He} asks if you would read, and say honestly whether the verses are good.
events.arc: The Student Who Outlived the Fame of a Master

effects.log: They are strong and strange, and a little overwrought. You tell {him} so, kindly.
Your voice does them justice. {npc} listens with closed eyes.
{npc} smiles, and does not quite believe you.

events.text: {npc} proposes to publish a collected edition, with every cost met out of {his} own purse. The Ministry of Rites refuses a licence: the master was a "troubler of rank". The word has outlasted the man. {npc} sits in the antechamber, small and stiff.
events.arc: The Student Who Outlived the Fame of a Master

choices.text: Appeal to the Ministry in person

effects.log: You argue the verses are older than the grudge. The clerk, bored, grants a limited licence.
{npc} stares at you, then grins. A hundred copies, hand-sewn, by lamplight, in a cellar.
{npc} stirs a cup in a long silence.

events.text: The edition goes out, a small, odd volume, and a few readers find it, then more. A young poet writes to say the verses changed {his} life. {npc} reads the letter, and again, and goes out for a walk to be alone with it.
events.arc: The Student Who Outlived the Fame of a Master

effects.log: You walk in the cool of the evening. {npc} says, finally, "I thought no one would."

choices.text: Send the young poet a gift

effects.log: A good brush. It arrives with no name on it.

events.text: The verses live in cellars and back rooms for a hundred years, passed hand to hand. {npc} lives to hear them quoted in a teahouse by a stranger who does not know the author. {He} says nothing, and orders another cup.
events.arc: The Student Who Outlived the Fame of a Master

choices.text: Raise a cup to the master

effects.log: You and {npc} drink in the corner. Neither says a name.

choices.text: Quote a line back to the stranger

effects.log: The stranger lights up. A friendship begins.

events.text: At the Star Sea Pavilion, {npc} grinds lenses for the astronomers, from a glass said to be fallen starlight cooled. It takes a century to grind one. The astronomers want it done faster. "A lens is slow," {he} says. "A star is slower. Let them wait." {He} offers you a chance to look through the latest.
events.arc: The Lens-Grinder of the Star Sea Pavilion

effects.log: A star you had never noticed fills the circle, trembling, with a ring of colours around it. It is a held breath.
"By not hurrying," says {npc}. "And by listening for the sound the glass makes when it is done."
The queue of astronomers sighs as one.

events.text: An astronomer of the Pavilion, impatient, pressures {npc} for a faster lens and threatens a replacement. {npc} grinds on, calm. You overhear the threat and the reply: "If you want a bad lens, buy one. If you want to see, wait."
events.arc: The Lens-Grinder of the Star Sea Pavilion

effects.log: You say the best lens is the one finished last. The astronomer glares, then relents.

choices.text: Offer to polish by hand for a night

effects.log: You rub glass with cloth until dawn. The lens is a little brighter, and you are a little blind.
The astronomer storms off. The lens keeps grinding.

events.text: The lens is finished at last. {npc} sets it in a brass ring and holds it up to the night. It shows a new star, and a new star after it, and another. The astronomers sit in awed silence. {npc} lowers the lens and says: "That is what the century was for."
events.arc: The Lens-Grinder of the Star Sea Pavilion

effects.log: The sky is full of unnamed small lights, each hanging like a patient thought. You lose track of time.
{npc} accepts the cup, but looks only at the sky.

events.text: You polish lenses at the Pavilion on winter evenings, a quiet hobby with a long reach. The astronomers call your lenses "adequate". {npc} calls them "good". You value the second word more than a title.
events.arc: The Lens-Grinder of the Star Sea Pavilion

effects.log: You grind one lens slowly, as taught. It is, by a long chalk, adequate.
