choices.text: Give a lens to a student

effects.log: The student cries into it.

events.text: The Ladies of the Nine Clouds Palace change their robes nine times a day, one for each cloud, and {npc} sews every one. The robes must be perfect and cannot be seen to be made. "A good seamstress is a rumour," {he} says. "The ladies are never to be told how it is done."
events.arc: The Seamstress of the Nine Clouds Palace

choices.text: Admire a robe and ask nothing

effects.log: The robe is beyond praise. {npc} watches you and relaxes, a little.
You thread. {npc} lets you hold the cloth. It is lighter than breath.

choices.text: Compliment the Ladies on their robes

effects.log: The Ladies glow. {npc} bows toward you, very small.

events.text: A Lady discovers a loose thread on the ninth robe of the day and goes cold. The Lady demands to know who sewed it. The hall is silent. {npc} steps forward, white, and says, quietly: "I did." The Lady begins to rise.
events.arc: The Seamstress of the Nine Clouds Palace

effects.log: You say the thread was yours, a gift of clumsiness. The Lady looks at you with contempt, and lets it go. {npc} stares.
You say the robes of the palace are a marvel, and a thread is a sign of a hand. The Lady, unexpectedly, softens.
The Lady waves it off, unwilling to be seen to care. {npc} lives.

events.text: {npc} begins to sew a robe in secret, in off hours, for no one: a plain robe, plain thread, no decoration. It takes three years. When it is done, {he} folds it and sets it in your hands. "For the one who spoke," {he} says. "Wear it badly."
events.arc: The Seamstress of the Nine Clouds Palace

effects.log: It fits like air. Everyone who sees it looks twice and cannot say why.

choices.text: Keep it folded in a chest

effects.log: It sits there, a perfect secret.

events.text: {npc} gives notice and retires to a hut on a hill, where {he} sews only for children, and badly on purpose, with wonky seams. The children adore it. The Ladies hear and send a carriage, which returns empty.
events.arc: The Seamstress of the Nine Clouds Palace

effects.log: You find {him} with a lapful of wonky robes, happier than you have ever seen.
It is returned with an extra patch.

events.text: The Hall of Precedence never sleeps, and {npc} has the night shift. No ministers, no petitions: only the hum of the lamps and the slow rearrangement of the ranking-boards by invisible hands. "They shuffle themselves," {he} says. "Nobody knows why. I just watch." You have come to file a late form.
events.arc: The Night Clerk of the Hall of Precedence

choices.text: File it and sit a while

effects.log: The hall is hushed. The boards move, gently, like leaves.

choices.text: Ask what the boards are doing

effects.log: "Ranking the dead," says {npc}. "And the nearly dead. And the interesting alive."

choices.text: Hand the form over and go

effects.log: {npc} stamps it, sleepily.

events.text: One night you find a board with your own name on it, high up, in letters of pale gold. {npc} is nowhere. A note on the desk reads: "It moved at midnight. I did not touch it. Some mornings I think the hall has opinions."
events.arc: The Night Clerk of the Hall of Precedence

effects.log: It is a ranking you do not recognise: not of power, but of how often you have been kind. It is higher than expected.

choices.text: Move your name down a rank

effects.log: The board refuses. It moves back with a tiny, stern click.
The board watches you go.

events.text: {npc} is found asleep at the desk, a pen in hand, one night in the dark. The boards have stopped moving. The clerk has not woken. A Court physician says it is nothing but a long overdue rest. The boards are silent until dawn.
events.arc: The Night Clerk of the Hall of Precedence

effects.log: You watch the hall until dawn. The boards stay quiet, as if politely waiting.
{npc} sighs in sleep.

events.text: {npc} wakes and finds the hall unchanged, the boards still, the lamps lit. "You kept it," {he} says. "You are on the list for a night shift." The list is not a joke. A board now bears your name beside {his}.
events.arc: The Night Clerk of the Hall of Precedence

choices.text: Take the shift once a month

effects.log: It becomes a quiet duty. The boards seem content.
The clerk keeps a chair for you.

events.text: The cloud-ferry to the Orchard Isle charges two stones for sealed passengers and four for rogues. The boatman, {npc}, collects at the plank. "Four," {he} says, without looking up. "Rogue fare. Do not blame me. The company sets the rate."
events.arc: The Ferry That Charged Rogues Double

choices.text: Pay four stones (4 Low-Grade Spirit Stones)

effects.log: You pay. {npc} gives a small nod, which could be shame.
{npc} grips the rail. "I am not the company," {he} says. You see that is true.
It takes a day and costs nothing. The view is good.

events.text: A sealed passenger sneers at the rogue fare as you board, loudly. The boat tilts with the weight of it. {npc} looks at the passenger, then at you, and says nothing. The ferry sets off through a silence like a blow.
events.arc: The Ferry That Charged Rogues Double

effects.log: You look at the clouds. The sneer dies of lack of attention.

choices.text: Ask the passenger a polite question

effects.log: The passenger is embarrassed into silence, and then, to your surprise, answers. A conversation of sorts begins.
The wind takes the sneer.

events.text: {npc} slips you a pair of tokens on the quay, small and plain. "A boatman's tokens," {he} says. "Two free passages. I give them to those I like. The company does not count them." It is quiet defiance in a pocket.
events.arc: The Ferry That Charged Rogues Double

effects.log: You nod. {npc} turns to the next fare.
You pass them on to a thin traveller with a heavy pack. {npc} sees and does not mind.

events.text: The ferry company changes the fare, in time, to a flat three for all. {npc} sends no note. But the next time you board, the boatman hands you a free cup of tea, with a nod that is half a smile. The planks are warm underfoot.
events.arc: The Ferry That Charged Rogues Double

choices.text: Raise the cup to the boatman

effects.log: The tea is hot and plain. The ride is short and good.

choices.text: Ride the ferry to the end of the line

effects.log: You do. It is a long way and a kind one.

events.text: The fare stays two and four for centuries. You take the cloud-path, and your legs grow strong, and the ferry-folk call you "the walker". The boatman, passing, always raises a hand. It is something. It is enough.
events.arc: The Ferry That Charged Rogues Double

effects.log: You do, every time.
The path whistles back.

events.text: {npc} keeps a shelf of jars, each holding rain from a different day: the rain of a wedding, the rain of a quarrel, the rain on the day the Marsh Isle floated free. "When I open a jar," {he} says, "it rains in the room, exactly as it did." {He} lifts a small jar toward you, shyly.
events.arc: The Collector of Remembered Rain

effects.log: A fine grey rain falls, in your hall. You smell a street you have never walked, and miss it.

choices.text: Ask which day it is from

effects.log: "The day I arrived above," says {npc}. "I never told anyone how it felt."
It is cold and weighty. The weight is an hour of someone else's grief.

events.text: A drought has gripped the Dry Isle for a century. The clouds will not come. The folk are parched and afraid. {npc} considers the shelf of jars. "A remembered rain is a fine rain," {he} says. "But it ends. These are the only rains I have."
events.arc: The Collector of Remembered Rain

effects.log: Two hundred jars go to the Dry Isle on a skiff. The isle drinks, and the rain falls in memory.
{npc} gives most and keeps the jar of arrival. The isle is saved and the shelf is a quiet place.

events.text: The Dry Isle sends a letter of thanks, with a small cloud-pine seedling in a pot. "It grew in your rain," the letter reads. {npc} plants it beside the shelf and waters it with the jar of arrival, once, with trembling hands.
events.arc: The Collector of Remembered Rain

effects.log: You kneel in the damp earth. The rain falls, soft and ancient.
The seedling takes the rain like a first breath.

events.text: {npc} now collects new rains, and labels them for the future: "the first day of spring", "the day a friend came". The shelf grows. You are given a jar on your own anniversary, labelled in a firm small hand.
events.arc: The Collector of Remembered Rain

effects.log: A gentle rain falls in your hall, warm and bright. You laugh without knowing why.

choices.text: Keep it for a hard year

effects.log: It will be there when needed.

events.text: A sky whale has drifted toward the Windward Isle, on a course that will crush the docks and the market. The elders argue. A few young hunters want to drive it off with spears of lightning. {npc}, the old whale-warden, holds up a hand. "It is a mother," {he} says. "The beast is lost. We turn it."
events.arc: The Whale That Had to Be Turned

effects.log: The elders hush. The hunters mutter. {npc} breathes out, shaking.
"With song," says {npc}. "And lanterns. And patience, which you may not have."
The whale draws nearer. The market empties.

events.text: The folk gather on the Windward quays with lanterns and drums, and sing the old turning-song, low and slow. The whale pauses. A great eye opens, ancient and tired. {npc} stands at the front, singing, barely audible. {He} looks at you, urgent.
events.arc: The Whale That Had to Be Turned

choices.text: Add your voice to the song

effects.log: Your voice joins a hundred. The whale tilts, ever so slightly, toward the open sky.

choices.text: Light a lantern line along the edge

effects.log: Lanterns glow in a long curve, a guiding river. The whale follows its light.
The beat is slow. The whale likes it.

events.text: The whale turns. It takes an hour. The huge flank slides past the docks with a creak like a mountain's sigh, and drifts away into the deep clouds. The folk fall silent, then weep. {npc} sits down on the quay and cannot rise.
events.arc: The Whale That Had to Be Turned

effects.log: You take an arm. {npc} leans on you all the way home.

choices.text: Sit beside {him} until the stars come out

effects.log: The two of you watch the dark clouds. One star blinks, and then another.

events.text: The whale returns once a century, to the same waters, and the Windward Isle holds a feast. The turning-song is sung by children now. {npc} dies content, and the whale passes the quay slowly, on the day of the funeral, one great eye turned toward the shore.
events.arc: The Whale That Had to Be Turned

choices.text: Sing the turning-song at the quay

effects.log: Your voice carries. The whale answers, low and long.

choices.text: Leave a lantern on the water

effects.log: It floats a while beside the great shadow.

events.text: On the Cold Reef, kites are flown in duels: lines crossed, threads cut, the loser's kite carried off by the wind. {npc} is the undefeated champion of three centuries. {He} challenges anyone who passes. Today {his} eye falls on you. "Well?" {he} says. "Fly something."
events.arc: The Kite Duelist of the Cold Reef

effects.log: You borrow a kite. It is a feather. {npc} grins, nasty with joy.
You watch {npc} cut a challenger in nine breaths. It is a thing of beauty.
{npc} snorts. "Everyone is only passing."

events.text: You lose in five breaths. The kite spins away. {npc} winds in, almost kind. "You fly too carefully," {he} says. "A kite is not a thing to keep safe. It is a thing to send." The words have an edge you cannot name.
events.arc: The Kite Duelist of the Cold Reef

effects.log: {npc} shows you how to let a kite go. It is harder than keeping it.
{npc} writes it on a sleeve, like a promise.

events.text: A year later you return. You have practised in the quiet of the evenings with a kite, a line, and a patch of wind. {npc} greets you with a nod. "Ready?" Two kites rise. This time they both stay up.
events.arc: The Kite Duelist of the Cold Reef

ok.log: Your line crosses, rasps and holds. The champion's kite spins and falls. {npc} salutes you, breathless.

fail.log: Your thread parts, and the kite sails off. {npc} claps you on the shoulder: "Better."

effects.log: You tie the kites together. {npc} laughs. The two fly as one.

events.text: After the duel, {npc} gives you a kite of {his} own making, plain and fast, with a line that sings. "For the next time," {he} says. You hang it in your hall and look at it often. Some mornings you fly it.
events.arc: The Kite Duelist of the Cold Reef

choices.text: Fly it from the reef each spring

effects.log: It becomes an annual duel, and a friendship.
It watches the room.

events.text: {npc} retires the champion's title and hands the line to a child. The child cuts three kites the first week and weeps with delight. {npc} stands behind the child, hands folded. "Let it go," {he} murmurs. "Let it go."
events.arc: The Kite Duelist of the Cold Reef

effects.log: The child's kite rises in the wind. The two of you say nothing.
The child grins and flies on.

events.text: At the foot of the Stair of Ten Thousand Steps, {npc} sits panting, a mortal in a dust-grey coat, who has climbed from the world below by a route no one thought existed. {He} holds a small bundle. "I have come to deliver a letter," {he} says. "And to ask a question. Which of you is the first I should ask?"
events.arc: The Pilgrim Who Climbed from Below

effects.log: {npc} straightens, eyes red. "Does my mother live up here?" {He} gives a name.

choices.text: Offer the pilgrim water and rest

effects.log: {npc} drinks. The hands shake. A small, sweet gratitude hangs in the air.

choices.text: Send for the Ministry of Arrivals

effects.log: The clerk comes with a form. {npc} stares at it, bewildered.

events.text: You search the ledgers of the Heavens for the name. Many days. An old clerk in the Archive of Arrivals finds it at last: the mother ascended three hundred years ago, took a new name, and lives on a quiet isle at the end of the fleet. You go to tell {npc}.
events.arc: The Pilgrim Who Climbed from Below

effects.log: {npc} listens, motionless. Then asks: "Will the old one know me?"
You and {npc} set out by skiff, a long quiet voyage. {He} says almost nothing.

events.text: The mother stands on the quay with arms crossed, older than the grandmother of the grandmother of anyone. {npc} steps off the skiff, bundle in hand. For a long time neither of them speaks. Then the mother says: "You climbed."
events.arc: The Pilgrim Who Climbed from Below

effects.log: You turn the skiff and wait out of sight. When you return, they are drinking tea on the quay.
You wait a long time. It is the right length.

events.text: {npc} stays above and takes up work in the kitchens of the quiet isle. The Ministry of Arrivals sniffs, and issues a certificate to the effect that a mortal cannot climb. The certificate is pinned in the kitchen, upside down.
events.arc: The Pilgrim Who Climbed from Below

effects.log: The soup is excellent. {npc} laughs more than you have ever heard.
It is the proudest wrong thing in the Heavens.

events.text: The sect you founded has three members, counting you, and its hall is a shed on the edge of a small isle. {npc}, the newest, is the best cook of the three. {He} has already redecorated the shed twice and started a vegetable patch. "A sect," {he} says, "is a household with a banner."
events.arc: The Sect of Three

effects.log: The shed becomes a home. The banner is a tea-towel.
You set a roster of dawn rites. {npc} complies, with a long-suffering look.
The beans come up crooked.

events.text: A grand sect sends a letter offering to absorb yours: "Three members is a hobby, not a sect." {npc} reads it aloud in a silly voice. The other member of the three rolls on the floor laughing. You are not sure whether to be hurt.
events.arc: The Sect of Three

choices.text: Reply with polite thanks and no

effects.log: The reply is a single line. The grand sect sends a pot of jam, to your surprise.
You think for a week. {npc} says nothing. You decline anyway.
It hangs by the door, a reminder.

events.text: {npc} turns out to be the sect's secret: the cook has a gift for arrays, and the vegetable patch is an unnoticed formation of great subtlety. The beans, the herbs, the rows: all tuned to the isle. The sect is, without announcement, quite formidable.
events.arc: The Sect of Three

effects.log: You and {npc} grin over supper. A sect of three with a secret is better than a sect of a thousand.

choices.text: Share the patch with the isle

effects.log: The isle comes to see. The patch is praised, and copied, and the neighbours have better beans.

events.text: The sect grows to seven, then twelve, but the shed remains. New members sleep in rows, and {npc} cooks for all, and the banner is still a tea-towel. At the yearly feast, someone proposes a proper hall. The vote is unanimous against.
events.arc: The Sect of Three

choices.text: Raise a cup to the shed

effects.log: It stands, creaking, in the sun.
It leaks a little less.

events.text: The sect is famous for its beans. Visitors come from three isles. {npc} sells a small pot of seed with a label: "Planted crooked, grown fine." The sect, which has only ever wanted a household, has become a small harvest of its own.
events.arc: The Sect of Three

effects.log: Your name is in the corner. {npc} sells it to the Ministry of Plants.

choices.text: Eat beans at the long table

effects.log: It is a perfect supper.

events.text: Every midnight, a bell tolls once on the Lantern Isle, and has done for a thousand years. {npc}, the ringer, does it by hand, from a rope that hangs through a hole in the floor of a tower no taller than a pine. "It is for the lost," {he} says. "Anyone out at that hour, anywhere. One note. They know where home is."
events.arc: The Midnight Bell of the Lantern Isle

choices.text: Stay up to hear it ring

effects.log: The note is round and warm. You feel a hand at your back, a long way off.

choices.text: Offer to ring it one night

effects.log: {npc} hesitates, then hands you the rope. The weight of it is quiet, enormous.
The bell rings across the water.

events.text: A storm cuts the rope one midnight, and the bell cannot be rung. {npc} stands under the dark tower with the frayed end in hand, rigid. "There is a skiff out," {he} says. "I can hear nothing. They will be lost."
events.arc: The Midnight Bell of the Lantern Isle

choices.text: Fly out with a lantern to guide the skiff

effects.log: You find the skiff in the fog, a family aboard, silent. You lead them in on the beam.

choices.text: Ring the bell with your hands

effects.log: You climb the tower and strike it. The note is wild and rough. The skiff turns toward it.

events.text: The skiff arrives, and the family clings to the quay. {npc} wraps them in blankets. A child asks who rang the bell. {npc} nods toward you. The child stares. Then the child bows, solemnly, as to a god.
events.arc: The Midnight Bell of the Lantern Isle

effects.log: The child giggles. The quay is warm.

choices.text: Return the child to the family

effects.log: The family is grateful beyond words.

events.text: The bell has a new rope, braided by the whole isle, strand by strand. It is thicker than the old and uglier, and rings the same. {npc} lets you ring it on the night of its renewal. The note goes out like a quiet hand.
events.arc: The Midnight Bell of the Lantern Isle

choices.text: Ring it and keep the rope

effects.log: You hold the rope a long moment. It sways.

choices.text: Add a strand of your own

effects.log: The rope has a little more of you in it.

events.text: A lamb of cloud, no bigger than a cushion, has wandered into the garden of the Meadow Isle, crying thinly. Cloud-lambs belong to flocks that graze the high pastures. This one has no flock. {npc}, the herd-keeper, kneels beside it. "Lost. Or left," {he} says. "It happens."
events.arc: The Orphan Cloud-Lamb

effects.log: It curls in your lap, soft as breath. It does not stop trembling for an hour.
You walk the pasture edges with a lantern, calling. Nothing answers.
It follows you to the gate and stops, small and sad.

events.text: The lamb thrives. It follows you through the market, stopping at stalls, sleeping on bolts of silk. The vendors adore it and charge you a little more. {npc} watches fondly and warns: "A cloud-lamb grows. They are not lap animals for long."
events.arc: The Orphan Cloud-Lamb

choices.text: Build a pen on the hill

effects.log: You and {npc} nail boards in a sunny spot. The lamb inspects and approves.

choices.text: Keep it in the house regardless

effects.log: The lamb eats a curtain. Then another.

events.text: One autumn dawn the lamb stands at the pen's edge, ears forward. On the far hill, a flock moves, grey as smoke. The lamb bleats once. {npc} puts a hand on your shoulder: "It knows," {he} says. "It has always known."
events.arc: The Orphan Cloud-Lamb

effects.log: The lamb trots out, looks back once, and runs. The flock opens to take it.

choices.text: Carry it to the flock yourself

effects.log: You walk the hill together. The flock lets the lamb in with a shy ripple.

events.text: Every autumn, the flock grazes on the hill. A lamb, grown, always stands apart at the edge, facing the pen. You leave a bundle of clover at the gate. It is gone by morning. {npc} says, softly: "That one remembers."
events.arc: The Orphan Cloud-Lamb

effects.log: The lamb comes to the fence for it. A small, steady bond.
The flock wanders on, quiet.

events.text: The great thaw comes: the high clouds, frozen for a season into hard pale plains, begin to crack and flow. The isles tilt on the shifting surface. Children skate between the pieces. A grandfather gives a warning, then a push.

effects.log: You skate. A crack opens behind you. You laugh, and keep going.

choices.text: Watch from the edge with a cup

effects.log: The thaw is a slow spectacle. The cup is hot.

events.text: The Isle of Hush sits in the eye of a permanent storm and has never known wind. The inhabitants are famous for their calm, their staring, and their remarkable hats. A visitor tries to hurry them, and they look at the visitor with mild pity.

choices.text: Slow down and stay a day

effects.log: You lose your hurry somewhere between breakfast and lunch.
They are made of wind-felt, an unusual thing. You buy none.

events.text: A courier of the high winds flies past with a bundle of letters, calling the isles by name. "Marsh! Pearl! Quill!" It slows near you and tosses one down. The envelope is blank, and warm, and the courier is gone before you can ask.

effects.log: It is a single dried petal. You do not know from whom.
It hangs there, as an unanswered question.

events.text: At the cloud market a stall sells shadows. "Ten for a stone," says the vendor, "cut to your size." You see a shadow that is exactly yours, a little taller, cut in a gentler light. You wonder who is wearing the other one.

choices.text: Buy the taller shadow (1 Low-Grade Spirit Stone)

effects.log: It follows you for a week, then slips off, cheerful.
The vendor shrugs: "Someone who stopped needing one."

events.text: A noodle-puller on the Steaming Isle pulls a single noodle the length of the quay, thinner than a thread, without breaking. Crowds gather to count the loops. At the end the puller bows and drops it in a pot, as if it were nothing.

effects.log: You lose count at three hundred. The puller winks.
The noodle is chewy, endless and delicate.

events.text: The Archive keeps a Lost-and-Found for jade slips: those left on benches, those left in teapots. Most are mundane: a shopping list, a half-written love poem. One says only, in a firm hand: "Remember to forgive." Nobody has claimed it in four hundred years.

effects.log: The clerk hands it over without a word. It sits in your sleeve like a kind weight.

choices.text: Leave it for someone who needs it

effects.log: The clerk sets it back on the shelf with great care.

events.text: On the night the moon is full, the surface of the Silver Lake becomes so still that you can walk across it, if you are quiet. A dozen people stroll its length with soft steps, lanterns bobbing. At the middle, nobody talks. The moon beneath your feet is intact.

effects.log: The moon looks up at you. You step off carefully, humbled.

choices.text: Stay on the shore and watch

effects.log: The walkers are silver shapes. It is a lovely thing to see.

events.text: A rain-house stands in the cloud-bamboo, a small hut with a roof made of listening-shells. On a rainy day it plays the rain back in lovely patterns: drip on drip. People sit inside with no tea at all, hearing the rain become a tune.

effects.log: The rain tunes itself. You wake at dusk with the melody in your head.

choices.text: Add a tap of your own

effects.log: Your tap joins the pattern. The shells approve.

events.text: A step on the Stair of Ten Thousand Steps has crumbled overnight. A crew of masons swarms the gap, and a long queue forms on both sides. A philosopher in the queue mutters that the stair is a metaphor. A mason replies that it is also a stair.

choices.text: Help the masons haul a block

effects.log: The block slides into place. The queue cheers.
You debate the stair. It is a metaphor. It is also a stair.

events.text: At the Glowworm Hour on the Marsh Isle, the lights go out and the worms come up from the reeds in clouds, blue-green and cool. The isle-folk turn their faces upward and say nothing. A child sings softly, and the worms hum back.

effects.log: The light is on your sleeves, your hands, your hair. You feel briefly like a spring.
The worms hum back. It is a good duet.

events.text: A ferry-whale carries passengers from isle to isle, on a back wide as a field. A small crowd rides, chatting, as the great beast drifts. A child asks the ferry-keeper if the whale ever minds. The keeper says: "Only when we sing off-key."

effects.log: The ride is slow and glorious. You nap on a warm back.
The whale hums approval.

events.text: A reef-crab leaves a gift on your doorstep each full moon: a small shell, a pebble, a single polished button. You have never seen the crab. You begin to leave a gift in return, a bit of cheese, a thimble. The exchange has run for a decade.

effects.log: The gifts grow stranger and kinder.

choices.text: Wait up to see the crab

effects.log: You see only a claw waving from the dark.

events.text: A kite has escaped from the Leeward Isle, and the Heron Isle hunts for it with nets and good cheer. It flits between the clouds, always just out of reach, to the delight of the children. At last it lands on your head.

effects.log: The owner is a small child, who hugs the kite and then you.
The kite carries you upward, a breath. Then you give it back.

events.text: In a crack of the Ash Isle ruins, you find a scrap of banner from the war of the immortals, bleached to white. A scholar tells you the colours have run out of it, but the weave is still a tell. You hold it, and something in your hand remembers a larger grip.

effects.log: The clerks admire it, and put it in a drawer.
It flutters faintly as you go.

events.text: Deep in a sealed grotto, you find a small cell with a straw mat and a clay cup. A note: "I never came out. The tea is still warm." The cup, to your slow horror, is. You leave it, and the mat, and back out softly.

choices.text: Say a quiet word to the cell

effects.log: You say thank you. It does not answer.
It is an ordinary cup, kept warm by something patient.

events.text: Behind a boulder on the Reed Isle, there is a garden on no map: a mossy square with a bench and a single pear tree. Someone has swept the path. You sit, and the pear drops a fruit into your lap, politely.

effects.log: It is perfect. You say so aloud, to the garden.
You sweep a few strokes. The garden seems pleased.

events.text: A very old immortal on the Moon Isle hums a tune. A passer-by stops: they have heard it. A second stops. A third. The tune is older than any of them, and they learned it, separately, from nobody. They sing it together, and find the verses match.

effects.log: The verses come out of you like water. You have no idea where you learned them.

choices.text: Ask the old immortal where it comes from

effects.log: "From before," says the old one, and stops humming.

events.text: A wedding is held on the Blossom Isle among a thousand cloud-peach trees in flower. The couple, three hundred years courting, finally agreed. The guests throw petals, and the petals rise instead of fall, and the couple walk out through a rising pink cloud.

effects.log: They drift upward and become part of the sky.
They wave. The petals stay in your hair for days.

events.text: There is a tiny tea-stall on a ledge halfway down the Cliff Isle. The only way to it is a rope. The proprietor, an ancient immortal, says the tea is no better than elsewhere, but the view is. A queue of nervous people hangs on the rope, breathing carefully.

effects.log: The tea is middling. The view is the whole sky.

choices.text: Look over the edge and decide against

effects.log: Wisdom has a flavour too.

events.text: Around the rim of an old starfall crater, the pear trees bear fruit that glows faintly at night. Orchardists harvest by lantern. They say the fruit tastes of the star that fell. You taste: it is sweet, cold, and slightly astonished.

effects.log: Your hands glow faintly for an hour.
The orchardists give you a basket and a song.

events.text: A neighbour is moving: the entire isle, in fact, to a new reef. The fleet gathers on the quays with ropes, towing the drifting home along. Everyone helps out of old friendship. At dusk the isle settles into its new berth like a cat on a cushion.

effects.log: The rope bites your palms. The isle slides into place.
The tea goes round. Nobody has ever been so grateful.

events.text: On the first morning of the year, a single flake of upward snow rises past your window. You watch it all the way up, and it takes a long time, and the world seems to be starting very gently.

choices.text: Make a wish on the flake

effects.log: It is a small, honest wish, for ordinary happiness.
The flake is lost against the sky.

events.text: A Minister of the Jade Court dozes in the middle of a long speech about precedence. The room goes still. A clerk carefully slides a cushion under the Minister's head. The speech, resumed in dream, makes more sense than the awake version.

choices.text: Take notes on the dream speech

effects.log: It is surprisingly lucid, and about bees.
The Minister sleeps on. The clerk gives you a grateful nod.

events.text: It is the birthday of the isle itself, one thousand and three, and the folk bake a cake the size of a boat. Everyone gets a slice, with a candle made of a small star. The oldest resident blows them out and is asked to make a wish for the isle. The wish is a quiet one.

effects.log: It is as sweet as a decade.
Your candle burns an hour longer than the rest.

events.text: A tribulation cloud has been drifting over the Quill Isle for three weeks, dark and grumbling, and has struck nobody. The isle-folk hang out their washing and ignore it. {npc}, the isle's weather-watcher, says the cloud is shy. "It was sent for a hermit who moved house. It has no one to strike, and too much pride to go home."
events.arc: The Tribulation Cloud That Would Not Strike

effects.log: You point out a retired hermit on the east quay. The cloud rumbles hopefully, and the hermit goes pale.
You tell the cloud about your week. It rumbles, then rains a little, politely.
The cloud sulks above the sheets. They dry, regardless.

events.text: The hermit, once found, refuses with great dignity. "I passed that tribulation three hundred years ago," the hermit would say, if not talking to a cloud. The cloud swells, offended. {npc} brings umbrellas and a stern look.
events.arc: The Tribulation Cloud That Would Not Strike

choices.text: Argue the hermit's case to the cloud

effects.log: You explain the paperwork. The cloud listens, in its way, and thunders once, a long low note.

choices.text: Hold an umbrella over the hermit

effects.log: The hermit takes it without thanks and with enormous relief.

events.text: The cloud has begun to follow you about the isle at a respectful height, like a large dog that has chosen. It does not strike. Children are no longer afraid of it. {npc} laughs: "It has decided you are the tribulation."
events.arc: The Tribulation Cloud That Would Not Strike

effects.log: You stand on the quay and nod. The cloud lets down a single, enormous, warm drop on your head.

choices.text: Walk it to the Ministry of Weather

effects.log: A clerk files it as "unattached, harmless". It is given a number and a corner of the sky.
It drifts away, rumbling. You feel oddly bereft.

events.text: The cloud returns each spring and hovers over the Quill Isle for a week, rumbling, and never strikes. The isle has made it a holiday. They call it the Courtesy of Clouds. {npc} sets out a chair for it, which it does not use.
events.arc: The Tribulation Cloud That Would Not Strike

choices.text: Bring a chair of your own

effects.log: You and the cloud keep each other company for a week.
It rumbles, a little shyly.

events.text: The cloud is entered in the Ministry's ledger and given a patch of sky to guard over the lanes. It grows busy and proud, and drops its shyness along with its rain. Once a year it passes the Quill Isle and rumbles a greeting, nothing more.
events.arc: The Tribulation Cloud That Would Not Strike

effects.log: You hum a long note. The cloud answers from far above.
It is good to see a thing settled.

events.text: On the Hightop Isle there is a terrace built for watching tribulations from a safe distance, with cushions, tea and a man who sells roasted chestnuts. {npc} runs it. "Ten stones for a good seat," {he} says. "A thousand years of lightning, and not a single complaint."
events.arc: The Terrace for Watching Other People's Tribulations

effects.log: A tribulation rolls past on the far horizon, small and fierce. The terrace applauds politely.
{npc} lets you carry the tray. The crowd is generous and lightning-struck, by turns.
They are embroidered with tiny storms.

events.text: A tribulation draws near, a big one, and the terrace falls quiet. Someone on the cloud-reef below is going through it, alone. {npc} lowers the tea tray. "We watch," {he} says, "but we do not clap when it is one of us."
events.arc: The Terrace for Watching Other People's Tribulations

choices.text: Stand and bow toward the reef

effects.log: The whole terrace stands with you. The lightning ends. A figure on the reef bows back, tiny against the dark.

choices.text: Send a skiff with towels and soup

effects.log: A skiff is sent with towels and soup. It arrives in time for the soup.
Silence is a sort of respect.

events.text: The one who passed the tribulation turns out to be a young potter, singed and radiant. The terrace gives {him} a cushion and a tea. {npc} says it is the first time in forty years that anyone has come up to the terrace afterward to say thank you.
events.arc: The Terrace for Watching Other People's Tribulations

choices.text: Raise a cup to the potter

effects.log: The terrace raises forty cups. The potter cries into the tea.
You say nothing. It is exactly right.

events.text: The soup arrives at the reef at the very moment the lightning ends. The potter gulps it and is revived. Afterward a pottery arrives at your door: one small cup, glazed with a storm. It is the best cup you own.
events.arc: The Terrace for Watching Other People's Tribulations

effects.log: The tea tastes faintly of ozone and kindness.
It catches the morning like a held breath.

events.text: At the centre of the great storm that circles the Western Reach there is a calm, and in the calm a small isle with a lamp. {npc} keeps the lamp. "Skiffs that lose the wind come to my light," {he} says. "In sixty years, three hundred and twelve have arrived, and each one thought it was dying."
events.arc: The Keeper of the Storm-Eye Light

choices.text: Sail in with a skiff of supplies

effects.log: The storm walls rise like a cathedral. You break through to still air and gold light. {npc} waves a spoon.
"It gets into your bones," {npc} says. "You begin to hear the storm's breathing."

choices.text: Admire the lamp from a distance

effects.log: It is a small flame for so large a duty.

events.text: A skiff limps in at midnight with a family aboard: a grandmother, two children and a cat. They are lost, and tired, and cross with each other. {npc} serves broth. The youngest asks if the storm will ever end. {npc} looks at you. "Tell them," {he} says.
events.arc: The Keeper of the Storm-Eye Light

choices.text: Tell them about the calm that returns

effects.log: You describe the storm's long habit of turning. The child nods and falls asleep on the cat.

choices.text: Offer to lead them out at dawn

effects.log: You promise it. {npc} nods slowly. It will not be easy.
It is hot and unfussy.

events.text: At dawn the storm leans in. You take the family's tiller and thread the wall by sound, the way {npc} taught you, listening for the thin place in the wind. The skiff shudders, groans, and breaks into a bright morning on the other side. The grandmother laughs aloud.
events.arc: The Keeper of the Storm-Eye Light

choices.text: Steer by ear through the wall

ok.log: You hear the thin place and take it. The skiff pops out dry as a loaf.

fail.log: You hear too many thin places. The skiff comes out the far side soaked and sound.

effects.log: A flash of the lamp, three short, one long. The skiff follows it home.

events.text: {npc} retires from the lamp at last and asks you to take it for a season. The lamp is simple: oil, wick, a bell. The work is hours of nothing and a few minutes of everything. You find the nothing is not empty. The storm breathes in the dark around you.
events.arc: The Keeper of the Storm-Eye Light

effects.log: You keep it for twenty years. A skiff arrives every few weeks. Each one thinks it is dying.

choices.text: Hand it to the next keeper

effects.log: A young person comes by skiff, shy and bright. The lamp does not seem to mind.

events.text: A petition to the Ministry of Moorings passes, by rule, across nine desks, each in a different hall, each manned by a clerk with a different stamp. {npc} has a petition about a leaking quay and has been at the first desk for eleven years. "The clerk is not rude," {he} says. "The clerk is only slow."
events.arc: The Petition That Must Cross Nine Desks

effects.log: You carry it to the second desk. The clerk there is slower, and kinder, and stamps it in green.

choices.text: Study the order of the desks

effects.log: There is a rule about the order, and a rule about the rule. You find the shortcut in a footnote.
Tea moves a petition an inch. It is something.

events.text: The fifth desk is manned by a clerk who has not looked up in a century. {npc} says the stamp is in a locked drawer, and the key is in the sixth desk, which cannot be reached until the fifth stamps. The petition rests on the desk like a small, patient bird.
events.arc: The Petition That Must Cross Nine Desks

effects.log: Under a rule from the Third Age, a petition may skip one desk if signed by a living witness. You sign. The clerk finally looks up.

choices.text: Wake the clerk with a bell

effects.log: The clerk jumps, apologises, stamps, and goes back to sleep. {npc} gapes.
You wait six days. It stamps itself, somehow, in the dark.

events.text: The petition reaches the ninth desk, and the ninth clerk reads the word "quay", and the word "leaking", and says: "Oh, we mended that years ago. Did no one tell you?" {npc} sits down on the floor of the hall and starts to laugh, and laughs for a long time.
events.arc: The Petition That Must Cross Nine Desks

effects.log: You laugh till the hall echoes. The clerks look up from their desks, and some of them smile.

choices.text: Ask the clerk for the receipt

effects.log: It is stamped nine times. It is a work of art.

events.text: The quay was mended years ago. A different petition, begun at the same desk a year later, has also reached the ninth clerk. It asks about a quay that was never leaking. {npc} frames both receipts. The clerks bow when {he} passes.
events.arc: The Petition That Must Cross Nine Desks

effects.log: They hang in the Archive, a joke that has the weight of a century.
You eat in the market and laugh at the long way round.

events.text: A rogue with no faction cannot file a petition at the Ministry of Prayers without a sponsor, a person of standing who signs for them. {npc}, a rogue of your own acquaintance, needs a hearing about a lost lantern-boat and has been turned away at the door eleven times. The doorman is not rude, only bored.
events.arc: The Petition That Needed a Sponsor

effects.log: The doorman looks at your plain sleeves and sighs. "Rogue for a rogue," the doorman says. "Wait there."
You spend a day in teahouses, asking. A retired marshal says yes, for a stone.
You argue; the doorman nods; nothing moves.

events.text: The clerk takes the petition with two fingers, as if it were damp. A rogue's petition is read last, after the day's Court business. By dusk the hall is empty but for {npc}, you, and a cleaner who sweeps around your feet. A clerk reads the first line aloud, slowly, with no tone.
events.arc: The Petition That Needed a Sponsor

effects.log: You speak plainly, without bowing. The clerk listens despite the hour.

choices.text: Hand over a small gift of tea

effects.log: The clerk looks at the tea, then at the clock, and reads on a little faster.
The cleaner offers you a rag. You decline.

events.text: The lantern-boat is found, rusted and half-sunk, in the Reed Isle shallows. The Ministry sends a form: "Matter closed." {npc} reads it twice and takes you to a teahouse for a drink. "They looked," {he} says. "For a rogue, that is rare."
events.arc: The Petition That Needed a Sponsor

effects.log: You raise your tea to a form that said what it said. {npc} cries a little, a good cry.
You and {npc} tow it back. It floats, which is more than anyone expected.

events.text: The retired marshal signs for a stone and a bow. The petition is read, in a slow bored voice, and filed. Nothing is found, nothing is lost. {npc} thanks you, and the marshal, and the doorman. The doorman, to everyone's surprise, nods back.
events.arc: The Petition That Needed a Sponsor

effects.log: The petition is in a drawer, and the drawer is in the Ministry. That is more than a rogue usually gets.
The marshal accepts, and tells a good story.

events.text: You have no isle. A rogue drifts, and sleeps where they are let. {npc}, the keeper of a tiny, empty isle, offers a season: "Mind the garden, feed the cat, do not touch the third drawer." The isle has a roof, a stove, and a view that costs nothing. The rogue's life is mostly the asking of small favours.
events.arc: The Wandering Immortal on a Borrowed Isle

effects.log: You sleep under a roof for the first time in a year. The cat inspects you at dawn and approves.
{npc} flushes. "Nothing. A family matter."
The sky is wide and free. You are very tired of it.

events.text: Neighbours on the nearest isles eye you from their quays. A rogue living on a borrowed isle is not a neighbour, merely an arrangement. A woman from the next isle leaves an unsigned note: "Garden fence is mine. Keep off." The cat sits on the note.
events.arc: The Wandering Immortal on a Borrowed Isle

effects.log: You re-set the posts and leave a pot of tea at the gate. The note is gone the next day, and a plum arrives in its place.
It reads "Understood." The reply is a fresh plum.
You weed the garden. The fence is not mentioned again.

events.text: The season ends. {npc} returns, thinner and brighter, and finds the garden thriving and the cat fat. {He} stands in the doorway a long time. "No one has kept it so well," {he} says. "Would you stay? It is a small isle, and it needs a keeper."
events.arc: The Wandering Immortal on a Borrowed Isle

effects.log: You take the isle. A rogue with an address is a lovelier creature than a rogue without.
You leave the cat a stone-weight of fish. The isle shrinks behind you.

events.text: The third drawer, when {npc} finally opens it, holds a hundred small clay animals, made by a child long grown. {He} says nothing for a while. "I could not give them away," {he} says. "Would you like one?"
events.arc: The Wandering Immortal on a Borrowed Isle

effects.log: It is a tiny, lopsided fox. It sits on your windowsill for a thousand years.
The room smells of old clay.

events.text: You keep the isle for a century and are known on the quays as the Rogue of the Tiny Isle. It is almost respectful. The fence-neighbour sends plums every autumn, unsigned. One year you send a plum back, and a note: "Signed."
events.arc: The Wandering Immortal on a Borrowed Isle

effects.log: The plums come with a signature thereafter, in a firm, vexed hand.
They are sweet and slightly sour, like all good neighbours.

events.text: A cloud-ferret, long as a scarf and soft as breath, has been sleeping in your tea chest for a week. It has eaten none of the tea and a good deal of the bread. {npc}, who knows the habits of sky creatures, says it has chosen you. "They do that. Once chosen, it is forever. Or until it finds a better chest."
events.arc: The Cloud-Ferret in the Tea Chest

effects.log: It drapes itself over your shoulders and falls asleep. You do not move for an hour.

choices.text: Ask {npc} how to care for it

effects.log: {He} lists eleven rules, three of them contradictory. "Mostly, it wants to be warm."
The ferret follows the chest, offended, and settles back in.

events.text: The ferret loves the market. It slips under stalls and returns with prizes: a thimble, a bead, once a small silver bell. Vendors begin to complain. {npc} says gently that a ferret keeps its own accounts, and that some of the bell may be owed.
events.arc: The Cloud-Ferret in the Tea Chest

choices.text: Return the bell with an apology

effects.log: The vendor laughs. "That ferret has taken it before." The bell is yours to keep, this time.

choices.text: Train it to bring only tea leaves

effects.log: A month of patience. It brings a leaf, then a sprig, then a whole branch.
The market adapts. Vendors set out a small tray of offerings for it.

events.text: One winter the ferret goes still. It lies in the chest for days, pale, breathing faint. {npc} says cloud-ferrets sleep for a season in the dark of the year. "It is not dying. It is going to a place you cannot follow." You sit beside the chest through the long nights.
events.arc: The Cloud-Ferret in the Tea Chest

effects.log: You sit with the ferret till the thaw. When the light returns, it opens one eye and yawns.
The lantern burns a season. The ferret wakes to light.

events.text: The ferret has grown sleek and wise. It has trained a dozen younger ferrets to bring tea leaves. A column of them now comes up the street each morning, bearing offerings. The vendors, once cross, bring honey.
events.arc: The Cloud-Ferret in the Tea Chest

effects.log: The tea is of the highest grade. You share it with the vendors.
It sniffs your hand, regal.

events.text: A wind-eel, thin as a thread and bright as a blade, swims in a green bottle on {npc}'s shelf. "It was a gift," {npc} says. "From someone who was mad at me." The eel presses against the glass and looks at you. {npc} sighs: "It wants to be out. But it will tear the roof off."
events.arc: The Wind-Eel in the Bottle

effects.log: You carry the bottle home with both hands. The eel whips back and forth, enraged and delighted.

choices.text: Open the bottle on a cliff

effects.log: {npc} agrees. On the Edge, you pull the cork, and the eel springs out, a ribbon of wind, and flies for the horizon.
It spins a small gale in its bottle, like a thought.

events.text: The eel has grown too big for the bottle. It rattles at night, and the glass sings. You take it to the roof and uncork it for an hour a day; it blows a hurricane in a teacup and returns, flushed, to its glass. {npc} sends a note: "Be careful. They learn."
events.arc: The Wind-Eel in the Bottle

effects.log: You throw feathers. The eel catches each one before it falls. A friendship forms.
A glassblower on the Marsh Isle makes one the size of a cask. The eel sulks, then loves it.
Discipline serves.

events.text: One dawn the eel is gone. The bottle is open, the cork on the floor, a feather in the neck. You find it later on a ledge with a dozen other eels, a long grey knot of wind, all humming. It sees you and unwinds, and swims once around your head. Then it goes.
events.arc: The Wind-Eel in the Bottle

effects.log: You stand for a long time with the empty bottle. The wind that evening is soft.
The wind answers, high up.

events.text: The wind-eel sails the sky on its own and comes back to the bottle each spring, to hover a moment on the sill. It has brought two children, thin as ribbon. You pour them tea in thimbles, which they do not drink, but admire.
events.arc: The Wind-Eel in the Bottle

choices.text: Offer the children a new bottle

effects.log: They come in, one by one, to look. None stays. All return.
The eels drift out and back again.

events.text: The Demon Realm keeps a feast in the dark of the year, the Night of Black Lanterns, when every house hangs a lantern of dark glass that gives light the colour of a bruise. {npc}, a neighbour of yours in the Realm, scrubs the steps. "You are a guest," {he} says. "Carry a lantern and ask nothing."
events.arc: The Night of Black Lanterns

effects.log: The glass is cold and the light is strange, grey-violet and soft. The street fills with figures with lanterns, all murmuring.
"We light the way for those who are not coming back," {npc} says. "It is a kindness, not a threat."
The work is quiet and good. {npc} approves.

events.text: The procession ends at a dark pool. One by one, people set their lanterns on the water. {npc} stops with {his} lantern in hand. "I have kept this one for four hundred years," {he} says. "Tonight I let it go." {He} looks at you, as if asking leave.
events.arc: The Night of Black Lanterns

effects.log: Your hand is over {his} on the glass. The lantern floats, a small bruise of light.
You stay at {his} side. The lantern floats on alone.

choices.text: Light one for someone of your own

effects.log: You think of a name, and the glass grows warm.

events.text: A visitor from the Jade Void Sect, in white among the black, stares at the pool in distaste. The Realm's neighbours go still. {npc} says softly: "The visitor is a guest also." The visitor looks at the lanterns, then at {npc}, and takes a lantern from a child. The lantern is set afloat.
events.arc: The Night of Black Lanterns

effects.log: The visitor nods back, awkward, human. Something eases in the dark.
The visitor sips the Realm's tea and says nothing.

events.text: You walk home through the dying lanterns. {npc} walks beside you, quiet and lighter. At the gate {he} says, "The Realm is not as you were told." You think of other things you were told. The black lanterns bob away on the pool.
events.arc: The Night of Black Lanterns

effects.log: The lantern waits for you. It does not flicker.
It is true, in its fashion.

events.text: Two chart-makers of the Star Sea Pavilion have not spoken in three hundred years, over a disagreement about whether the star Ember-in-the-Reed lies to the left or right of the Fish. {npc} says left. The other says right. Both are positive, and both are, annoyingly, brilliant. The Pavilion keeps two versions of every chart.
events.arc: Two Chart-Makers of the Star Sea Pavilion

effects.log: You spend a week with a glass. The star shifts, as stars do, and you see it is both and neither.
{He} is delighted. The other chart-maker sends a cold note.
You draw an empty page with a dotted line. It offends both, equally.

events.text: The two chart-makers are given a joint commission for the grand chart of the Western Reach. They sit at one table and do not speak. Ink flows. Each corrects the other's margin in smaller and smaller letters until the page is a thicket of notes. They have never been so happy.
events.arc: Two Chart-Makers of the Star Sea Pavilion

effects.log: Neither takes it. Both drink it when you leave.
You suggest a single scale for the chart, one both can fault. They both do. It is accepted.
You watch a rivalry that has become a marriage.

events.text: The chart is finished and hung in the Pavilion's hall. Beneath it, in the tiniest hand, a joint line: "We were both right, and the other is insufferable." The signatures are one beside the other. The hall guides read it aloud to visitors, with relish.
events.arc: Two Chart-Makers of the Star Sea Pavilion

effects.log: The hall laughs. The two chart-makers pretend not to hear.
The stars move above it, as they must.

events.text: {npc} wins the argument by outliving the other by a fortnight. {He} hangs a chart with the star on the left. The next morning, quietly, {he} paints a second star on the right, and signs it with the other's name.
events.arc: Two Chart-Makers of the Star Sea Pavilion

effects.log: You say nothing. The chart hangs. The stars, in their wisdom, agree.
You drink to two old fools.

events.text: A heaven-born child, born on a floating isle and never farther than the next, has found a story-book about the world below. {npc}, who is the child's tutor, says the book is nonsense. "Floors that do not move, a sky that does not drift. It has no sense." The child wants to know if it is true.
events.arc: The Heaven-Born Child Who Asked About the Ground

effects.log: The child is astonished. "Where does the water go?" The question has no good answer, and you try.
{npc} nods approvingly. The child scowls and reads on.
The child thinks it is probably true, because the book is so silly.

events.text: The child begs for a look, and the Ministry of Passage will not allow it: no heaven-born goes below without leave. {npc} sighs. "They have heard of a window, in the Archive. A peepshow into the world beneath." The child folds a tiny paper boat and drops it off the quay.
events.arc: The Heaven-Born Child Who Asked About the Ground

choices.text: Take the child to the Archive window

effects.log: The window shows a single morning in a mortal field. The child watches the cows with a stunned face.

choices.text: Tell the child what you remember of below

effects.log: You describe the smell of earth after rain. The child goes quiet. "Show me," they say.
It has caught on a cloud-pine. You return it, damp.

events.text: The child grows up. At a hundred, they ask the Ministry for leave to go below as a guest, to see the field, the cow, the rain. The leave is granted for a single day. {npc} packs a bundle. You see the child to the edge of the Stair. "I will bring you a handful of earth," they say.
events.arc: The Heaven-Born Child Who Asked About the Ground

choices.text: Walk them down the first flight

effects.log: The steps lengthen into mist. The child goes on alone, small and brave.
The day, when it comes, is long.

events.text: The child returns, flushed and smeared with dirt. They have a handful of earth in a handkerchief and a lump in the throat. "It smells like rain," they say, "even when it is dry." They plant a seed from the handful in a cup on your windowsill, and a green thing grows.
events.arc: The Heaven-Born Child Who Asked About the Ground

effects.log: It becomes a small, odd, ordinary plant. You keep it a thousand years.
They shrug, pleased.

events.text: A letter has arrived in the post-sparrow's beak, grimy and addressed to "the Immortal Who Was My Great-Great-Grandfather". It was written by a mortal descendant, far below, in a careful, misspelled hand. {npc}, the post-keeper, says such letters are rare and usually prayers in disguise.
events.arc: A Letter Sent Up From Below

effects.log: The descendant asks nothing. They only write that the family still tells your name, and that the old pear tree you planted is in flower.
{He} reads it in a gentle voice. When {he} reaches the pear tree, {he} stops.

choices.text: Put it on the shelf unopened

effects.log: It sits there, humming faintly, the way letters do.

events.text: You write back. The reply takes a mortal season to arrive, with a sketch of the tree and a pressed blossom. The descendant, a child of twelve, asks about the sky, and whether the clouds are warm. The child has never met anyone who has been above them.
events.arc: A Letter Sent Up From Below

choices.text: Tell the child the clouds are warm

effects.log: You describe the sky, the isles, the long noon. The letter will be kept in a box.
A feather of cloud-silk, a pinch of starlight. It goes by sparrow and the reply comes in raptures.
The tree, you write, is old and wise.

events.text: Years pass in the mortal calendar. The letters from below grow slower, shakier, and then a different hand arrives: the child's own daughter. The child has gone. A last note is enclosed. It reads only: "The clouds are warm. Thank you." {npc} pours you tea.
events.arc: A Letter Sent Up From Below

effects.log: The line begins again. You learn the mortal names of a whole family, season by season.

choices.text: Keep the note by the window

effects.log: It faces the sky it described.

events.text: The letters go on for centuries, and the family grows beyond counting. Each autumn a sparrow brings you a pressed pear blossom. The old tree has long since fallen below, but a descendant has planted another, and another. You keep every blossom in a jar.
events.arc: A Letter Sent Up From Below

choices.text: Add a blossom of your own to the jar

effects.log: You press a cloud-peach flower with the others. A strange, mixed sweetness.
It goes by sparrow, bright against the dark.

events.text: Every year the wind-tossed hats of the whole Heron fleet come down on one isle, the Isle of Hats, where the folk stack them on the quay and hold a festival. You lost a hat on the last storm. {npc}, the festival marshal, says you may claim it, if you can describe it, and may wear anyone else's while you decide.
events.arc: The Festival of Lost Hats

effects.log: It was grey with a band of green. {npc} produces seven grey hats with green bands. All are wrong.
You choose a floppy purple one with a feather. You become a different, braver person.
There are eight thousand. Sorting is a form of meditation.

events.text: The hat-queue moves slowly. A very old immortal ahead of you has been looking for a hat for sixty years, the same one, a travelling hat from a lost voyage. {npc} has put out a hundred possible hats for {him}. The old immortal tries them one by one, in silence, and sets them down.
events.arc: The Festival of Lost Hats

effects.log: You dig for a day. At the bottom is a hat the colour of an old road. The old immortal stops.
You listen to the tale of the voyage. It is a long one, with weather and a goat.
The old immortal tries it. It does not fit, but is worn with dignity.

events.text: The hat, when found, is not the right one. The old immortal turns it in their hands and says, slowly: "No. But it is a good hat." They wear it away down the quay, upright, with a faint smile. {npc} watches. "Sixty years," {he} says. "Best outcome we have had."
events.arc: The Festival of Lost Hats

effects.log: The hat tips. You smile at the sea of hats.
You choose one that nearly fits.

events.text: Your own hat turns up three years later, mailed from an isle on the far edge of the fleet, with a note: "Wore it for a season. It is a good hat. Sorry." It is slightly sun-faded and has been to places. You wear it proudly.
events.arc: The Festival of Lost Hats

effects.log: The marshal nods. A new tradition: hats come home better travelled.

choices.text: Mail it onward with a note

effects.log: It goes out again, a small, patient wanderer.

events.text: Two tea pavilions stand on opposite sides of the Twin Isle, each run by an immortal who has refused to admit the other exists since the last war. {npc} owns the Eastern. The Western is run by someone {he} calls "that person". Each serves a tea the other says is swill. Customers must choose, and are watched while choosing.
events.arc: The Tea Masters of the Twin Pavilions

effects.log: {npc} serves you personally, and talks of nothing but the other pavilion's faults.

choices.text: Drink at both, one after the other

effects.log: You sip, savour, and say nothing. Both pavilions go cold on you.
The other person pours your tea in silence. A great deal is conveyed.

events.text: A cloud-storm takes the roof off the Eastern Pavilion in the night. At dawn the Western tea master stands in the ruin, in an apron, holding a ladder. {npc} stares from the street. "I came to look," says the other. "I stayed to mend." A long silence.
events.arc: The Tea Masters of the Twin Pavilions

effects.log: You haul planks. The two masters do not speak, but they pass nails.
You hold it steady. {npc} climbs up, glaring, and does not fall.
Neither pavilion's recipe. A new one.

events.text: The roof is mended, and the two masters sit side by side on the new ridge-beam with a bowl of tea between them. Neither says thank you. Neither says sorry. They drink in the same silence they kept for three hundred years, but it has a different grain.
events.arc: The Tea Masters of the Twin Pavilions

effects.log: You slip away. At dusk the two pavilions share a lamp.
The masters look at it, and at you, and make room.

events.text: The rivalry survives. Each pavilion, though, has quietly put a small table out front, with a free bowl for the other's customers. The Twin Isle becomes the best place in the Heavens to drink tea and be disliked by both owners at once.
events.arc: The Tea Masters of the Twin Pavilions

choices.text: Raise a bowl to the feud

effects.log: It is a good feud. It will outlive you.
The bowl is hot and generous.

events.text: Each evening a lantern is lit on the next isle, across the reef-channel, and each evening you light yours. Neither of you has ever met. {npc}, who lives across the water, sends a small cloud-boat with a note: "Your lantern is crooked." It is.
events.arc: The Neighbour Across the Reef

effects.log: The next evening a note arrives, "Better." You cannot tell if it is a joke.
A pause, then a laughing reply. The correspondence begins.
It is your lantern. The note says nothing more.

events.text: The cloud-boat goes back and forth over the channel at dusk, carrying notes, then small gifts: a biscuit, a pressed flower, a poem written on a bay leaf. {npc} turns out to be a gardener, with a dry wit and a fear of crowds. You have still not met.
events.arc: The Neighbour Across the Reef

choices.text: Propose a meeting on the reef

effects.log: A pause of three days, then: "Tuesday. I will bring biscuits and be nervous."
You are in no hurry. Neither is {he}. The letters grow thick.
It is lit at once, brighter than any other.

events.text: The reef at dusk, a Tuesday. {npc} arrives in a clean coat, holding a basket of biscuits and a plant in a pot. You are both silent. Then {he} says, "Your lantern is still crooked." You laugh so hard a heron leaves the reef.
events.arc: The Neighbour Across the Reef

effects.log: The evening goes by like a sentence you want to keep reading.
It is lit that night on {his} isle, a little crooked.

events.text: You write for forty more years and never meet. Then one day the notes stop, and you cross the channel at last. The isle is empty, the garden tidy, a single note on the table: "Your lantern was never crooked. I just wanted to talk." You light your lantern, a little crooked, that night.
events.arc: The Neighbour Across the Reef

effects.log: It burns through the night. Perhaps it is seen.
It is a small, warm, sad thing.

events.text: A tribulation cloud drifts past the Plum Isle at breakfast, towing its own small thunderhead and trailing a stream of lightning like a torn sleeve. The isle-folk look up, nod, and pass the jam. "That is the one from last year," says a grandmother. "It has put on weight."

effects.log: The cloud grumbles. A single drop of rain lands in your jam.
The cloud passes. The jam is excellent.

events.text: The Ministry of Weather pins its forecast to the notice-board: "Tribulation, scattered, over the Eastern Reach. Light lightning, heavy ambition. Carry a cloak." A small crowd gathers to read it, as if the ambition were their own.

effects.log: The crowd listens with a certain relish.
The day turns out fine. The cloak is warm.

events.text: On a day of rare calm, a group of friends picnics on the rim of the storm-eye, spread out on the still cloud while the wall of the storm circles slowly around them. They say it is the only place a person can eat in peace. The sandwiches are excellent.

effects.log: You eat under a ring of thunder. It is the loveliest lunch of the decade.
The wall passes like a slow dancer.

events.text: The oil-sellers of the Western Reach bring lamp-oil to the storm-eye light in a convoy of skiffs, shouting in the wind. The keeper, at the dock, counts each barrel with a pencil. The count is three barrels short. Every sailor says it is the wind. The keeper says nothing and brews tea.

effects.log: The barrels are heavy and the wind rude. The keeper pours you a bowl.
The keeper smiles. "All of them. Gently."

events.text: On Stamp Day the Ministry of Precedence opens its great doors, and the public may bring any document to be stamped for a copper. The queue is a mile long. A woman has brought a loaf. The clerk stamps the loaf. The queue cheers.

effects.log: The stamp reads "Seen". You wear it with pride.
You make a note.

events.text: A petition is read in the Court Hall, a good six hours of it, on the matter of a missing doorknob on the Isle of Kettles. The petitioner, an ancient immortal in a faded cap, reads each word with a scholar's care. No one interrupts. By the end, the Hall has agreed to find the knob.

effects.log: The vote is unanimous. The doorknob is not found, but the effort is thorough.

choices.text: Offer to look for the doorknob

effects.log: You find it in a drawer. It was never missing.

events.text: At the Bridge Market a toll-keeper charges you double. "Rogues pay more," says the keeper, not unkindly, tapping a notice on the post. "Rules." You hand over the stones, and the toll-keeper gives you a bun, at a quarter price, as an unwritten apology.

choices.text: Pay the double toll (2 Low-Grade Spirit Stones)

effects.log: You pay, bun in hand, and cross the bridge with quiet dignity.

choices.text: Turn back and go round by skiff

effects.log: The long way takes an hour. The sky is lovely.

events.text: A teahouse on the Court Terrace has a sign: "Members of the factions only". The doorman looks at your sleeves and turns away. Inside, someone is laughing at a joke that is not for you. You find a bench in the wind and drink from your own flask.

choices.text: Sit in the wind and drink

effects.log: The tea is good. The bench is fine. The sky has no sign.

choices.text: Leave a polite note for the owner

effects.log: It says, "Your tea smells lovely." It is left on the step.

events.text: No ferry will carry a rogue after dark without a seat-ticket bought a day before. You wait on the quay with other rogues, a quiet row, wrapped in coats. Someone shares a flask. Someone tells a long, funny story. By dawn, the row is friends.

effects.log: You tell one of your own. The quay laughs.
Hot, sweet, and gone in a minute.

events.text: A drifter's fire burns on a small cloud-raft, miles from any isle. A traveller sits by it, boiling something. "Stay," says the traveller. "The sky is cold." You sit, and you both look at the stars. Nothing is said for an hour. It is the best company you have had in years.

effects.log: Dawn comes slow and gold. You part without names.
The fire flares. The traveller smiles.

events.text: A wind named Old Sourpuss blows over the Heron Isle each autumn and takes one hat from every head, out of spite. This year it takes yours. You hear a high, petty chuckle as the hat flutters off. The wind has a long memory and a short temper.

choices.text: Shake a fist at the wind

effects.log: The wind blows harder. You are rather pleased.
It rises, spinning, a small brown star.

events.text: A courier sparrow arrives, out of breath, with a letter nine years late. It apologises in chirps and shakes its feathers. The letter is a wedding invitation. The wedding is long over. The couple, you learn, are now celebrating their first anniversary of their second marriage.

effects.log: You send a vase. It arrives only a little after the vase from the postman.
The sparrow eats a whole cake and sleeps for a week.

events.text: On the Steaming Isle they make dumplings the size of a lamp, steamed over a vent that sighs warm clouds. The dumpling is split by two people with a long thin knife, to a cheer. Inside, a soup of cloud-broth, sweet, hot, and slightly electrical.

effects.log: The soup scalds your tongue and warms your bones.

choices.text: Hold the knife for the cheer

effects.log: The cheer is yours. The soup is everyone's.

events.text: An archivist on the Quill Isle collects Ministry stamps: all nine thousand. Each is mounted on a card with date, desk and hall. The collection is, to the archivist, a history of the Heavens told entirely in ink. They show it to you with the quiet joy of someone who has found the right shelf.

effects.log: Nine thousand small seals. You find a favourite: a tiny snail.
The archivist's eyes shine.

events.text: At the Mirror Hour the lake at the foot of the Willow Isle stills, and the sky holds itself upside down in the water. A line of folk stand at the edge with a single pebble each. When the clock bell rings they let the pebbles fall together. The sky shivers and mends.

effects.log: The ripple spreads. The sky wobbles, and holds.
You keep it in your pocket for a century.

events.text: The cloud-bamboo of the Hush Isle whispers when no one listens and goes silent when you do. A scholar has spent two centuries trying to catch it. They are very patient, and very wrong, and they love the grove.

effects.log: You hum a tune, and the bamboo whispers.
They sip, still listening past you.

events.text: Halfway up the Stair of Ten Thousand Steps stands a tiny inn with eight beds and a very large cat. The innkeeper has never gone down or up in six hundred years. Guests are given a bowl of soup and a view. The cat sits on the guest book.

choices.text: Take a bed for the night

effects.log: The soup is warm. The cat is a pillow.
You sign, with a cat-pawed flourish.

events.text: On the Sunrise Peak of the Eastern Isle a bell is rung at the first light by whoever arrives first. A queue of the most punctual immortals in the Heavens stands there each night, in blankets, to win the privilege. This year it is a child in slippers. Nobody grumbles.

choices.text: Ring the bell with the child

effects.log: The note rolls across the clouds. The queue cheers.
It is the same dawn as ever, and each time new.

events.text: The shearing of the cloud-sheep on the Meadow Isle is a day of music and cake. Each sheep is led to a stool, sat upon, and gently relieved of its mist. The fleeces are stored in sacks and sold by the bolt. The sheep trot off, lighter and pleased with themselves.

effects.log: The sheep sighs and goes limp with bliss.
It is soft as a held breath.

events.text: There is a bench at the Edge of Heaven where people sit and watch the end of everything. It is always occupied. An old man has sat there for a thousand years, and a young woman for a day. They have shared a flask. The young woman asks the old man what the edge is for. "Looking," the old man says.

effects.log: You watch the edge. It is very large and very quiet.
Both accept. The edge says nothing.

events.text: In the cold season a sky-whale sings under the Greyfin Isle, deep and slow, and the folk on the quay lay their ears against the stone. Each hears something different. A fisherman hears a lost voice. A child hears nothing and is sad. The whale, as it passes, adds a gentle note.

choices.text: Press your ear to the stone

effects.log: You hear a low, patient kindness.
You hum together until it hears something.

events.text: In the hot spring on the Steam Isle, the gossip is as warm as the water. A minister has been seen carrying a pie. A marshal has lost a sock. A rumour spreads that the Ministry of Fog is secretly run by a goose. All present are certain of it by noon.

effects.log: The water holds you. The goose rumour grows.

choices.text: Start a rumour of your own

effects.log: It is about a heron and a flute. It spreads at once.

events.text: The night market on the Lantern Isle opens at moonrise. Each stall hangs a different lantern, so that the street is a procession of colours, ruby, lime, indigo. A vendor sells you a lantern with a moth already inside. The moth glows politely.

effects.log: You cross the colours one by one. At the end the sky is the loveliest.
It lights your way, a little sleepily.

events.text: A cat lives in the old war ruins on the Ash Isle, among the toppled columns. It follows travellers at a distance and sits on the highest stone, watching. A guide says it has been there since the war. It looks, to your eye, quite fed.

effects.log: The cat accepts it with a long unblinking look.

choices.text: Ask the guide about the war

effects.log: The guide tells it for an hour, then asks if you saw the cat.

events.text: A sealed grotto on the underside of the Tern Isle repeats everything said inside it, a day later and in a different voice. You say "hello". Next day, a courteous echo says "hello" back, and adds, "How is the weather?" You say it is fine. The grotto sighs.

effects.log: It answers kindly, a day late.

choices.text: Leave it a cup of tea

effects.log: The cup is empty by the next day.

events.text: A ferry runs between two isles that are on no list. It is poled by an old immortal who takes no fare and asks nothing. The isles are small, green, and empty, except for a single bench each. You sit on one, and look across at the other. It is peaceful, and you do not ask why.

effects.log: You ride twice and leave them in peace.

choices.text: Leave a small gift on the bench

effects.log: A flower. It is gone when you return.

events.text: On the oldest step of the Stair, worn almost smooth by a million feet, there is an inscription. A scholar has spent a century on one word. You run a finger along it and the word, whatever it was, comes to you softly, as if it had been waiting.

effects.log: It echoes briefly, a very old sound.
You tell no one. It becomes a small private lantern.

events.text: At the end of spring the peach orchard on the Vermilion Isle sheds all its petals in one night, and the dawn brings a pink rain that rises. Children chase the petals upward, shouting, then fall back laughing. An old gardener leans on a rake and says nothing, content.

effects.log: You catch three. They dissolve into sweetness.
The path is ankle-deep in pink.

events.text: Every full moon, a choir of old immortals gathers on the cliffs of the Bell Isle and sings into the gulf. They are not good, but they are loud, and the echoes from the abyss add a certain bass. The listeners on the other isles cover their ears, then smile.

effects.log: You are no better, and no worse. The abyss sings back.
The song crosses the gulf, thinned and kind.

events.text: You have invited forty people to dinner, and sixty come. The table is a plank on two barrels. There are three potatoes. By midnight the plank has become a banquet: everyone brought a dish. The potatoes are the worst thing on it and the most remembered.

effects.log: They are gone in a minute. People remember.
The generosity is the real meal.

events.text: It is an ordinary Tuesday, the sky is a pale ordinary blue, the isles drift in their ordinary way, and nothing at all happens. A bee wanders by. A distant bell rings once. You feel a quiet, enormous contentment.

effects.log: The contentment lasts the whole afternoon.
It is a short, good page.

events.text: On the Pearl Isle everyone greets everyone by name on the quay, by long habit, in a ritual that takes ten minutes. "Good morning, Pelun. Good morning, Quill. Good morning, Hush." You are greeted by name, and, to your astonishment, you know it back.

effects.log: The ritual is a loop of small kindnesses.
The names are like a soft chant.

events.text: A heaven-born child on the Marsh Isle has caught a baby tribulation cloud in a jar, no bigger than a fist, grey and crackling. {npc}, the child's parent, drags you in to look. "It sparks on the curtains," {he} says. "Please tell the child it must go back." The child is holding the jar like a lamp.
events.arc: The Child Who Kept a Tribulation Cloud

effects.log: You ask its name. "Grumble," says the child. The jar crackles in a friendly way.
A hairline crack, and a tiny blue spark. You tape it with cloud-paper.
It zaps your finger, gently, in thanks.

events.text: Grumble grows. It outgrows the jar, then the cupboard, then the room, and drifts up to the ceiling, where it sulks and drips. The child sleeps beneath it. Neighbours complain about the rumbling. {npc} stands in the middle of the floor with a bucket.
events.arc: The Child Who Kept a Tribulation Cloud

effects.log: You and {npc} nail a netting over the garden. The cloud floats there, content, a small private storm.

choices.text: Ask the Ministry of Weather about a licence

effects.log: A clerk issues a form: "Domestic Tribulation, Class Small." It costs two stones and a promise.

choices.text: Suggest it be returned to the sky

effects.log: The child cries. {npc} looks at you, then at the ceiling, then away.

events.text: The cloud is large now, and the child nearly grown. One night it rumbles at the roof and does not stop. It wants to go. The child stands on the garden wall in the rain and tells it to wait. It waits. The child cries, and the cloud rains with them for an hour, warm.
events.arc: The Child Who Kept a Tribulation Cloud

effects.log: You say nothing. The rain stops. The cloud lifts, slow and silent, and goes north.
It spits a small spark in farewell.

events.text: The licence is stamped, the cloud is a registered resident, and the Ministry sends an inspector every spring. The inspector, a tall quiet clerk, ends up drinking tea with the child and the cloud. The child grows up to be a clerk of weather. The cloud sits on the office roof.
events.arc: The Child Who Kept a Tribulation Cloud

choices.text: Raise a cup to the Ministry

effects.log: The inspector nods, solemn, and sips.
It sparks, pleased.

events.text: Two lamp-keepers of the Western Reach want to marry in the storm-eye, where the sky is still and the thunder walks around them like a guest. {npc}, the couple's friend, asks you to help carry the feast through the storm wall. "The storm will not mind," {he} says. "It is invited."
events.arc: A Wedding in the Eye of the Storm

effects.log: You hold it over your head through the wind. It arrives intact except for the frosting.

choices.text: Hold the lantern at the bow

effects.log: You lead the skiff by the thin light. The wall of cloud parts like cloth.
You tend the garland. It smells of salt.

events.text: The wedding goes well till the storm wall tightens, as storms do when a thing has been said aloud. Thunder rolls toward the still centre. The guests look up. The couple stands at the altar, hand in hand, calm as stone. {npc} whispers: "Sing. They always back off for a song."
