events.arc: A Wedding in the Eye of the Storm

effects.log: It is a hymn, badly pitched. The storm rumbles, hesitates, and goes round.

choices.text: Hold the wall back with your qi

ok.log: You brace and push, and the wall stays a long breath. The vows are said in a hush.

fail.log: The wall presses in. The vows are said quickly, in the lee of a table.

effects.log: It is rescued, a little damp.

events.text: The vows end, and the storm passes outside. The guests step into the still, drink the cloud-wine, and dance on the cold moonlit cloud. The couple dance last. {npc} wipes an eye. "They will keep the light," {he} says. "Together, for ever."
events.arc: A Wedding in the Eye of the Storm

effects.log: The cloud is firm under your feet. The thunder keeps time.
The cake is cut. It tastes of wind and happiness.

events.text: The couple keep the lamp for forty years. Skiffs that lose the wind come to a light and a kitchen and two people who laugh a great deal. You visit on every anniversary, with a cake carried through the wall on your head. The frosting is always gone by arrival.
events.arc: A Wedding in the Eye of the Storm

effects.log: It becomes a tradition. The storm learns the shape of your hat.
It is warm and quick and arrives dry.

events.text: The Ministry of Fog is the one office in the Heavens that no one can find. It moves with the weather, and its doors open only at dawn on foggy days. {npc} has a petition about a lost path and has searched for the Ministry for eight years. "I once found its steps," {he} says. "They led nowhere. I was there a month."
events.arc: The Petition to the Ministry of Fog

effects.log: You walk into a grey so thick you feel your own sleeves. A bell rings softly from somewhere.

choices.text: Ask the Ministry of Precedence where it is

effects.log: A clerk says: "Where the fog is thickest." The clerk is quite serious.

choices.text: Wait on the quay for dawn

effects.log: The fog comes in. You sit. Nothing.

events.text: You find a door, plain and grey, in a wall that is really only mist. A porter with a lantern waves you in. The hall is long and white, desks fading into distance. A clerk looks up, as if from very far away. "Petitions?" says the clerk. "Say it low. The fog listens."
events.arc: The Petition to the Ministry of Fog

effects.log: The clerk writes it on a scrap of mist. It dissolves. "Received," says the clerk.
The paper goes grey and soft in your hand. The clerk smiles. "Many do that."
The ceiling is a drift of cloud.

events.text: The answer to the petition comes a year later, as a patch of fog drifting in at dawn across {npc}'s garden, forming for an hour the shape of a path. {npc} walks it, with a lantern, to a small hill {he} had lost for forty years. It is exactly as it was.
events.arc: The Petition to the Ministry of Fog

effects.log: The fog fades. The hill is warm and green. {npc} weeps and plants a stone.

choices.text: Send a thank-you into the mist

effects.log: A note dissolves. It is accepted.

events.text: The petition, written, dissolves as well. No answer comes. {npc} goes back to look for the Ministry again, and finds it, twice, and again it takes the petition, and again nothing. After a few years {he} does not mind. "It is the looking," {he} says. "It is the fog."
events.arc: The Petition to the Ministry of Fog

effects.log: You and {npc} walk into fog on a quiet morning. Something is never found. It is a good tradition.

choices.text: Leave a lantern at the quay

effects.log: It is lit every dawn by someone unknown.

events.text: Two poets of the Jade Court have written replies to each other's verses since before most of the Court was born. {npc} writes the first line of every exchange; the other writes the last. Each pair is posted at the Archive. They have never spoken. They sign with different seals. The Court says the quarrel is the finest poem of the age.
events.arc: The Poets Who Have Replied to Each Other for Six Centuries

effects.log: The first line is a rain-song; the answer is a drought. You laugh and want to weep.

choices.text: Write a verse of your own

effects.log: {npc} reads it aloud to the reading-room, politely, and says: "Not yet."
The ink is good. It goes in a drawer.

events.text: {npc} comes to you, shaken. The other poet has stopped replying. Three months of silence. "I have written eleven first lines," {he} says, "and no answers." The Archive keeps a seat for the other poet. It is empty. The reading-room is quiet in a worried way.
events.arc: The Poets Who Have Replied to Each Other for Six Centuries

choices.text: Go to find the other poet

effects.log: You track the seal to a quiet isle. A very old figure lies by a window, pen in hand, asleep.

choices.text: Write an answer in the other's style

effects.log: {npc} reads it, and weeps, and does not post it.
The silence is long. It teaches a great deal.

events.text: The other poet is old and tired, not dead. They have written an answer for each of eleven first lines, folded in a drawer, and fell asleep over the twelfth. They wake, blink, and ask for tea. {npc} arrives at the door at the same moment, out of breath, and the two stare at each other for the first time in six hundred years.
events.arc: The Poets Who Have Replied to Each Other for Six Centuries

effects.log: They speak at once, and stop, and laugh. It is not a poem. It is better.
You close the door. Inside, a long murmur starts.

events.text: The exchange ends. The Archive posts a final pair, side by side: {npc}'s last line and an answer that is only a blank space, signed in both seals. The Jade Court is silent for a day. Then someone starts a new exchange, and someone replies. It goes on, a little looser.
events.arc: The Poets Who Have Replied to Each Other for Six Centuries

choices.text: Begin an exchange of your own

effects.log: You write a first line and leave it on the sill. Within a week, it is answered.
It is the most eloquent thing in the Archive.

events.text: The Nine Clouds Palace weaves the cloud-silk that dresses the Heavens, and {npc} is its weaver-mistress, three thousand years at the loom and still scolding apprentices about knots. "A good cloud is woven, not cut," {he} says. No one dares correct {him}, and {he} has noticed that you have a loose thread.
events.arc: The Weaver-Mistress of the Nine Clouds Palace

effects.log: {npc} snaps it off with a bite. "Thank you for the opportunity," {he} says. It is gone.
The loom is the size of a hall. The thread is starlight. {npc} lets you pass a shuttle once.

choices.text: Carry a bolt for the apprentices

effects.log: It is heavier than a whale. Nobody applauds.

events.text: A rival palace, the Star Sea Pavilion, sends a bolt of its own silk, marked "finer". The Nine Clouds weavers go stiff. {npc} fingers the cloth. "It is finer," {he} says, to the horror of the hall. "And it will tear in a hard wind. Let us weave one finer and stronger."
events.arc: The Weaver-Mistress of the Nine Clouds Palace

effects.log: You wear both through a gale on the Western Reach. The Star Sea silk rips. The Nine Clouds silk bends.

choices.text: Suggest a blend of the two

effects.log: Weavers of both houses, forced into a room, argue for a week. A hybrid is born.
The bolts are folded away. The tension remains.

events.text: The hybrid silk, named Twin Cloud, is a sensation, and the two houses declare a truce at a ceremony where they share a spool. {npc} cuts the first length in person. "It is not my thread," {he} says. "It is ours." The hall stands and applauds.
events.arc: The Weaver-Mistress of the Nine Clouds Palace

effects.log: Weavers weep openly. It is a very silk occasion.

choices.text: Take a scrap of Twin Cloud

effects.log: It is cool and strong and slightly iridescent.

events.text: The Nine Clouds silk wins the test and the Palace crows for a decade. {npc} warns the apprentices against pride. "A thread that has proved itself," {he} says, "should still be checked for fray." A year later a fray is found. The loom is quiet for a day.
events.arc: The Weaver-Mistress of the Nine Clouds Palace

effects.log: You and the apprentices re-weave a hand's width. It takes a night. It is perfect.
It stands, waiting, like a horse.

events.text: In the Demon Realm a guest is sacred, and a guest who is fed three meals may not be harmed by the house for a season. {npc} is a lord of a small border hall and takes the rule very seriously. "Sit," {he} says. "Eat. You are safe for three meals, and four if you are polite."
events.arc: The Rule of the Guest in the Demon Realm

effects.log: The food is dark, smoky, and delicious. A hound sleeps against your leg.
"Old," says {npc}. "From before the Realm had borders. We kept it when we lost the rest."
The hall is hung with black glass. {npc} nods slowly.

events.text: At the second meal a rival lord arrives with a stern face and a dagger of black jade, and is also made to sit and eat. The two lords glare over the soup. {npc} calmly ladles. The rule holds the table like a hand. "No harm in my hall," {he} says, "and no harm in yours."
events.arc: The Rule of the Guest in the Demon Realm

effects.log: The rival takes it, frowning. The dagger stays in the sheath.
Both lords love hounds. The talk goes late.
The soup is peppery and perfect.

events.text: By the fourth meal, the two lords are trading dog stories, and the dagger lies on the table by the salt. In the morning they swear a truce on the old rule, and a bell rings in the hall. {npc} says: "That was the best fourth meal I ever served."
events.arc: The Rule of the Guest in the Demon Realm

effects.log: You sign your name beneath theirs. The Realm remembers a guest.
It rides in your sleeve, warm.

events.text: The rival leaves in the morning, and the rule is broken in no way. Years later {npc} hears that the rival's hall burned, and that the rival was fed and housed three meals in the Jade Void Sect, of all places, and left unharmed. The two halls exchange gifts at the new year.
events.arc: The Rule of the Guest in the Demon Realm

choices.text: Carry a gift between the halls

effects.log: You carry a black jade dagger one way and a jar of pickled plums the other.
It has kept more people than any wall.

events.text: A goose, vast and white, has taken up residence at your gate. It honks at anyone who passes, bites the tax-collector, and has no registration. {npc}, the neighbour, says: "It is a Goose of the Upper Reach. They guard. They also adopt." The goose looks at you with a cool, level eye.
events.arc: The Goose of the Unregistered Isle

effects.log: It eats a bag of grain and a loaf and leaves a single feather in thanks.
{He} laughs. "You cannot register a goose. A goose registers you."
The goose bites the gate. You open it.

events.text: The goose guards you with fierce attention. It bites a tax-collector, two inspectors, and a minor minister. A complaint is filed with the Ministry of Beasts. {npc} says gently that the goose is protected by an old statute. The inspector is unconvinced.
events.arc: The Goose of the Unregistered Isle

effects.log: You cite the Third Age Beast Accord, section nine: "Geese may not be moved." The inspector retreats.

choices.text: Offer the inspector tea and a goose-proof hat

effects.log: The inspector dons the hat and drinks the tea. The goose approves.
The goose bites the clerk who comes for it.

events.text: The goose is eventually recognised as a Resident Guard of the Isle. It wears a small badge and bites only by appointment. The inspector brings it a loaf each month, in a spirit of appeasement. A friendship grows, wary and wonderful.
events.arc: The Goose of the Unregistered Isle

effects.log: It is the best guard in the Heavens and the worst conversationalist.
It suits you.

events.text: The goose does not stay. One spring it leaves, in the night, with a honk, and a long white feather on your pillow. {npc} says geese come only when they are needed. "It stayed as long as you needed guarding," {he} says. "Which is a compliment, I think."
events.arc: The Goose of the Unregistered Isle

effects.log: It rests in a jar, white as a held breath.

choices.text: Put out a loaf in case

effects.log: It is gone in the morning, though no goose is seen.

events.text: A rogue with no isle and no faction drifts alone, and the sky is wide. {npc}, a fellow drifter, offers to share a skiff on a long journey across three fleets, splitting the poling and the tea. "Ill not talk much," {he} says. "I find a silence is good company."
events.arc: The Long Drift With a Stranger

effects.log: The skiff is small and patched. {npc} hums when poling, tunelessly. You sleep well.
"Nowhere," {he} says. "It is a good road."
The sky is wide and a little lonelier than before.

events.text: At the first fleet, the quay-folk will not sell to rogues. The two of you sit by the water and eat dry bread. A child, not yet taught to look down on drifters, brings a bowl of hot soup and sits. The child asks what it is like to have no isle. {npc} looks to you.
events.arc: The Long Drift With a Stranger

effects.log: You describe the sky, the freedom, and the cold. The child listens with a stern face and nods.
The child beams. {npc} smiles into the soup.
The child accepts a crust and goes away pleased.

events.text: At the third fleet the road splits. {npc} turns the skiff gently toward a small, dim isle you have never seen, and says quietly: "This is the end for me." There is a hut on the shore and a garden gone to seed. "I am going home," {he} says. "I did not know I had one. Come in?"
events.arc: The Long Drift With a Stranger

effects.log: The hut is warm. The garden bursts back to life. The two of you sit by the fire and talk for the first time.
You wave from the skiff. {npc} stands at the door a long time.

events.text: The skiff drifts through the fleets, patched and cheerful, and you and {npc} become a pair of familiar sights: two rogues with a kettle. Quay-folk learn your names. A baker keeps a loaf for you. A drifter's life is not a lesser one, you decide, only a longer road.
events.arc: The Long Drift With a Stranger

effects.log: You travel for a century. The kettle is never cold.

choices.text: Tip your hat to a baker

effects.log: The loaf is warm.

events.text: Once a year the Dove Isle releases its slow birds, big grey birds that fly at the speed of a walking man and cover a distance in a day that a sparrow does in an hour. The folk cheer them on. {npc}, the bird-warden, hands you a bird. "Hold it kindly," {he} says. "It has waited all year."
events.arc: The Festival of Slow Birds

effects.log: It is warm and heavy and entirely unhurried. It blinks once.
It opens its wings and, with great dignity, steps off the quay and begins to glide.
A great grey slow shower of birds climbs the sky.

events.text: You are asked to follow a bird, as the festival custom is: a skiff each, in the wake of one slow wing. Your bird takes a leisurely path toward the Quill Isle and stops over a pond for a doze. {npc}, aboard the next skiff, calls over the wind: "Do not hurry. It knows."
events.arc: The Festival of Slow Birds

effects.log: The bird leads you through a golden day. You pass a hundred small isles you had never seen.
The bird flaps once, offended. You slow down.
The skiff drifts on. The bird, in front, drifts too.

events.text: At dusk the birds settle on the shore of the far isle, a huge grey flock of quiet shapes. People step off the skiffs and sit among them. Nobody speaks. A bird leans a head on your shoulder. {npc} says: "That is the festival. That."
events.arc: The Festival of Slow Birds

effects.log: The night is cold and the birds are warm. You sleep.
{He} nods, wrapped in a bird.

events.text: Your bird comes to the sill of your house each year after, a day late and a little greyer. It does not ask for food. It stays an hour and leaves. You leave a dish of seed out. Some years it eats. Some years it does not. It comes anyway.
events.arc: The Festival of Slow Birds

effects.log: A tiny, steady rite. The seed is never quite finished.
It cocks a grey head.

events.text: Two heaven-born youths of the Garland Isle race every spring up the Stair of Ten Thousand Steps, and neither has ever won. They tie by a breath, then by a hair, then by a feather. {npc} is one; the other is a cousin. Today {he} asks you to judge, for the first time in a decade. Both look at you with white faces.
events.arc: The Heaven-Born Who Raced Every Spring

effects.log: You stand at the top with a bell. You have never been so nervous.
A race down instead of up. {npc} frowns, then grins.
They find another judge, a heron, who pecks a feather and calls it a draw.

events.text: The race runs. The two rivals pound up the steps, neck and neck, breathing hard. At the last hundred steps one stumbles, and the other, without a word, stops to haul the stumbler up. They cross the line hand in hand. You ring the bell. It rings, loud and unsure.
events.arc: The Heaven-Born Who Raced Every Spring

effects.log: Both groan. Both grin. The crowd roars.

choices.text: Award the race to the one who stopped

effects.log: The crowd goes quiet. {npc} hangs the garland on the cousin. The cousin refuses it.
They gulp it side by side.

events.text: The spring race becomes a different race: the two cross the line together every year, and a third child joins, then more. The Garland Isle makes a festival of it. {npc} is grey and wise now, and tells the children: "Stop for the one who falls. It is the whole of the race."
events.arc: The Heaven-Born Who Raced Every Spring

choices.text: Cheer from the top of the Stair

effects.log: The bell rings and rings. Some tears are real.

choices.text: Hand out water at the finish

effects.log: The crowd is thirsty and grateful.

events.text: The garland hangs on a peg in the cousin's hall for three hundred years, never worn. The two never race again, and never speak of it. They drink tea every spring on the same bench at the top of the Stair, and look at the view. It is the best friendship either of them has.
events.arc: The Heaven-Born Who Raced Every Spring

effects.log: They make room. The view is a thousand isles.
Some quiet things should stay quiet.

events.text: A cook at the Ministry of Prayers kitchen, {npc}, comes to you pale. The prayers from the world below have thickened this season, thousands in a day, all asking for the same thing: rain. A drought is wasting a distant land. {npc} says the clerks are overwhelmed and the Ministry will not act until the proper forms arrive.
events.arc: News From Below That Reached the Kitchen

effects.log: A clerk shrugs: "Mislaid in the Fog." You and {npc} stare at each other across a pile of prayers.

choices.text: Read some of the prayers aloud

effects.log: You read ten. They are plain: a child, a farmer, an old woman with a goat. {npc} cannot listen to the last.

choices.text: Say it is not in your hands

effects.log: You say it is not, and it is not. It sits badly.

events.text: You and {npc} take the prayers to a minor Ministry of Weather clerk who owes {npc} a favour. The clerk, after a long silence, says: "A cloud-fleet is idle over the Eastern Reach. With the right signature, it might drift south." The signature belongs to a marshal who is hard to find.
events.arc: News From Below That Reached the Kitchen

effects.log: You search four isles. The marshal is on a fishing trip, in a hat, and is reluctant to read.

choices.text: Forge nothing, and ask the clerk to stretch the rule

effects.log: The clerk agrees to stretch a rule by a hand's width. It is enough.
It passes through your hands in a hurry.

events.text: The cloud-fleet drifts south by degrees. A week later a letter arrives by sparrow, from a mortal child, thanking "the kitchen." {npc} reads it three times, then props it against the stove. "We cook for the dead and the living," {he} says. "Today we cooked for the living."
events.arc: News From Below That Reached the Kitchen

choices.text: Leave a note for the sparrow

effects.log: You write "Thank the rain." It goes down.
The soup is rich and plain.

events.text: The marshal signs, after a lecture, and the fleet drifts south. The drought breaks in a week. The marshal, rather pleased with the outcome, takes a long holiday. The Ministry of Weather sends you a note: "Please come again." You do not, on the whole, wish to. But it is a nice note.
events.arc: News From Below That Reached the Kitchen

effects.log: It hangs in the kitchen window, a small emblem.
The marshal has caught nothing and is content.

events.text: Among the rogues of the sky there is a custom: a single small lamp, passed from drifter to drifter, never kept longer than a season. {npc} gives it to you at a campfire on a lonely cloud. "It was lit before I was born," {he} says. "It has been given to a thousand. Now you."
events.arc: The Lamp That Passes Between Drifters

effects.log: It is warm and a little worn. Its light is the colour of a candle seen through tea.
"Nobody knows," says {npc}. "That is the point."

choices.text: Hold it for a moment and pass it back

effects.log: The lamp feels heavy for its size. {npc} nods.

events.text: You carry the lamp for a season through towns where drifters are barred from the inns. Its light draws other drifters to your fire: old, young, quiet, loud. A pot of stew appears. A fiddle. A thin child with a bundle. The lamp seems to know them.
events.arc: The Lamp That Passes Between Drifters

effects.log: The fire is crowded and very warm.

choices.text: Ask the child where they are bound

effects.log: The child says: "Away." You give the child the best seat.
A reel, badly. Everyone dances.

events.text: The season ends. You must pass the lamp on. The child you sheltered volunteers, shy, and takes it in both hands. The lamp glows a little brighter. "I will carry it," says the child, "to the edge, and then beyond." You watch the light dwindle into the dusk, small and steady.
events.arc: The Lamp That Passes Between Drifters

choices.text: See the child to the edge of the fleet

effects.log: You walk the quay together. The lamp is a point of gold against the dark.
The lamp flickers once, as if to wave.

events.text: You hand the lamp on at the next fire, to a stranger, with a short speech that you did not plan. The stranger says thank you, and the lamp passes on. You think of all the hands. You are, you decide, one of the thousand. It is not nothing.
events.arc: The Lamp That Passes Between Drifters

choices.text: Tell the stranger the lamp's story

effects.log: You tell what little you know. The stranger repeats it back, adding a line.

choices.text: Light a candle of your own

effects.log: It burns small and steady beside the lamp.

events.text: Once a decade the noon on the Orchard Isle lasts three days. The sun stays high, the shadows stay short, and everyone is excused from work. {npc}, the orchardist, sets out long tables beneath the peach trees and says: "The Long Noon is for lying down. Anyone who is busy will be sent home."
events.arc: The Long Noon on the Orchard Isle

choices.text: Lie down under a peach tree

effects.log: You lie in the dappled warmth. A peach falls beside you, and you eat it without rising.
{npc} gives you a cloth and a long look. You set. You do not hurry.
{npc} laughs. "The Noon forgives all."

events.text: On the second day of the Noon a stranger arrives in black, hurrying, with a satchel. They are a clerk of the Ministry of Precedence, sent to deliver a summons. {npc} leads them to a table and puts a peach in their hand. The clerk, by degrees, forgets the summons. The satchel lies unopened in the grass.
events.arc: The Long Noon on the Orchard Isle

effects.log: You talk about nothing. The clerk laughs for the first time in a century.
The satchel is placed behind a tree. The clerk, unknowing, sleeps.
It is taken with a sigh.

events.text: On the third day the noon ends. The shadows lengthen, slow as syrup. The clerk wakes, picks up the satchel, and looks at it. "I will deliver it tomorrow," the clerk says, and puts it back down. {npc} smiles. "There is always a tomorrow," {he} says, "and next Noon is ten years off."
events.arc: The Long Noon on the Orchard Isle

choices.text: Toast the end of the Noon

effects.log: The tables are cleared. The peaches are gone. Everyone is rested.
The shadows are your own again.

events.text: The hidden satchel is found by a goat the next morning. The summons is delivered a decade late, to a person who has forgotten the offence. The Ministry files it as "Resolved". The clerk is promoted. You never confess. The peaches, that year, are the best.
events.arc: The Long Noon on the Orchard Isle

effects.log: It is a very small crime and a very ripe one.
It accepts, indifferent.

events.text: The Jade Void Sect and the Star Sea Pavilion exchange one student each decade, as a courtesy. {npc} arrives from the Pavilion with a telescope the length of a boat and a habit of staring at the ceiling. The Sect assigns the student to your cell. "I find roofs fascinating," {he} says. "They are so close."
events.arc: The Exchange Student From the Star Sea Pavilion

effects.log: You clear half the cell. {npc} sets up the telescope in the window and trains it on a spider.
You lead a tour. {npc} looks at the sky the entire time, and tells you a great deal about it.
{npc} drinks and does not look away from the roof.

events.text: The Sect disapproves of the telescope. A senior disciple says that watching the stars is idle, and that the Jade Void looks inward. {npc} blinks. "But the inward is so small," {he} says, and is sent to scrub the courtyard. You scrub beside {him}, and learn the names of a hundred stars in a single afternoon.
events.arc: The Exchange Student From the Star Sea Pavilion

effects.log: You argue the stars are a mirror. The disciple frowns, and assigns you the scrub as well.
The courtyard is clean by dusk. You know the Weaver, the Goat, the Fish.
The stone is bright. The silence is full of stars.

events.text: When the decade ends, {npc} returns to the Pavilion with a chest of Jade Void scrolls and a new habit of looking at the floor. You go with {him} to the quay. {He} hands you the telescope. "I have another," {he} says. "Look up now and then. The ceiling will keep."
events.arc: The Exchange Student From the Star Sea Pavilion

effects.log: It sits in your window. At dusk you look at the sky and not the ceiling.

choices.text: Return a scroll to the Pavilion

effects.log: It crosses the sea in a bundle.

events.text: The telescope is confiscated by the Sect Elder for a season, then returned in secret with a note: "Interesting spider." The Elder, you learn later, spent a year looking at the sky and wrote a short book of verse. It is not displayed.
events.arc: The Exchange Student From the Star Sea Pavilion

effects.log: It is rough and sincere. You tell no one.
It is received without comment.

events.text: A shop on the Marsh Isle sells umbrellas for lightning, with a rubber-wood handle and a tiny bell that rings when a bolt is near. The shopkeeper swears by them. The one customer who bought one returned it, singed and grinning, and bought a spare.

effects.log: It rings once in a distant storm. You stay dry.
It chimes, sweet and thin.

events.text: A rainbow comes down on the Garden Isle in one piece, like a dropped scarf, and lies draped over the roofs. The residents are uncertain what to do with it. A grandmother hangs the washing on it. It holds.

effects.log: It is soft and bright, a little bouncy.
The colours stain it faintly gold.

events.text: In the middle of the storm-eye the hush is so deep that a dropped pin sounds like a bell. Skiff crews learn to whisper. A young sailor sneezes, and the sound travels round the wall of cloud and comes back as thunder. Everyone laughs, in whispers.

effects.log: It returns as a distant, delighted rumble.
You hear your own heart, a drum in a cathedral.

events.text: A teahouse perched on a floating raft follows the storms at a distance, brewing cups for the watchers. The proprietor knows the winds by name and the lightning by mood. "Good bolt," says the proprietor, pouring. "Dry, with a hint of citrus."

effects.log: It tastes of copper and rain. Your hair rises.

choices.text: Ask the proprietor about the winds

effects.log: There are forty-one by name. The proprietor recites them all.

events.text: Two minor ministers each insist the other must enter the hall first. They stand at the door for eleven hours. The hall behind them fills with waiting guests. Finally a cleaner mops between them, and they both step back in alarm, and enter together.

effects.log: The Court is, at times, a fine comedy.
They both refuse, then both accept.

events.text: In the Jade Court, a ledger is kept of who stands higher than whom, and the ledger is revised every year, in a hall full of quills. Clerks hold their breath as the page is turned. A clerk finds that a rival has been moved up a place. A quiet murmur passes through the hall.

effects.log: You stand where you stood, which is a small relief.
It is taken without a glance.

events.text: Two ancient immortals haggle for a bolt of cloud-silk. They have haggled over the same bolt for six hundred years. The stall-keeper gave up long ago and now sells tea to the spectators. Today, the price finally drops by a hair. Both sit down heavily, exhausted and moved.

effects.log: The two glare at you, then at each other. A third bolt is brought out.
The tea is hot. The haggling resumes.

events.text: A silk-seller at the Bridge Market tells you the price of a bolt is four stones. A faction member beside you is quoted two. You notice. The seller notices you noticing and goes pink. You say nothing and look at the silk. The seller drops the price to three, and then to two, mumbling.

effects.log: You buy the bolt. The seller will not meet your eye.
The seller calls after you. You keep walking.

events.text: A singer stands on the Dove Bridge each evening, singing a single sad song in a very old language. The words are lost, but the tune is clear. Passers-by slow, and stop, and cry a little, and go on. The singer takes no money. A cat sits by the singer's feet, like a punctuation mark.

effects.log: The song finishes. You feel lighter, oddly.

choices.text: Leave a coin in the cat's dish

effects.log: The cat accepts it with dignity.

events.text: Anglers on the Opal Lake fish for clouds, with rods of bamboo and lines of silk. A big one takes hours to land. This morning, a young angler hooks a stormcloud by accident, and the whole lake goes dark. The angler, with great courage, cuts the line. The storm sulks away.

effects.log: You catch a small pink cumulus and release it.
They are pale, and very proud.

events.text: On the night of the star-rain, the whole sky of the Eastern Reach is full of falling sparks, each a different colour, silent as snow. The isles hang lanterns to catch them. A spark lands in a lantern and is carried home like a small coal. It glows in the hearth for a week.

choices.text: Catch a spark in a jar

effects.log: It hums faintly. You set it by the bed.
It is a very long moment, in several colours.

events.text: In the qi-kitchen of the Spice Isle the pepper is grown in pots of lightning-struck soil and tastes of heat that arrives a moment after the thought of it. A cook adds three grains to your broth. You feel it arrive in the next corner of your body.

effects.log: You sweat gently for an hour. Everything is bright.

choices.text: Ask the cook for a pot of seeds

effects.log: The cook gives you three. You plant them.

events.text: In the Archive of Jade Slips there is a ladder as tall as a tree, and a clerk who climbs it each morning to reach the high shelves. The clerk is afraid of heights. Each morning, the clerk closes both eyes, climbs, and fetches. The Archive has never lost a slip.

effects.log: The clerk descends with a sigh of relief.
It is a very small fear and a very big ladder.

events.text: In the cloud-bamboo grove of the Reed Isle a flute-maker cuts a single stalk each autumn, turns it, drills it, and tests it at dawn. The sound of the first note, the maker says, is the only thing that matters. Fifty years of flutes lie in a cabinet. Each plays only its first note.

effects.log: It is clear and a little sad.
It plays a thousand notes, none like the first.

events.text: A hermit on a peak of the Greyhorn Isle has not spoken in two hundred years. Hikers leave offerings of tea and rice cakes at the foot of the path. The offerings are always gone by morning. Once, a note was left in return: a single character, which the scholars have spent a decade on. It means "Salt".

effects.log: The next day the salt is gone, and a pebble lies in its place.
It is gone. The hermit is, evidently, fond of sweets.

events.text: On a hill of soft cloud, picnickers lie in rows and are rolled gently down by their children. The hill is damp and bouncy and smells of rain. A grandmother, rolled, comes to rest at the bottom and lies there giggling for a good five minutes.

effects.log: It is a wonderful, dizzy, soft descent.
You lie in the damp and giggle.

events.text: A bottle is found at the Edge of Heaven, wedged in a crack, with a note inside. It reads: "To whoever finds this: I was here. I looked. It was big. Be well." There is a date nine thousand years ago and a smudged signature. The finder pins it to a post for passers-by to read.

choices.text: Add a line of your own

effects.log: You write "Still big. Still well." and pin it.
It is a very small, honest thing.

events.text: A sky-whale passes slowly above the Pearl Isle, so large its shadow takes a quarter of an hour to cross. Everyone stops what they are doing. A tea-seller sets out cups. The whale breathes out, a slow warm mist, and the cups fill with dew. It is the best tea the seller has ever served.

effects.log: It tastes of high places.
A great slow eye turns, and closes, and opens.

events.text: There is a spring on the Veil Isle that whispers the name of every person who drinks from it. You bend and drink. The spring whispers your name, and then, quietly, another name, one you did not tell it. It is a name you had forgotten, and had lost long ago.

effects.log: The spring is still. The name is yours again.
The spring says only your own name.

events.text: Will-o-wisps rise from the Fen Isle at dusk and, if you hold out a lantern, will light it. They are rather vain, and require compliments. "What a beautiful glow!" you say to the first. It brightens at once, and moves in. Your lantern is lit for a month.

effects.log: It glows for you all evening.
The candle burns a faint green.

events.text: In the mud by the Fen Isle you find the pawprint of a mist hound, wide as a plate and gone grey at the edges. The track fades into fog in three steps. A hunter tells you it is a young one, lost from its pack. The pack will find it by sound. The hunter hums low and long.

effects.log: A distant howl answers.
The print is gone by noon.

events.text: A cloud carp has taken up residence in the teapot of a quiet pavilion. The proprietor does not mind, as it keeps the tea warm. Customers are told it is "an unusual leaf". A child asks why the leaf has fins. The proprietor says it is a very special tea.

effects.log: It tastes of high water and sweet bread.
It bubbles contentedly.

events.text: The walls of a ruin on the Ash Isle have grown a garden: ivy, thyme, small blue flowers. A caretaker, an ancient immortal in a straw hat, tends them with great tenderness. "War ended long ago," the caretaker says. "The walls have been so patient."

effects.log: The stones drink the water deeply.
It is warm in the sun, and remembers.

events.text: A bell rings under the cloud sea, deep and slow, from a sunken isle that has been there for twelve thousand years. Divers who have heard it say it is sad, and divers who have not say it is an echo. You listen one night from a skiff, in the dark, and it is both.

effects.log: The last stroke fades. You sit a long time.
Nothing answers, but the water stills.

events.text: In the roots beneath a cloud-pine on the Rosy Isle there is a table laid for two. A kettle steams. The cups are warm. No one is there. A note says: "Sit." You sit. Someone, somewhere, is very pleased.

effects.log: The tea is jasmine and a small, pleasant dusk.
You leave a biscuit.

events.text: On the slope of the Elder Isle a stone is carved with a riddle, in a hand older than the Jade Court: "What is heavy when you hold it and light when you let go?" Visitors have been guessing for ten thousand years. The usual answers are wrong. A child says: "A grudge." The stone, to everyone's alarm, seems to hum.

effects.log: The stone hums a second time.
The stone is silent, politely.

events.text: The pool in an old starfall crater shows a sky that is not above it. You see a night of different stars, a moon with a crack, a distant wheel of light. A watcher tells you it is the sky the star fell from. The pool shows it faithfully, and sadly, and without complaint.

choices.text: Study the stars in the pool

effects.log: You memorise one constellation. It fits nowhere above.
The sky shivers and settles.

events.text: A neighbourhood potluck on the Heron Isle ends with nineteen desserts and no main dish. Everyone brought the thing they love. They eat dessert for dinner with great solemnity, then agree it was the best meal of the year and promise to repeat the mistake.

choices.text: Take seconds of the third pie

effects.log: It is a good pie.

choices.text: Propose a main dish for next time

effects.log: The idea is rejected, kindly.

events.text: A soft rain falls on your isle for the whole afternoon, straight down, unhurried, tapping the roof in patterns. You sit by the window with a cup. Nothing is required of you. The kettle sings once. The rain agrees.

effects.log: The afternoon is long and warm.
It is a short line, and enough.

events.text: Each dusk the fishing-skiffs of the Sandal Isle come home with lanterns lit, and the folk on the quay count them in. One is late. Nobody says so, but the quay waits a little longer. At last a small light rounds the headland. A cheer goes up, low and warm.

effects.log: The skiff is tied. Everyone goes home.

choices.text: Light a lantern for the late skiff

effects.log: You hold it high until the skiff is in.

events.text: {npc}, your friend of four hundred years, tells you over tea that the tribulation cloud has been sighted. It will arrive in nine days, and {he} intends to stand on the Bare Reef and meet it alone. "It is a private matter," {he} says, and stirs the tea much longer than the tea requires.
events.arc: Waiting Out a Friend's Tribulation

choices.text: Offer to wait on the reef

effects.log: {npc} says no, twice, and then yes. Your cushion goes in the skiff.
You and {npc} haul talismans and sandbags. It is oddly cheerful, like packing for a picnic.
You say you will light a lamp in your window that night. {npc} nods.

events.text: The cloud arrives early, a day before the sky promised. It sits above the Bare Reef like a lid, dark and slow. {npc} walks out onto the reef in a plain coat. You wait at the edge of the water, holding a flask. The first thunder comes as a low, plain note, like a door opening in a distant house.
events.arc: Waiting Out a Friend's Tribulation

choices.text: Stay as far as the edge allows

effects.log: You stand with the flask in the wind. The lightning is white and exact. You do not look away.
You sing, low and badly, an old fleet song. It carries over the water in the gaps between bolts.

choices.text: Light a lamp on the shore

effects.log: It is a small light against a very large dark.

events.text: The last bolt lands. The cloud thins and slides off over the horizon like a tired animal. On the reef stands {npc}, scorched at the hem, hair on end, with a look of baffled joy. {He} walks the whole way in without a word, and sits on the wet stones next to you and takes the flask.
events.arc: Waiting Out a Friend's Tribulation

effects.log: You pour. {npc} drinks. After a while {he} laughs, helplessly, for a quarter of an hour.
{He} is shivering and shining. It is a good coat to lose.

events.text: The song is heard on the reef. {npc} tells you later that in the third bolt {he} lost count of everything but the tune, and that this was the moment it let go. "Dreadful singing," {he} says. "Thank you. Never stop." You are asked to sing at every tribulation that follows among your friends.
events.arc: Waiting Out a Friend's Tribulation

choices.text: Become the Singer of the Reef

effects.log: You sing at nine tribulations in the next age. You do not improve. It does not matter.
You pass the song on to a better voice.

events.text: {npc}, a retired steersman, has asked the Ministry of Precedence for the right to a seat at the Spring Banquet of the Jade Court. Not a good seat. Any seat. "I steered the Court's own isle for nine hundred years," {he} says, "and have never been asked to sit at it." The petition has been ruled upon for forty years.
events.arc: The Petition for a Seat

choices.text: Take the petition to a clerk

effects.log: The clerk is courteous and slow. "It will be considered," says the clerk, in the tone of a closing door.
You collect nineteen signatures from old shipmates. They sign with shaking hands and ready jokes.
{He} laughs. It is not a small thing to be fed.

events.text: The Ministry answers with a form: the petition may be granted if three Ministers of rank will vouch for the petitioner at the banquet itself, in person, at the door. {npc} reads it three times. "That is a seat only for those who already have one," {he} says. The form has a stamp in the shape of a laurel.
events.arc: The Petition for a Seat

effects.log: The first says maybe, the second says later, the third has gone to a wedding.
You tell the story at a tea pavilion in front of forty people, and a Minister in the back goes red.
Even a petition needs a nap.

events.text: The Spring Banquet. {npc} arrives at the door in a borrowed coat, and the three Ministers, as the fates have it, are all in sight. One steps forward, flushed. "I steered with this one in the great drift," the Minister says. "Seat {him} beside me." The doors open. The hall rustles.
events.arc: The Petition for a Seat

effects.log: You are given a stool at the foot of the table, and a very old cup. {npc} weeps into a soup spoon.
You stay outside, cheerful, and the cook sends out a plate.

events.text: The Ministers dither, then rule, in the end, to seat {npc} at the Banquet in the year of the next drift, which is nine hundred years off. {npc} reads this with the calm of a man who has steered through worse. "I shall be there," {he} says. "Save me a stool." The Ministry writes the date in a very small hand.
events.arc: The Petition for a Seat

effects.log: You carve a mark in your own stool for the day. It is in the ledger of the future.
Nine hundred years. It is not so long.

events.text: A clerk of the Ministry of Prayers comes to your door holding a single sheet. "An answer," {npc} says, uneasy. "To a prayer you made four hundred years ago, when you were new here. It was misfiled. It has just surfaced in a drawer." You cannot remember what you asked for.
events.arc: The Answer That Took Four Hundred Years

effects.log: It reads: "Yes. Be patient." You laugh, and cannot stop.
{npc} looks it up. It was for a garden. You have had one for three hundred years.
{He} sighs. "At least someone is gentle about it."

events.text: You are asked to come to the Ministry to receive the answer formally, since the Ministry, on finding a late answer, is obliged to apologise. The apology takes an afternoon. It is long, graceful, and in three tenses. A tray of cakes is brought. The clerks line up to say sorry in turn.
events.arc: The Answer That Took Four Hundred Years

effects.log: You nod at all forty. By the end you are very fond of the clerks, and a little drunk on cake.

choices.text: Ask for the apology to be shortened

effects.log: The Ministry is, as one, appalled. A shorter apology is composed. It is almost as long.
They are good cakes.

events.text: A second letter comes in the clerk's hand: another answer, to another prayer, found in the same drawer, this one older still. It is for a sorrow you thought long forgotten. The answer is a line, a single line, and it is kind. You hold it a while in the quiet.
events.arc: The Answer That Took Four Hundred Years

effects.log: It lies in a drawer of your own, now. It is the right place.
The smoke rises, a thin warm column.

events.text: The Ministry, shamed by the misfile, decides to open every drawer in the archive. The search takes sixty years and returns eleven thousand answers. A great many are delivered to people who have since gone or died. The clerks, it is said, were never so tired or so well loved.
events.arc: The Answer That Took Four Hundred Years

effects.log: You deliver nine. One is received by a child of the person who prayed. The child smiles.
They are on their feet at all hours.

events.text: {npc}, a rogue of twenty years, has bought a small isle at a discount, a leaky, forgotten rock, and wants a mooring licence to tie it to a reef. Rogues may own an isle but may not moor it without a faction's backing. "They say it is for safety," {he} says. "They also say it is for the best."
events.arc: The Rogue Who Wanted a Mooring

effects.log: You write three drafts. The third is courteous, brief, and has a joke on page two.

choices.text: Look for a faction willing to back it

effects.log: You visit four halls. The Star Sea Pavilion shrugs. The Nine Clouds Palace says maybe. The Jade Void is out.
{He} accepts, grateful, and tells you the story of the isle.

events.text: The Ministry of Moorings returns the application with a note: "Insufficient backing. Please consult a faction." {npc} reads it aloud, in a voice that has gone flat. The isle drifts a little farther on its tether each night. "I will lose it," {he} says. "It will drift off one night and I will not even know."
events.arc: The Rogue Who Wanted a Mooring

choices.text: Tie it to your own isle for now

effects.log: You string a line and a bell. The isle jingles gently by your window. It is a very odd neighbour.
A junior clerk grants a one-year provisional berth, in tiny script. It is a small kindness, and not nothing.
The isle bobs. You talk of old voyages.

events.text: The year runs out. At the last day a letter arrives from the Nine Clouds Palace: an elderly weaver has read the story and offered to back the licence, as a small repayment for a kindness fifty years ago that you have both forgotten. {npc} cries openly, in the street, and so does the weaver.
events.arc: The Rogue Who Wanted a Mooring

effects.log: The signature is a small flourish. The licence is stamped. The isle sits still for the first time in a year.
The isle sits at its berth, tidy as a hat.

events.text: The bell-and-line system works for years. {npc}'s isle bobs at your window like a pet. You become used to its shape. At last {npc} finds a backer and moves the isle away. You stand at the window a long time, and the line, still tied, goes slack and trails in the air like a thin goodbye.
events.arc: The Rogue Who Wanted a Mooring

effects.log: It hangs in your hall and rings in the wind. It rings for the isle.
The isle waves back, with a loose rope.

events.text: A chick has fallen from a thunder-sparrow's nest onto your sill, small and grey and shivering with crackles. It cheeps in a voice that raises the hair on your arms. {npc}, who knows birds, says the parents do not return for fallen chicks. "You may keep it," {he} says. "Or you may carry it, like a sweet, to a nest that will take it."
events.arc: The Thunder Sparrow Chick on the Windowsill

effects.log: You warm it in a scarf. It sparks quietly, content, and eats a spoonful of crushed seed.
{npc} points the way. You climb a ridge with a chick in your hat, and find a flock sitting in thunder.

choices.text: Put out a bowl of seed

effects.log: It is gone in a minute. The chick flaps, thrilled.

events.text: The chick grows, and its voice breaks into thunder. It flies a clumsy lap around the room and takes the lampshade with it. The neighbours begin to ask questions. {npc} suggests a training perch outdoors, away from the rafters, and, for the nights, a metal bowl for it to spark into.
events.arc: The Thunder Sparrow Chick on the Windowsill

effects.log: You nail a perch to the garden wall. The bird adopts it at once, and glares.

choices.text: Take it to a flying lesson

effects.log: A flock leader gives it a place at the back of a class. It falls off the first branch and bounces.
The shade is a lost cause, but a happy one.

events.text: The thunder sparrow is full-grown, a storm in a feather coat. It brings gifts to the sill each spring: a bent nail, a bright button, once a small silver bell. It stays for the thunder season each year and leaves with the first clear sky. The bird has two chicks of its own now.
events.arc: The Thunder Sparrow Chick on the Windowsill

effects.log: They cheep in a chorus. The perch is crowded and full of sparks.
The seed is gone by dawn.

events.text: The flock takes the chick, with grave and ruffled courtesy. You return to the ridge each spring to find it, and cannot tell which of a hundred it is. Then one day a bird alights on your shoulder, sparks once, and flies. {npc} says: "That is the one."
events.arc: The Thunder Sparrow Chick on the Windowsill

effects.log: A hundred small heads turn. The thunder is mild.
The flock answers in a roll of low thunder.

events.text: A reef-crab the size of a footstool clambers up the steps of your isle one evening and sits on the porch, snapping gently. {npc}, your neighbour from across the channel, watches from the rail. "They do that," {he} says. "They are looking for someone steady. It will stay as long as you are boring."
events.arc: The Reef-Crab That Followed You Home

choices.text: Offer it a bowl of water

effects.log: It dips a claw, nods, and settles. The porch creaks.
"Longer than us," {he} says. "They always do."
You use the back door for a week.

events.text: The crab begins to sweep. It sweeps the porch, the steps, the path, and then your neighbours' paths, with its great pale claw. Complaints arrive: it has swept up a doormat, a cat, and a minor poet. The cat returned in a bad temper. The poet is still being looked for.
events.arc: The Reef-Crab That Followed You Home

effects.log: You draw chalk lines. It obeys with immense seriousness, and sweeps only the lines.

choices.text: Apologise to the neighbours with pastry

effects.log: The pastry works. The poet is found, in a hedge, composing.
Your path has never been so clean.

events.text: The crab sheds its shell, a great pale husk, and crouches beside it, soft and exposed. It lets no one near for a week. You sit on the porch at a respectful distance, with a lantern, and at night put out small bits of fish. It does not eat them. It watches you watch.
events.arc: The Reef-Crab That Followed You Home

effects.log: You do not sleep much. On the eighth day a bright new shell stands where the old one was.

choices.text: Leave it fish and go in

effects.log: The fish is gone each morning.

events.text: Years pass. The crab sweeps, snaps and sulks, and your porch is the cleanest in the Heavens. When it dies, quietly, on a warm afternoon, the neighbours bring flowers for the great pale shell and set it among the reeds. {npc} says: "Best boring you ever did."
events.arc: The Reef-Crab That Followed You Home

effects.log: The shell is left in the reeds. It sings, faintly, in the wind.
It sits in a jar, an odd and loyal trophy.

events.text: The Demon Realm sends an envoy once a decade to the Cloud Market, to trade black glass for cloud-silk, and the market, rather than feeling honoured, feels watched. {npc}, the envoy, is a tall figure in dark robes with a very large hat. "I am here to be stared at," {he} says wearily. "Please hurry."
events.arc: The Envoy of the Demon Realm at the Cloud Market

effects.log: You hang the black glass. It shimmers in the lantern light. The crowd steps closer, curious.

choices.text: Stand near the envoy and be seen

effects.log: The crowd stares at you, too. It is an education.
The envoy accepts with a nod. The hat stays on.

events.text: A merchant of the Cloud Market spits on the ground by the stall and mutters about "demon trinkets". The envoy does not blink. The crowd goes quiet. A stall-keeper from across the aisle steps forward, takes a bolt of the black glass, and hangs it in her own window. "Best glass I have seen," she says.
events.arc: The Envoy of the Demon Realm at the Cloud Market

effects.log: She waves a hand. "I like it." The merchant goes pink and leaves.
It hangs in your window and turns the sunrise violet.
You do not say a word. The envoy glances at you.

events.text: The market ends. The envoy packs, slow and tired. Before leaving {he} hands you a small black bead. "A guest-token," {he} says. "Show it at any hall of the Realm, and you will be fed three meals." The bead is warm in your hand. {He} puts on the hat and goes into the dusk.
events.arc: The Envoy of the Demon Realm at the Cloud Market

effects.log: It sits in your sleeve like a small ember.
The envoy does not turn, but the hat dips.

events.text: The black glass becomes a quiet fashion on the isles, and by the next decade nearly every window of the Cloud Market has a pane. The envoy comes back a little less weary. The market no longer stares. It buys, and the envoy sells, and the hat, in the end, comes off.
events.arc: The Envoy of the Demon Realm at the Cloud Market

effects.log: The envoy takes off the hat. The face beneath is quite young, and nervous.
The market is happy.

events.text: Once an age the Star Sea Pavilion shows its Unfinished Chart, a map of the heavens left blank in a corner for a star not yet found. {npc}, a chart-warden, leads visitors past the blank. "We may fill it in," {he} says, "or the star may. Whichever comes first." The visitors stand around the blank in reverent hush.
events.arc: The Festival of the Unfinished Chart

effects.log: There is a faint glimmer in your mind where the star should be.

choices.text: Ask what the star will be

effects.log: "Small," says {npc}. "Gentle. We think it will look like a lamp left on."
It is a good thing to bow to.

events.text: A visitor from below, a mortal scholar on a scholarship from the Court, arrives at the Pavilion with a notebook of observations. The Pavilion tolerates the visitor with a certain stiff air. The scholar has found a star not on any chart. {npc} reads the notes, and goes pale, and then red.
events.arc: The Festival of the Unfinished Chart

effects.log: A week of nights and glass. The star is real. It is faint, grey, and lopsided.

choices.text: Praise the scholar to the Pavilion

effects.log: The Pavilion mutters. The scholar is led to the dais with great suspicion and a cup of tea.

choices.text: Offer the scholar a place to rest

effects.log: The scholar sleeps for a day.

events.text: The new star is entered in the blank corner of the Unfinished Chart, in the scholar's hand, with the scholar's name beneath it. The Pavilion stands in silence, and then, to its own surprise, applauds. The scholar, who had expected a lecture, weeps. {npc} says: "We never said it had to be one of us."
events.arc: The Festival of the Unfinished Chart

effects.log: The hall is loud with old hands. The scholar is mobbed with tea.

choices.text: Take the scholar to see the star

effects.log: You look together through the long glass. It is faint and wonderful.

events.text: The Pavilion argues for forty years about whether a mortal can be named in a chart of the heavens. The corner stays blank. The scholar dies below, in old age, and a letter comes up: "Keep the corner for another." {npc} places the letter in the blank, framed.
events.arc: The Festival of the Unfinished Chart

effects.log: You write "Someone will." It hangs in the hall.
The blank is full of possibility.

events.text: A heaven-born child, a frail and earnest one, has asked to be your apprentice in lamp-lighting. {npc} says the child has no talent for flame and an excessive devotion to it. "I will be quite good," the child says, seriously. "I have read about it." Your lamps are low and plain.
events.arc: The Heaven-Born Apprentice of the Lamp-Wright

effects.log: The first week is a flood of questions and spilled oil. The child is cheerful and wholly undeterred.

choices.text: Test the child with a hard wick

effects.log: The child lights it on the fifth try, singed, grinning.

choices.text: Send the child to read more

effects.log: The child returns, a week later, with another book.

events.text: The apprentice's lamps are wrong. They are too bright, or too dim, or too blue. A neighbour complains. Another, oddly, comes to say they are lovely. The apprentice has begun to light the lamps for moods: a quiet lamp, a hopeful lamp, a lamp for the end of a long day. People are asking for them by name.
events.arc: The Heaven-Born Apprentice of the Lamp-Wright

choices.text: Let the child follow the gift

effects.log: You give up a corner of the workshop. The child fills it with strange lamps.

choices.text: Teach the child the old rules first

effects.log: You spend a season on wicks and oils. The child learns, and loses nothing of the strangeness.
It makes you feel, absurdly, that tomorrow will be a good day.

events.text: The apprentice is grown now, a lamp-wright in earnest, and sets a lamp in your window the day you move to a new isle. It is a lamp for a person with a long road ahead and good company. You do not recognise the shape of it. It is perfect. The apprentice stands at the door with a shy, fierce look.
events.arc: The Heaven-Born Apprentice of the Lamp-Wright

effects.log: It glows a gentle gold. The apprentice breathes out.
The apprentice bows. It is a very small, very low bow.

events.text: The apprentice leaves to found a workshop of lamps on the Eastern Reach, and sends, each new year, a lamp in a box with a note. The notes grow longer. The lamps grow stranger. They fill your halls with a soft and varied light, and when visitors ask where the lamps come from, you say: "A student."
events.arc: The Heaven-Born Apprentice of the Lamp-Wright

effects.log: You write a long letter. The reply is a lamp the shape of a heart, or perhaps a pear.

choices.text: Hang the lamps in a row

effects.log: They glow like a conversation.

events.text: A clerk of the Ministry of Prayers visits with an odd report: below, in a mortal valley, a shrine has been raised to you, though you have never been there and done nothing. "Prayers are arriving," says {npc}. "About rain, mostly, and a lost goat." {He} looks embarrassed. "I think it is a mistake. They have you confused."
events.arc: The Shrine That Mortals Built to the Wrong Immortal

effects.log: They are plain and sincere. A boy asks for {his} goat. An old man asks that the roof hold.
{npc} sets it down in a ledger. The shrine, however, remains.
It is not a bad thing to be mistaken for.

events.text: The prayers pile up. The goat is lost for good. The boy prays once, quietly, then again, in a smaller voice. {npc} says the Ministry cannot answer prayers sent to the wrong address. But you could. It would be, strictly, a private act. "It is not done," {he} says. "It is also not forbidden."
events.arc: The Shrine That Mortals Built to the Wrong Immortal

effects.log: You drop through a cloud in a plain coat, and walk a hillside until a bleating leads you to a ravine. The goat is stuck, indignant, unharmed.
A warm light touches the hillside. The boy sees it and looks up, baffled.
The shrine is quiet. You feel it, a little.

events.text: The boy has grown, the goat has died, the shrine stands. The boy, now a man, brings a pot of tea and leaves it each morning at the altar, and you, above, receive a faint warmth every dawn. {npc} says it is the only prayer in the ledger that has never asked for anything.
events.arc: The Shrine That Mortals Built to the Wrong Immortal

effects.log: You send a warm breath each dawn. It is a quiet correspondence.
The tea you make above is the same tea.

events.text: The shrine falls to ruin over the centuries, then is rebuilt by a descendant who does not know whom it honours. The Ministry gives up correcting the ledger. You become, by a mistake and a goat, the minor patron of a quiet valley. It is a very small office. You find you like it.
events.arc: The Shrine That Mortals Built to the Wrong Immortal

effects.log: You sign the ledger. A line of prayers for the valley appears at once.
It is clean and plain. A pot of tea waits on the altar.

events.text: On the night of the Open Doors, every house on the Quay Isle leaves its door ajar, and any stranger may come in for tea, a bun, and one story. The tradition is two thousand years old. {npc}, who has lived on the isle all that time, is hanging a lantern on the latch. "I am nervous every year," {he} says. "Tonight it will be someone."
events.arc: The Festival of Open Doors

effects.log: You enter eight houses. At each, the tea is hot, and the story is better than the last.
You sit by {his} open door. For an hour, nobody comes. Then someone does.
Open doors on both sides, a gold corridor.

events.text: A stranger enters {npc}'s house at midnight, hooded, thin and shy, with a bundle. The stranger asks for tea. {npc} makes it with trembling hands. The stranger does not tell a story. {He} looks at the stranger, then at you. "Perhaps there is none tonight," {he} says. "That is allowed."
events.arc: The Festival of Open Doors

effects.log: The tea is drunk. The silence is warm. When the stranger leaves, a small stone is on the table.

choices.text: Tell a story of your own

effects.log: You tell a short one. The stranger smiles, half hidden, and nods.
The stranger takes it with both hands.

events.text: The stone on the table is small and grey, with a thin crack, and warm. {npc} cannot say whose it is. You put it on the sill. Next year, on the Open Doors, a hooded figure comes to the window and takes it, bows low, and leaves a new stone in its place, a smooth round one, the colour of dusk.
events.arc: The Festival of Open Doors

effects.log: It is cool and quiet. It sits next to a bowl of old tea.

choices.text: Say thank you to the dark

effects.log: The dark is kind.

events.text: You tell your story at the Open Doors, and the stranger carries it away. In some other place, at some other time, a person tells it again. The story changes in the telling. Years later you hear it, from a ferry-hand, and find it better than you wrote it.
events.arc: The Festival of Open Doors

effects.log: You let it be. The story belongs to the road.
The ferry-hand laughs and takes it.

events.text: Two isles, Hearth and Hollow, moored side by side for ten thousand years, quarrel about where one ends and the other begins, and every season they do it in song. {npc}, the choir-master of Hearth, calls the music "a grievance in four parts". Hollow answers in six. Visiting listeners find the debate gorgeous and the content incomprehensible.
events.arc: The Isles That Quarrelled by Singing

effects.log: The Hearth choir sings, the Hollow choir answers. You cry at a modulation.
"A line of reeds," says {npc}, tired. "It has moved."
Both sides accept them.

events.text: You are asked to survey the boundary, as a neutral party, because you have no isle of your own on either side. You walk the line of reeds with a measuring cord, and find that it has not moved. It is in exactly the place the two treaties say. Both choirs have been quarrelling about something else.
events.arc: The Isles That Quarrelled by Singing

choices.text: Tell both choirs what you found

effects.log: There is a long silence, then a laugh from the Hollow side, then a half-hearted answer from Hearth.

choices.text: Quietly ask {npc} what the quarrel is really about

effects.log: {He} looks at the sky. "A broken harp," {he} says. "Nine hundred years ago. It was never mended."
The quarrel goes on, beautifully.

events.text: You and {npc} take the broken harp to a harpist on the Pearl Isle, who mends it in a single night. At the next boundary song, the two choirs perform together, the harp between them, for the first time in nine hundred years. The audience is not sure at first what it is hearing. Then it is.
events.arc: The Isles That Quarrelled by Singing

effects.log: The harp is out of tune, a little. It is lovely.
You are quickly joined.

events.text: The choirs keep quarrelling, but the quarrel has changed: it is now about whether the harp should be tuned a hair sharp or a hair flat. {npc} says it is the best quarrel Hearth has ever had. Hollow, on the other side of the reeds, is smug in six parts. A new composer arrives, who can resolve nothing.
events.arc: The Isles That Quarrelled by Singing

effects.log: It is better than the old. It is nearly pleasant.
No one minds.

events.text: The long cold season comes to the isles, and the shelters of the factions are closed to rogues by a rule older than anyone remembers. A drifter must find a roof, or build one, or freeze in a skiff. You go from door to door on the Heron Isle. At each, a bolt slides. At the last, {npc} opens, a stout widow with a pot on the boil, and says: "In. Do not tell the neighbours."
events.arc: The Winter Without a Roof

effects.log: The room is small and smells of soup. A cat sits on your boots.

choices.text: Offer to chop wood for it

effects.log: "There is a pile," says {npc}. "It is a large pile."
You rest in a skiff under blankets. The cold is clean.

events.text: In the evenings the two of you play an old game of cards and tell the stories of your long lives. {npc} was once a Ministry clerk and left it for reasons {he} will not say. A neighbour knocks, sees you, and goes stiff. "A rogue in the house?" the neighbour says. "It is not done." {npc} looks at the neighbour, mild and steely.
events.arc: The Winter Without a Roof

effects.log: You say you will leave in the morning, and thank {him}. {npc} says nothing. The neighbour, abashed, brings a pie.
{He} says: "My roof, my guest." The neighbour goes. The pie is left by the door, later, without a note.
The cat sits on the cards.

events.text: The thaw comes. The sky opens in long clean strokes, and the skiffs of the fleet come out of the harbour. {npc} presses a coat into your hands, the lining quilted by hand. "A rogue should have a coat," {he} says, "that someone made for them." You sleep that night in a skiff under the new coat and are warm for the first time in a decade.
events.arc: The Winter Without a Roof

effects.log: Every winter, for a hundred years, you knock on the same door. It always opens.
It is the finest thing you own.

events.text: You chop the wood, a great pile, and stack it in the shed in neat rows. {npc} watches from the window and tells you the shed has not been so tidy in thirty years. The neighbours see. By spring, three neighbours have left firewood at your skiff, without a word.
events.arc: The Winter Without a Roof

effects.log: The shed fills. The skiff rides low.

choices.text: Light a fire on the quay

effects.log: The quay gathers, and warms, and talks.

events.text: At the Celestial Ministries there is a clerk, {npc}, who remembers every petition ever filed in the Hall of Petitions, and can recite them. Nobody knows how. It is a skill that cannot be taught or sold. The Ministry treats {him} as a sort of national treasure and avoids having any conversation with {him} lest it be quoted. "I recall," {he} says to you, brightly, "yours."
events.arc: The Clerk Who Remembered Every Petition

effects.log: {npc} recites it. You had asked for a window that faced east. You do now.
{He} hesitates, as if no one has asked in years. "Yes," {he} says. "I would like that."
{He} blushes to the collar.

events.text: The Ministry decides to digitise, in jade slips, the whole Hall of Petitions, and {npc} is told to recite for three years while scribes copy. The scribes tire and complain. {npc} recites on, tireless, polite, a little lost. By the second year {he} has begun to leave out the dull ones. No one notices.
events.arc: The Clerk Who Remembered Every Petition

effects.log: You listen for a day to the petitions of strangers. They are small and large and all human.

choices.text: Help the scribes with the copying

effects.log: Your hand cramps. The petitions of three hundred years pass through you.
They vanish at once.

events.text: The recitation ends. The Ministry holds a ceremony, and {npc} is given a cap of honour. {He} puts it on and gazes at the room. "I recall," {he} says, "that I was supposed to say something." The room waits. "I recall that I was going to say thank you." The room applauds a long time.
events.arc: The Clerk Who Remembered Every Petition

effects.log: You stand. The hall rises.
{He} nods in thanks.

events.text: The scribes finish the slips, and the Hall is put in order. {npc} retires to a quiet isle and does nothing, perfectly, for centuries. Once a year, a letter arrives at your door in a very neat hand. It says only: "I recall you." It is the finest thing that is ever written to you.
events.arc: The Clerk Who Remembered Every Petition

effects.log: The letters go on, short and warm.

choices.text: Keep the letters in a box

effects.log: They accumulate quietly.

events.text: A great wind sheers the top off a cumulus above the Plum Isle and sends it sailing in pieces over the roofs. The folk run out with baskets and catch the larger pieces. By evening, every kitchen on the isle is whipped light and sweet. A poet calls it the best weather of the decade.

effects.log: It dissolves on your tongue, cold and clean.

choices.text: Help a neighbour with a basket

effects.log: The basket is quickly full.

events.text: At dawn the dew-collectors of the Silver Isle walk the grass with spoons, gathering the first drops into jars. They say dew at first light is the sky's memory of the night. A jar sells for a stone. A bad day is a dry one. A good day makes the whole isle shimmer.

effects.log: The dew is cold and has a faint taste of stars.
The isle is a pearl in the first light.

events.text: A picnic for the retired on the Greybeard Isle is cancelled when a tribulation cloud drifts over the lawn and sits down. The retired, to a man, are delighted. They know the sound of a good cloud. A chair is set out for it. A sandwich is offered, and refused, and eaten by the cloud's thunder.

effects.log: The cloud rumbles. The retired applaud.

choices.text: Sit and listen to the stories

effects.log: Every one of them has met this cloud before.

events.text: A skiff, once saved by the storm-eye light, returns after twenty years with a barrel of oil and a card: "We are the ones who thought we were dying." The keeper reads it twice, tucks it into the lamp, and burns the first drops of the new oil that night. The flame is exactly the same.

effects.log: It is a good barrel.
It is the best thank-you note you have ever seen.

events.text: From inside the storm-eye the wall of cloud is a vast circle of grey on all sides, rising to a round of blue overhead. It is the shape of a well. Gulls circle in it without hurry. You feel, for the first time, quite small and quite safe at once.

choices.text: Stay a while and look up

effects.log: The round of sky is very bright.
They wheel in widening gyres.

events.text: There is a rule of the Jade Court that cushions must be three fingers thick for ministers, two for marshals, and one for everyone else. A clerk with a ruler goes down the rows. The cushions are measured, adjusted, and measured again. A guest sits on the floor out of embarrassment. It is, by the rules, correct.

choices.text: Sit on the floor with the guest

effects.log: The floor is cool and honest.
It is within a hair of the right thickness.

events.text: A tea-seller works the long queue outside the Hall of Petitions, with a cart that rolls slowly down the line. The queue is a year long. The tea-seller knows the names of everyone, and the number of their petition, and how long they have left. The tea-seller is the only one who is ever hurried.

effects.log: The tea is hot and kind.

choices.text: Ask the tea-seller how long you have

effects.log: "Years," says the seller. "But the tea is quick."

events.text: A stall sells starlight in jars, three grades: clear, pearly, and "what the star was thinking". The clear is cheap and the thinking is not. You sniff the thinking. It smells of someone about to say something kind and not quite doing it.

choices.text: Buy a jar of the pearly (2 Low-Grade Spirit Stones)

effects.log: It glows on your shelf, calm and milky.
The seller gives it for a smile.

events.text: At the Cloud Market a stall-keeper refuses to sell you tea because you wear no faction badge. A little crowd looks on. An old immortal in a Jade Void robe steps up, buys a cup, and hands it to you with a bow. "A gift," says the stranger. "From someone who has been where you stand." The stall-keeper looks at the ground.

effects.log: You drink. The tea is strong.
You share. The stranger grins.

events.text: Behind the main aisle of the Cloud Market runs a back alley where the rogues set out their goods on blankets: patched cloaks, home-brewed wine, repaired lamps. The prices are fair. The jokes are better. A rogue woman sells charms she calls "ordinary luck". You buy one. It works rather well.

effects.log: It is a plain knot of thread. You feel better.

choices.text: Sell a small thing of your own

effects.log: It goes in minutes. The alley hums.

events.text: A bridge between the Quill and the Willow isles has a toll of one line of poetry. The keeper writes each line in a long scroll. After a thousand years the scroll has become the longest poem in the Heavens, and it is, remarkably, quite good. You pay your line. It sits near the middle.

choices.text: Pay a line of your own

effects.log: The keeper reads it with approval and writes it.
It is moving, in a patchwork way.

events.text: A small wind has been following you round the isle for a week, tugging your sleeve. Today it carries a faint scent of cinnamon and distant rain. It wants something. You open the window, and the wind enters, brushes the room, finds nothing, and lays itself down on the floor with a sigh.

effects.log: It rests there, content, a long while.

choices.text: Open the door and let it go

effects.log: It leaves, tugging a sleeve in thanks.

events.text: In a corner of the Hush Isle a wind blows through a row of hollow reeds, played by nobody, every evening. People gather to listen. The tune is never the same twice. A child asks if the wind is lonely. The musician, who is a very old immortal, says: "Only when nobody listens."

effects.log: The last note is a long sigh.
The wind adjusts, politely.

events.text: A baker on the Dumpling Isle hides a tiny folded note in one bun in a hundred. The notes are small kindnesses: "You are enough." "Drink some water." "That was brave." Customers bite, wonder, and sometimes weep. The baker, who is shy, never looks at who finds one.

effects.log: Your note says: "Slow down." You do.

choices.text: Leave a note in a bun for a stranger

effects.log: The baker nods without looking up.

events.text: The porridge-makers of the Eastern Reach have been arguing about the right amount of salt since the First Age. The argument is carried on in a series of cooks' contests, none of which is decisive. At the last one, the winner is a child who adds no salt, and a great deal of cream. It is declared a draw.

effects.log: You taste eleven. Each is the best.
The child bows.

events.text: The Archive of Pearl has moved a room again. This time the Hall of Astronomy has slid sideways over the Hall of Tides, and the two have fallen into a conversation. A young clerk is sent in with a notepad. The clerk returns an hour later, pale. "They are in agreement," the clerk says. "About everything."

effects.log: Two sets of scrolls whisper together. It is an unsettling harmony.
You write down "ask later".

events.text: In a jade slip from the Third Age, an archivist finds a faint tea-ring. A careful reading reveals that the original copyist had paused mid-sentence to drink. The pause is notated in a margin note: "Hot." The archivist smiles, and files the slip with great tenderness.

effects.log: Hot. You taste the tea across three thousand years.

choices.text: Add a ring of your own

effects.log: You set a cup on a spare slip. It is a small act of continuity.

events.text: A ferry across the Sapphire Lake is poled by an old immortal with a dog. The dog collects the fares in a cap and counts them with its nose. It has not yet been wrong. Passengers are delighted. On the far shore, the dog is given a biscuit and allowed to sniff the sun.

effects.log: It sniffs your coin, approves, and licks your hand.
It eats it with great ceremony.

events.text: A shelter in the cloud-bamboo is just a roof on four poles, and under it, on rainy days, six or seven strangers sit and wait. They do not speak. The rain drums. When it ends they all stand at once, nod, and go separate ways. It is the best conversation you have had all week.

effects.log: The rain is a kind of company.
The others nod back.

events.text: A runner on the Stair of Ten Thousand Steps carries letters up and down, and has done for four centuries. The runner does not seem to tire, and once, asked why, said: "I do not count." You decide to try that for an hour. Somewhere around the three-thousandth step, you forget what a step is.

effects.log: The stair loses its edges and becomes a slope.

choices.text: Carry a letter for the runner

effects.log: It is light and easy.

events.text: Halfway up a peak on the Greyhorn Isle there is a flat rock where hikers eat lunch. Everyone says the same thing as they sit: "Oh, the view." A hiker with an unusual sandwich, a slab of fried cloud, is asked about it by six strangers. By dessert they are friends.

effects.log: It is accepted, and replaced with a slice of someone else's.
The hiker grins and gives out the recipe.

events.text: On the Hill of Bells each stone has a small bell tied to it, and the wind rings them in turns. Walkers stroll through the music, and the notes shift as they move. At the summit, one bell is larger, and silent. A sign reads: "For the one who ought to come." No one has rung it yet.

effects.log: The bells follow you in a warm wave.
It does not ring, but trembles.

events.text: Gulls at the Edge of Heaven carry messages for a fee of one fish. The messages are always short. "Fine." "Come soon." "I am sorry." One is addressed simply "To the sky". The gull seems to know where it goes. It drops the note off the Edge and watches it fall.

effects.log: It says "Thank you". The gull flies out of sight.

choices.text: Read the notes on the Edge-post

effects.log: A hundred small sentences.

events.text: A school of sky-whale calves is led past the Greyfin Isle in a line, each hugging the tail of the next. A teacher whale chides them in a low voice. The calves bump each other, breach clumsily, and sink back. The crowd on the quay sighs as one at their awkwardness.

effects.log: One waves a fin, then dives in embarrassment.
It is a lesson in patience.

events.text: A hot spring under a teahouse floor has been enclosed in a stone cup the size of a bathtub, and customers soak while they sip. The proprietor mixes the tea with the spring-water, which makes the tea faintly effervescent. It is, by all accounts, the best bath in the Heavens.

effects.log: The water is warm and fizzy.
