It tickles the nose.

events.text: At the Lamp Festival of the Reed Isle each person hangs a lantern, but most are too shy to hang their own. A tradition has grown of hanging a neighbour's lantern instead. By midnight every house is lit by someone else. It is the best way to learn who loves you.

effects.log: You choose the quietest one. It glows.

choices.text: Find your own, hung by another

effects.log: It is a plum-red lantern, well hung.

events.text: Notices go up for the Season of the Thunder Sparrows: where the flocks will land, which hills are closed to walkers, how loud the thunder will be. A child, asked what the hunt is for, says: "To watch." The hunters carry only spyglasses and thermoses of tea.

effects.log: You watch a flock land on a hill, storms folded in their wings.
They are written in cheerful chalk.

events.text: A wind serpent has curled up for a nap on the roof of the pavilion. It is the length of three skiffs and weighs nothing. The proprietor has covered it with a quilt. Customers are asked to sip softly. The serpent breathes out, once, and the lanterns all sway the same way.

effects.log: You sit in the hush. It is nearly holy.
The serpent sighs and lets you.

events.text: A flight of stairs in the Ash Isle ruins climbs twelve steps and stops in the air. Walkers climb and stand at the top and look at the sky, just to say they did. Some leave a pebble. The pebbles have piled into a cairn. No one knows what the stair was for.

effects.log: The view from the top is the same view, a little higher.
It joins the cairn.

events.text: A small wooden door set into the underside of an isle is warm to the touch. Behind it, you hear a faint domestic clatter. You knock. The clatter stops. After a long time a voice says, kindly: "Not today, thank you." You back away, comforted, though you cannot say why.

choices.text: Leave a loaf by the door

effects.log: It is gone, later, and a button is left in its place.
A small laugh from behind the door.

events.text: In a hollow of the Moss Isle live the mushroom folk, tiny, round, very polite. They have a town hall the size of a thimble and a mayor who wears a feather. A visiting giant, you are told, is a great event. You are offered a sip of dew from a bowl the size of a pea. You accept with great care.

effects.log: It tastes of cold green mornings.
The mayor bows lower.

events.text: The oldest cloud-pine of the Elder Isle has a record of every visitor in its rings. A tree-warden shows you: here a storm, here a wedding, here a very hard winter. The warden finds a ring from the year you came to the Heavens and puts a gentle finger on it. It is a thin, green, hopeful ring.

effects.log: It is smooth and warm.
You lose count at four thousand.

events.text: On the night the moon-lilies open on the Pale Isle, the whole slope is white, and everyone walks very softly. A child asks a question out loud, and every flower turns toward the sound. The child stops, startled, and says "sorry" in a whisper. The slope sighs, and turns away.

effects.log: You pass through the white slope without a word.
A lily turns to you.

events.text: On the Swallow Isle a swing hangs from a cloud-pine over the cliff, high as a tower. The folk take turns on it at sunset, shrieking. It is perfectly safe, as the rope is spun from sky-silk, and perfectly terrifying. A grandmother goes on it first, every night, in a hat.

effects.log: You swing out over nothing and back. Your stomach stays at the top.
She is calm and magnificent.

events.text: Children of the Cinder Isle play a game in an old starfall crater, rolling pebbles up the inner slope. The pebbles roll back. The child whose pebble stays longest wins. A pebble that stays is called a "star-friend", and is kept. The crater is half full of friends.

effects.log: It rolls up, and up, and back.
The child looks very pleased.

events.text: On the long ferry from the Orchard Isle to the Tern Isle, the passengers sing round songs, each adding a line. By the end, the song is nonsense and everyone is in tears from laughing. The ferry-hand collects the lines in a notebook, and is said to have the longest song in the Heavens.

effects.log: It is applauded.
The sea of cloud rolls past.

events.text: A cat sits in your window at the end of the day and looks at the sunset with the air of a critic. The sky is magnificent. The cat gives it a low grade, and goes in. You consider the sky again. It is a little over-orange, perhaps. It is still magnificent.

effects.log: The cat flicks an ear.
It is a very good one.

events.text: On the Marsh Isle a clock stands in the square that tells the tides of the cloud-sea, not the hours. The islanders read it as easily as bread. A visitor asks the time and is baffled by the reply: "Half-ebb, rising." Everyone agrees that this is what time is.

effects.log: It takes a day. After that, hours seem arbitrary.

choices.text: Ask what the next tide brings

effects.log: "Fish," says an islander. "And weather."

events.text: In the Demon Realm lamps are not lit but tempered. {npc}, an ember-smith, hammers each flame into shape on an anvil of black glass and sells it by the hand-span. {He} takes on a new apprentice every century, and this century {he} has looked at you across the counter for a long while.
events.arc: The Ember-Smith of the Demon Realm

effects.log: {npc} points at a basket the size of a barrel. You carry it all morning.

choices.text: Ask what a good flame sounds like

effects.log: "Like a held breath," {he} says. "Come back at dusk and I will show you."
{He} wraps it in a leaf. It purrs in your sleeve.

events.text: At dusk {npc} shows you the quenching: a flame plunged into cold wind until it holds its shape. "Most flames want to be bigger," {he} says. "A good smith teaches them to stay the size they are." Your first flame comes out the shape of a lopsided pear. {He} nods, kindly, and says it will do.
events.arc: The Ember-Smith of the Demon Realm

effects.log: It sits on your sill and burns a steady, ridiculous gold.
You ruin eleven flames and the twelfth comes out almost round.
You walk home with warm hands.

events.text: Years on, {npc} sets out a lamp-festival and gives you the centre stall. The lamps of your making are plain, small, and even. A crowd of Demon Realm folk lingers in front of them. "Honest light," one says, and buys three. {npc} stands at the back of the hall with {his} arms folded, and does not trouble to hide the pride.
events.arc: The Ember-Smith of the Demon Realm

choices.text: Give the profit to the smithy

effects.log: The stones go into the glass-stock. The anvil is re-faced that spring.

choices.text: Share the stall with other apprentices

effects.log: It becomes a row of apprentices, shoulder to shoulder.

events.text: {npc} grows old and slow, and hands you the hammer on a night when the wind is perfect. "Do not make my flames," {he} says. "Make yours." You temper one that comes out nothing like {his}, a tall pale flame, shy and straight. The black glass rings. {npc} laughs, and sits down on the anvil-stool at last.
events.arc: The Ember-Smith of the Demon Realm

effects.log: The sign is repainted with both your names. The hammer is warm in your hand.

choices.text: Keep the tall flame as a gift to {him}

effects.log: {He} keeps it by the bed, where it does not flicker.

events.text: {npc} keeps the great dome of the Star Sea Pavilion and has counted the same sky every night for four hundred years. Tonight the count is one short. "A small one, in the Ladle," {he} says, very quietly. "It was there at the last turn." The charts are consulted, and then the other charts.
events.arc: The Dome-Keeper Who Counted Missing Stars

effects.log: You turn pages until dawn and find the star in a margin note, annotated "will return."
The two of you sit under the dome with a flask. Nothing happens, slowly.
{npc} is grateful that the dome is quiet.

events.text: The margin note was in the hand of {npc}'s own teacher, three hundred years gone. It says the star goes out for a season each age and comes back brighter. "Why was I not told?" {he} asks the empty room. Then, because the dome is vast and kind, {he} begins to laugh at it, in small spurts.
events.arc: The Dome-Keeper Who Counted Missing Stars

choices.text: Copy the note for the dome-book

effects.log: The book gets a footnote. {npc} blots it with a sleeve.
The tea steadies {his} hands.

events.text: For sixty nights the Ladle has a gap. Then one evening a pale light flickers in it, no brighter than a candle behind a curtain. {npc} does not cry out. {He} takes off {his} hat and holds it to {his} chest while the star settles into its place, and the dome, for a moment, hums.
events.arc: The Dome-Keeper Who Counted Missing Stars

effects.log: The two of you sign the page. The ink dries before the star stops trembling.
It rings once, low, over the Star Sea.

events.text: The star never comes back. {npc} counts, season after season, and the count stays short. In time {he} amends the dome-book, kindly: "One star walked on. We kept the seat." Visitors ask about the empty place in the Ladle, and {he} says, "It is not empty. It is saved."
events.arc: The Dome-Keeper Who Counted Missing Stars

choices.text: Add your name to the book

effects.log: The page now reads "kept by two." It is a small kindness to a very large sky.

choices.text: Leave a lamp in the gap

effects.log: A tiny flame burns where the star was.

events.text: The sect you founded has grown to nine halls, and one of them, the Hall of Morning Sweeping, is run by {npc}, who joined you in the first year and has not once asked for anything. {He} comes to you now with a ledger. "The Hall has forty-one members," {he} says, "and no one knows what it is for."
events.arc: The Hall of Morning Sweeping

effects.log: "Waking up," {he} says. "Somebody must be first." You write it down.

choices.text: Declare it the heart of the sect

effects.log: You give a speech on brooms. Forty-one people nod gravely.
The broom is lighter than expected.

events.text: The Hall of Morning Sweeping asks for a bell, a hot bath for the members, and a day off each season. The other halls object loudly. The Hall of Letters says that sweeping is not cultivation. The Hall of Swords says that it is a defence against dust. {npc} waits in the corner, not arguing, as if the matter were weather.
events.arc: The Hall of Morning Sweeping

choices.text: Grant the bath and the day off

effects.log: The other halls grumble for a week and then borrow the bath.

choices.text: Hold a debate between the halls

effects.log: The debate runs eleven hours. The Hall of Swords wins on points and loses the argument.
The bell sounds at dawn. Forty-one people wake.

events.text: A century on, the Hall of Morning Sweeping has the cleanest steps in the sky and the happiest members of any hall. Disciples of other halls begin to ask to join it for a year. {npc} accepts all of them, and sets each at a single step for a month. "Learn one thing," {he} says, "before you learn anything."
events.arc: The Hall of Morning Sweeping

choices.text: Make the year in the Hall required

effects.log: The sect becomes known for its manners. Visitors remark on the swept air.
The Hall stays small and fond.

events.text: Ten years pass, and {npc} turns up at your door with the ledger and a shy look. "The Hall is closing," {he} says. "Not from failure. We have swept everything." You walk the grounds and every step is clean. The members stand in the courtyard, a little lost, holding their brooms at their sides.
events.arc: The Hall of Morning Sweeping

choices.text: Give the Hall a new work: the gardens

effects.log: The brooms go into the garden, and the Hall reopens in spring.
They drink tea on the swept stones, a thing they had never done.

events.text: A heaven-born child is carried into the tea pavilion on the Mulberry Isle, swaddled in cloud-silk, and named {npc} for the season of the birth: the Season of Slow Rain. The whole isle files past to say a word to the infant. {He} sleeps through all of them, except yours, at which {he} opens one eye.
events.arc: The Child Named for a Season

effects.log: The eye closes. You are fairly sure it approved.
A silver bell for a cot. {npc}'s parents tie it on at once.
The queue behind you thanks you.

events.text: The child is thirty, which on the Mulberry Isle means barely walking. {npc} toddles up to you at the market with a fist full of petals and says, in very clear words, "I have decided to be a cloud." The mother shrugs. You are expected to answer.
events.arc: The Child Named for a Season

effects.log: "A tall one," {he} says. "With no thunder." The plan is noted.
A ribbon for a cloud. {He} ties it to {his} wrist and rises on tiptoe.
{He} nods the way the very small nod.

events.text: Eighty years on, {npc} comes to your door with a travelling pack and a face like a closed shutter. "I am going to see the Edge of Heaven," {he} says. "Everyone says it is only a place. I want to say it to its face." You see in the set of {his} chin that the cloud was never a game.
events.arc: The Child Named for a Season

effects.log: Three jars and a map with one crossed-out route. {He} takes them both.

choices.text: Go with {him} as far as the last isle

effects.log: The two of you ride a skiff in companionable silence.
{He} accepts the wish with a bow.

events.text: Two centuries later, a stranger stops you on a cloud-bridge: a tall figure, thin, quietly shining, trailing a ribbon from {his} wrist. It is {npc}, grown and free of the isle. "I found it," {he} says. "It is only a place. Come and see how kind it was."
events.arc: The Child Named for a Season

choices.text: Say you would be glad to

effects.log: You go, and the place is kind. There is a bench at the end of the world, and someone has left it a cushion.

choices.text: Tell {him} to come to tea instead

effects.log: The story takes an afternoon, and is worth every minute.

events.text: {npc}, a rogue with no isle and no faction, sells dried pears from a basket at the foot of the cloud-bridge, where the stall rent is nothing because no one else will stand there. The wind comes up through the planks and carries the pears off. "I would pay rent for a better spot," {he} says, "if anyone would let me."
events.arc: The Rogue Who Earned a Stall

choices.text: Speak for {him} to the market warden

effects.log: The warden says rogues stand where rogues stand. Your word is noted, and not used.

choices.text: Buy a bag and keep returning

effects.log: A dozen visits and a dozen bags. The pears are very good.
The wind is playful and the basket is light.

events.text: A rogue may take a stall only after a "season of proof": three months in which {npc} must sell, tidily and without complaint, in the worst spot, under the eye of a clerk. {He} does it with a stiff back. A faction stall across the way charges triple for the same pears and is never asked to prove anything.
events.arc: The Rogue Who Earned a Stall

choices.text: Tell the clerk what you see

effects.log: The clerk writes it down and looks uncomfortable. It is a small crack.
The friends you gather buy out the basket. The clerk counts nine sales.
You sit on an upturned crate and watch the sky.

events.text: The season of proof ends. The clerk, stiffly, grants {npc} a stall licence with a stamp the colour of a bruise. {He} is given a spot on the main bridge, two stalls from the Jade Void tea-seller, who sniffs. {npc} hangs a sign: "Pears. No faction. No hurry." The queue is long by noon.
events.arc: The Rogue Who Earned a Stall

effects.log: It is straight enough. It is perfect.
It tastes of the sun and of a bridge in the wind.

events.text: The crowd you gathered stays. {npc} sells out before noon three days running, and the market warden, noting the crowd, quietly moves {him} to a better place without calling it a favour. "I will take it," {he} says. "I will not pretend it was kind." That, you think, is the better reply.
events.arc: The Rogue Who Earned a Stall

choices.text: Say you will bring a crowd again

effects.log: You do. It becomes a habit on the bridge.
You share it on the bridge in the wind.

events.text: A star-moth lands in your window at the turning of the year, silver-winged and no larger than a thumbnail, and refuses to leave. {npc}, the lamp-wright next door, says moths of this sort live a thousand years and attach themselves to lamps, not people. "Yours must be a lamp," {he} says, looking at you over the sill.
events.arc: The Star-Moth That Outlived Three Lamps

choices.text: Give it a lamp of its own

effects.log: You light a small one in the window. The moth circles it twice and settles.

choices.text: Name it and keep it close

effects.log: You call it Wick. It flutters to your shoulder and sleeps there.
It comes and goes, and stays.

events.text: Wick has grown. Its wings now reach the span of your hand and glow faintly when it is happy. It follows you to the market and the tea pavilion and, once, to a meeting of the Court, where it perched on the Minister of Precedence and was not asked to leave. Wherever it lands, quiet falls.
events.arc: The Star-Moth That Outlived Three Lamps

effects.log: The archivists let it sleep in a lantern. The scrolls near it brighten.

choices.text: Keep it out of the Court

effects.log: You take care. It sulks in a sleeve for a week.

choices.text: Let it choose where to land

effects.log: It chooses, as always, wisely.

events.text: The lamp you lit for the moth has burned out after three hundred years. Wick flutters round the cold glass in the window, dim, confused. {npc} comes by to look at it with a long face. "They do not like to outlive their lamps," {he} says. "I can make a new one, if you will let me."
events.arc: The Star-Moth That Outlived Three Lamps

effects.log: The new lamp is made from your old one's glass, relit. Wick sighs.
The flame is yours, and the moth knows it.

events.text: Seven centuries on, Wick lies still in the lantern in your window. It does not move, and the glow in its wings has dimmed to the colour of pearl. You hold it in your hands a long time. When the sun comes up it is gone, and where it lay there is a small pale dust, bright in the light, like a faint star.
events.arc: The Star-Moth That Outlived Three Lamps

choices.text: Scatter the dust over the Star Sea

effects.log: It drifts out in a fine silver line and joins the stars.

choices.text: Keep a pinch in a locket

effects.log: The locket is warm all your years.

events.text: Every nine decades the isles of the Larch Fleet drift apart for a long season, each toward its own winds. {npc}, the Fleet's oldest steersman, goes from isle to isle with a hand-bell, saying goodbye. {He} stops at your door. "Four hundred years since the last parting. Some of us will not be back."
events.arc: The Fleet That Parted at the Season of Drift

effects.log: A wind-chime. {He} hangs it from the bell on the pole, and they sing together.

choices.text: Offer to steer one of the isles

effects.log: You take a rope. It is a hard drift and an honest one.
{He} says everyone does, and no one does. You will.

events.text: The Fleet drifts. Your isle catches a cold current and falls into a corner of the sky where nobody sails. The nights are long and the neighbours are all new. A fogbound isle drifts alongside, with a lamp at the prow and a small, bright voice calling hello across the gap.
events.arc: The Fleet That Parted at the Season of Drift

effects.log: You trade stories across a hundred yards of cloud. It is a new friendship.

choices.text: Keep to your own isle for the season

effects.log: You mend, read, and let the quiet in.
They wave back, which is something.

events.text: When the Fleet gathers again, nine decades later, the isles ring into place one after another like keys on a bunch. {npc} is on the dock with the same bell, grey, thin and cheerful. "I counted," {he} says. "Fourteen of us missing. Eleven came back with new friends." You stand together and watch the ropes come in.
events.arc: The Fleet That Parted at the Season of Drift

effects.log: They shake hands with {npc}. The Fleet has one more name in its book.
Everyone rings it once.

events.text: When the Fleet gathers again, you are the one on the dock with the bell. {npc} is not there, and a note in the ledger says only: "Drifted on." You ring the bell for each missing name. The wind-chime you once gave still hangs from the pole, and for a long time it sings with the bell.
events.arc: The Fleet That Parted at the Season of Drift

effects.log: You carry it to every isle in turn, saying goodbye and hello.

choices.text: Write the note in the ledger

effects.log: You write: "Thank you." It will do.

events.text: {npc}, a clerk of the Ministry of Prayers, comes quietly with a ledger and says that someone you knew in the mortal world, long ago, has died below. It was an old age, and gentle. "I thought you would want to hear it from a person," {he} says. "Not from a notice."
events.arc: The Grave You Cannot Visit

effects.log: You sit. The tea goes cold. It is a small mercy to have someone beside you.

choices.text: Ask for a name and a place

effects.log: {He} writes them on a slip. The place is a hill you remember.

choices.text: Thank {him} and go for a walk

effects.log: The walk takes you to the edge of the isle and back.

events.text: You cannot visit a grave below. The stairs are long, and the rule is old, and a path down would cost a year of standing and a year of your life. So you do the next thing: you plant a peach on the edge of your own isle, in the direction of the hill. It is a small seedling. It leans toward the ground.
events.arc: The Grave You Cannot Visit

effects.log: The seedling takes. You talk to it, now and then, without meaning to.

choices.text: Say a few words over it

effects.log: You say the person's name aloud. The wind carries it down.
It lives on rain and sky.

events.text: A hundred years pass. The peach bears fruit, small and hard and very sweet. You do not eat the first. You set it on a plate under the tree and sit with it until evening. The clerk of the Prayers arrives with a new ledger, sees the tree, and sits beside you without a word. {npc} eats the second one.
events.arc: The Grave You Cannot Visit

choices.text: Share the fruit with the Prayers clerks

effects.log: The Ministry has a bowl of your peaches by the gate each autumn.
It is sweet. It tastes of a hill.

events.text: The tree grows old and tall, and each year you say the name when the blossom comes. A heaven-born child asks who it is for, and you tell the story, in the plainest words. The child listens, solemn. "Then it is not a tree," says the child. "It is a letter." You think that is the right word.
events.arc: The Grave You Cannot Visit

effects.log: The child waters it every week, and says the name too.
The tree needs nothing more.

events.text: {npc} has tied knots for six centuries and now is said to know eleven thousand. On the dock of the Reedy Isle, {he} sits and ties a mooring rope in a hitch that, in the old books, no one has seen since the war. A crowd gathers. "It is a hobby," {he} says, red to the ears. "I tie them to calm down."
events.arc: The Immortal Who Mastered Knots

effects.log: {He} teaches you the three-turn hitch. It takes a week and holds forever.
The crowd cheers. {npc} bows to the rope.
The rope seems to tie itself.

events.text: The Ministry of Moorings summons {npc} to a hearing: its hitches are so good that no boat on the Reedy Isle can be untied by anyone else. The harbour-master has been stuck for a week. "It is not a fault," {npc} says. "It is a safety." The hearing is held on the dock, over a tangle of rope.
events.arc: The Immortal Who Mastered Knots

effects.log: You argue that a knot you cannot untie is a knot you can trust. The room mutters.
You pick at it for an hour, and it falls open at last, to a roar of cheers.
You sit in silence on the dock.

events.text: The harbour-master and {npc} agree on a compromise: every knot gets a small hidden tail that can be pulled by anyone who knows the trick. The trick is published as a pamphlet, "A Short Account of Gentle Hitches," in nine hundred copies. It is the Reedy Isle's bestselling book for a hundred years.
events.arc: The Immortal Who Mastered Knots

choices.text: Take a copy to the archive

effects.log: The archivists shelve it between a poem and a map.
{He} inspects it for a long time and says nothing, which is high praise.

events.text: {npc} grows old and stops tying. The ropes of the Reedy Isle are all in the hands of apprentices now, and they hold, mostly. One evening {he} sits with a bit of string and fumbles a knot, and looks at it, and laughs. "It is a bad one," {he} says. "I like it." You keep it in your sleeve for the next five hundred years.
events.arc: The Immortal Who Mastered Knots

effects.log: It never comes undone. You never try.

choices.text: Teach the apprentices the bad knot

effects.log: They tie it to be kind.

events.text: You and {npc} have been neighbours for six centuries, and have a fence between your gardens of peaches and plum. This morning {he} has moved it a hand's breadth. Nothing is said. In the evening you move it back a hand's breadth and a little more. This is how the quarrel begins.
events.arc: The Two Gardens and the Fence Between Them

effects.log: By week's end the fence has crossed the lawn twice. You are quietly pleased.

choices.text: Go and ask what is wrong

effects.log: {He} says nothing is wrong. Then, over a cup, something is.
The fence stays crooked, and so do you.

events.text: The quarrel has grown too large for a fence. {npc} will not take your greeting at the market, and you will not give it back. A mutual friend, a tea-seller, carries sour messages in both directions. "You are both acting like two old trees," the tea-seller says. "Too stubborn to bend."
events.arc: The Two Gardens and the Fence Between Them

effects.log: The letter is stiff and short. It is also a start.
The fence is a wall now. The quiet is thick.
The tea-seller shrugs. "Fence, mostly."

events.text: {npc}'s answer comes in a basket of plums over the fence. No letter. The plums are the best of the year. You eat the first on your knees by the wall and laugh at yourselves. The next morning the fence is gone and a bench sits where it was. Neither of you has said who built it.
events.arc: The Two Gardens and the Fence Between Them

choices.text: Sit on the bench at dusk

effects.log: {npc} turns up with tea. The bench holds both of you.
The plums and peaches share a plate.

events.text: You never speak again of the fence, and by the time the isle drifts into a new season you cannot remember who started it. {npc} grows quiet and old, and one day goes to a farther isle. You find the fence, mended, and a plank of it left on your side, with a mark carved: "Thank you for the nine hundred good years."
events.arc: The Two Gardens and the Fence Between Them

choices.text: Carve a reply on the plank

effects.log: You write: "Same." It seems enough.

choices.text: Plant a plum by the fence

effects.log: The tree takes well.

events.text: In the Demon Realm every stall at the night market sells its goods twice: once at dusk, to the buyer, and once at dawn, back to the seller, at a smaller price. It is thought a matter of manners. {npc}, a trader, takes you round and explains the custom. "Nothing is truly owned," {he} says. "Only borrowed with ceremony."
events.arc: The Night Market Where Everything Is Sold Twice

effects.log: It costs two stones. It is the best lantern you have owned for a night.

choices.text: Ask to be shown the dawn sale

effects.log: {npc} promises, and then tells the tale of how it was invented.
No one minds. Browsing, here, is its own trade.

events.text: At dawn you carry the lantern back to the stall. The seller counts the price carefully, hands over a quarter of what you paid, and bows. You bow back. {npc} watches and says nothing, and then says, "That, my friend, is a Demon Realm friendship. You return what you were lent, and leave smiling."
events.arc: The Night Market Where Everything Is Sold Twice

effects.log: You get one stone back, and a friendly nod.

choices.text: Keep the lantern, pay the difference

effects.log: The seller is moved. It is an unusual thing to do.

choices.text: Ask what happens to a lantern no one buys

effects.log: "It is sold to the night," says {npc}.

events.text: {npc} invites you to the trader's feast, held at dawn when the stalls close. Everything on the table has been sold twice and eaten once. A great shared pot of noodle soup goes round. You are asked to say a few words. You say, awkwardly, that the custom has made you feel borrowed and welcome, and the room cheers.
events.arc: The Night Market Where Everything Is Sold Twice

choices.text: Raise a cup to the custom

effects.log: The cup is raised in unison. It is full of something warm and strange.
Washing the pot is a high honour.

events.text: You return to the night market a century later with a gift, a lantern you made. The stall-keeper, white-haired now, looks at it a long time. "Dusk or dawn?" they ask. "Dusk," you say. They place it in the front of the stall, between a mask and a bowl, and the lantern sells for nine stones before you finish your tea.
events.arc: The Night Market Where Everything Is Sold Twice

choices.text: Take the nine stones back to the smith

effects.log: The smithy is delighted. You are asked to make more.
It is cheaper than you hoped.

events.text: {npc} joined the Star Sea Pavilion as an apprentice navigator, and cannot read a chart. The letters swim, the lines slide. All the others pity {him}. {He} comes to you at the end of the week, and says, in a low voice, "I can feel where the stars are, and I cannot say how. May I tell you?"
events.arc: The Navigator Who Could Not Read Charts

effects.log: {He} describes a sense like a pulse behind the ears. It is a rare gift.
With a cloth on, {he} points to nine stars in a row. Eight are right.
The secret is a small, warm weight.

events.text: The Pavilion's masters find out, and are divided. One says a navigator who cannot read the charts is a menace. Another says the charts are only a crutch. The master of charts, a stern old figure, requires {npc} to sit an examination in front of the whole Pavilion, with chart in hand. {He} looks at you across the hall.
events.arc: The Navigator Who Could Not Read Charts

choices.text: Stand by {him} in front of the masters

effects.log: You speak for {him}, plainly. The master of charts raises an eyebrow.

choices.text: Offer to read the chart aloud for {him}

effects.log: The two of you work as one voice. It is a clever arrangement.
You wait. The hall is silent for an hour.

events.text: {npc} passes the examination, in a way: {he} points out the star the master of charts had misdrawn for two centuries. The hall is stunned. The master of charts bows, slowly, and says, "A navigator needs to know where the stars are. The charts are for those who do not." {npc} is given a seat on the high dais.
events.arc: The Navigator Who Could Not Read Charts

effects.log: {He} drinks it quickly, and cries, a bit.
Some victories are best left to the one who earned them.

events.text: {npc} and you start a small school for navigators who cannot read, in a corner of the Pavilion. It has four students the first year and eleven the second. The charts on the wall are replaced with a single bare slate and a bell. The Pavilion's masters pretend not to notice it, and send their own students there by night.
events.arc: The Navigator Who Could Not Read Charts

effects.log: You teach them to listen for the sky. They are surprisingly good.
They are used as kites.

events.text: Fifty years ago a disciple of the sect left in anger over a matter of seating. Today {npc} stands at your gate in travelling clothes, a little rumpled, holding a tin. "Tea," {he} says. "From the eastern isles. I have been carrying it for a decade, and I did not know whom to give it to."
events.arc: The Disciple Who Left and Came Back for Tea

choices.text: Take the tin and invite {him} in

effects.log: {He} comes in like a cat testing a floor.

choices.text: Ask about the old quarrel first

effects.log: {He} laughs. "It was a very small chair."

choices.text: Brew the tea at the gate

effects.log: The two of you drink it standing.

events.text: {npc} walks the grounds of the sect and stares at the changes: the new hall, the pond, the rows of juniors. The elders look away. The Hall of Letters hastily clears a chair. At the evening meal, {npc} sits at the foot of the table and says nothing, and eats everything on the plate, and the juniors watch with round eyes.
events.arc: The Disciple Who Left and Came Back for Tea

choices.text: Offer {him} a seat at the high table

effects.log: The elders object. You overrule them, quietly.
{He} seems content there, with a bowl.
The ladle is heavy and the soup is hot.

events.text: {npc} asks, after a week, to rejoin the sect. The elders hold a council in the Hall of Letters. The council is long. Every elder makes a speech, and most of them contradict one another. In the end the vote is nine to seven, and you give the deciding word. {npc} waits outside, holding an empty tin.
events.arc: The Disciple Who Left and Came Back for Tea

effects.log: The doors open. {npc} walks in with a face like an unlatched window.

choices.text: Offer {him} a place as a guest instead

effects.log: {He} accepts with a bow, and stays for a century.

events.text: {npc} stays a season and then leaves again, this time on good terms. "I came to see if the chair was still there," {he} says. "It is. It is smaller than I remembered, and so am I." You walk {him} to the gate. {He} leaves behind an empty tin on the step, with a sprig of tea-leaf pressed inside.
events.arc: The Disciple Who Left and Came Back for Tea

choices.text: Keep the tin in the hall

effects.log: It sits on a shelf by the door as a reminder of mercy.
{He} waves back, once, without turning.

events.text: The twins of the Quince Isle, {npc} and a sibling, are indistinguishable at thirty, the age when a heaven-born child may first walk the stairs alone. This morning they have swapped names. The isle takes it well. Their mother does not. "I always knew which was which," the mother sighs to the baker, "until this week."
events.arc: The Heaven-Born Twins Who Swapped Names

effects.log: You guess wrong with some confidence. They both applaud.

choices.text: Call them both by both names

effects.log: It seems to please them. The confusion is complete.
Tea is poured with a sigh, and a smile.

events.text: The swap lasts a year, then ten. It stops being a joke and becomes a way of life. Each twin gets the other's letters, debts, and friends. {npc} tells you over a rail on the long stairs that it is oddly freeing to be someone else, but also that {he} has begun to miss {his} own name. "It is like a coat that someone else has been wearing."
events.arc: The Heaven-Born Twins Who Swapped Names

effects.log: {He} shakes {his} head. "Not yet. Not until they ask."

choices.text: Say a name is a coat you can choose

effects.log: {He} thinks about this on the stair for a full minute.

choices.text: Walk with {him} up to the landing

effects.log: The landing is bright and the wind is gentle.

events.text: A century on, the twins come to your door together, in each other's coats, and hand you a card. It reads: "We have swapped back. We would like you to be the first to call us by our own names. We would like you to say them out loud." You do. It sounds, to all four ears, very strange and right.
events.arc: The Heaven-Born Twins Who Swapped Names

effects.log: The twins link arms. One of them laughs and one of them cries.
It is warm.

events.text: The twins never swap back. At two hundred they stop explaining it, and the isle simply calls them what they are called. Their mother lives to see it and says, at last, "I know which is which. It is just that I know it the other way round." The twins hold her hand, one on each side.
events.arc: The Heaven-Born Twins Who Swapped Names

choices.text: Raise a cup to the family

effects.log: The family laughs. It is a good laugh.
One red, one blue. They swap them at once.

events.text: {npc}, the keeper of a small hall of the Celestial Ministries, has written you a letter. A rogue may not enter the Hall of Weights and Measures, but the keeper has found a rule, deep in the statutes, allowing an "exceptional guest by invitation." "It has not been used in nine hundred years," {he} writes. "Come on a Tuesday."
events.arc: The Rogue Admitted as an Exception

effects.log: You are told to wear plain clothes and to leave at noon. You agree.
{He} replies: "Because the weights need someone who does not care who owns the scale."
You write a courteous refusal. The keeper replies with a smile.

events.text: In the Hall of Weights and Measures, every scale is exact and every clerk is wary. You are given a cloth and a weight of a thousand grains, and told to check it. The clerks watch with folded arms. The weight is one grain light. You say so. A gasp goes round the hall, and then a very small cheer.
events.arc: The Rogue Admitted as an Exception

effects.log: You spend the afternoon at it. Nineteen weights are off.
The keeper walks you to the door with great courtesy.

choices.text: Take a cup of tea with the clerks

effects.log: They thaw, a degree.

events.text: The keeper makes you "Guest Examiner of Weights" for the afternoons of every Tuesday. It is an unpaid, honorary, and awkward title, but a title all the same. Clerks of the Hall begin to nod to you in the market. A faction steward, seeing it, offers you a seat at the next banquet, and the steward's voice cracks over the word "rogue."
events.arc: The Rogue Admitted as an Exception

effects.log: You sit among the factions for one night and are served first for once.

choices.text: Decline and send the seat to a friend

effects.log: The friend is baffled and delighted.

events.text: You keep your Tuesdays. No further invitation comes, and the clerks of the Hall go back to looking over your shoulder. But the keeper sends a small package every year at the turn of the season, a single exact grain of gold, with a note: "In case you doubt it was real." You keep them in a jar on the shelf. The jar fills slowly.
events.arc: The Rogue Admitted as an Exception

effects.log: After five hundred years it is full, and so is the memory.
The letters are short and warm.

events.text: A mist-hound pup, grey and loose-limbed and made mostly of fog, was left at your door in a basket by {npc}, who runs the hound-stables on the next isle. "It will not hunt," {he} says. "It will not even bark. It follows people home. I thought it should follow someone good."
events.arc: The Mist-Hound Pup Who Learned the Isle

effects.log: It curls up on your cushion and blurs a little at the edges.
"Fog," {he} says. "Evening fog. And now and again a biscuit."

choices.text: Say you will think about it

effects.log: {npc} leaves the basket anyway, with a little bow.

events.text: Within a decade the pup is the size of a calf and has learned every path on your isle. It guides the lost back to their doors in a mist, and growls only at those who cheat the ferry. The neighbours have given it a name, Pebble, and there is a shrine to it by the dock, hung with bits of biscuit.
events.arc: The Mist-Hound Pup Who Learned the Isle

choices.text: Walk the isle with Pebble each morning

effects.log: The two of you cover it in an hour. Pebble disappears into the fog and returns smiling.

choices.text: Train it to find lost things

effects.log: It finds three keys, a left shoe, and a letter from a century ago.
It roams, and always returns.

events.text: A bad fog rolls in over the Fleet and a skiff of children goes missing in the white. Pebble lifts its head, sniffs, and is gone in the mist like a thread pulled out of cloth. Hours pass. Then there is a bark, the first bark of its life, and a line of small figures comes out of the white, each holding a bit of the hound's tail.
events.arc: The Mist-Hound Pup Who Learned the Isle

effects.log: The children are cold and happy. Pebble is given every biscuit on the isle.
{He} just shrugs. "It chose well."

events.text: The pup grows old on your isle, and fades, a little, at the edges. One evening it lies down on the dock where it was first brought in, and the fog gathers over it like a blanket. In the morning there is only mist and a dent in the cushion. The neighbours leave biscuits at the shrine for a long time.
events.arc: The Mist-Hound Pup Who Learned the Isle

effects.log: The biscuits are replaced every week. Pebble is not forgotten.

choices.text: Walk the isle alone at dawn

effects.log: The mist feels like company.

events.text: The Anchor Isle was due at the Meeting of Fleets a century ago and has just now floated into the harbour, tattered, laden with sleepy passengers and a very apologetic steersman. {npc} steps off, bows to the harbour-master, and says, "We took a wrong turn at the second cloud. It was a very pleasant wrong turn."
events.arc: The Isle That Arrived a Century Late

effects.log: The passengers eye the bun with the longing of a century. It vanishes.
{npc} tells it in one breath, and it is a fine tale, with a goat in it.
Mooring takes nine hours, and no one minds.

events.text: The Meeting of Fleets was long over. Its decisions had been made without the Anchor Isle, and some of them are unkind to it. The Anchor Isle has been struck off the roll of mooring rights, its seat given to another. {npc} reads the notice in silence. "We never meant to be late," {he} says. "We only meant to be slow."
events.arc: The Isle That Arrived a Century Late

effects.log: You speak at the harbour office. The clerks hear you out, with caution.

choices.text: Offer your own isle's berth for the season

effects.log: It is cramped but friendly. The Anchor Isle moors alongside.
The tea house is warm and the clerks do not follow.

events.text: The harbour office, after a week, rules that the Anchor Isle has been "present in spirit" for the whole of the century, and restores its mooring. The seat goes back. The isle's passengers hold a feast on the quay, and the whole harbour is invited. The goat from the tale is led in, in a ribbon, to a round of applause.
events.arc: The Isle That Arrived a Century Late

choices.text: Raise a cup to the goat

effects.log: The goat accepts, with dignity.
It lasts into the small hours.

events.text: The Anchor Isle moors beside yours, and the two isles are inseparable for a thousand years. Children cross the rope-bridges between them without a thought, and elders play long games in the middle. When the day comes that the Anchor Isle drifts on, {npc} stands at the rail with the goat and waves, and your whole isle waves back.
events.arc: The Isle That Arrived a Century Late

choices.text: Tie a lantern to the rope-bridge

effects.log: It burns till the isle is a speck in the sky.
They wish you a slow one.

events.text: You have kept, in a cupboard, a small tin of candles given to you by a friend below, years ago. The tin has {npc}'s mark on the lid, a tiny bird. {npc}, a neighbour on your isle who knows what the bird means, stops at your door on a cold evening and says, "The first of the month, down there, is the day they burn candles for the gone."
events.arc: The Candle Burned for a Mortal Friend

choices.text: Light a candle at the window

effects.log: The flame stands straight in the cold air. It is a small, steady flame.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to light it with you

effects.log: The two of you sit by the flame. {He} says nothing, and it is a comfort.

choices.text: Keep the tin and decide later

effects.log: It goes back on the shelf, warm to the touch.

events.text: You burn a candle on the first of every month. At first it is an effort, and later a habit, and eventually a kind of company. The isle's children notice and ask what it is for. You explain in the plainest words: "It is for someone who is not here." One of them brings you a candle of her own, hand-dipped, crooked.
events.arc: The Candle Burned for a Mortal Friend

effects.log: It smokes a little, which is also a kind of speech.

choices.text: Tell the child the whole story

effects.log: The child listens with grave attention. It takes an hour.

choices.text: Say it is a private matter

effects.log: The child nods, and understands, in the way of children.

events.text: The tin empties. You light the last candle at the window and watch it burn all the way down. When it gutters, you are surprised to find you are not sad but quiet, like a room after music. In the morning a child leaves another tin at your door, with a note: "From all of us. Please keep going."
events.arc: The Candle Burned for a Mortal Friend

effects.log: The candles are crooked and many. You light one at once.

choices.text: Plant the last stub in the garden

effects.log: In spring a small flower comes up where it was buried.

events.text: You hold the candle for a mortal friend every first of the month for six hundred years. The neighbours join in, one by one, until the whole isle lights a window on the same night. Travellers passing in skiffs see the row of tiny flames and ask what festival it is. A child says, "It is the one we keep."
events.arc: The Candle Burned for a Mortal Friend

effects.log: It becomes an isle custom, and then a fleet custom.

choices.text: Keep your own window dark that night

effects.log: You sit by the others and watch them burn.

events.text: {npc} collects echoes. Not sounds: echoes. {He} stands at the foot of a cliff with a small jar and a patient expression, and calls out, and waits, and then claps the lid on. "This one is from the Weeping Cliff," {he} says, handing you the jar. "Put your ear to it." You hear your own voice, a hundred years old, and rather charming.
events.arc: The Immortal Who Collected Echoes

effects.log: "Patience," {he} says. "And a good jar, with a narrow neck."
It answers, a moment late, in a voice not yours.
There are nine hundred, labelled in a careful hand.

events.text: {npc} invites you on a collecting trip to the Hollow Reef, whose echoes are said to be the finest of the sky. The skiff is stuffed with jars. At the reef {he} stands, hands cupped, and calls one note; the answer rolls round the stone like a ball in a bowl and falls, finally, into the neck of the jar.
events.arc: The Immortal Who Collected Echoes

effects.log: You hold it steady. The echo lands in it with a faint chime.
Yours is the worst echo of the day. {He} treasures it.
It has a deep, hollow, gentle voice.

events.text: {npc}'s collection is opened to the public in a hall on the Chime Isle. Each jar is labelled with the place and the year. Visitors walk the aisles with their ears to the glass, and cry, or laugh, or both. The most requested is a jar from a cliff that has since fallen. The echo is all that remains of the cliff.
events.arc: The Immortal Who Collected Echoes

choices.text: Give a jar of your own to the hall

effects.log: It is shelved between a canyon and a well.
Each jar is a small door.

events.text: When {npc} grows old and tired, you inherit the keys of the hall, and the nine hundred jars, and the quiet duty of listening. On the last evening you open the jar from the Weeping Cliff, the first one you ever heard, and your own young voice says its small hello. You laugh, once, and shut the lid gently.
events.arc: The Immortal Who Collected Echoes

effects.log: You hold the keys for a thousand years. Children are brought in for their first echo.
It is a goodbye, tucked in a jar.

events.text: {npc} has been your friend for eight hundred years and has never once been on time. {He} arrives a day late for everything: dinners, funerals, weddings, the one tribulation you ever stood in. {He} is arriving now, three days after your birthday, with a present and a look of extreme innocence. "I was nearly early," {he} says.
events.arc: The Friend Who Always Arrived a Day Late

effects.log: The present is a tiny jade clock with no hands. You laugh.

choices.text: Tell {him} off in a friendly way

effects.log: {He} bows and takes it, smiling, as one who has heard it for centuries.
{He} sits, delighted.

events.text: You tell {npc} that this year you have planned a trip, and that the skiff leaves at dawn on the first of the month. {He} promises faithfully. On the first of the month, at dawn, the dock is empty. You wait a day. On the second, {npc} turns up at a run, hair wild, with a bag. The skiff has gone.
events.arc: The Friend Who Always Arrived a Day Late

effects.log: It costs three stones, and the ride is bumpy and lovely.

choices.text: Say the trip can wait a day

effects.log: You both laugh. The trip becomes a day late too.
The tide comes in at its own pace.

events.text: For once, {npc} turns up first. {He} is early, by an hour, standing on your doorstep with a basket, a book, and the air of someone who has not slept. "I thought you might need me," {he} says. It is a hard day: the news from below has reached you. {He} says nothing about the lateness, and stays three days.
events.arc: The Friend Who Always Arrived a Day Late

effects.log: The silence is shared. It is the best present of the age.
The tea is the right strength for a hard day.

events.text: {npc} is late to your leave-taking, too: you set out on a long drift, and the dock is empty, and you sail without {him}. Three days later a skiff overtakes you in the clouds, with {npc} at the tiller, bareheaded and delighted. "On time," {he} says, "for the second half." You give {him} the hand-clock back, still handless, and say it is perfect.
events.arc: The Friend Who Always Arrived a Day Late

effects.log: The two of you sail on, a day apart and always together.

choices.text: Share a flask on the open sky

effects.log: It is a good flask.

events.text: {npc} is the herald of the Jade Court and has announced every entry for five hundred years in a bell-clear voice. This morning, at the spring audience, it fails halfway through a minister's name. A silence falls. The minister waits. {npc} stands on the dais with a crimson face and a dry throat, and holds up a hand.
events.arc: The Court Herald Who Lost a Voice

choices.text: Step up and finish the name for {him}

effects.log: Your voice carries; the name is finished; the audience resumes.
A page passes it up. {npc} drinks, and the voice does not come.
The hall holds its breath, and so do you.

events.text: The Court is unsure what to do. A herald without a voice is a bell without a clapper. The Ministry of Precedence debates for a month and decides that {npc} must be retired with honour. It is a fair decision, and it breaks {his} heart. {He} comes to you in the evening and says, "I did not know I was so much my voice."
events.arc: The Court Herald Who Lost a Voice

choices.text: Offer to help {him} find another work

effects.log: You walk with {him} through the Court's many halls, looking at each in turn.

choices.text: Speak up for {him} at the Ministry

effects.log: You ask for a different kind of herald: a writing one.
There is little to say. You sit.

events.text: The Court makes {npc} the first "Herald of the Written Word," who announces by brush, a name a day, on a long scroll that hangs beside the throne. The calligraphy is the finest in the hall. Visitors stop to read the day's names and ask who the brush belongs to. {npc} has grown a new sort of grandeur, a quiet one.
events.arc: The Court Herald Who Lost a Voice

choices.text: Buy a scroll of the names

effects.log: It is a lovely thing to hang in a window.

choices.text: Read the day's names aloud for {him}

effects.log: The scroll sounds fine in your voice.

events.text: A century on, {npc}'s voice returns, a little cracked, a little low, like a bell recast. The Court holds an audience to hear it. {He} says one name only, and it is yours. You are not sure what to say. The hall applauds. {He} bows, and says, quietly, "I wanted the first word to be a kind one."
events.arc: The Court Herald Who Lost a Voice

effects.log: The audience laughs and weeps together.
You walk out in the sun.

events.text: In the Demon Realm, the oldest lamps are not lit with matches but borrowed from the lamp next door. A child walks the lane at dusk carrying a single live flame in a cup, calling at each door: "A spark for your lamp?" The doors open, one after another, and the lane lights up like a string of beads.

effects.log: The child lights it, with a bow.

choices.text: Walk the lane with the child

effects.log: The lights come on in order.

events.text: The Demon Realm drinks its tea black as a well, with a pinch of ember-salt, and serves it in cups so thin that they are drunk in one swallow. A host who offers a second cup is saying: stay. A guest who accepts it is saying: I will. You are offered a second cup.

effects.log: It is bitter and warm, and the host beams.
The host nods and does not mind.

events.text: A mask-seller in the Demon Realm lays out a dozen faces on a cloth: a laughing one, a frowning one, a sleeping one, a mask with no features at all. "The last one is for days when you wish to be nobody," they say. "It sells best at the turning of the year."

effects.log: It is surprisingly restful.
It is a gift for a friend.

events.text: The Star Sea Pavilion keeps a tea-room under the dome where the night-watch takes breaks. A sign reads "Quiet, please: the stars are listening." On the counter is a plate of star-shaped biscuits, freshly baked, and a small card: "Take two. Leave a thought."

choices.text: Take two and leave a note

effects.log: You write: "The Ladle looks fine tonight." It goes in the jar.

choices.text: Sit under the dome with a biscuit

effects.log: It tastes faintly of cinnamon and distance.

events.text: A Star Sea Pavilion ink-maker grinds night-ink from soot and a drop of old starlight, so that a chart drawn in it brightens in the dark. This week the batch has come out slightly too bright. Every chart in the east wing glows by day and the clerks have taken to wearing hats indoors.

choices.text: Help the clerks with a lid

effects.log: You cap the pots, and the glow subsides.
They are, honestly, a fine sight.

events.text: The roof of the sect's oldest hall leaks in the one corner where the Elder of Letters keeps her best scrolls. A junior has been quietly placing a basin beneath it for ten years and emptying it at night. Today you find the basin and the roof both, and a note in a young hand: "Please do not tell."

choices.text: Mend the roof and say nothing

effects.log: A day of tiles and a clean basin.
The junior blushes to the ears.

events.text: A new cook has joined the sect and cooks everything as if for a thousand. The disciples eat in grateful silence, then in groaning silence. The portions are huge. The cook, asked to scale back, looks stricken and says it is the only way they know to say they care.

effects.log: You do. It takes an hour.

choices.text: Teach the cook to make small plates

effects.log: The cook learns, with visible effort.

events.text: Every sect needs a gate-bell, and yours has been silent for a century. A junior finally asks why. You realise no one remembers who rang it last. A search of the shed finds a small clapper in a drawer and a note: "Do not ring unless you mean it."

effects.log: The bell hums for a whole minute.

choices.text: Hang the note by the gate

effects.log: It becomes a motto.

events.text: A heaven-born child on the Willow Isle takes the first of the long stairs alone, with a bag, a bun, and a very serious face. The whole isle watches from windows. At the top step the child turns, waves, and goes in. A sigh runs round the neighbours like wind in barley.

effects.log: The child, small as a button, sees you.

choices.text: Hold a bun in reserve for their return

effects.log: It is a long stair, and you are ready.

events.text: A heaven-born child turns one hundred today. On the Poplar Isle this is marked by a cake in the shape of a very small isle, with candles for each decade. The child blows once and the whole island of cake sails off the table. The neighbours catch it in a net and eat it where it lands.

effects.log: It is soft, and tastes of honey.
Off-key, and loved.

events.text: Your cloud-lamb has grown fat on the Orchard Isle's clover and stands in the middle of the lane, refusing to let a cart pass. The carter yells, then laughs, then yawns. The lamb turns a calm eye on the whole scene and settles down. The cart is turned round. The lane is, for the day, the lamb's.

effects.log: It leans into the hand.

choices.text: Lead it home with a clover leaf

effects.log: It follows with great dignity.

events.text: A thunder sparrow chick has taken to sleeping in your hat, and occasionally lets off a small rumble in its dreams that rattles the cups. Tonight it has outdone itself: a clap so loud the neighbours come to the door. You hold up the hat, apologetic. The neighbours, melting, ask if it eats.

effects.log: It purrs in thunder.

choices.text: Apologise with a plate of buns

effects.log: The neighbours forgive on the spot.

events.text: As two fleets cross in the open sky, every isle rings its bell once. It takes an hour for the whole sound to run down the line and back. A steersman on the nearest isle, tiny in the distance, holds up a flag, and you hold up yours, and for a moment the sky is a very large room full of friends.

effects.log: It joins the chorus.
It flaps in the open wind.

events.text: Two small fleets that have been neighbours for centuries decide to merge at the season of drift. The merger takes three weeks of speeches, ropes and good cake. At the end, a signal flag is raised over the dock: two knots of colour, braided into one. Both steersmen cry.

effects.log: Your hands remember how.
It is good, and enormous.

events.text: A clerk of the Ministry of Prayers brings you a slip: a mortal you once knew has had a child. The child is named for you. The clerk asks if you would like to send a gift down. The rules allow only a gust of wind, which will seem coincidence. You think for a long while.

choices.text: Send the gust, warm and gentle

effects.log: A breeze, down in some far yard, ruffles a cradle.

choices.text: Keep the news to yourself and smile

effects.log: It is a quiet joy.

events.text: A leaf drifts up the cloud-stair on a thermal and lands in your tea. Written on it, in faded ink: a line from a mortal poem, with your name misspelled. Somewhere below, a child is learning to write and has sent a leaf upward for luck. The leaf is soft, small, and entirely sincere.

choices.text: Press the leaf in a book

effects.log: It stays green for a hundred years.
It will take years to arrive.

events.text: An immortal at the Mirror Lake sorts pebbles by the sound they make when dropped. There are nine thousand in a grid on the shore. They will not tell anyone what the sounds are for. When asked, they smile and drop one. It goes plink. They nod, satisfied, and make a note.

effects.log: It goes plonk. They write it down.

choices.text: Sit and listen to the plinks

effects.log: It is oddly restful.

events.text: A retired marshal has devoted a century to pickling clouds. The jars line a cellar on the Brine Isle, labelled by weather: "Light drizzle", "Hail, mild", "Sunset, late." They taste, according to the marshal, of the moment they were put away. You taste "Fog, morning." It tastes like waiting.

effects.log: It glows faintly on the shelf.
The marshal looks astonished and pleased.

events.text: The toll-keeper of the Silver Bridge takes no coin, only a small story, which is written into a long book kept in a hut. Today you pay with one from your first century, about a goat who found a flute. The toll-keeper writes it down, frowns, asks for the ending, and waves you through.

effects.log: The goat plays the flute. The toll-keeper beams.
The toll-keeper writes: "Lost." It is a fair ending.

events.text: A skiff-boy stands on the dock with a ticket in his hand and a very worried look. He has lost the isle he was told to deliver a parcel to. "It was here a week ago," he says. "It was a big one, with a green roof." You both look at the empty water.

effects.log: The master points two isles east.

choices.text: Give him a sandwich and a compass

effects.log: He sets off with confidence.

events.text: The Wind of the East has been in a mood all week: it has stolen three hats, upset a tea-tray, and blown the Minister of Precedence's wig clean off the dais. On the fourth morning it sulks round the corner of the Weather Office. A clerk opens a window and says, "Come in and tell us what is wrong."

effects.log: The wind murmurs for an hour, then calms.
It sweeps past, grateful.

events.text: The Letter Winds of the Fourth Season carry mail between isles without a skiff, if the letters are folded small and the wind is asked politely. A beginner's letter, folded wrongly, lands in a pond. A better-folded letter reaches its target in an afternoon. You fold yours. You fold it eleven times.

effects.log: It rises, turning like a leaf.
You arrive before the wind does.

events.text: A bathhouse on the Spring Isle is heated by a small, shy hot spring which turns bashful if watched. The attendant leaves the room, and the water rises in clouds. The bath is perfect only when no one is thinking about how perfect it is. You settle in and try to think about something else.

effects.log: The water warms by a degree.

choices.text: Count the tiles on the ceiling

effects.log: There are three hundred and four.

events.text: The week of the thousand-year peach arrives with a quiet sort of ceremony: a single fruit ripens on an old tree in the Orchard Isle's centre. The gardeners stand around it with cloths. When it falls, it is cut into a hundred thin slices, and one is given to each person who has ever helped the tree.

effects.log: It tastes like an old spring afternoon.
The child is awed.

events.text: A jade slip in the east archive has a smudge across its third line, where some past reader pressed a thumb. The archivists have debated for a century whether to clean it. The smudge, they say, is part of the record: the thumb of someone who cared. You are asked to cast the deciding vote.

effects.log: The smudge stays. The archivists bow.
The line is restored. The thumbprint is saved in a drawer.

events.text: A kitchen on the Jade Void isle is cooking for a thousand with a single flame, said to be the oldest on the isle, that must never go out. A cook feeds it a spoon of oil each hour and sings to it. Tonight it has begun to sulk. The cook asks you for a song.

effects.log: The flame swells and settles.
The flame sways in time.

events.text: Far out, a sky whale sings a long, low line across the cloud sea. The notes pass under the isles and shake the teacups. Travellers say it is a greeting, or a question, or a joke. A child on the dock sings back, flat and delighted. After a long pause the whale sings the same flat note back.

effects.log: The two of you hold still until the sound fades.
The whale does not mind.

events.text: The silver carp of the Chime Reef run once a year, and the whole isle turns out with nets and lanterns. The aim is not to catch them but to count them, a tradition of three hundred years. This year the count is lower, and the oldest counter, a dry old woman, writes the number slowly and looks at the sky.

effects.log: You count to fourteen hundred, and lose track.
They glide round it, glittering.

events.text: At the edge of the Last Terrace stands a bench with a plaque: "For the one who is waiting." No one has ever found out who put it there. A kettle sits beside it in winter, kept warm by a spell nobody remembers casting. You sit down. The view is the end of the world. The bench is very comfortable.

choices.text: Pour a cup from the kettle

effects.log: It is hot, and tastes of pine.
You wait. Nothing arrives. It is a lovely wait.

events.text: The roads of the Demon Realm shift with the moods of the ground, and {npc} makes maps that last a single week. A new map is drawn every Sunday on wet slate and rubbed out the Saturday after. "Nobody wants a map that lies," {he} says, and offers you a rag. "Come and rub out the old one with me."
events.arc: The Mapmaker of the Shifting Roads

effects.log: The roads smear into grey. It feels like erasing a weather.

choices.text: Ask to draw the new one

effects.log: {He} hands over the chalk. Your first road leads straight into a wall.

choices.text: Buy last week's map as a souvenir

effects.log: It is wrong in nine places, which is its charm.

events.text: You walk the roads with {npc} on survey, a slow tour of valleys that rearrange themselves while you look. A bridge is there, then a ramp, then a long gentle stair. {npc} sketches fast and swears softly at a hill that moves out of frame. "Rough work," {he} says. "But nobody ever got lost with a map that tried."
events.arc: The Mapmaker of the Shifting Roads

effects.log: You hold it against the wind. The hill returns, and {he} sketches it.
It is called "Late Again". {He} writes it in.

choices.text: Rest on a stone that stays put

effects.log: It stays, remarkably.

events.text: A traveller arrives at the mapmaker's hut at dusk, half-lost, with an old map of {npc}'s from years ago clutched in a fist. It is no use now, of course, but the traveller says it was the only paper that had ever been kind. {npc} takes it, looks at it, and for the first time in centuries, frames a map.
events.arc: The Mapmaker of the Shifting Roads

effects.log: It goes on the wall above the slate. The hut feels warmer.

choices.text: Share a cup with the traveller

effects.log: The traveller sleeps by the fire.

events.text: The day comes when the ground in the valley settles, and the roads stop shifting. The mapmaker is out of work. {npc} walks the new, fixed roads for a week, unable to believe it. Then {he} draws one last map, permanent this time, on a sheet of real paper. It is plain and exact, and {he} signs it with your name beside {his} own.
events.arc: The Mapmaker of the Shifting Roads

effects.log: It hangs beside the traveller's old map.

choices.text: Walk the fixed road to the next valley

effects.log: It is dull and lovely.

events.text: {npc} bakes ash-bread, the black loaf of the Demon Realm, in an oven fired with cooled embers from the night before. Each loaf is said to hold a day's worth of warmth. The queue starts at four in the morning. {He} spots you in the line and calls, over the heads of the others, "You, there. You look as if you need bread."
events.arc: The Baker of Ash-Bread

effects.log: It is heavy, black, and sweet, and warm all the way through.
Your arms ache within minutes. {npc} laughs, kindly.
The baker works like a drummer.

events.text: The Demon Realm has a rule that ash-bread must never be sold, only given, and the baker is paid in gifts: a mended coat, a song, a basket of eggs. {npc} shows you a shelf full of them. "A fair trade," {he} says. "I give what I can make. They give what they can." One shelf holds only a feather, and {he} refuses to say why.
events.arc: The Baker of Ash-Bread

choices.text: Bring a gift for the shelf

effects.log: You bring a small bell. It is hung with the others.
It was from a friend who flew off. The baker will say no more.

choices.text: Say it is a good rule

effects.log: {He} nods and passes you the heel of the loaf.

events.text: A hard winter comes to the Realm, and the queue doubles. {npc} bakes day and night, and the shelf of gifts grows thin; the oven is nearly out of embers. Then, one by one, neighbours arrive with armfuls of fuel and sit by the door to keep the fire going. By dawn the line is a ring of people, and the bread comes out as warm as ever.
events.arc: The Baker of Ash-Bread

effects.log: You carry coals until your arms ache.
The oven glows.

events.text: The feather, it turns out, belonged to a friend who still comes by once a century, to taste the bread. {npc} has been saving the heel of the loaf for the friend, though the friend has not come in two hundred years. You are asked to keep the shelf in order when the baker is gone. It is a small trust, and an enormous one.
events.arc: The Baker of Ash-Bread

effects.log: You dust it each spring. The feather stays.

choices.text: Promise to leave the heel out

effects.log: You do, for centuries.

events.text: A great brass telescope in the Star Sea Pavilion has, for forty years, been pointed at the wrong end of the sky. {npc}, the keeper, will not move it. "It has been looking there so long," {he} says, "that I believe it knows something." The astronomers sigh. The telescope stares at a patch of black.
events.arc: The Telescope That Looked the Wrong Way

effects.log: You see nothing but dark, which turns out to be very interesting.

choices.text: Argue that it should be turned

effects.log: The keeper is stubborn. The argument is long and cordial.
{He} is touched, and says nothing more.

events.text: You look every night for a month. The dark is not quite empty: a patch, very faint, shifts like a breath. {npc} stands behind you with a notebook, whispering numbers. On the thirtieth night, the patch brightens by a hair. "There," {he} says. "I told them." The astronomers, summoned in their night-caps, gather round the eyepiece.
events.arc: The Telescope That Looked the Wrong Way

effects.log: One by one they peer in, and each one goes silent.

choices.text: Record the patch in the dome-book

effects.log: The page now carries a small, shaky drawing.

choices.text: Sit on the floor and breathe

effects.log: It is a bigger night than you expected.

events.text: The patch brightens through the next decade into a faint pale star, new and unnamed. The Pavilion holds a naming. {npc} stands on the stool and says the name, softly: a very old, ridiculous word for "waiting". The astronomers clap. The telescope is, for the first time in forty years, unlocked and turned to look at something else.
events.arc: The Telescope That Looked the Wrong Way

choices.text: Raise a cup to the new star

effects.log: It glows faintly. The telescope turns with a creak.
{He} sticks it in the eyepiece.

events.text: The patch fades again in a century. {npc} is unfazed. "A star is an event," {he} says, "not a possession." The telescope is left pointing at the dark, and the keeper teaches the junior astronomers to look for what is there before it is there. It becomes the Pavilion's most beloved lesson, though it is the least useful.
events.arc: The Telescope That Looked the Wrong Way

choices.text: Teach the lesson to a junior

effects.log: You teach it in an hour. The junior tilts a head.
It is quiet and large.

events.text: The Star Sea has tides, though no one agrees what the moon is. {npc} reads them: three times a day, {he} walks to the end of the Pavilion jetty with a stick and a bucket, dips the stick, and announces the tide in a voice like a bell. "Rising," {he} calls. Nobody ever checks. Nobody has ever needed to.
events.arc: The Tide-Reader of the Star Sea

effects.log: The stick comes up wet, silvery. It smells of far places.
"The stick," {he} says. "And a feeling about my knees."
"Rising," {he} agrees, and writes it down.

events.text: A young astronomer builds a machine to read the tides without a stick. It clicks and whirrs and prints the answer on a card. The Pavilion is delighted. {npc} stands by the machine, watches it work, and says nothing for a week. On the eighth day, the machine and {npc} give different answers. The tide, the Pavilion finds, sides with {him}.
events.arc: The Tide-Reader of the Star Sea

choices.text: Offer to check the machine's gears

effects.log: The gears are fine. The tide is simply odd today.
{He} grumbles about knees and is secretly delighted.
You let the rivalry settle on its own.

events.text: The young astronomer and {npc} become unlikely colleagues. They share the jetty, one with the machine and one with the stick, and the Pavilion posts both numbers on a board. When they differ, the tide is said to be "in two minds." Tea is made. The machine stays, and so does the stick, and the Pavilion has never been more accurate.
events.arc: The Tide-Reader of the Star Sea

effects.log: It is good tea for a quarrel that is not one.
It says: "Rising, perhaps."

events.text: {npc} retires and leaves you the stick. It is dark, smooth, and warm from long use. On the first morning you walk out to the jetty alone and dip it. The Star Sea laps coldly at the wood. You wait. The feeling in your knees, which you did not know you had, says: "Rising." You say it aloud, and the bell of the Pavilion rings.
events.arc: The Tide-Reader of the Star Sea

effects.log: You read the tide three times a day for a thousand years.

choices.text: Keep the stick and decline the post

effects.log: It hangs by your door.

events.text: A portrait of you as founder is to hang in the main hall of the sect you founded, and {npc}, the court painter you have hired, has made you look about forty years younger, and noticeably more handsome. "It is how you will be remembered," {he} says, defensive. "No one wants a founder with a squint."
events.arc: The Founder's Portrait Painted Too Young

effects.log: You hang it. It looks very noble and not at all like you.

choices.text: Ask {him} to paint you as you are

effects.log: {He} sighs, mixes grey, and paints the squint.

choices.text: Take it home and hang it over a door

effects.log: It is a good door.

events.text: Visitors to the hall comment on the portrait. Some say it looks wise. Some say it looks smug. An old traveller stops in front of it and laughs, long and loud, then walks up to you and bows. "I knew you at forty," the traveller says. "You were exactly like that, except for the hair." The disciples, listening, snort.
events.arc: The Founder's Portrait Painted Too Young

effects.log: It is a good laugh, and it lasts all through lunch.
The disciples love you for it.
You bury yourself in a ledger.

events.text: A century on, the portrait is the sect's most famous object. Juniors pass it with a bow; a legend grows round the "founder who never aged." You are asked to confirm it at a gathering. A whole hall of faces turns towards you, awed. {npc}, older, from the back, mouths: "Say yes."
events.arc: The Founder's Portrait Painted Too Young

effects.log: The hall sighs, happy. {npc} winks.

choices.text: Tell the true story with a grin

effects.log: The hall bursts into laughter and applause.
The hall interprets it as it likes.

events.text: The honest portrait goes up in the dining hall instead. Squint and all. The disciples feel closer to it than to the grand one, and bring it small offerings: a dried flower, a pebble, a spoon. {npc} looks at the work, in time, with a different sort of pride. "That is the only one I would keep," {he} says.
events.arc: The Founder's Portrait Painted Too Young

effects.log: The two of you hang side by side, a founder in two ages.
The painter bows.

events.text: {npc} is the treasurer of the sect you founded, and reports with a grey face that the stone-chest in the vault is short by nineteen stones. It has been short for years, a little each season. No theft, no loss, only a slow leak. "It is as if the chest drank them," {he} says. The vault smells of old rain.
events.arc: The Treasurer and the Leaking Stone-Chest

effects.log: You count it twice. The numbers do not agree.
{He} is not reassured, but relieved to hear it.
They are long and surprisingly pretty.

events.text: The leak turns out to be a hairline crack in the vault floor, beneath which a family of mouse-geckos has made a home. They have been pulling stones through one at a time and building a nest of glittering rocks. {npc} gets down on hands and knees and addresses the lair. "Gentlemen," {he} says, "that is the sect's money."
events.arc: The Treasurer and the Leaking Stone-Chest

effects.log: You offer a plate of crumbs for the stones. The geckos consider it.
The geckos look hurt. The vault is sound again.
They are industrious and bright-eyed.

events.text: The geckos accept a treaty: one plate of crumbs a week for the nest, and the stones returned at the turn of each season. They keep it perfectly, with a tiny pile of nineteen stones at the crack on the first morning of spring. The treasurer weeps. The treaty is signed with a stamp of three small footprints.
events.arc: The Treasurer and the Leaking Stone-Chest

effects.log: You press your seal next to the footprints.
It becomes a treasure of the vault.

events.text: The crack is sealed. The geckos move to the garden, where they are soon beloved by juniors, who feed them crumbs and name them after elders. {npc} feels bad about it for a century, and slips a handful of crumbs under the vault door each week, out of old guilt. The geckos never return, but now and again a small stone is left on the sill.
events.arc: The Treasurer and the Leaking Stone-Chest

effects.log: The two of you keep a small tradition.
It is a sweet smooth thing.

events.text: {npc}, heaven-born and two hundred years old, tells you with great seriousness that {he} wishes to live one day as a mortal does. "No qi. No stairs. No skiffs," {he} says. "I want to know what a day is, if you cannot do anything about it." You say it sounds tiring. {He} says that is the point.
events.arc: The Heaven-Born Who Wished to Be Mortal for a Day

effects.log: You write a list: breakfast, error, tiredness, supper.

choices.text: Warn {him} it may not be what {he} hopes

effects.log: {He} nods, undaunted, and writes your warning down.

choices.text: Offer to lend a plain coat

effects.log: {He} puts it on and spins, thrilled.

events.text: The day is a Tuesday. {npc} wakes without flying, walks to the baker's on foot, queues for the bread, and drops it. {He} stands in the lane looking at the bread, flabbergasted. A passing child hands over another loaf, and then {he} is crying, and laughing, and says "I did not know it would matter so much."
events.arc: The Heaven-Born Who Wished to Be Mortal for a Day

effects.log: You trudge up a hill, share a loaf, and are very tired by dusk.
You wave from the lane and leave the day to its owner.
It is your turn to drop it.

events.text: At dusk {npc} sits on the stairs with blistered feet and a face like a lamp. "That was the best day of my life," {he} says, "and I never want another." The two of you eat cold bread. {He} asks if you will keep the secret, and you say you will. The stars come out, and {he} leans on your shoulder and sleeps.
events.arc: The Heaven-Born Who Wished to Be Mortal for a Day

effects.log: It is a long way. You do not mind.
A blanket is found.

events.text: {npc} tries the day again, a century on. It is not the same. The bread does not fall. The hill is easier. The magic of the first, {he} tells you, was in not knowing how it ends. "A mortal gets one first day," {he} says. "I wasted mine in the telling." You laugh, and agree.
events.arc: The Heaven-Born Who Wished to Be Mortal for a Day

effects.log: You suggest a long walk with no destination. {He} accepts.
The tea is warm.

events.text: A heaven-born child named {npc} is brought to the Bamboo Isle school at age nine, which is to say forty-five years of ordinary growing. The teacher, an old calligrapher, hands {him} a brush and says "Copy this." The child copies the page upside down, with such grace that the teacher stares at it for a very long time.
events.arc: The Child Who Taught the Teacher

effects.log: It has a rhythm the right side up one lacks.
The teacher coughs, and says "It is... novel."
