{He} puffs up, then pretends not to.

events.text: The child, set to learn the old strokes, invents new ones. The teacher is at first alarmed and then enchanted. Within a decade the school is writing a hand never seen before: loose, round, a little crooked, as if a bird had been taught the alphabet. Parents are scandalised, then enrolled.
events.arc: The Child Who Taught the Teacher

choices.text: Help the child write a primer

effects.log: The primer is eleven pages long and a bestseller.

choices.text: Defend the new hand to the parents

effects.log: You are persuasive, for once.
It comes out like a startled bird.

events.text: The old teacher steps down and hands the school to {npc}. It is a quiet day, a Sunday. The two of them share a table in the empty schoolroom, and the teacher takes up a brush and copies, shakily, one of the child's strokes. "I learned more from you," the teacher says, "than you from me." {npc} says nothing, and wipes the brush.
events.arc: The Child Who Taught the Teacher

effects.log: You set out three cups. The room is warm with ink.
You slip out the door.

events.text: The new hand spreads through the isles and, in time, is taught in every school of the sky. People forget that it began as a child's mistake. {npc}, a grown immortal now, is asked to write a history of it and writes only one line: "It was the teacher who said yes." The preface is that line alone.
events.arc: The Child Who Taught the Teacher

choices.text: Read the preface at the next festival

effects.log: The hall applauds, and a few eyes fill.

choices.text: Tell the teacher's story to a student

effects.log: The student writes it down, crooked.

events.text: {npc}, a rogue with a toolbox and no faction, walks the Celestial Ministries' corridors with a pass that reads "Contractor, Temporary." The clocks of the Ministry have been wrong by an hour for decades, and no clerk is permitted to repair them. {He} is permitted only because a rogue cannot be blamed for a clock.
events.arc: The Rogue Who Mended the Ministry's Clocks

effects.log: You steady the ladder. A clerk eyes you, then looks away.
It is a bun and a flask. {He} eats it on a stair and says it is the first lunch in the Ministry.

choices.text: Tell a clerk the clocks are fine

effects.log: The clerk blinks, then nods.

events.text: The first clock {npc} mends strikes noon with a sound the Ministry has not heard in a century. A clerk drops a tray. Another bursts into tears. The sound runs down the corridors in a bright, brazen wave, and every clerk stops writing for a moment and listens, as if recalling the name of an old friend.
events.arc: The Rogue Who Mended the Ministry's Clocks

effects.log: A small, delighted applause breaks out.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to mend the next one

effects.log: {He} smiles with the whole face.
The sound hangs in the stairwell a long time.

events.text: The Ministry, delighted by the clocks, offers {npc} the title of "Honorary Mender of Time," unpaid, without a rank, which is an insult to anyone but a rogue. {He} takes it. The title comes with a small brass badge. A clerk sees it on {his} coat and, with a flicker of reluctance, holds a door open.
events.arc: The Rogue Who Mended the Ministry's Clocks

choices.text: Raise a cup to the badge

effects.log: The tea-house toasts it. {npc} blushes.
It is only a door, but it opens.

events.text: When the last clock is mended, the Ministry has no more work for a rogue. The badge is not renewed. {npc} packs the toolbox without complaint and walks the corridor one last time, listening to the hours ring in order. At the gate a clerk hands over a very small clock, wrapped in cloth. "From all of us," the clerk says, "who were not allowed to say thank you."
events.arc: The Rogue Who Mended the Ministry's Clocks

effects.log: It ticks bright and exact.
You say goodbye at the toll.

events.text: {npc}, a rogue cook with no hall, has been hired for a single night to help in the back kitchen of the Spring Banquet: peeling, stirring, carrying. A faction cook points {him} to a corner and a pile of roots. "You will not enter the hall," the cook says. "Rogues are served by the kitchen, not by the front."
events.arc: The Rogue Allowed in the Banquet Kitchen

effects.log: Roots by the hundred. You lose track after the first one.

choices.text: Ask the head cook for a better station

effects.log: The head cook shrugs. "Rules are rules." But a stool is found.

choices.text: Bring a cup of tea to the corner

effects.log: {He} accepts with a small nod.

events.text: Halfway through the banquet the sauce, the great sauce, curdles. The head cook turns pale. A hundred dishes wait for it. {npc} walks to the pot, tastes, adds a pinch of something from a pocket, and stirs. The curdle smooths. The head cook stares. "Don't," {npc} says, mildly, "tell them it was a rogue."
events.arc: The Rogue Allowed in the Banquet Kitchen

effects.log: The sauce goes out. The hall sighs over the first spoonful.

choices.text: Tell the head cook to credit {him}

effects.log: The head cook, sweating, says "perhaps."
It is heavy and fragrant.

events.text: A Minister, tasting the sauce, asks for the cook. The head cook, flushed, brings out {npc}, who stands in the hall in an apron, blinking at a thousand faces. The Minister bows. "I have not tasted that sauce," says the Minister, "since the great drift." There is a pause. A rogue has been named in the hall.
events.arc: The Rogue Allowed in the Banquet Kitchen

effects.log: The hall follows, slowly, and the noise swells.
{He} wipes {his} hands and bows.

events.text: The sauce is served at every banquet thereafter, and its maker is never named. {npc} is hired again each year as a "temporary helper," at the same pay, in the same corner, with the same pile of roots. {He} does not mind. {He} smiles at the sauce, as it goes out, like a parent at a school gate.
events.arc: The Rogue Allowed in the Banquet Kitchen

effects.log: The two of you share the peel and the tea.
It is always good.

events.text: A small wind-serpent, no thicker than a rope, has coiled itself on your roof and fallen asleep. {npc}, the neighbour, points it out with a rolling pin. "It came in with last night's gale," {he} says. "They get tired. Give it a day and it will go." The serpent opens one eye, regards you, and shuts it.
events.arc: The Wind-Serpent Who Borrowed the Roof

effects.log: You walk softly under the roof for a week.

choices.text: Set out a saucer of milk-cloud

effects.log: The serpent drinks it politely.
It flicks a tail.

events.text: The serpent does not go. It stays through the spring and into the summer, curled around your chimney, whistling in the evenings. The sound is cheerful and a little off-key. The neighbours come to listen. Tea is made on your doorstep. A small crowd forms nightly under the eaves, and the serpent whistles to them, shy and proud.
events.arc: The Wind-Serpent Who Borrowed the Roof

effects.log: Chairs, cups, and a serpent. It is one of the best nights of the year.
It learns three notes in a week, and holds them with great pride.
The street hums.

events.text: One autumn night the serpent rises from the roof in a long silver curl and joins a passing gale. It does not look back. You stand in the yard and hear the whistle fade over three isles. In the morning there is a single scale on the roof, bright as a coin. {npc} takes it down with reverence and hands it to you.
events.arc: The Wind-Serpent Who Borrowed the Roof

choices.text: Keep the scale on the sill

effects.log: It catches the first light each day.
You whistle the three notes.

events.text: The serpent returns every autumn, for a night, on the first gale. It circles the roof once, whistles three notes, and goes. The neighbours gather in the yard at dusk and wait. The three notes are the tune you taught it. By the fifth century, the whole isle can whistle them, and children do, in the lanes, without knowing why.
events.arc: The Wind-Serpent Who Borrowed the Roof

effects.log: You and the children whistle the three notes at dusk.

choices.text: Leave the roof bare for it

effects.log: The serpent coils on the old tiles.

events.text: Two isles of different fleets, the Heron and the Marten, are to marry, in a manner of speaking: the heirs have fallen in love. {npc}, the Heron's steersman, comes to you for advice on the ceremony. "Which fleet hosts?" {he} asks. "Which cake do we cut? What if the isles do not like each other?" You say that isles have rarely been consulted.
events.arc: The Wedding Two Fleets Shared

choices.text: Suggest meeting halfway in the sky

effects.log: A neutral patch of cloud, with a bridge of rope. {He} writes it down.

choices.text: Offer to help with the cake

effects.log: You are drafted. The cake is enormous.
{He} sighs and thanks you.

events.text: The wedding is held on a patch of open sky between two fleets, with the isles moored at each end of a rope bridge a mile long. Guests cross from both sides in lantern-light, meeting in the middle, where the couple stand. Nobody can hear the vows. They are sung by the wind, which has been paid in advance, and is moved to tears.
events.arc: The Wedding Two Fleets Shared

choices.text: Cross the bridge with the guests

effects.log: It sways and sings. Halfway, you meet a stranger who is a cousin.

choices.text: Stay on the Heron side and watch

effects.log: You see the lanterns meet, a bright thread.
The wind carries your toast along.

events.text: The two isles, after the wedding, move closer. A decade later they are moored side by side, and a tourist cannot tell where one ends and the other begins. The Heron and Marten fleets become one, with a new flag: two birds, wings touching. {npc} is made harbour-master of the new fleet and, to your delight, hangs your name on a plank by the dock.
events.arc: The Wedding Two Fleets Shared

choices.text: Sit by the plank with a cup

effects.log: The dock is quiet, with the sound of ropes.
They are shy and kind.

events.text: The wedding bridge is left up between the isles, and becomes a tradition: every year, on the same day, the two fleets cross it and swap a gift. The gifts get stranger as the centuries pass. One year it is a sack of pebbles, another a single sea-shell. {npc}, old and wise, still takes the first step.
events.arc: The Wedding Two Fleets Shared

choices.text: Bring your own gift to the bridge

effects.log: You bring a pebble. It is accepted with solemn thanks.
The procession is a ribbon of lamps.

events.text: {npc} has steered the Larch Fleet through ten thousand seasons, and announces it will be the last. {He} gives the news in the wheelhouse over a cup, in a plain voice, as if reading a bill. "My hands are going," {he} says. "I want to give the fleet over while I still know how to be useful." The fleet is quiet at the news.
events.arc: The Steersman's Last Season

effects.log: {He} nods. "Come at dawn. I will not repeat myself."

choices.text: Say the fleet will not manage without {him}

effects.log: {He} snorts. "It managed before I was born."
The cup is warm in both hands.

events.text: You spend the season at the wheel beside {npc}, learning the winds. It is hard, and humbling. A wind named Old Sourpuss shoves the isle sideways. A cloud-reef looms. You turn too late, and the hull groans along the stone. {npc} says nothing at first, then: "That was the correct way to do it badly. The next is the correct way to do it."
events.arc: The Steersman's Last Season

effects.log: The second try is better. The third is almost smooth.
{He} pours without comment. The reef drifts by.
The hands move like water.

events.text: On the last day of the season, {npc} lets go of the wheel, and the fleet watches from every deck. You turn the isle through the final reef alone. The ropes sing. The fleet comes into harbour like a flock of geese, every isle in its place. {npc} stands on the dock, small, and takes off {his} cap.
events.arc: The Steersman's Last Season

choices.text: Offer the cap back to {him} with a bow

effects.log: {He} refuses, and puts it on your head.
It sounds for a long time.

events.text: The Larch Fleet gets a new steersman, a quarrelsome young one who has never met the winds and does not like them. {npc} watches from the dock with a cup of tea, and says nothing. When the young steersman fails, {he} calls across the water: "Correct way to do it badly!" The fleet laughs. The steersman learns.
events.arc: The Steersman's Last Season

effects.log: {He} waves back with the cup.

choices.text: Pour out a cup for the wind

effects.log: Old Sourpuss accepts.

events.text: A thin clear note drifts up the cloud-stair, from far below. {npc}, a clerk of the Ministry of Prayers, hears it first and carries the news to you. "It is a song," {he} says. "A very old person is singing it, down there, to nobody. The Ministry has forwarded it to you, as the name on the song is yours."
events.arc: The Last Song of a Mortal Friend

effects.log: It runs three minutes. It has no words. It is simply a person, singing.
{npc} looks it up. It is a friend of long ago, now eighty.
The two of you listen, side by side.

events.text: The song is repeated each dusk for a month. You learn it by heart, a plain tune of five notes. You hum it at your window. A neighbour asks what it is, and you tell the truth, in a few sentences. The neighbour is quiet, and then hums the tune back, a bit off.
events.arc: The Last Song of a Mortal Friend

effects.log: It takes an evening. The neighbour carries it away like a warm coal.
It is a private thing, worn like a coat.
Five notes on a slip of jade.

events.text: One dusk, the song stops. {npc} comes to your door with the news in a soft voice, and no ledger. You thank {him}, and sit. After a while you sing the five notes yourself, aloud, in the quiet of the room. They sound very small. They carry a very long way. The window is open, and the night wind takes them down.
events.arc: The Last Song of a Mortal Friend

choices.text: Sing it until the lamp burns low

effects.log: The song fills the room, and then empties it.
It is enough.

events.text: The tune spreads up the stairs, hummed by clerks, ferrymen and children. Nobody knows where it came from. It is called "the Five Notes" and played at dusk on the long terraces. A visiting musician writes it into a symphony. The symphony is performed, in time, in the Jade Court, and you attend, and weep, quietly, in the back.
events.arc: The Last Song of a Mortal Friend

choices.text: Tell no one it was a gift

effects.log: It stays a secret, between you and the wind.
The music takes you.

events.text: {npc} has set out to paint every cloud in the sky, one by one, in a notebook, and has so far reached the letter C. "There are rather many," {he} says, wiping a brush. "I have a system. They go in by shape, mood, and what they were about to do." A small crowd watches over {his} shoulder, enthralled.
events.arc: The Immortal Who Painted Every Cloud

effects.log: It runs to eleven hundred volumes. The paintings are small and perfect.
{He} paints it at once, and names it after you.
It moves like a thought.

events.text: The notebooks need a house. {npc} builds a long, low studio on the Bluebell Isle, with north windows and nine hundred shelves. A cloud drifts in through the window one afternoon and settles over a desk. {He} paints it with trembling hands, and when it is done, the cloud floats off, looking pleased. The studio is soon full of cloud visitors.
events.arc: The Immortal Who Painted Every Cloud

effects.log: Your arms ache and the shelves fill.

choices.text: Stay for tea with the clouds

effects.log: The clouds are polite guests and leave a faint dew.
The shelf shimmers.

events.text: A century later, {npc} has reached the letter M and has become cloud-famous. Clouds queue to be painted. Some travel for years from the Edge. A storm cloud arrives, huge, grey, and shy, and asks, in a rumble, if it may be painted without thunder. {npc} says yes, and does it, and the portrait is the finest in the studio.
events.arc: The Immortal Who Painted Every Cloud

effects.log: The grey is soft and deep. It is the best thing in the book.
It trembles, pleased.

events.text: {npc} never reaches Z. When the time comes, {he} hands you the brush and notebook, saying, "There are always more clouds than anyone can paint." You paint, badly, a single small cloud over the Bluebell Isle. It looks back at you, and drifts off, delighted. The studio stays open for a thousand years.
events.arc: The Immortal Who Painted Every Cloud

effects.log: You paint a cloud a week for ages.
The shelves are dusted.

events.text: {npc} announces at breakfast that after six hundred years of study, {he} has produced the perfect boiled egg. A hush falls. {He} cracks it with a spoon. It is a very ordinary egg, which, {he} says, is the whole point. "Every other egg has been trying to be something," {he} says. "This one is simply an egg."
events.arc: The Immortal Who Perfected the Boiled Egg

effects.log: It is warm, soft, and exact. You have never felt so completely at breakfast.
"Nine minutes," {he} says. "And a quiet mind."
The egg takes a bow.

events.text: The perfect egg spreads. Cooks from three isles come to watch {npc} boil, and fail to match it. A rival chef sulks. A young admirer follows {him} for a month. A letter arrives from the Jade Court asking for a demonstration. {npc} writes back: "It is only an egg." The Court insists.
events.arc: The Immortal Who Perfected the Boiled Egg

effects.log: You carry the pot. The Court is rapt.
{He} sighs with relief and does.

choices.text: Boil a bad egg for comparison

effects.log: It is dreadful. The comparison is complete.

events.text: At the Jade Court, {npc} boils the egg before four ministers and a crowd. It is served. The ministers eat in silence. One removes a hat. After a long pause, the oldest says: "It is just like the egg my mother made." Nobody speaks. {npc}, to everyone's surprise, begins to cry, and says, "That is the whole point."
events.arc: The Immortal Who Perfected the Boiled Egg

effects.log: {He} blows {his} nose and bows.
It is as good as the first.

events.text: {npc} retires from eggs, and takes up soup. The soup is awful. {He} is delighted by this. "Imperfect," {he} says, spooning it, "is where the next six hundred years begin." You eat three bowls, out of loyalty and curiosity, and by the third you are ready to admit it is, in its way, wonderful.
events.arc: The Immortal Who Perfected the Boiled Egg

effects.log: It is a list of mistakes.
{He} glows.

events.text: {npc} and you have been friends for a thousand years, and have fallen into the habit of competing to be more modest. At every gathering the two of you bow lower than the other, give the better seat, refuse the better dish. The room watches, weary. This evening {npc} has offered you the seat of honour, which you have politely declined for the ninth time.
events.arc: Two Old Friends Racing to Be Humble

effects.log: You insist. {He} insists. The room withdraws for tea.

choices.text: Take the seat, just to end it

effects.log: {He} is aghast, then relieved, then amused.
You sit together. It holds, barely.

events.text: The contest escalates. {npc} gives away an isle, in honour of your example. You give away yours. The recipients, two bewildered bakers, are told to keep them. Neither of you is allowed to refuse. The following morning, you are both homeless, cheerful, and sitting side by side on a rock in the middle of the sky.
events.arc: Two Old Friends Racing to Be Humble

effects.log: You laugh till you are weak. {He} joins in.

choices.text: Ask the bakers for a bed

effects.log: The bakers find you a spare room, with pastry.

choices.text: Sit and look at the sky

effects.log: It is large and indifferent.

events.text: The bakers return the isles with a note: "We could not accept such generosity." The two of you stare at the note, then at each other. A joke has become a trade, and the trade is done. The isles are yours again, with the pastry shop thrown in. You and {npc} sign a pact in cake icing, to be proud and say nothing.
events.arc: Two Old Friends Racing to Be Humble

effects.log: It is the best document you have ever signed.
It crumbles on the wall.

events.text: The contest gradually softens into something warmer. The two of you stop competing. Instead, you swap seats at dinner, quietly, and nobody comments. {npc} once says in an offhand way, "I am glad it is you I am humble to." It is the best thing anyone has said to you in a century. You are too humble to answer.
events.arc: Two Old Friends Racing to Be Humble

effects.log: The cups meet in the middle.
They are very fine shoes.

events.text: {npc}, your neighbour of five hundred years, has announced that {he} is moving. Not house, but isle: the whole Quill Isle, with its orchard, its cat, and its crooked chimney. "The winds are better in the south," {he} says. "Come and visit." You look at the rope that has joined your isles for as long as you can remember.
events.arc: The Friend Who Moved a Whole Isle Away

effects.log: You haul at the lines for a day and a night.
{He} smiles sadly and says the winds are the winds.

choices.text: Say nothing, and bake a loaf

effects.log: {He} takes it with a quiet thanks.

events.text: The Quill Isle sails away on a clear morning. You stand on the dock with a cup and watch it grow small. For the first time in centuries the sky beside your window is empty. The cat, you are told, has stowed away on your roof. It looks at you with large dismissive eyes. You are a pet-owner now.
events.arc: The Friend Who Moved a Whole Isle Away

effects.log: It eats and leaves a shrug of fur.

choices.text: Send a letter after the isle

effects.log: It will take a season to arrive.
It is vast, and gives nothing back.

events.text: A year later a skiff arrives with a parcel: a jar of the south wind, sealed with wax, and a tin of jam. The note says, "Open the jar when you miss me." You do not open it. You put it on the sill, and look at it, and are comforted. The cat sleeps beside it. The south wind sits in the jar, patient.
events.arc: The Friend Who Moved a Whole Isle Away

effects.log: It stays, a promise on the shelf.

choices.text: Open the jar for a moment

effects.log: A warm breeze runs through your hair and out the window.

events.text: A century on, the Quill Isle sails back, tattered and sun-bleached, and moors in its old place. {npc} climbs down the rope in a hat that has seen a great deal of weather. "The winds were better," {he} says. "But the neighbours were not." The cat leaps down from your roof and steps across the gap without looking back.
events.arc: The Friend Who Moved a Whole Isle Away

effects.log: They fit as if never gone.

choices.text: Pour a cup for the traveller

effects.log: The tea and the traveller are both hot.

events.text: The Jade Void Sect keeps a choir of nine great bells, each as tall as a house, rung at dawn by nine ringers. {npc}, the choirmaster, is short a ringer for the seventh bell, whose rope has worn out three apprentices already. {He} looks you over from head to foot and says: "You have the shoulders."
events.arc: The Jade Void Bell Choir

effects.log: You pull. The bell moves, and your arms with it.
{He} sniffs. "There are no lighter bells. There are only lighter people."

choices.text: Watch the practice from the side

effects.log: It is loud, and then beautiful.

events.text: The seventh bell is the lowest, a note felt in the feet rather than heard. The choir rings at dawn on the first of the month, and the whole isle hums. You learn to lean into the rope, to wait for the sway, to let go. By the third week you can ring it half a minute without a shudder. {npc} grunts, which is praise.
events.arc: The Jade Void Bell Choir

effects.log: You ring in an empty hall. The bell listens.
Eight ringers, eight answers.
They tingle.

events.text: The Jade Void rings the dawn for a visiting delegation of ministers. Nine bells in nine notes: a chord that shakes the dust from the beams. The seventh comes in a little late, and a little loud. The delegation, hushed, thinks it is on purpose. {npc} looks up at you in the gallery and mouths: "Perfect." You do not believe a word.
events.arc: The Jade Void Bell Choir

effects.log: They bow back. A minister dabs an eye.

choices.text: Share a cup with the ringers

effects.log: You drink in silence, ears ringing.

events.text: {npc} retires and leaves the baton to you. You teach new ringers, a new nine, each with their own sway and their own quarrel with their rope. The choir rings for a thousand years, and not once the same way twice. Visitors say it is the sound of the isle thinking. You say it is just bells.
events.arc: The Jade Void Bell Choir

effects.log: You hold it as one holds a hand.
It is as low as ever.

events.text: At the Nine Clouds Palace, a fan is not for cooling but for saying what the mouth cannot. {npc}, the palace fan-maker, paints each blade with a phrase in a language of folds and flutters: a half-closed fan means "later," a trembling one "perhaps." {He} has been asked to make a fan for you, and has questions. "What would you like it to say?"
events.arc: The Fan-Maker of the Nine Clouds Palace

choices.text: Ask for a fan that says "thank you"

effects.log: {He} smiles. "That is the hardest. I will need a month."

choices.text: Ask for a fan that says "no"

effects.log: {He} laughs. "Easy. Everyone wants those."
{He} nods, pleased by the trust.

events.text: The fan arrives in a lacquered box. It is plain, pale, and almost weightless. When you open it a quarter, the whole court seems to hear a gentle word. A minister, passing, bows, as if thanked. You try it again, closing it slowly. A clerk stops to look back, startled. You have begun speaking a tongue you cannot read.
events.arc: The Fan-Maker of the Nine Clouds Palace

effects.log: You learn three phrases in a week and one by accident.

choices.text: Gift a fan to a friend

effects.log: The friend opens it, and, understanding, smiles.
Silence is also a phrase.

events.text: At a banquet, a rival of the palace sends you a fan, wrapped in silk, with a sly note. Opened, it says, in a flutter anyone could read, "I know." You hold it a moment. Then you open your own, half, and tilt it, a gesture that reads, to any who know, "Of course you do." The court exhales. The rival laughs from the other end of the hall.
events.arc: The Fan-Maker of the Nine Clouds Palace

effects.log: A quarrel becomes a friendship across the table.
The silk goes back in the box.

events.text: {npc} retires, and you carry a fan you never open at the end. It says, {he} told you, the thing you meant to say when you asked for it. You still do not know what that is. At the funeral of an old friend, you hold it half open, and a hush falls over the room, and you understand, finally, what it is for.
events.arc: The Fan-Maker of the Nine Clouds Palace

effects.log: You never open it again.

choices.text: Pass it to a young courtier

effects.log: The young courtier bows over it.

events.text: {npc}, an inspector of the Celestial Ministries, has spent a month inspecting the Tern Isle for compliance with the Weather Statutes, and has now discovered that it was supposed to inspect the Tarn Isle. The Tern folk, who were delighted to be inspected, are stricken. The Tarn folk, unvisited, are miffed. {npc} stands at your door with a ream of reports.
events.arc: The Inspector Who Inspected the Wrong Isle

choices.text: Offer to help rewrite the reports

effects.log: You and {npc} change every "Tern" to "Tarn," and then see the problem.

choices.text: Suggest keeping the Tern reports as a kindness

effects.log: {He} stares at you, then brightens.
{He} drinks it standing.

events.text: The Ministry is told. A senior clerk, bald and thorough, calls a hearing. {npc} stands in front of a long table of senior clerks, explaining that the Tern Isle has been praised, fed, and thoroughly commended. The clerks ask what is the harm. The Tern Isle delegate, in the back, says: "None. We would like to be inspected again."
events.arc: The Inspector Who Inspected the Wrong Isle

effects.log: You describe the month: tea, tidy gutters, and a genuine joy in compliance.
The Tarn folk, too, deserve a visit. The hearing agrees.

choices.text: Sit at the back and listen

effects.log: The hearing takes four hours.

events.text: The Ministry rules that both isles should be inspected, annually, in alternating years, so that neither is neglected, and that {npc} is to remain the inspector of both. Both isles celebrate. A banner, hung across the harbour, reads: "Compliant, Ish." {npc} shakes your hand twice and cannot finish a sentence.
events.arc: The Inspector Who Inspected the Wrong Isle

choices.text: Raise a cup to the inspector

effects.log: The harbour sings.
It is hung straight, mostly.

events.text: The Ministry rules that the Tern Isle must now be inspected as a matter of record, since the reports exist, and that the Tarn Isle must be inspected some other time, which is never fixed. {npc} sighs. Years later, on a clear morning, {he} turns up at the Tarn Isle with a bag of sweets and an apology. It is received like a festival.
events.arc: The Inspector Who Inspected the Wrong Isle

effects.log: The street is lined with paper flags.
The scene is a pleasure.

events.text: In the Demon Realm, once a year, the sky lets fall a fine grey ash that is not burning, but warm. Children run out into the lanes with open mouths and open palms. A baker says it tastes of old bread. A poet says it tastes of old hours. The ash stays on the ground for a day, then lifts, in a slow bloom, back to the clouds.

effects.log: It is warm as a sleeping cat.

choices.text: Stand in it with the children

effects.log: Your coat goes grey, to your delight.

events.text: A stall at the Demon Realm market sells the echoes of words that no one has said yet, bottled in thin glass. The seller, a calm figure in a long robe, explains that they are cheaper than the real thing. "You open one when you are about to say it," they say, "and it saves a great deal of trouble."

effects.log: It smells faintly of regret.
The seller shrugs, not offended.

events.text: The gatekeeper of the Demon Realm's eastern road asks every traveller one question: "What are you carrying that is not in your bag?" Answers are written in a book. Today a trader says "worry." A child says "a song." A traveller says nothing and is waved through with a smile.

effects.log: The gatekeeper writes it down, nods, and waves you in.
The gatekeeper laughs, and you pass.

events.text: On clear nights the apprentices of the Star Sea Pavilion fly kites on the dome roof, long silk ones with a single lantern in the tail. They are not for pleasure but for calibration: a kite with a lantern is a fixed point the astronomers can measure against. It is also, undeniably, for pleasure.

effects.log: The kite rises into the stars.
The lantern is relit.

events.text: The Star Sea Pavilion keeps a cat to chase the moths out of the lenses. The cat has become suspiciously famous. Visitors leave offerings: fish-scale charms, tiny silk hats, a miniature telescope. The cat sits on the pile with an air of cosmic ownership and permits no one to touch the telescope.

effects.log: The cat accepts it as tribute.
The cat blinks slowly.

events.text: The Pavilion's archive of star-charts is kept cold, and the archivists drink their tea very hot. A rule requires that no cup be set down on a chart. Rule or not, every chart in the east wing wears a faint ring. A cleaner works through the rings with a cloth, and calls them "the astronomers' signatures."

choices.text: Fetch a cup for the cleaner

effects.log: The cleaner takes it with thanks.

choices.text: Trace a ring with a finger

effects.log: It is still faintly warm.

events.text: The youngest disciple of the sect you founded bows to you each morning with such care and speed that the bow ends in a small stumble. For a year you have said nothing. This morning the disciple lands on a broom and sweeps a whole row of cups to the floor. The silence is long. You are, you realise, laughing.

effects.log: The disciple is mortified and grateful.
It is a bow like a feather.

events.text: Rain duty at the sect means standing under the eaves of the Hall of Letters with a bucket and a very long face, ready to move the scrolls if the roof leaks. Today a junior has fallen asleep on duty, bucket on lap. It starts to drip. The scrolls hold. The bucket quietly fills, and the junior, in sleep, shifts it just in time.

effects.log: The scrolls are safe.
The junior purrs.

events.text: The anniversary of the sect's founding is marked with a banquet at which the founder (you) is expected to say a few words. Every year you say the same four, and every year the disciples cheer as if it were the first. This year a junior asks you to say a different four. You have, you find, no others.

effects.log: The cheer is very loud.
The cheer is even louder.

events.text: A heaven-born child on the Meadow Isle has lost a tooth, a first one, at the age of sixty. The isle assembles for the ritual: it is placed in a cloud-pine and the child is made to spin three times. It is said the tooth grows into a new one, in the form of a small star. The child spins, and nothing happens, and then the pine twinkles.

effects.log: The child curtsies, dizzy.
The child takes it, gap-toothed.

events.text: A heaven-born child sits on the third step and asks every passer-by the same riddle: "What do you do when the last stair is the first?" Most people shrug. An old minister goes pale and sits down. The child, looking as though a lesson has landed, writes the minister's name in a small book.

effects.log: Your answer is "Turn round." The child looks impressed.

choices.text: Ask the child to explain it

effects.log: "I do not know," says the child. "Isn't it good?"

events.text: A mist-hound is sitting on your doorstep, damp and wide-eyed. Its collar says, in a careful hand, "Not lost: waiting." You search the lane for its owner. The lane is empty. The hound, reading your face, wags the tip of its tail. It has, evidently, chosen.

choices.text: Bring it in and dry it

effects.log: It steams happily by the fire.

choices.text: Leave a bowl on the step

effects.log: It eats and stays.

events.text: A cloud carp has taken up residence in your washing-tub. It rolls in the suds, burbling soft bubbles, and has refused all offers of a proper pond. A neighbour tells you it must be "between lives." The carp, hearing, looks mildly offended, and blows a bubble the size of a plum.

effects.log: The carp swirls and approves.
It nibbles, content.

events.text: When two fleets meet in a narrow channel, a gong is struck, three times, to say who yields. The crews have argued for centuries over who strikes first. Today both gongs ring at once, and the sound is a single, strange chord. The steersmen look at each other, surprised, and both lower their flags.

effects.log: Both crews bow.
The fleets pass in turn.

events.text: A fleet in the far north sends a message by lantern to a fleet in the far south: "We are cousins." The answer comes back the next night: "We know." The two fleets have not met in six centuries. A skiff is sent to fetch them. It returns with a hundred cousins, a goat, and a half-eaten cake.

effects.log: The dock fills with hugging.

choices.text: Fetch a pot of tea for the lot

effects.log: The tea runs out quickly.

events.text: It has rained below for three days, a steady grey rain that reaches even the upper terraces as a faint drumming. A clerk of the Prayers says it is a good year for the harvest below. You think of a field, a hand, a bowl of rice, and are surprised by how warm the thought feels. The rain goes on.

effects.log: It is a lullaby.

choices.text: Say a quiet word of thanks

effects.log: It is sent down with the drops.

events.text: On the night of the mortals' lantern festival, tiny lights float up through the clouds like fireflies, carried by thermals. A few reach the upper terraces and hover, shivering, over your balcony. Each carries a paper tag: a wish, a name, a prayer. You read three. They are all, in the end, requests for kindness.

effects.log: It asks for a good harvest.

choices.text: Light a lantern of your own

effects.log: It joins the ones below.

events.text: An immortal at the Quiet Lake has skipped one stone, every morning, for nine hundred years, and recorded the number of skips in a ledger. The record is thirty-one. The average is four. The immortal says that the record is meaningless, but keeps the stone that made it, polished, on the sill.

effects.log: It makes six. The immortal writes it down.
The stones are lined in order.

events.text: In a bamboo grove, a retired marshal has trained a hundred wind-whistles into a tune, hung at different heights so that a breeze through the grove plays an old fleet song. The marshal sits on a bench and conducts the wind with a finger. The wind, it is said, is proud of itself.

choices.text: Sit on the bench and listen

effects.log: The tune is sweet and plain.
The marshal nods.

events.text: A painter on the Cloud Bridge draws a portrait of every traveller who crosses, in chalk on the planks, free of charge. By evening the bridge is a gallery of faces; by morning the wind has taken them. "That is the point," the painter says. "They are a gift to the wind." Your portrait looks astonishingly like you.

effects.log: The painter bows.

choices.text: Watch the wind take your face

effects.log: It goes in a grey puff.

events.text: The wind has taken your hat. You see it sailing over the lane, high, tilting, like a bird making up its mind. A child gives chase with a net on a pole. The hat leads her a merry dance over three roofs, a chimney, and a pond. In the end it lands on the head of a very surprised minister.

effects.log: The minister gives it back with a smile.
It suits them.

events.text: A kitchen on the Plum Isle has a wooden spoon that has stirred the same soup pot for seven hundred years, and has, in the opinion of the cooks, opinions. When a stew is wrong, the spoon will not stir. When it is right, it hums. Today it hums. The cooks sit very still and let it.

effects.log: It tastes of everyone who ever ate it.
It hums a little louder.

events.text: A page whose job is to strike the Jade Court's noon gong has been late three times this month. A minister begins to mutter. The page, hearing, strikes the gong with such unexpected force that a vase falls. The minister goes quiet. The page, rubbing a sore wrist, says "On time, Excellency."

choices.text: Hand the page a cup of water

effects.log: The page gulps it.
The page flushes.

events.text: A clerk of the Ministry of Weather forgot, for once, to schedule the hail. A small round of it falls on the Elm Isle at midnight, unannounced. The folk run out in nightgowns and stand in the moonlit lane catching hailstones in their hands. It is the best night the isle has had in a decade.

effects.log: It is cold as a star.
You share a laugh.

events.text: One peach tree in the Orchard Isle blooms a whole season late every year. The gardeners have tried to correct it with pruning, warming, lecturing. Nothing works. This year the late blossoms open on the day of the first snow, a pink blaze against white, and the gardeners stop correcting.

effects.log: The petals and snow mix.
The gardeners laugh softly.

events.text: A nap on the edge of the Last Terrace, with your feet over the abyss and a cushion at your back, is said to cure a hundred minor ailments and one major boredom. The Terrace keeper charges a stone for the cushion. You pay it. You sleep like a stone. When you wake, someone has covered you with a blanket.

effects.log: The sleep is deep and sweet.
It is hard, and also fine.

events.text: The nights of the Demon Realm are twice as long as the days, and {npc} fills them. Every evening {he} sits at the crossroads under a hanging lamp and tells one story, never the same, to whoever has come. The rule is that no one may leave before the end. Tonight the tale is about a door that opens only for the lost. You have come in out of the cold.
events.arc: The Storyteller of the Long Nights

effects.log: The tale goes on until the lamp is low. You leave feeling lighter.

choices.text: Ask for a tale of your own

effects.log: {He} considers you. "Tomorrow," {he} says. "Come early."

choices.text: Bring a flask for the circle

effects.log: It goes round, and returns empty.

events.text: You return early. {npc} takes your tale down on a strip of paper, by asking questions: where you were born, what you fear, what you forgot. The story that comes out is nothing like what you told. It is shorter, odder, and truer. {He} tells it that night without naming you, and the crossroads goes quiet in the way of a held breath.
events.arc: The Storyteller of the Long Nights

choices.text: Listen as a stranger to your own tale

effects.log: It is strange to be told what you are. You do not mind.
{He} says no. "An ending is not a thing you can borrow."
You are stopped at the edge of the lamplight by a gentle cough.

events.text: Years on, the crossroads lamp gutters. {npc} is too tired to climb the stool. A crowd gathers and begs for the tale. You stand, a little shaky, and say that you will tell it for tonight. Your voice is steadier than you thought. You tell the one about a storyteller and a lamp. When you finish, {npc}, in the dark, begins to clap.
events.arc: The Storyteller of the Long Nights

effects.log: You tell a tale every night after, until the lamp burns bright.
The stool is cold.

events.text: You keep the secret of the ending. {npc} tells the tale one final time, in a voice like worn silk, and ends it without a flourish. "That is how it goes," {he} says. The crowd sits very still for a while. Then they go home in twos and threes, carrying the story like a lit coal. The lamp at the crossroads is never relit.
events.arc: The Storyteller of the Long Nights

choices.text: Keep a seat at the crossroads

effects.log: You sit there each evening, listening to the wind tell it.
The road is long and quiet.

events.text: The border bridge of the Demon Realm has an odd toll: {npc} takes no coin, only a joke, which {he} writes in a thick ledger and rates out of ten. A poor joke is turned back and told to improve. A good one is waved through with a bow. You have been standing at the barrier for an hour trying to think of one.
events.arc: The Toll-Collector Who Collected Jokes

choices.text: Offer an old joke about a goat

effects.log: {npc} rates it a four. "Vintage, but tired," {he} says.

choices.text: Offer a joke you made up on the spot

effects.log: It is terrible. {He} gives it a six for courage.
{He} tells a very good joke. You cross, laughing.

events.text: The ledger is a famous thing, and visitors come just to read it. It has recorded fourteen thousand jokes across seven hundred years. Many of them are terrible; a handful are masterpieces. {npc} shows you the page where the oldest is kept, a pun so ancient it has lost its meaning, and has gained a kind of dignity.
events.arc: The Toll-Collector Who Collected Jokes

choices.text: Offer a joke worth a ten

effects.log: You search your memory and find one. {He} laughs so hard the ink spills.
You spend an afternoon among centuries of laughter.
It deserves its dignity.

events.text: A day comes when the border closes for a ceremony and the bridge is empty. {npc} sits on the rail with the ledger in {his} lap and says, quietly, "I have not laughed in a year." You know that is not true. You tell the goat joke again, slowly, badly, and {he} laughs till {he} falls off the rail and has to be fished out.
events.arc: The Toll-Collector Who Collected Jokes

effects.log: The two of you lie on the bridge laughing.
{He} is grateful and still giggling.

events.text: {npc} retires, and the ledger is sent to the archive, where it is read by scholars who do not laugh. You visit it every year and read a page aloud to an empty room. The room, in the end, laughs. Somewhere in the stacks, a frowning archivist drops a book and begins, to their own surprise, to giggle.
events.arc: The Toll-Collector Who Collected Jokes

effects.log: The ritual becomes part of the archive.

choices.text: Leave a joke in the margin

effects.log: Someone will find it.

events.text: {npc} has kept the night-watch of the Star Sea Pavilion for seven hundred years and has never once seen the dawn. The shift ends an hour before it, and {he} goes straight to bed, curtains drawn. "I have an arrangement with the sun," {he} says. "I do not look and it does not insist." A junior, new, wants to know why.
events.arc: The Night-Watch That Never Saw Dawn

choices.text: Ask the junior to leave it alone

effects.log: The junior shrugs. {npc} looks relieved.

choices.text: Offer to stay the extra hour with {him}

effects.log: {He} hesitates, and then says "Perhaps."

choices.text: Pour a cup for the night-watch

effects.log: The cup steams in the dark.

events.text: You sit with {npc} in the last hour. The dome is full of stars, deep and slow. The east begins to pale. {He} grips the rail. "It was a dawn, once," {he} says, "a bad one. I do not like to talk about it." You nod and say nothing, and the grey moves across the dome, and {he} does not turn.
events.arc: The Night-Watch That Never Saw Dawn

choices.text: Stay quiet until the light comes

effects.log: The light comes, plain and gentle. {npc} lets out a long breath.
The room goes dim. {He} gives you a small smile.
It is a very old, very small tune.

events.text: {npc} sees the dawn, the first in seven centuries. It comes up gold on the Star Sea and sets the dome-glass aflame. {He} says nothing for a long time. Then: "It is smaller than I remembered." You laugh, and {he} laughs, and the watch ends in a flood of warm light. The junior, passing with a broom, bows to the sun.
events.arc: The Night-Watch That Never Saw Dawn

effects.log: The kitchens are warm and loud. {He} eats three buns.
It is a good sun.

events.text: {npc} never looks at the dawn again, but now sets a chair by the east shutter and listens to it come up, a little at a time, through the slats. The sound is faint: a thin bird, a stir of wind, a clock. "That is enough," {he} says. You keep the chair dusted, and the shutter oiled, for a thousand years.
events.arc: The Night-Watch That Never Saw Dawn

effects.log: It is a good chair and gets good use.
The tea is always hot.

events.text: {npc} comes to the Star Sea Pavilion archive late one evening, wrapped in a long coat, and asks to speak to an astronomer with no witnesses. {He} unwraps a chart: a very fine one, and false. "I forged this," {he} says, "four centuries ago, in a bad year, to pay a debt. It has hung in the east wing since. I would like to take it back."
events.arc: The Chart Forger's Apology

effects.log: The story is long, tired, and sorry.
{He} flinches. The master arrives with a lamp.

choices.text: Take the chart and look at it

effects.log: It is a wonderful forgery.

events.text: The false chart has misled four generations of navigators. A few skiffs have gone astray; none lost. The east wing's best map, the pride of the Pavilion, is a lie. The master of charts says nothing for a full minute. Then: "It is still the best chart we have of that sector. Perhaps because the lie was drawn by someone who loved the sky."
events.arc: The Chart Forger's Apology

choices.text: Propose keeping it, with a note

effects.log: The Pavilion adds a card: "A beautiful error."

choices.text: Propose a true one beside it

effects.log: The two hang together, side by side.
{npc} cannot hold it for shaking.

events.text: The forger is asked, as penance, to draw the true chart, and takes ten years. The result is exquisite: a copper-plated sky that shames the old lie. It is hung beside the forgery. Visitors cannot tell them apart, and the Pavilion prints a leaflet to help. The forger, in a corner, is overheard saying "I did my best."
events.arc: The Chart Forger's Apology

effects.log: {npc} blushes like a boy.
It is sweetly written.

events.text: The false chart stays on the wall, with its card. Over time it becomes a favourite of the junior astronomers, who learn to read its errors as a map of a kind: the errors of a person who wanted the sky to be beautiful. {npc}, old, is sometimes seen standing in front of it, hands behind {his} back, smiling.
events.arc: The Chart Forger's Apology

effects.log: The two of you look at the beautiful error.
{He} nods slowly.

events.text: Two disciples of the sect you founded, {npc} and a fellow from the Hall of Swords, have asked leave to marry. It is the first wedding in the sect's history, and the rule-book is silent. The elders are alarmed. The cooks are thrilled. {npc} stands in your doorway, hands knotted, asking, "May we?"
events.arc: The First Wedding in the Sect

effects.log: The doorway fills with sunshine. {He} runs off to tell the Hall of Swords.

choices.text: Ask the elders to write a rule

effects.log: It takes three days and four drafts, and the rule is three lines.
{He} sits on the edge of the chair.

events.text: The wedding is planned by committee, and the committee cannot agree on anything. The Hall of Swords wants a procession; the Hall of Letters, a poem; the Hall of Morning Sweeping, a clean path. The cooks want a banquet. {npc} comes to you in despair. "It is going to be everything," {he} says. "I wanted something small."
events.arc: The First Wedding in the Sect

effects.log: The elders protest. You overrule them. {npc} weeps with relief.

choices.text: Let each hall add a piece

effects.log: The wedding grows to a fortnight. It is glorious.
You learn the words the night before.

events.text: The small wedding is held in the garden at dusk, with nine guests and a single bell. The couple stand beneath a plum tree. You say the three lines of the sect's new rule. A bird sings in the wrong key. Afterwards the cooks bring out a plain dish of noodles, and everyone eats in the half-dark. It is the best meal of the century.
events.arc: The First Wedding in the Sect

effects.log: You raise a cup of tea. Everyone drinks.

choices.text: Wash the bowls with the others

effects.log: Your sleeves get wet.

events.text: The long wedding is a joy and an ordeal: a fortnight of processions, poems, brooms, and banquets. By the end, the couple are exhausted and everyone else is in love with the sect. A sign is hung over the gate for the following year: "Please marry here." The elders blush. {npc} sends you a card, signed in two hands.
events.arc: The First Wedding in the Sect

choices.text: Keep the card on your desk

effects.log: It is the happiest object in the room.
The elders groan.

events.text: The sect library keeps a ledger of borrowed scrolls, and one entry has been outstanding for four hundred years. {npc}, the librarian, brings it to you with a wince. "Taken by a disciple long gone," {he} says. "A treatise on lanterns. I should like it back before I retire." The disciple, the ledger says, is now an immortal on the Far Reef.
events.arc: The Overdue Book of the Sect Library

effects.log: The letter is polite and a century late.
{He} stares at you. "It is two weeks by skiff."
{He} sighs, patient as a stone.

events.text: You reach the Far Reef after a bumpy fortnight and find a grumpy old immortal on a rock, surrounded by lanterns. "Yes," says the immortal, before you can speak. "The book. I have been meaning to return it. I read it every year." The lanterns, you note, are all alike, and all perfect. The treatise lies open on a stool, annotated in nine hands.
events.arc: The Overdue Book of the Sect Library

effects.log: The immortal clutches it. "Not yet. Another decade."
The immortal is moved. "I would like that."
Each is better than the last.

events.text: A copy of the treatise is made, and the original stays on the Far Reef, with a note in the ledger: "Lent for life." The library's shelf of lantern books is complete for the first time in four centuries. {npc} dusts the new copy and weeps a little onto it. "Four hundred years," {he} says. "And I was so cross."
events.arc: The Overdue Book of the Sect Library

effects.log: The two of you place it between a poem and a map.
It arrives with a lantern.

events.text: The immortal on the Far Reef, grateful, sends the sect library a lantern of astonishing beauty, along with a note: "Overdue fee." It is hung in the reading room, and its light is the colour of old paper. {npc} reads under it every night and is, for a hundred years, content.
events.arc: The Overdue Book of the Sect Library

effects.log: The light is kind to eyes.

choices.text: Add the lantern to the ledger

effects.log: You write: "Received, with thanks."

events.text: {npc}, heaven-born and barely eighty, has been left a garden on the Pear Isle by a grandparent who walked off to the Far Reef. It is large, wild, and entirely unsorted. A note on the gate reads: "Everything here is a small trouble. Welcome." {npc} stands among the weeds with a trowel, looking at you for guidance.
events.arc: The Garden a Grandparent Left a Heaven-Born Child

effects.log: The weeds fight back. The bed is cleared by dusk.

choices.text: Advise {him} to learn the garden first

effects.log: {He} sits and watches. By evening {he} knows the paths.

choices.text: Leave a loaf on the gate

effects.log: It is eaten by morning.

events.text: The garden teaches. The roses bloom out of order; the cabbages are alive with opinions. A plot of mint has swallowed a small shed. {npc} sets up in the mint, and finds in the shed a wooden chest. It holds a hundred seed packets, each labelled in the old gardener's hand with a note: "Plant when ready. Do not hurry."
events.arc: The Garden a Grandparent Left a Heaven-Born Child

effects.log: A summer's work. Some labels are jokes.
It sprouts into a tiny golden tree by morning.
They wait.

events.text: A hundred years on, the garden is a marvel, a quilt of paths and beds, a place the Pear Isle comes to on festival days. {npc} greets the visitors from the shed door. A tall figure, bent, in a shabby coat, stops at the gate and gazes in. It is the grandparent, home at last. They look at the garden, and at {npc}, and say nothing at all.
events.arc: The Garden a Grandparent Left a Heaven-Born Child

effects.log: You see the old one take the child's hand, and the two walk the paths.
They wave back.

events.text: The golden tree grows slowly, a branch a century. {npc} tends it with a bucket and a lullaby. Years later it flowers once, in a single night, and the flowers are tiny stars. The Pear Isle gathers in the garden under them. {npc} says, in a whisper, "I did not hurry."
events.arc: The Garden a Grandparent Left a Heaven-Born Child

effects.log: The petals fall on your sleeves.

choices.text: Pick one petal for a book

effects.log: It stays gold.

events.text: {npc}, a heaven-born prodigy of forty, has mastered three schools and four instruments and is tired of being praised. {He} meets you on the stairs with a small bag and says: "I should like to be unremarkable for a while. Where does one go?" You suggest the Reed Isle, where nobody has ever done anything of note.
events.arc: The Prodigy Who Wanted to Be Ordinary

choices.text: Pack a lunch for the journey

effects.log: {He} takes it with a grave bow.

choices.text: Warn {him} the Reed Isle is very dull

effects.log: "Splendid," says {npc}.
{He} accepts, grateful for the company.

events.text: On the Reed Isle {npc} takes up weaving baskets, badly. The baskets leak, and tilt, and some collapse. The isle's folk, who have never seen anything done well, are charmed. {He} writes you: "I have never been so happy. They think I am slow." You write back with a basket-shaped loaf, which arrives squashed.
events.arc: The Prodigy Who Wanted to Be Ordinary

effects.log: You sit in a field of baskets, cracked and lovely.
It arrives squashed again.
It is a good letter.

events.text: A decade into basket-weaving, {npc} makes a perfect basket by accident. It stands upright, holds water, and does not leak. {He} stares at it in dismay. "I did it again," {he} says. The isle cheers, and hangs it on the wall as a warning. You visit, and find {him} sitting beside it, quietly delighted and quietly aghast.
events.arc: The Prodigy Who Wanted to Be Ordinary

effects.log: {He} says "thank you" like the defeated.
It is out of the way.

events.text: {npc} stays a century on the Reed Isle, weaving crooked baskets, and then, on a calm morning, walks down to the dock. "I think I have been ordinary long enough," {he} says. "I would like to be remarkable again, but on purpose." You hand over the leaking basket, a farewell gift, and {he} carries it back up the stairs with a joyful stagger.
events.arc: The Prodigy Who Wanted to Be Ordinary

effects.log: The stairs are long and bright.
{He} bows.

events.text: {npc} is a rogue with no school and no faction, but a gift for explaining things. Every afternoon {he} sits outside the wall of the Jade Void school with a slate, and answers the questions of any pupil who comes to the hedge. The pupils are not supposed to. The masters pretend not to notice. {He} greets you with a tin of biscuits.
events.arc: The Rogue Who Taught Outside the Wall

effects.log: You learn three things about the sky, and one about patience.

choices.text: Bring a bench for the hedge

effects.log: It is the first furniture the hedge has seen.
It is a good biscuit.

events.text: The Jade Void masters summon {npc} and say, with weary courtesy, that rogues may not teach, and that the school's pupils may not consult them. {He} listens with folded hands. "I teach nobody," {he} says. "I answer questions. It is quite a different thing." The masters confer, and look at the sky, and look at their shoes.
events.arc: The Rogue Who Taught Outside the Wall

choices.text: Speak up for the hedge school

effects.log: You say pupils learn better outside than in. A master coughs.
The masters grunt, and promise to think.
It is enough, for a moment.

events.text: The Jade Void rules that {npc} may answer questions "from outside the wall, in good faith, without credit or fee." It is a grudging ruling, and a gift. The pupils give {him} a hand-embroidered sash. {He} wears it on the slate. The hedge, in time, becomes the best-attended classroom in the school, and its roof is the sky.
events.arc: The Rogue Who Taught Outside the Wall

choices.text: Raise your cup to the hedge

effects.log: Pupils and rogue drink together.
The questions are good ones.

events.text: The masters never rule. The hedge school continues as a thing that does not exist, with a hundred pupils and a rogue, and a bench. Years on, a master of the Jade Void, retired, is seen sitting at the back with a slate and a shy look. {npc} nods to the old master, as to any pupil. The master asks a question about clouds.
events.arc: The Rogue Who Taught Outside the Wall

effects.log: The master waves back with the slate.
It is shared in silence.

events.text: The Lantern Prize of the Jade Court is awarded each year to the best lamp-wright in the sky, and rogues are not permitted to enter. {npc}, a rogue lamp-wright, has made the finest lamp of the age, and cannot show it. {He} turns it in the hand. "A faction friend could carry it in for me," {he} says. "Under another name. I am not proud of the idea."
events.arc: The Rogue Who Won the Lantern Prize

effects.log: You wrap the lamp in your coat. It is warm against you.
{He} nods slowly. "Then what do I do with it?"
It glows like a held word.

events.text: The lamp enters the contest under a faction name, and the judges are entranced. They ask the lamp-wright to step forward. A faction friend does, confused, and is overwhelmed with praise. Meanwhile {npc} sits in the back row, a shabby coat, watching the judges argue about the lamp. The prize is awarded. The friend turns, aghast, and points at the back.
events.arc: The Rogue Who Won the Lantern Prize

choices.text: Stand and say the maker's name

effects.log: The hall hushes. A rogue has made the finest lamp in the sky.

choices.text: Let the friend take the prize

effects.log: The prize goes home with the wrong person.
They go through several expressions.

events.text: The Court, embarrassed, debates whether a rogue-made lamp can be awarded. A very old judge says the prize was meant for the best lamp, not the best affiliation. After forty minutes of grumbling, the vote is nine to eight. {npc} is called to the dais. {He} walks up in a shabby coat and the hall rises. {He} takes the prize in both hands and says nothing.
events.arc: The Rogue Who Won the Lantern Prize

effects.log: The hall is loud for a full minute.
{He} drinks, and is steadier.

events.text: {npc} never learns who took the prize that year. The ledger says only: "Awarded, by proxy." The lamp itself is unrecognised, and quietly sold, and hangs in the corridor of a faction hall, admired by all and credited to no one. {npc} says it is fine. {He} visits the corridor sometimes, at night, and stands beneath it.
events.arc: The Rogue Who Won the Lantern Prize

effects.log: The lamp hums in the dark.

choices.text: Tell the story to a friend

effects.log: It is passed down in whispers.

events.text: A jade tortoise, the size of a table, is plodding across the rope-bridge to your isle, on the third day of its journey from the one before. {npc}, the bridge-warden, keeps count. "Four centuries to cross the bridge once," {he} says. "It has been over and back nine times. I think it is lost." The tortoise stops and blinks at you.
events.arc: The Jade Tortoise Who Walked Between Isles

effects.log: It eats politely, in nine minutes.

choices.text: Walk beside it for a stretch

effects.log: You cover forty yards in two hours. It is a very good walk.
It looks grateful, in its way.

events.text: The tortoise settles on your isle in the sun by the pond, and does not move for a year. The children bring it flowers. The poet laureate writes an ode, of nine thousand lines. The bridge-warden brings a chair. When it finally yawns, the whole isle gathers round, and it says, in a slow deep voice, a single word: "Pleasant."
events.arc: The Jade Tortoise Who Walked Between Isles

choices.text: Sit in the sun beside it

effects.log: Time stretches out. Everything is warm.
It considers the question for a month.
It blinks twice, which is high praise.

events.text: After a century of sun, the tortoise rises, shakes off a layer of lichen and a small bird, and sets off again across the bridge. The isle lines up to watch. Nobody speaks. It walks, without looking back, for a day and a night. A child runs after it with a flower and tucks it into a crack in the shell, where it stays for ages.
events.arc: The Jade Tortoise Who Walked Between Isles

effects.log: The slow back recedes into the mist.
It is a pleasant, slow stroll.

events.text: The tortoise stays. In the end it is made the isle's mascot, then the isle's councillor, then the isle's clock: when the tortoise has crossed the lawn, it is noon. The calendar, once a matter for committees, is the tortoise. {npc} keeps a chart of its progress and calls it the most reliable timepiece in the sky.
events.arc: The Jade Tortoise Who Walked Between Isles

effects.log: It is a quarter past tea.
It is called "Eventually."

events.text: {npc}, a night-baker on the lower terraces, tells you that a stray cat comes each night to sit on the warm oven. It is silver and sleepy, and has a way of dozing off mid-purr. "Customers say they dream better after petting it," {he} says. "Half the terrace is addicted. I wonder if it has a name."
events.arc: The Dream-Cat of the Night Terraces

effects.log: The purr runs up your arm. You yawn for a minute.
It opens one eye. You get the sense it prefers "Mew".
It is warm and soft.

events.text: You begin to dream vividly. Shapes of towers that fold into bridges; a long road of lamps; a tea-house where a figure waits just out of sight. Each morning you wake with a little more of the dream remembered. {npc} says the cat has "taken a liking." The cat curls on your pillow when you return home, as if it had always lived there.
events.arc: The Dream-Cat of the Night Terraces

effects.log: Your notes run to a hundred pages.

choices.text: Follow the road in the dream

effects.log: The dream road leads to a door you almost open.
It sleeps, and so do you.

events.text: The dream finally opens its door. The figure at the tea-house turns out to be yourself, old, calm, and holding a cup. You sit opposite, and the old self says only: "It goes well." You wake with the taste of tea in your mouth. The cat is purring like a hive. It has never been prouder.
events.arc: The Dream-Cat of the Night Terraces

choices.text: Thank the cat with a fish

effects.log: It accepts the fish and no further comment.

choices.text: Sit with the cat at dawn

effects.log: The sun comes up on a purr.

events.text: The dream-cat is a legend by the next century. Neighbours request an hour of its company for their sleepless nights. You open your home as a hostel for cats, tired folk, and long naps. The cat presides from the best cushion. Its descendants, silver and sleepy, spread across the terraces, and the lower isles have never slept so well.
events.arc: The Dream-Cat of the Night Terraces

effects.log: It runs on tea and gentle snoring.
The purr is familiar.

events.text: Once a year, the harbour-master of the Larch Fleet counts the isles, aloud, from the dock, and every isle answers when its name is called. {npc} has done this for six hundred years. This year, the count is one short. A name has been called, and nothing answered. {He} stands very still on the dock.
events.arc: The Annual Count of the Fleet

effects.log: You take a skiff round the Fleet in the grey morning.
"The Moth," {he} says. "A small one. A tailor lives there."

choices.text: Stay on the dock and wait

effects.log: The hours pass slowly.

events.text: The Moth Isle is found hanging in a pocket of fog, three miles astern, tangled in a net of wind-weed. The tailor sits on the porch, sewing, unconcerned. "I was meaning to catch up," the tailor says. "The moorings slipped in the night." You and {npc} fix a rope to the tailor's porch and begin the long tow home.
events.arc: The Annual Count of the Fleet

effects.log: It takes all day. The isle follows, creaking.
The rope runs better to a tune.

choices.text: Sit on the porch and watch the tailor sew

effects.log: The stitches are small and beautiful.

events.text: The Moth Isle rejoins the Fleet at dusk, to cheers. The count is taken again; this time every isle answers. {npc} says the last name, "Moth," and the tailor, from the porch, calls "Present!" It is the sweetest word of the year. The harbour-master wipes {his} eyes on a sleeve and writes the number, with a flourish, in the ledger.
events.arc: The Annual Count of the Fleet

choices.text: Offer a cup to the tailor

effects.log: The tailor takes it, stitching.
You add it to your own almanac.

events.text: The count is never one short again. The Fleet adds a new custom: on the night before, every isle lights a lamp and rings a bell, so that a straggler might find home by sound. The Moth Isle, always last, is the loudest. {npc} listens from the dock, counting not the isles, but the bells, and finding them all.
events.arc: The Annual Count of the Fleet

choices.text: Ring your bell with the others

effects.log: It is one among many.
The sound is like a flock of birds.

events.text: Two isles of different fleets, the Pine and the Quarry, have drifted into one another in the night and are caught, their cliffs grinding gently like two cows at a gate. {npc}, a steersman of the Pine, appears on your balcony in a nightshirt. "They will not part," {he} says. "I must ask for advice. I am not accustomed to being tangled."
events.arc: The Two Isles That Drifted Together

effects.log: A rope in the dark is a fine thing.

choices.text: Suggest waiting for the wind to shift

effects.log: {He} sighs, and sits, and waits.
Tea is brewed on a tilted table.

events.text: The isles are stuck by an ancient spur of rock that has caught the Quarry's overhang. A crowd from both isles gathers along the seam. The Quarry folk are polite and puzzled; the Pine folk, polite and puzzled. A child on the Quarry side passes a bun across the gap to a child on the Pine. They eat, in silence, with the solemnity of diplomats.
events.arc: The Two Isles That Drifted Together

choices.text: Organise a tug from both sides

effects.log: Forty hands on one rope. It creaks.

choices.text: Ask the rock to let go

effects.log: You speak to the spur. It seems to listen.
The seam becomes a street fair.

events.text: The isles part with a deep creak and a sigh. A shower of grey dust falls. The crowds on both sides cheer. Somebody on each isle weeps. For a week, the two isles drift apart, and then, to everyone's surprise, together again, and moor side by side with a rope. {npc} says, "Well, if they insist."
events.arc: The Two Isles That Drifted Together

effects.log: It is caught and tied by a Quarry child.
The glass tinkles.

events.text: The spur of rock is chipped away, politely, over the following season, and a new bridge is built where it was. The Pine and the Quarry become a double isle, with a market in the middle and two sets of rules for everything. {npc} admits it is chaos. It is also, {he} says, the most fun {he} has had.
events.arc: The Two Isles That Drifted Together

effects.log: Two kinds of tea, three kinds of fish.

choices.text: Cross the bridge for the view

effects.log: It is a fine view.

events.text: Years ago a mortal friend pressed a packet of seeds into your hand, saying: "Plant these when you are settled." You never did. {npc}, a gardener on your isle, finds the packet in a drawer while helping you move, and holds it up, yellowed. "These are old," {he} says. "Very old. May I look?" You nod. {He} opens it with a care that is almost reverent.
events.arc: The Seed Packet From Below

choices.text: Ask if the seeds can grow

effects.log: "After this long? Perhaps," {he} says. "Let us try."
{He} listens and is quiet, and folds the packet again.
It is very light.

events.text: The seeds are planted in a clay pot on the sill. Nothing comes up for a month. You water, and talk, and are embarrassed to be talking. Then, on a still morning, a green thread breaks the soil. It is thin, pale, and unmistakable. {npc} bends beside you, and neither of you says a word. The leaf opens.
events.arc: The Seed Packet From Below

effects.log: It grows an inch a week. You keep a count.

choices.text: Tell the plant a story of your friend

effects.log: You tell it the whole thing. The leaf trembles.

choices.text: Move the pot into the sun

effects.log: It leans toward the light.

events.text: The plant flowers in a small, plain, yellow bloom. Mortals call it a dandelion, {npc} says, and a weed, but also a clock, and a wish. You pick the seed-head carefully. At the window, you blow. The seeds float out over the clouds, a hundred tiny parachutes, drifting down toward the ground. Some, at least, will land.
events.arc: The Seed Packet From Below

effects.log: They vanish into the blue, bright as sparks.

choices.text: Keep one seed in a locket

effects.log: It fits exactly.

events.text: You keep the plant for centuries, and it spreads gently over the isle, in cracks and corners, in the gutters of the temple, between the stones of the lane. Visitors ask what it is. You say: "It is a letter from a friend." The weed-pullers of the isle quietly leave it alone. In spring the lanes are gold.
events.arc: The Seed Packet From Below

choices.text: Plant a row by the gate

effects.log: The gate looks gentler for it.
It does, quietly.

events.text: {npc}, an archivist on the Pearl Isle, asks you a strange question over tea: "Do you remember the name of your first teacher? Below, I mean?" You search. The name is on the tip of your tongue and will not come. {He} nods, unsurprised. "It goes," {he} says. "It goes for all of us. The mortal names go first."
events.arc: The Teacher Below Who Is Now Forgotten

effects.log: You get an outline: round spectacles, a patient hand.
"Write them down while you can," {he} says.
The tea is poured. The question lingers.

events.text: You spend a month trying to recall. The outline sharpens: a thin man, a cough, a habit of tapping the chalk. A song they sang when the class was restless. The name does not come, but the song does, entire. You hum it for {npc}, who writes down the notes and sends them off to a friend in the Music Archive.
events.arc: The Teacher Below Who Is Now Forgotten

effects.log: The archivists listen with folded arms, then with wet eyes.
It is a private song.

choices.text: Write the tune on a scroll

effects.log: The scroll is pale and neat.

events.text: A letter arrives from the Music Archive: the song is catalogued under "Unattributed, mortal, old," and a note says that, by a happy chance, a family below has kept the same tune for generations, and the name is attached to it. The name is the one you could not find. It reads, simply, a surname, and a place, and a year.
events.arc: The Teacher Below Who Is Now Forgotten

effects.log: It comes back like a returning tide.

choices.text: Put the letter in a drawer for later

effects.log: It will keep.

events.text: You never find the name. But you teach the song to the children of the isle, in the autumn, and they sing it on the long terrace in the evening light. A passing ferryman stops to listen, and asks where it comes from. You say: "From a teacher." The ferryman nods. It is, you think, a good enough name.
events.arc: The Teacher Below Who Is Now Forgotten

effects.log: Your voice is low among the high ones.

choices.text: Leave the song in the air

effects.log: It lingers.

events.text: {npc} has made it a life's work to learn every lullaby in the sky: the isle songs, the ferry songs, the ones hummed by parents of seven hundred different kinds. {He} keeps them in a book of small black dots, and sings them, one a night, from a window of the Moon Isle. The neighbours say the isle sleeps better than any in the Fleet.
events.arc: The Immortal Who Learned Every Lullaby

effects.log: A tune drifts over the roofs. You are asleep in minutes.

choices.text: Offer a lullaby of your own

effects.log: {He} writes it in the book. "I did not know that one," {he} says.
{He} blushes and nods.

events.text: A traveller from the Far Reef comes with a lullaby that is not on any list: a four-note thing, sung by a grandmother with no teeth to a child who would not sleep. {npc} listens, eyes closed, and writes the dots down with a hand that trembles. "It is the first new one in three hundred years," {he} says. "It is perfect."
events.arc: The Immortal Who Learned Every Lullaby

effects.log: The traveller is surprised, and bows.
The copy is ink and care.
You get two right.

events.text: The book of lullabies is published in a single copy, bound in blue silk, and placed in the Moon Isle's cradle-house. Visitors to the isle sing one to a child, and then add a page of their own. The book is thick now, with unbalanced margins and eight thousand pages. {npc} sleeps in the cradle-house in a chair, and the children fall asleep before the second verse.
events.arc: The Immortal Who Learned Every Lullaby

effects.log: You write a lullaby you do not remember learning.
The room is soft.

events.text: {npc} sings the last of the lullabies, and leaves the book on the sill. In the morning the window is open and the song is still in the air, hanging like a net of silk. The isle wakes late, rested, and silent. Somewhere on the long terrace a child sings the first verse of a song nobody recognises. It is, they say, the lullaby for the singer.
events.arc: The Immortal Who Learned Every Lullaby

effects.log: It comes to you as if learned in a dream.
The room is quiet.

events.text: {npc} has made a hobby of walking every stair in the sky, one by one, and noting each in a battered book. There are forty thousand stairs. {He} has done thirty-one thousand, and is in no hurry. "Each stair is a small opinion," {he} says, on the landing of the Cherry Isle. "I like to hear them all." The book is warped by wet.
events.arc: The Immortal Who Walked Every Stair

effects.log: It is a short one, ten steps, and has a fine view.

choices.text: Ask which stair is the best

effects.log: "The one you are on," {he} says, then adds, "Also the Cherry."
Every entry is a sentence, and a sketch.

events.text: You accompany {npc} for a season, up and down the stairs of three isles. Some are narrow as a hair. Some are broad enough for a procession. The oddest is a stair that goes down only: no way up. A sign says "Return by another route." {npc} laughs until {he} has to sit on the bottom step.
events.arc: The Immortal Who Walked Every Stair

effects.log: It leads to a garden you have never seen.

choices.text: Carry {his} pack up the long stair

effects.log: The pack is lighter than the book.
The view is good for resting.

events.text: The last stair, the forty-thousandth, is in the cellar of an old court, a plain stone flight of six steps to a plain door. {npc} stands on the bottom step with a pencil. "I did not think I would feel so little," {he} says. {He} climbs it, writes the entry, and closes the book. Then {he} laughs, and says: "I will start again."
events.arc: The Immortal Who Walked Every Stair

choices.text: Offer to walk the second round

effects.log: You shake on it. The first stair of the second round is the cellar.
{He} grins, already packing.

events.text: The book of the stairs is placed in the Cherry Isle library, in a glass case, open at the page of the forty-thousandth. A card lists the entries, and a second card lists the stairs that have since fallen. {npc} is outliving stairs now: sixteen are gone. {He} says it is the oldest work in the world, listening to what remains.
events.arc: The Immortal Who Walked Every Stair

choices.text: Add a stair to the book

effects.log: You note a stair on your own isle.

choices.text: Read the card of fallen stairs

effects.log: It is a quiet list.

events.text: {npc} and you have a tradition: on the first of each year, each writes a poem on the same subject and exchanges it with the other. This year the subject is "the last light of a winter day." You read {his} poem on the Pine Isle terrace and it is your own, almost word for word, but reversed: the last line first, the first line last.
events.arc: The Friends Who Wrote the Same Poem Backward

effects.log: It works. It is a bit better backward.
{He} swears not. "It came to me in a dream."

choices.text: Pin both poems on a wall

effects.log: They hang there in the winter light.

events.text: The two of you test it. You write a poem about a quiet river; {he} writes the reverse in another house, with no contact. When you meet again, the poems are mirrors. It happens nine times. A scholar from the Archive hears of it, and sends a clerk with a magnifying glass and a long list of questions.
events.arc: The Friends Who Wrote the Same Poem Backward

effects.log: The clerk takes notes, bewildered.
{npc} and you share a glance and a laugh.
The clerk accepts, awkward.

events.text: The scholars conclude that your minds have come so close in a thousand years that they now rhyme. A paper is published. It is called "On the Mirror Friendship," and is cited for centuries. You and {npc} read it together over tea and decide it is correct, but a little sad. "We should have been surprised," {he} says, "instead of wise."
