events.arc: The Friends Who Wrote the Same Poem Backward

choices.text: Write a mirror poem about that

effects.log: It comes out the same, backwards, in an hour.
It swirls.

events.text: You stop trying to explain it. Each year you write your poems and leave them on a shared sill, one on each side of the window, and each year they reflect. Eventually you stop looking at them as a puzzle and read them as a conversation. {npc} dies first. You write your poem, and set it on the sill, and wait. The next morning there is another.
events.arc: The Friends Who Wrote the Same Poem Backward

effects.log: It is a mirror. It says what you meant.
The breeze turns the page.

events.text: You and {npc} have not spoken for sixty years. The quarrel was about nothing: a borrowed saw, a cutting remark at a banquet. Now you stand on opposite ends of the Cloud Bridge, each waiting for the other to cross. The planks creak in the wind. {He} looks at the sky and you look at the water, and neither moves.
events.arc: The Long Silence Between Old Friends

effects.log: The first plank is the hardest. {He} flinches.
The wind rises and drops. No one crosses.
You walk to the end of the isle and sit.

events.text: You meet in the middle of the bridge. Neither of you speaks. A skiff passes underneath, its pilot whistling. {npc} clears {his} throat and says: "I still have your saw." You stare. It was a cheap saw, rusted, ugly. "I never could bring myself to return it," {he} says. "It reminded me of you. It was a very bad saw."
events.arc: The Long Silence Between Old Friends

effects.log: You laugh till the bridge shakes.
{He} looks wounded, then pleased.
It is the simplest thing and the hardest.

events.text: The saw is brought on the next skiff, wrapped in blue silk, and presented on your doorstep. It is as bad as remembered. You hang it in the shed, and every time you pass it you smile. {npc} visits on the first of each month. The two of you build nothing. You sit on a bench, talk, and look at the saw.
events.arc: The Long Silence Between Old Friends

choices.text: Keep the saw on the wall

effects.log: It stays there for centuries.
Tea and silence, again.

events.text: The wind decides the matter. A strong gust throws the bridge-planks crooked, and you and {npc} both end up in the middle of the sky, clutching one rope and each other. When it is over, you are laughing, and shaking, and no longer angry. "I forgive the saw," {he} says. "I do not know about you."
events.arc: The Long Silence Between Old Friends

choices.text: Say you forgive the saw too

effects.log: The bridge creaks. It holds.
You walk together.

events.text: The Ministry of Precedence has received a petition to settle which side of a doorway a minister should leave by. The doorway is that of the Hall of Seals. {npc}, the doorkeeper, brings the question to you with a tired face. "Left or right," {he} says. "Nine ministers have walked into one another. We cannot settle it. We cannot be seen to settle it."
events.arc: The Ministry and the Question of the Door

choices.text: Propose that both walk through at once

effects.log: {He} blinks. "Is that a door or a wall?"
{He} sighs. "The Hall of Seals does not widen."
{He} drinks it standing.

events.text: The Ministry of Precedence meets on the matter and decides that the left door is for ministers and the right for marshals, but that a marshal who is also a minister must use the centre, a thing which does not exist. A carpenter is called. He builds a centre door in a week. It is purely decorative, and ministers are forbidden to use it.
events.arc: The Ministry and the Question of the Door

effects.log: It is painted with a small, wise face.
A clerk gasps. Nothing falls.
They are all bowing to each other.

events.text: The decorative door becomes the most beloved door of the Hall, and the doorkeeper, {npc}, oils its hinges daily. Ministers pause beside it to straighten their hats. A tradition arises that anyone who walks through it has earned a wish. The Ministry of Precedence takes offence, and then does not. The door is never officially opened.
events.arc: The Ministry and the Question of the Door

choices.text: Make a wish at the door

effects.log: You wish for small things. They arrive.
It purrs.

events.text: You walk through the centre door and nothing happens, which in the Hall of Seals is itself a scandal. A clerk faints. A page runs for tea. {npc} stands frozen beside the doorframe, then begins to laugh, holding the wall. By evening the story is in every tea-house. The Ministry, embarrassed, quietly amends the rule: anyone may use the centre door, on Tuesdays.
events.arc: The Ministry and the Question of the Door

effects.log: You become a regular, and a minor legend.

choices.text: Hold it for the next minister

effects.log: The minister bows.

events.text: Two lamp-sellers in the Demon Realm have shared a stall for nine centuries and have not spoken for eight. Today a child asks them, in a very small voice, whose lamp is better. They look at one another. Both say, at once, "Mine." Then both begin, helplessly, to laugh, and keep laughing until the child leaves.

effects.log: The lamps burn side by side.

choices.text: Take the child to the next stall

effects.log: The child looks relieved.

events.text: Travellers in the Demon Realm add a stone to the cairn at each crossroads, saying a name aloud. The cairns are tall now, and weathered, and the names they carry are mostly forgotten. You add a stone and say the name of someone you miss. The cairn seems to settle, a little, as though pleased.

effects.log: The stone is cold and the name is warm.
It rolls into a gap.

events.text: In the Demon Realm a guest who finishes the stew is asked to leave a spoonful in the pot for the next. This custom has produced stews of enormous age, shaped by travellers from three hundred years. The one before you tastes of salt, ginger, and many farewells. You leave a spoonful of your own, and a thought.

effects.log: The stew is now partly yours.
The host laughs. "It has none."

events.text: The Star Sea Pavilion takes its tea at the hour the last star sets, a cup each, sipped in silence on the long terrace. No one speaks. The cups clink once, softly, as the star goes out. A visiting scholar, unaware, begins a sentence, and the whole terrace turns slowly to look at them. The scholar finishes it in a whisper.

effects.log: The tea is faintly sweet.
The scholar is grateful.

events.text: A boy of fifty rings the Pavilion's dusk-bell, at the exact moment the first star shows. He has been wrong by a few seconds for a year. The astronomers agree he is right and the star is wrong. A notice is posted: "The bell is correct, the sky will adjust." The boy is proud for a week.

effects.log: He grins from ear to ear.
It is, grudgingly, a few seconds late.

events.text: In a quiet map-room of the Pavilion, a lone astronomer unrolls a chart of a sky that has not been seen in nine hundred years, an old arrangement before the stars drifted. They spread it on a table and smooth it with a hand. The old stars look back at them in neat ink. The astronomer says, softly, "Hello again."

effects.log: The old sky is strange and dear.
It is a private reunion.

events.text: A cat has been stealing fish from the kitchen of the sect you founded, brazenly, in the middle of the day. The cook has chased it with a ladle and a net. It escapes by the roof. At the evening meal it is seen on the head table, washing a paw, while the elders pretend not to notice. The cook gives up.

effects.log: It purrs through the whole meal.

choices.text: Tell the cook to let it be

effects.log: The cook mutters, then smiles.

events.text: The sect you founded is rearranging its halls, and the move is chaos: scrolls in baskets, swords in barrels, a junior asleep in a wheelbarrow. The Hall of Morning Sweeping sweeps the new path before anyone uses it. Everyone, even the elders, carries something. By dusk the new hall is in order, and the old one echoes.

effects.log: Your arms ache.

choices.text: Sweep the old hall one last time

effects.log: It is bittersweet.

events.text: On the first day of the year the whole sect assembles in the courtyard to write its resolutions on slips and burn them in a bowl. The slips are all different: one asks for patience, one for a better sword, one for cake. Yours burns with the rest. The smoke rises in a thin column, straight as a spear.

effects.log: It is short and honest.
The smoke curls and joins.

events.text: A heaven-born child tells you, gravely, that the moon is made of cheese, and that the cheese is owned by the Minister of Weather. You ask how they know. The child looks at you with huge eyes and says: "Everyone knows." You decide, for the time being, not to correct them.

effects.log: The child is delighted.
"The sharp kind," says the child.

events.text: A heaven-born child has adopted a rock. It is a plain grey one, found on the Lantern Isle. The child feeds it breadcrumbs, tucks it in at night, and has given it a rank. It is a Captain. The rock has not yet disobeyed an order. You are asked, formally, to salute it.

effects.log: The rock accepts with dignity.
The crumb is placed carefully.

events.text: A dust-sprite has moved into your study, the small kind that lives in sunbeams and eats the lint. It is the size of a thumb and extremely proud. When you sweep, it hides in the broom. When you read, it sits on the page and corrects your grammar by tapping. Its taste in verbs is excellent.

effects.log: It taps approval.
It bows, thimble and all.

events.text: The goose of the isle has gone missing, and the whole lane is out searching with lanterns. It is found, at last, asleep in a large bonnet on the doorstep of the Ministry of Moorings, where it has laid an egg on a form. The clerk who opens the door is gentle. The form is stamped, "Received."

effects.log: It honks, once, in your ear.
It is surprisingly warm.

events.text: At dusk a line of lamps is lit along the Fleet from stern to bow, one isle at a time. The light runs along the line like a spark along a fuse, and then holds, in a long gold thread. A steersman at the rear says it looks like a necklace. A steersman at the front says it looks like a road. Both are right.

effects.log: It joins the thread.
The thread wavers in the wind.

events.text: The two oldest isles of the Fleet exchange a gift every century. This year it is a pot of jam from one and a bell from the other. Both are placed in the middle of the harbour, and the whole Fleet eats the jam and rings the bell. It is a poor jam and a good bell. The Fleet says so, cheerfully.

effects.log: It is a little sour.
It rings long.

events.text: A clerk of the Ministry of Prayers reminds you that today is the name-day of a mortal you once knew. You do not need reminding. You light a stick of incense and place a sprig of plum by the window. The wind brings in a smell of rain from below, and for an hour you do not move.

effects.log: The hour passes.
It sounds quite small.

events.text: You look down through a thin place in the clouds and see, very far below, a small round moon on a pond. A mortal child is trying to catch it with a bucket. You laugh, and then you do not. The child pours the pond out on the grass and looks into the empty bucket, puzzled. Then the child starts again.

effects.log: The thin place seals over.

choices.text: Blow the child a breath of wind

effects.log: The pond ripples, and the moon appears.

events.text: A stall at the Cloud Market repairs holes in clouds: a patch of vapour, a stitch of fog, a coat of fresh mist. The stallholder is gentle with each, and charges by the width of the hole. A child brings in a torn cloud the size of a handkerchief. The stallholder mends it for free, and gives it back with a bow.

effects.log: The seam vanishes.

choices.text: Tip the stallholder a kind word

effects.log: The stallholder beams.

events.text: Two immortals at the Cloud Market haggle over a clock for the sixth day running. The clock is very ordinary. The haggling is magnificent: sighs, scorn, bows, a sudden walk-out, a return. By evening the price has barely moved. A crowd has gathered. At sunset the clock is sold, and both parties embrace and weep with joy.

effects.log: The crowd cheers.
It ticks, a little fast.

events.text: A busker on the Long Stair plays a fiddle with only one string, and plays it astonishingly well. People pause on the steps, hats in hand. A child asks why only one string. The busker says: "The others were too good at disagreeing." The child accepts this, and the busker plays on.

choices.text: Drop a stone in the hat

effects.log: The busker nods.

choices.text: Sit on the step and listen

effects.log: The note rings in your ribs.

events.text: A sky whale passes over the isle at midday, and its shadow is a cool moving island on the lawn. Children chase the shadow across the grass, shrieking. Elders lift their faces to feel the chill. The whale, with enormous courtesy, slows for a moment, and the shadow lingers. Then it moves on, and the sun is back.

effects.log: It is cool and deep.
It dips a fin, perhaps.

events.text: A storm of the gentle sort rolls over the Fleet, with soft thunder and a fine warm rain. The isles shut their shutters, and every kitchen brews a pot. The sound of rain on roofs and the smell of tea mix over the whole Fleet. A neighbour knocks, bearing a plate of sesame cakes. It is the best kind of weather.

effects.log: The plate is soon empty.
It is a long lullaby.

events.text: An old immortal sits to the neck in the Spring Isle's hottest pool every dawn, reciting the names of every cloud they have ever seen. They are on the letter T. A fresh towel waits on the bank. A cup of cooled tea stands beside it. They say, between names, that a bath is the best excuse for remembering.

choices.text: Sit by the pool and listen

effects.log: The names are small and bright.
The immortal thanks you, steaming.

events.text: The thunder sparrows come each year for nine days, and the isle holds a count, not a hunt: each bird is noted, named, and left to fly. A child spots a pale one with a notched feather and shouts. The old counters nod. It is the same bird, they say, that came when the child's grandparent was a child. The child writes its name.

effects.log: You count fifty, and lose track.
The sparrows pounce.

events.text: On the fallen terraces of an old isle from the war of the immortals, a family has laid out a picnic on a broken floor. They say it is the best spot in the sky: wind, view, and no one else. A faded mosaic of a lion peers up from beneath the cloth. They offer you a pastry. It is wonderful.

effects.log: It is warm and flaky.
The lion has one eye left.

events.text: On the Cliff Isle someone has hung a swing from a single hook over the abyss. A sign says "For anyone who has forgotten how." You sit. A neighbour gives a push. The world rushes up, the sky stretches out below, and you laugh aloud like a person of a hundred years ago. The swing carries on a long time.

effects.log: The view is endless.
They shriek with delight.

events.text: In the courtyard of an ancient hall, there is a stone worn to a shallow dip by generations of feet. The caretaker says that at dawn, a faint light fills the dip, like water. No one knows why. Visitors are invited to place a foot in it, one at a time, and think of someone they have lost. You wait your turn.

choices.text: Step in and think of them

effects.log: The stone is warm.
Someone else is waiting, shyly.

events.text: On the ground floor of the Ministry of Precedence there is a small door marked Lost and Found. Behind it {npc} has kept the shelves for four centuries: umbrellas, a shadow in a jar, one sleeve, and a tag reading “one name, unclaimed”. {He} asks, kindly, whether you have lost anything lately.
events.arc: The Office of Lost Property

choices.text: Describe a thing you lost long ago

effects.log: {npc} writes it on a card and files it under Hopeless. {He} says that is where the best things end up.
The tag has waited longer than the Ministry has had a roof. {npc} says someone always comes in the end.

choices.text: Hand in a ribbon you found

effects.log: It is logged with great ceremony, and you feel oddly honest for the rest of the day.

events.text: A year on, {npc} sends a note: something of yours has turned up. It is a cup you broke on a mountain ninety years ago, mended with gold lacquer by someone you never met. The form to reclaim it has eleven lines, and one asks why you let it go.
events.arc: The Office of Lost Property

choices.text: Write the truth on that line

effects.log: You write that you were ashamed of the crack. {npc} reads it and stamps it without a word.

choices.text: Write that it was an accident

effects.log: The form is accepted. The cup is cold in your hand, the way untrue things are.
It still belongs to you in the way unclaimed things do, and the thought is a comfort.

events.text: {npc} retires at last and gives you the key to the little door. “Someone must keep the lost,” {he} says. “You are the first who told the truth on the form.” The shelves are yours now, and the cup sits among them with a card that reads Found.
events.arc: The Office of Lost Property

choices.text: Take the key and keep the shelves

effects.log: By the century's end the shelf of reunions is longer than the shelf of the lost.

choices.text: Give the key to a young clerk

effects.log: You teach the clerk the card system and visit with tea. The door stays open.

events.text: {npc} retires with the cup still on the shelf. The new clerk is brisk and keeps no cards, and by spring the shadow in its jar has gone to a back room, the nameless tag with it. A note arrives, unsigned: “Some things want keeping a long time.”
events.arc: The Office of Lost Property

choices.text: Ask the new clerk where the tag went

effects.log: The clerk looks it up and finds it in a drawer. It goes back on the shelf, a little crooked.
You think of the tag now and then. It is a long time before you forgive yourself the form.

events.text: The Calendar Office keeps the day, and the isles never agree on it. The Leeward Isle runs eleven days behind and is proud of it. {npc}, the senior reckoner, asks you to carry a corrected almanac to three isles that dislike being corrected.
events.arc: The Calendar Office That Added a Day

effects.log: Two isles accept, one sulks. {npc} says that is a better average than the Office has had in a century.

choices.text: Carry it with a gift of tea

effects.log: Tea softens most corrections. Two isles thank you, and the third offers you a chair.

choices.text: Tell {npc} the isles can keep their own days

effects.log: {npc} sighs and sends someone else. You feel lighter and slightly unhelpful.

events.text: The third isle has celebrated the same spring festival for a century and will not move it. {npc} proposes a remedy: add a day to the isle's calendar, one that belongs to no month. It is irregular. It is also the kind of thing the Office has never dared before.
events.arc: The Calendar Office That Added a Day

effects.log: You write the petition in your own hand. {npc} signs it before you finish the last line.
The Office has always held the line. {npc} says that, too, is a kind of kindness.

choices.text: Take no side and drink the tea

effects.log: The tea is good. The decision, made without you, is neither better nor worse.

events.text: The extra day is granted. The third isle holds its festival on it, and the lanterns that night are the oldest the sky has seen. The next year the Office finds it has a day it cannot account for. {npc} files it under Gifts and says no more about it.
events.arc: The Calendar Office That Added a Day

choices.text: Spend the extra day on the isle

effects.log: You are given a seat and a bowl and no questions. It is the best day of the year.

choices.text: Write the day into the almanac in gold

effects.log: It becomes the only gilded entry in the book. People ask about it for centuries.

events.text: The line is held. The third isle keeps its own calendar and the fleet learns to say “their Tuesday” when it means a Tuesday that is not the fleet's. {npc} visits yearly with a corrected almanac, which is politely set on a shelf and never opened.
events.arc: The Calendar Office That Added a Day

effects.log: The two of them argue happily over tea for an afternoon. It is the oldest friendship on the isle.
Some corrections are really visits. You understand it late.

events.text: The Ministry of Weather keeps a small window for complaints, and {npc} has sat behind it for three centuries. Today a line has formed: an isle that wants less hail, a tea-house that wants more mist, and an elder who wants the thunder to start later. {He} asks if you would hold the stamp while {he} fetches tea.
events.arc: The Window for Weather Complaints

choices.text: Hold the stamp and say nothing rash

effects.log: You hold it for an hour. It is amazing how often people need only to be heard.
The line leaves happy. {npc} returns, looks at the pile, and says gently that you have promised hail to a wedding.
{npc} manages the line alone, and manages it well.

events.text: The elder's complaint returns every year, and every year the Ministry replies with the same form. This year {npc} puts the form down and asks you what the elder is actually complaining about. It is a strange question to be asked across a counter.
events.arc: The Window for Weather Complaints

choices.text: Visit the elder and find out

effects.log: The elder is complaining about the silence the thunder leaves. It is a loneliness, not a weather.
The reply is clear, kind and entirely beside the point. The elder frames it anyway.
{npc} nods slowly. Forms are, after all, forms.

events.text: You find the elder lives alone on a small isle and has no one to say good night to. The thunder was the only voice that answered. {npc} arranges a gentle thunder at dusk, once a week, and sends a clerk to sit on the porch for the first one.
events.arc: The Window for Weather Complaints

effects.log: The thunder rolls in, small and polite. The elder says good night to it and then to you.
The weekly thunder becomes the smallest and most loved service of the Ministry.

events.text: The reply is filed, framed and answered by a long letter that no clerk reads. {npc} says it is the nicest complaint they have ever received, and asks permission to stop answering it. The elder, informed, is delighted: now there is a real correspondence.
events.arc: The Window for Weather Complaints

effects.log: You become the odd courier of a friendship between a window and a porch.
They do. It takes two centuries to arrange, and goes well.

events.text: At the foot of the Long Bridge a stool and a tally-board belong to {npc}, a clerk of the Ministry of Roads. {He} counts every immortal who crosses and has done so since before the bridge had railings. The count is for no purpose anyone remembers. {He} marks you down with a small, courteous nod.
events.arc: The Ministry Clerk Who Counted Footsteps

choices.text: Stop and ask what the count is for

effects.log: "For the count," says {npc}, with a smile that suggests the answer is deeper than it sounds.
You are recorded as Unhurried. It is the only title you have ever earned without trying.
The tally has your hurry on it, in a neat small stroke.

events.text: Years later you meet {npc} on a dark morning, closing the board. The bridge has been counted one hundred and nine million crossings. Someone in the Ministry has finally asked for the numbers, and {he} wonders aloud what they will find in them.
events.arc: The Ministry Clerk Who Counted Footsteps

effects.log: Together you find a pattern: the whole sky crosses more slowly on the evening before a festival.
{npc} accepts it with grace, and then goes home and cries a little, you later learn.

choices.text: Offer to carry the board to the Ministry

effects.log: It is a heavy walk, and you are glad you did it.

events.text: The Ministry publishes the pattern as a gentle finding. The festival evenings are named after it, and a small bench is placed at the foot of the bridge with {npc}'s name carved into the arm. {He} sits on it every morning now and counts, and does not mind that the count has a meaning.
events.arc: The Ministry Clerk Who Counted Footsteps

effects.log: Neither of you says a word, and the bridge fills and empties.

choices.text: Bring a flask of tea for the count

effects.log: It is the first thing {npc} has ever been given for the work.

events.text: {npc} does not return after that morning. The board hangs on its hook, and the tally ends on an even number. A new clerk is not appointed. Instead, people take turns, each making one mark when crossing, and the bridge keeps its own count, somehow, in a hundred hands.
events.arc: The Ministry Clerk Who Counted Footsteps

choices.text: Make a mark every time you cross

effects.log: It takes a lifetime. It becomes a quiet prayer.

choices.text: Hang a small lantern at the board

effects.log: It burns through the night. People set their palms on the board in passing.

events.text: Isles drift, so every map above is wrong by evening. In the Map Room of the Ministry of Roads {npc} refolds maps all day, pressing the new routes into old creases, so that no sheet is ever replaced, only amended. “A map is a kind of letter to the traveller,” {he} says, handing you one with warm fingers.
events.arc: The Map-Folder of the Ministry of Roads

choices.text: Ask for a map of your own route

effects.log: It is folded so that your destination lies exactly on a crease. You find this either comforting or alarming.

choices.text: Offer to hold the paper while {he} presses

effects.log: The creases remember the isles that moved. You learn how the sky has been rearranged.
The map in your sleeve rustles like a small bird.

events.text: A frightened courier bursts in: a map has been lost on the way to the Jade Court, and with it the only chart of a sealed channel between two reefs. {npc} stands very still. “It has to be refolded from memory,” {he} says. “I have the creases. I do not trust my hands.”
events.arc: The Map-Folder of the Ministry of Roads

effects.log: You hold the sheet while {npc} dictates the folds. It takes the night and most of your patience.

choices.text: Offer to find the lost courier's route

effects.log: You walk the road backward and find the map snagged on a sapling.
The room is very quiet. You regret it by morning.

events.text: The map is refolded and delivered. It is not exactly the same as the lost one, and the Court never notices. {npc} puts a new crease at the very centre and says, shyly, that it is for you: a fold that means “the person who held the paper”. It will never be unfolded now.
events.arc: The Map-Folder of the Ministry of Roads

choices.text: Ask to see the other creases

effects.log: {He} shows you a room full of them, each one a person who helped. You are in good company.
Some thanks are best left folded.

events.text: The lost map is found and the refolded one quietly discarded. {npc} is oddly sad to see the original return, with its old creases and a twig stuck in the fold. “It was better when I had to make it again,” {he} says. You both look at the twig for a long time.
events.arc: The Map-Folder of the Ministry of Roads

choices.text: Press the twig into the map

effects.log: It stays there, dried and flat, a fold of its own. The Court never remarks on it.

choices.text: Tell {npc} the folding was good work

effects.log: It is the first praise {he} has heard in two centuries.

events.text: Below the Ministry of Tribute is a canteen where the clerks of eleven desks eat in silence, because no one wants to hear anyone's paperwork. {npc} runs it, stirring a pot that has not been emptied since the first clerks sat down. {He} serves you soup with a look that says “sit”.
events.arc: The Canteen of the Overworked Clerks

choices.text: Sit and eat in silence like everyone else

effects.log: The soup is plain and very warm. Something in your shoulders comes down.
"It is not a story," says {he}. "It is a stock." Then, after a pause, {he} tells it anyway.

choices.text: Take it away to eat at your desk

effects.log: It gets cold. {npc} marks you down as a person who cannot sit.

events.text: The clerks go on silent strike, in their own way: no one orders. Three days of untouched pots. {npc} says the clerks are tired, not rebellious, and asks you to carry a message to the Chief Clerk: that the clerks want, simply, a half-hour at noon in which no one asks them for anything.
events.arc: The Canteen of the Overworked Clerks

effects.log: The Chief Clerk reads it twice and then says yes, with a stiffness that hides relief.

choices.text: Carry it with a plate of soup

effects.log: The Chief Clerk eats, in silence, and the rest follows from there.

choices.text: Say it is not your place

effects.log: {npc} nods slowly, and sets down the ladle.

events.text: The half-hour is granted. At noon every desk empties, and the canteen fills with eleven offices of clerks who eat, and look at one another, and begin to talk. {npc} stands at the pot with a face that does not quite know what to do. Within a year there is a second pot.
events.arc: The Canteen of the Overworked Clerks

choices.text: Help carry the new pot in

effects.log: It is a very large pot, and you are given the first bowl.

choices.text: Bring a song for the noon half-hour

effects.log: The song is bad. It is sung by everyone, and then it is a custom.

events.text: The Chief Clerk eats the soup and is changed by it. By the end of the season the half-hour exists, but nobody has quite the courage to take it, and the canteen goes back to silence. {npc} keeps the pot hot regardless. “Someone will,” {he} says. You have your doubts. You keep coming.
events.arc: The Canteen of the Overworked Clerks

choices.text: Be the first to talk at the noon half-hour

effects.log: It starts as an awkward remark about the weather. By the third week there are five conversations.
You choose the quiet, and the quiet, being chosen, is kinder.

events.text: The Pasture Isle keeps clouds as other places keep sheep. {npc} herds them every dawn with a long crook and a whistle that is half song, driving small white cumulus toward the edge to graze on the morning mist. One has wandered off the isle, and {he} asks, without much hope, if you can fly a little way.
events.arc: The Cloud-Shepherd of the Pasture Isle

choices.text: Fly out and herd the stray home

effects.log: The stray cloud follows your whistle badly and your qi well. It comes home with a rumble of apology.

choices.text: Offer {npc} your help with the whole flock

effects.log: You spend an afternoon learning that you cannot drive a cloud, only lead one.
{npc} whistles alone. The cloud, you hear later, found its own way back.

events.text: A storm in the east rolls the flock together into one great grey mass, and {npc} cannot tell which cloud is which. The dark ones will rain on the herb terraces. The pale ones are lambs and must not be wet. {He} asks if you will hold the lambs while {he} turns the dark ones away.
events.arc: The Cloud-Shepherd of the Pasture Isle

effects.log: You draw them in like a handful of wool. Rain falls on the terraces and not on a single lamb.
You and {npc} drive the storm away with whistles and crooks. It leaves, grumbling.
The storm passes. You are dry and mildly ashamed.

events.text: {npc} gives you a lamb-cloud that was too small to survive the winter, wrapped in a blanket of wool. “Take it,” {he} says. “It likes you, and I am getting old.” The cloud follows you everywhere after, a small white thing at your heel, and rains very gently on your shoes.
events.arc: The Cloud-Shepherd of the Pasture Isle

effects.log: It grows slowly, over centuries, into a fine pale cumulus that sleeps over your roof.

choices.text: Return the lamb to the pasture each spring

effects.log: It grazes in the mist and comes home to you in autumn. This suits you both.

events.text: The storm is turned, and the herd, relieved, falls asleep in the lee of the isle. {npc} thanks you with a small crook, hand-carved, that whistles in the wind. “It will call a cloud,” {he} says. “Do not tell anyone how.” You never find out how, but clouds do turn their heads.
events.arc: The Cloud-Shepherd of the Pasture Isle

choices.text: Keep the crook as a keepsake

effects.log: It hangs by your door and hums in good weather.

choices.text: Give it to a heaven-born child

effects.log: The child becomes a shepherd in fifty years. {npc} claims the credit.

events.text: The undersides of the isles are hung with roots, and roots left alone grow into everything. {npc} prunes them from a hanging seat under the Orchard Isle, snipping and tying with the sky yawning beneath. {He} offers you the spare seat and a small pair of shears, and says the view is better from below.
events.arc: The Root-Pruner Beneath the Isle

choices.text: Climb down and take the seat

effects.log: Hanging under an isle, you see how it is stitched to the air. {npc} is right about the view.
It is a quiet, trusting kind of work. Your hands do not forget it.
The seat swings, small against the clouds. You are not tempted.

events.text: A root of the Orchard Isle has grown across a gap and taken hold of a neighbouring isle, two hundred paces away. Both isles are now tied, and as the fleet turns, the root strains. {npc} must cut it, but it is the oldest root, and {he} says it has been the isle's only handshake with the next.
events.arc: The Root-Pruner Beneath the Isle

effects.log: You free the root bit by bit. It retreats to the Orchard side like a hand returning to a sleeve.

choices.text: Cut the root cleanly and quickly

effects.log: It is done, and the isles sway apart. The silence afterward is a little cold.
The Ministry of Roads is consulted. The reply takes thirty years.

events.text: The root, loosened, curls back and sprouts a small flower at the tip. The neighbouring isle sends over a pot of its own soil, with a note: “For the next handshake.” {npc} plants the flower in it and hangs it from the seat. It blooms at dusk and smells faintly of two isles.
events.arc: The Root-Pruner Beneath the Isle

effects.log: You visit it once a season for as long as you live. It always blooms for you.

choices.text: Carry a second pot to the neighbouring isle

effects.log: It is welcomed with enormous seriousness and a small cake.

events.text: The root is cut, and the two isles drift apart, as fleets do. {npc} stays under the Orchard Isle that season, silent, with the cut end in {his} lap. “It was the oldest thing here,” {he} says. You sit with {him} until the wind changes. Next spring, the stump sprouts a green shoot facing away from the neighbour.
events.arc: The Root-Pruner Beneath the Isle

choices.text: Tell {him} the shoot is a new beginning

effects.log: {npc} does not answer, but plants a little marker beside it.
Some grief is a one-person job. You send tea.

events.text: Even the stars tarnish, and above the clouds someone is paid to polish them. {npc} climbs a long ladder each night, rag in hand, and rubs the minor stars one by one until they shine. {He} offers you the next rung and says the stars like company, though they never say so.
events.arc: The Star-Polisher and the Dimming One

choices.text: Climb the ladder and take a rag

effects.log: The star is warm and a little ticklish. It shines for you in a way you do not forget.
A steady ladder is half the work. {npc} says so, and means it.
From below the stars look entirely clean. You do not mention it.

events.text: One minor star, polished every night for four hundred years, has begun to dim no matter the rag. {npc} brings you a lantern, a flask and bad news: the star is not tarnished, it is tired. {He} does not know whether to keep polishing, let it rest, or give it a night off, which has never been done.
events.arc: The Star-Polisher and the Dimming One

choices.text: Say let it rest for a night

effects.log: The star goes dark for one night. The sky seems to hold its breath, and the star is brighter after.
You and {npc} polish it by turns until dawn. It shines on, a little warily.

choices.text: Say it is only a star

effects.log: {npc} gives you a long look and says nothing.

events.text: The star, rested, comes back slowly, and then it begins to twinkle in a pattern. {npc} thinks it is a word. After a season of watching, you both agree it is a word, and the word is “thanks”. {He} takes off the cap and stands under it for a long time.
events.arc: The Star-Polisher and the Dimming One

effects.log: It is a small, foolish gesture. The star twinkles twice.

choices.text: Write the word in the star-chart

effects.log: The chart-makers are baffled and delighted. It is the only note of its kind.

events.text: The star is polished through the night and is bright, if wary, at dawn. {npc} gives up the ladder the next spring and teaches a young heaven-born to climb it, rag and all. The star, you are told, dims again a century later, and the young one lets it rest, gently, as {npc} once did.
events.arc: The Star-Polisher and the Dimming One

effects.log: Retired, {he} still counts the stars from a window, and says they need less polish than people think.
The young one blushes and promises to rest the star again, someday.

events.text: The mill on the High Quay turns only for one wind, a gentle west-wind named Hollow Pell, who comes through twice a year and will not be hurried. {npc} the miller grinds the isle's grain in those two weeks and sits idle the rest of the year. {He} says idleness is a trade too, if you do it properly.
events.arc: The Miller Who Ground Only on a Named Wind

choices.text: Sit with {npc} and wait for the wind

effects.log: You wait a full month. The wind arrives like a guest who has forgotten the time. It is worth the month.

choices.text: Offer to speed up the wind with a charm

effects.log: {npc} politely declines. A wind is not a servant.

choices.text: Say a mill should run all year

effects.log: "Then it would grind sorrow," says {npc}, without heat.

events.text: This year Hollow Pell does not come. The grain waits. The isle begins to mutter that the mill is useless. {npc} walks to the edge every dawn and calls the wind by its name. {He} asks you to call as well, since a wind answers a second voice more quickly than one.
events.arc: The Miller Who Ground Only on a Named Wind

effects.log: You call for a week. On the eighth morning, a faint stir lifts your hair.

choices.text: Go to the Ministry of Weather and ask

effects.log: The clerks tell you the wind has been sulking over a lost hat. They will see what can be done.

choices.text: Say the wind has gone for good

effects.log: {npc} keeps calling. You feel the weight of having said it.

events.text: The wind comes, and with it the lost hat, which has been carried over three isles and returned with great dignity. Hollow Pell rises through the mill, sails turning, and the grain falls as fine as snow. {npc} laughs aloud. It is the first time in a century you have heard {him} do so.
events.arc: The Miller Who Ground Only on a Named Wind

choices.text: Help bring the flour to the isle

effects.log: You carry bags down the quay, and the isle forgets it ever doubted the wind.

choices.text: Ask for a handful of the first flour

effects.log: It makes the loaf of the year. It tastes faintly of a western summer.

events.text: The Ministry finds the hat, sends a dignified apology, and the wind returns grudgingly. But the mill, ground too fast, is never quite the same, and the grain has a hint of haste in it. {npc} says nothing. The isle eats the bread and finds it good enough, which is the worst thing {he} has ever heard.
events.arc: The Miller Who Ground Only on a Named Wind

choices.text: Tell {npc} the bread is fine and mean it

effects.log: You make an effort to mean it. By the third loaf it is true.

choices.text: Offer to wait for the wind next year

effects.log: You will. It is a promise worth keeping.

events.text: Every cloud-skiff that crosses at night carries a lamp, and every lamp must be oiled. {npc} walks the quay at midnight with a can and a rag and a little song, oiling each lamp as the skiffs come and go. {He} hands you the can and asks if you would like to learn the quiet trade of keeping other people's light.
events.arc: The Oiler of Ferry Lamps

effects.log: It is surprisingly delicate. A lamp has moods, and the oil is a kind of conversation.
{npc} corrects your pitch, and by dawn you know all four verses.
The lamps pass like slow fireflies. {npc} nods at each one.

events.text: One night a skiff arrives with a lamp that will not take oil. It burns without it, a steady green, and the pilot says it was a gift from someone they cannot name. {npc} looks at it a long time and then at you: “It is a ghost-lamp,” {he} says. “It burns for someone who will not come.”
events.arc: The Oiler of Ferry Lamps

choices.text: Sit with the pilot and hear their story

effects.log: The pilot lost a friend to the sea of clouds. The lamp is how they look for them.

choices.text: Offer to oil the lamp anyway

effects.log: You pour oil that does not soak in. It beads on the glass like tears.

choices.text: Keep the pilot company with silence

effects.log: Silence is allowed. You both stare at the green flame.

events.text: The pilot tells you the friend's name, and you carry it to the Ministry of Registers, who find it listed as only “drifted”. The pilot is given a seal, a bench on the quay, and a lamp-hook that will always be kept free. Every night after, the green lamp hangs there and no one else takes the hook.
events.arc: The Oiler of Ferry Lamps

choices.text: Visit the green lamp on its hook

effects.log: You sit with the pilot on quiet nights. Neither of you needs to say much.

choices.text: Add your own lamp beside it

effects.log: The two flames burn side by side. People begin to leave small lamps at the quay.

events.text: The pilot thanks you and goes. The green lamp is taken off the skiff at last, and given to {npc}, who hangs it on the quay's far end where no skiff comes. It burns there all night, a single green flame, and the skiffs steer a little wide of it out of respect.
events.arc: The Oiler of Ferry Lamps

effects.log: It is a small and strange duty. You keep it for a century.
It burns alone, which may be what it wants.

events.text: A small shed at the cloud quay is hung with slings, bandages and a hundred tiny bells. {npc} heals the beasts that fall ill at the quay: a thunder sparrow with a cold, a cloud carp with a sunburn. {He} hands you a roll of linen and says that if you can hold a creature still you are already a healer.
events.arc: The Healer of Sky Beasts at the Quay

choices.text: Hold a trembling sparrow while {he} works

effects.log: The sparrow bites, then sleeps in your palm. {npc} says that is the real cure.
A quay full of invalid beasts is a quiet and gentle place. You keep it supplied.

choices.text: Keep clear of the biting end

effects.log: A sensible way to live, you tell yourself.

events.text: A young whale calf is beached on the far side of the quay, its song faint and its breathing strange. It is too large to be moved. {npc} says there is a way, but it needs someone who can sing low and long and hold a note for hours, steady as a keel.
events.arc: The Healer of Sky Beasts at the Quay

choices.text: Sing the low note for the calf

effects.log: You sing until your throat gives out. The calf stirs and floats a little higher on each breath.

choices.text: Fetch the Steersman to haul it

effects.log: The Steersman Ohwa arrives with a line of skiffs. The calf comes off the quay on a tow of lanterns.
{npc} sings alone. You hear the note go on till morning.

events.text: The calf lifts at dawn, shakes its flukes, and sings you a song so sweet that the whole quay stops to listen. {npc} sits down on the shed step with {his} bandages in {his} lap and weeps. The calf circles twice and goes up into the light, and every year on that day it returns to sing once at the quay.
events.arc: The Healer of Sky Beasts at the Quay

choices.text: Wait for the calf each year

effects.log: It always comes. You never miss one in the century that follows.

choices.text: Record the song on a jade slip

effects.log: The slip is kept at the shed and played to sick beasts. It works better than you would think.

events.text: The skiffs haul the calf off the quay and into the deep air, singing as it goes. {npc} writes up the case in a ledger that hangs from the shed door. “They always go,” {he} says. “That is the point of a quay.” You help {him} sweep the shed, and find a small bell on the floor that rings all by itself.
events.arc: The Healer of Sky Beasts at the Quay

choices.text: Hang the bell by the door

effects.log: It rings whenever a beast is brought in. It has never been wrong.

choices.text: Keep the bell in your sleeve

effects.log: It rings in your sleeve when someone, somewhere, needs hands.

events.text: The heaven-born children of the Bamboo Isle learn first how to fall, since the edge is always near. {npc} teaches the class: a ring of small figures tumbling off a low terrace onto a cushion of cloud. “Falling is only flying you have not yet admitted,” {he} says, and invites you to watch.
events.arc: The Class Where Heaven-Born Learn to Fall

effects.log: The children are solemn and graceful, and one lands upside-down to cheers.
You catch four. They giggle at being caught, and fall again on purpose.
You trust the cushion, and the children.

events.text: One child, the quietest in the class, will not fall. {He} stands at the terrace edge each day with clenched hands and shakes {his} head. {npc} asks you to speak with the child. “I cannot make them,” {he} says. “A fear like that is no one's to take.”
events.arc: The Class Where Heaven-Born Learn to Fall

choices.text: Sit with the child and say nothing

effects.log: You sit a week of afternoons. On the eighth, the child takes your hand and steps off.

choices.text: Tell the child about your own first fall

effects.log: The tale is silly and true. The child laughs, and then falls, laughing.

choices.text: Tell {npc} to push the child gently

effects.log: {npc} refuses, politely, and you feel the rebuke for years.

events.text: The child falls, lands, and sits up covered in cloud-dust. The whole class cheers, and the child, astonished, takes a bow. {npc} wipes {his} eyes with a sleeve. “Twelve hundred pupils,” {he} says, “and I still cry at this one.” The child becomes a courier, years on, and never drops a letter.
events.arc: The Class Where Heaven-Born Learn to Fall

effects.log: The child gives you a tiny cushion made of cloud-dust as a gift.

choices.text: Tell {npc} how well it was done

effects.log: It is a rare kind of conversation: two grown immortals, each happy for different reasons.

events.text: The child falls by choice and then never again. Years later the child is the one who steadies the class, gentle and exact, never losing the memory of the terrace edge. {npc} gives the child a wooden bell and says, “Ring it when someone is afraid.” It rings often, and always kindly.
events.arc: The Class Where Heaven-Born Learn to Fall

choices.text: Ask the child how it feels now

effects.log: "Like I borrowed the sky and gave it back," says the child.

choices.text: Carry the bell for a day as a favour

effects.log: You ring it once. A child nearby looks up and steps down from a high stair.

events.text: Each century the heaven-born sit the Examination of the Seven Stairs, and the top scorer is sent away to serve in the far Ministries. The students dread the post. {npc}, the proctor, notices on the first morning that every paper has the same wrong answer in the same place. {He} puts down the pen and looks at you, as the only other adult in the hall.
events.arc: The Examination Everyone Failed on Purpose

choices.text: Say nothing and watch the proctor decide

effects.log: {npc} breathes out slowly. "A pact," {he} says, and does not report it.

choices.text: Ask {npc} what the students are afraid of

effects.log: "Leaving," says {npc}. "Every one of them has a friend."
{npc} gives you an unreadable look and folds the papers.

events.text: {npc} cannot let the exam stand: the Court expects a name. {He} comes to you with a proposal. If a new rule could be written, letting the top scorer choose to stay, the pact would be unnecessary. It means petitioning three Ministries that have never agreed on anything.
events.arc: The Examination Everyone Failed on Purpose

effects.log: The drafting takes a year and four pots of tea. The language is elegant and impossible to refuse.
You tell them the pact is known and tolerated. Several cry with relief.
You are polite, and unhelpful, and unnoticed.

events.text: The rule passes in the face of three Ministries' sighs: the top scorer may choose to stay or to go. At the next examination the best student, a thin shy student with a stammer, takes the paper and answers every question correctly. The student stays. So do all the others, by choice.
events.arc: The Examination Everyone Failed on Purpose

effects.log: {npc} takes the praise stiffly and then admits {he} did very little.
The students climb all seven together. Nobody is left on a lower step.

events.text: The students, relieved to be seen, stop the pact the next year and sit the exam honestly. The top scorer goes to a far Ministry and writes weekly letters that are read aloud in the hall. {npc} saves them all in a box, and shows it to you only once. It is a short box, and a heavy one.
events.arc: The Examination Everyone Failed on Purpose

choices.text: Write a letter back to the student

effects.log: It takes you a month. You are surprised at how much you have to say.

choices.text: Tell {npc} the box is worth the post

effects.log: {npc} nods, though not convinced. The next year the box is longer.

events.text: The heaven-born of the Bamboo Isle play a game at recess with rules so complicated that the adults avoid it. {npc} supervises with a long face. A boy has been sent off the field for “breathing wrongly,” and the argument has reached the fourth appeal. {He} asks you to referee the final one.
events.arc: The Recess Rules of the Heaven-Born

effects.log: Both sides speak at once. The rules, you realise, are being made up as the argument continues.

choices.text: Rule in favour of the youngest

effects.log: The youngest is delighted. The oldest says the ruling is unprecedented, which pleases everyone.

choices.text: Say recess is for running about

effects.log: They stare at you with open pity. You go away.

events.text: The game's rules, written down by a clever child, run to nine hundred pages. The children ask you to bind them into a book. {npc} reads one page and slowly sits down. “There is a rule,” {he} says, “that forbids rules from being read aloud.” {He} asks what you think should be done with the book.
events.arc: The Recess Rules of the Heaven-Born

choices.text: Bind it and keep it in the archive

effects.log: It becomes a minor work of legal literature. Scholars read it for the humour.

choices.text: Burn the book and play without it

effects.log: The children are horrified, then relieved, then begin inventing new rules from scratch.
The pages are rearranged by the children into a better order.

events.text: The book is read, and the Ministry of Precedence adopts three of its rules. {npc} puffs out {his} chest. The children, hearing, are indignant: those were the silly ones. A new edition is demanded, and for a year there are fierce discussions on the lawn, as cheerful as ever.
events.arc: The Recess Rules of the Heaven-Born

effects.log: You are named in the preface as a "friend to the game".

choices.text: Tell them the silly rules are the best

effects.log: The children are won over. Recess ends in a truce, then in a picnic.

events.text: The book is burned. The game is played again from nothing, and within a season is just as complex as before. {npc} looks at the new rules with resignation and a small smile. “It is not the rules,” {he} says. “It is the arguing.” The children look up and wave.
events.arc: The Recess Rules of the Heaven-Born

effects.log: You lose every appeal, and it is the best afternoon of the year.

choices.text: Bring a snack for the new rules

effects.log: Snacks are admitted as a valid argument by all parties.

events.text: A rogue with no isle and no faction has no one to lend or to share. You learn this at the Low Market, where {npc}, another wanderer, sits on an upturned crate counting stones into small piles and back again. “You count too,” {he} says to you. “Everyone without a patron counts. It is the only prayer we have.”
events.arc: The Rogue Who Counted Every Stone

effects.log: Counting aloud is a ritual. It steadies the nerves and, oddly, the purse.

choices.text: Say a patron would be worse

effects.log: {npc} laughs bitterly. "Said by one who has never had one," {he} says, without malice.
The stone-piles click behind you like beads.

events.text: {npc} needs a loan: three stones to buy a licence for a night stall. The market charges rogues double for the licence, and {he} has a recipe that sells itself. No faction will vouch for the stall, and no rogue has stones to spare. {He} does not beg. {He} only shows you the three small piles.
events.arc: The Rogue Who Counted Every Stone

effects.log: The loan is made with a handshake. {npc} writes your name on the first page of a new ledger.
Your word counts for little, but it counts. The licence is halved.
{npc} nods and puts the piles back in {his} sleeve, which is worse than an argument.

events.text: The stall opens and the recipe sells. Within the year {npc} repays the loan with interest in the form of a lifelong supply of the best dumplings in the Low Market, and a stool at the stall that is yours alone. The rogues of the market begin to say that a stone lent is a stone kept.
events.arc: The Rogue Who Counted Every Stone

choices.text: Eat at the stall each week

effects.log: The dumplings are excellent. The stool is warm. You feel, for once, expected.
A little guild forms, informal and kind. The licence fees are shared.

events.text: The market halves the fee for a vouched stall, and {npc} opens with fewer stones and more nerve. The stall is modest and the dumplings fair. {He} never mentions the favour, but when you pass, there is always a steamer pushed to the front, and a nod that means more than a debt paid.
events.arc: The Rogue Who Counted Every Stone

choices.text: Accept the nod and the steamer

effects.log: Gratitude does not have to be a sum. You eat.

choices.text: Recommend the stall to the market

effects.log: Business picks up. {npc} sends you a card in thanks, with a single pressed leaf.

events.text: A note of debt, written by a wandering rogue five centuries ago, has passed from hand to hand across the sky, and {npc} holds it now. “It says whoever carries it is owed ten stones,” {he} says, “by someone named Yun-A who has never been found.” {He} wants to be rid of it, but cannot bring {him}self to burn it.
events.arc: The Debt Note That Passed Through Seven Hands

effects.log: The paper is soft as cloth. The signature wanders across the page like a drifter itself.

choices.text: Offer to buy it for a stone

effects.log: {npc} thinks about it. "A debt is worth less than a story," {he} says.
You walk away. {npc} puts the note back in {his} sleeve.

events.text: You take the note, and with it the long task of tracking the name. At a tea-house on a far isle, an old woman says she knew a Yun-A once, a wanderer who died poor. Her granddaughter might know more. The trail is five isles long, and the note is worth ten stones that no one will ever pay.
events.arc: The Debt Note That Passed Through Seven Hands

choices.text: Follow the trail to the granddaughter

effects.log: It takes a year and many ferries. The granddaughter is cooking when you find her.

choices.text: Hand the note to a ministry clerk

effects.log: The clerk files it in a drawer of debts that no one owes. It is finished, and sad.
You keep the note in your sleeve, and sometimes think of it.

events.text: The granddaughter reads the note, laughs, cries, and shows you a shelf where Yun-A's other debts sit, each marked “paid in full” in the same wandering hand. She pays the ten stones herself, then hands them back to you with the note. “Ancestors lend,” she says. “They always lend. The only debt is to keep going.”
events.arc: The Debt Note That Passed Through Seven Hands

choices.text: Accept the stones and the note

effects.log: You carry both, and the note is lighter than before.

choices.text: Refuse the stones, keep the note

effects.log: You say you will carry it for her. She weeps again, kindly.

events.text: The clerk files the note under Unpayable, and the Ministry stamps it with a wax seal that makes it, officially, a memory. The ten stones are never paid. You walk away feeling that something small and absurd has been laid to rest. In the sleeve where the note was, you find, for no reason, a stone.
events.arc: The Debt Note That Passed Through Seven Hands

choices.text: Keep the stone as a charm

effects.log: It is warm, like something returned.

choices.text: Leave the stone on the next beggar's step

effects.log: You walk on, and the debt is, in a way, paid.

events.text: A cloud-skiff ferries rogues between the poor isles for half what the licensed lines charge, and {npc} keeps a small book of who owes what. The book is full of crossings given on trust. {He} offers you a ride at the old price, and asks nothing for it but your name in the margin.
events.arc: The Rogue Ferryman Who Kept a Debt Book

effects.log: The skiff is slow and mended. The book smells of tea and old rain.
The book is not offended. It records you as “Paid”, a word that is oddly rare.
You save your pride and lose a day.

events.text: The licensed lines have complained to the Ministry of Roads that the rogue ferry undercuts them. {npc} is summoned. {He} brings the debt book as evidence, thinking it a defence. It reads like a list of the poor. The clerks seem uncertain what to do with it. {He} asks if you will speak for the ferry.
events.arc: The Rogue Ferryman Who Kept a Debt Book

effects.log: You say it is a service, not a rival. The hearing hushes. Not everyone is moved, but some are.
You count out stones, and the clerks note it down without enthusiasm.

choices.text: Say you were only a passenger

effects.log: {npc} nods without anger. The hearing continues without you.

events.text: The Ministry rules that the rogue ferry may continue, provided it runs a “free line” on certain days, carrying those who cannot pay. {npc} had been doing so for years without the paper. The paper is hung in the wheelhouse, framed, with the debt book under it. You are named a “witness for good standing”.
events.arc: The Rogue Ferryman Who Kept a Debt Book

choices.text: Ride the free line on its first day

effects.log: The skiff is full, quiet and grateful. You sit among them.

choices.text: Offer to keep the book for a season

effects.log: The ledger is heavy with trust. You write in it with care.

events.text: The fines are paid, the line continues, and the ferry runs on trust alone. {npc} never forgets the stones you spent and records it in the book as a gift, not a loan. Years later, when the ferry is old, a small plaque appears on the wheelhouse listing your name among its friends. It is not large. It is warm.
events.arc: The Rogue Ferryman Who Kept a Debt Book

choices.text: Ride the old ferry once more

effects.log: It is worn and slow. {npc} lets you steer it, for a bit.

choices.text: Send a gift for the wheelhouse

effects.log: A lamp, a new cushion. The ferry is the cleaner for it.

events.text: On the roof of the Ministry of Tribute are forty hives of cloud-bees, and {npc} is the Ministry's beekeeper. The honey is for state banquets, but the bees seem to prefer the paperwork: they nest in the files. {He} asks you to help smoke them out of an archive without offending either party.
events.arc: The Keeper of the Ministry's Bees

effects.log: The bees leave in a long polite line. The files smell of honey for a century.

choices.text: Persuade the bees with a flower

effects.log: A bee takes your flower to the queen, and the colony relocates. {npc} is impressed.

choices.text: Leave the files to the bees

effects.log: A clerk finds a lawsuit written in wax. It is unreadable and very handsome.

events.text: The honey of the year is ready, and the Minister wants it served at a banquet for guests of the Divine Realm. The bees have chosen to make it bitter this year, perhaps from grief, perhaps from tea-leaves. {npc} is anxious. “It is the best honey I have ever made,” {he} says, “and the worst for a banquet.”
events.arc: The Keeper of the Ministry's Bees

choices.text: Serve it as a bitter honey

effects.log: You write the menu card yourself. The guests are charmed by its honesty.

choices.text: Blend it with a sweeter honey

effects.log: It is pleasant and forgettable, like most banquets.
The Minister is cross, then curious. The bitter honey is tasted, privately, and approved.

events.text: The banquet is remembered for the bitter honey. A guest from the Divine Realm asks for the recipe and is told that it is a secret of the bees. {npc} is invited to serve it again, and refuses, courteously: the bees do not do the same thing twice. The Ministry, to its credit, understands.
events.arc: The Keeper of the Ministry's Bees

effects.log: {He} blushes into {his} beard and goes back to the hives.

choices.text: Ask for a jar of the bitter honey

effects.log: It is strange and good. You keep it for sorrows.

events.text: The blended honey is served and forgotten. The bees, offended, withhold their best the following year. {npc} spends the autumn in the apiary, apologising to each hive. By winter the honey is back, sweet, and the files are bee-free. The Ministry never learns how close it came to an absence.
events.arc: The Keeper of the Ministry's Bees

effects.log: It is a long, humbling afternoon, and the bees accept it.

choices.text: Bring the bees a gift of flowers

effects.log: They hum over the flowers for days. The truce holds.

events.text: The border towns of the Demon Realm are quiet places, with low houses, long tables, and a market on the thirteenth day of every month. {npc} runs an inn where guests of both realms sleep without comment. {He} sets down a bowl of black-bean broth and tells you that everyone is welcome until they are not.
events.arc: The Innkeeper at the Border of the Demon Realm

choices.text: Eat and ask about the rules of the house

effects.log: "There is one," says {npc}. "Do not leave the table angry." You find it hard to break.

choices.text: Pay for your night and sleep

effects.log: The bed is firm and the quilt is red. You wake rested.
{npc} looks at you with absolute calm. "Then do not eat it," {he} says.

events.text: Two travellers arrive on the same night, one a Court clerk and the other a Demon Realm soldier, and each sits at an opposite end of the long table. The rule of the inn is that no one speaks until the broth is finished. They finish. Silence thickens. {npc} looks at you and tilts {his} head at the empty seat between them.
events.arc: The Innkeeper at the Border of the Demon Realm

choices.text: Sit between them and ask a small question

effects.log: You ask where each of them grew up. It turns out they grew up two valleys apart.
The silence lasts until midnight and then breaks, quietly, over a second bowl.

choices.text: Pick a side and talk to one

effects.log: The other feels it. {npc} says nothing, but the broth tastes thinner.

events.text: The two leave in the morning, still not friends, but walking at the same pace. {npc} says it is the best kind of peace the inn can make. A month later a letter arrives, signed by both, thanking the house and asking, as a joke, whether the long table could be made longer. {He} orders more wood at once.
events.arc: The Innkeeper at the Border of the Demon Realm

effects.log: It takes a week and many strong opinions. The grain of the wood is beautiful.

choices.text: Carry the letter to the Jade Court

effects.log: It is read, to your surprise, aloud. The Court seems moved.

events.text: The silence breaks over a second bowl, and the two, by dawn, are arguing about the best route to the next isle. {npc} serves them breakfast and does not look up. “The inn does its work,” {he} says to you quietly, “without anyone noticing it has.” You, noticing, decide to say nothing, which is its own kind of thanks.
events.arc: The Innkeeper at the Border of the Demon Realm

choices.text: Leave a stone under the bowl

effects.log: The coin is found a day later. {npc} puts it in the box for the next traveller.

choices.text: Praise the broth on your way out

effects.log: {npc} bows deeply for the first time in your acquaintance.

events.text: When hail falls on the roofs of a small isle, {npc} of the Ministry of Weather arrives with a ledger and a ladder, to count the damage. {He} is polite, thorough and slow. Today the isle is a school, and the roof is dented like a drum. {He} asks if you will help count dents, since two sets of eyes are less wrong than one.
events.arc: The Adjuster of Hail Damage

effects.log: There are four hundred and nine. The children cheer each time you call out a number.
It is not glamorous. The roof gets counted all the same.

choices.text: Say you have no head for numbers

effects.log: {npc} counts alone, quietly, in the cold.

events.text: The Ministry's repair fund is small, and the school roof needs a hundred stones to mend. {npc} tells you in confidence that the fund will not cover it. The school is poor, and the children have nothing to give. {He} says, carefully, that rules sometimes bend when a witness is willing to sign.
events.arc: The Adjuster of Hail Damage

effects.log: The report is bent just enough, and the fund approves. {npc} thanks you with a small nod.

choices.text: Raise the stones from the isles around

effects.log: You go door to door. The stones come in fives and tens.
{npc} folds the report and says nothing. The roof stays dented.

events.text: The roof is mended with the Ministry's stones, and the children paint the new tiles in bright colours. {npc} visits once a year to count, not damage, but dents of the happier sort, where children have bounced balls on the roof. The ledger now has two columns: hail, and play.
events.arc: The Adjuster of Hail Damage

effects.log: You paint a small cloud with a smile. It is the only one on the roof.
It is an honour to hold a ledger so full of small things.

events.text: The isles give, and the roof is mended without the Ministry. {npc} writes in the report that the repair was “by private generosity”, a phrase the Ministry rarely sees. {He} frames it, and the school, on the anniversary, hangs a banner reading Thank You, Everyone. A hundred hands have written their names on it, yours among them.
events.arc: The Adjuster of Hail Damage

choices.text: Sign the banner in a corner

effects.log: The ink dries slowly, warm in the sun.
Tea and banner, sky and school. It is a good afternoon.

events.text: To hang a lamp over any public water above the clouds, you need a licence from the Ministry of Lights, and {npc} issues them. {He} sits at a desk by the lake, stamping slowly and tastefully. A hundred lamps float above the water for each licence, {he} says, and every one must be stamped, though no one checks.
events.arc: The Clerk Who Licensed Lamps

choices.text: Ask how the stamp is chosen

effects.log: "By the lamp," says {npc}. "It must look like it will not be missed."

choices.text: Apply for a licence to hang a small lamp

effects.log: The form is two lines long. You receive a stamp that is, very faintly, warm.

choices.text: Hang a lamp without a licence

effects.log: It is spotted by a passing clerk in a minute. You pay a small fine.

events.text: A rogue wanders to the desk and asks for a licence. {npc} reads the form and frowns. Rogues are not permitted to hang lamps over water: it is a rule from the old Ministry, nobody remembers why. The rogue says nothing, but their lamp, already lit, sits in their palm like a small star.
events.arc: The Clerk Who Licensed Lamps

effects.log: You say the rule is a relic. {npc} looks tired, then pulls out a pen.

choices.text: Offer to sponsor the lamp yourself

effects.log: Your name goes on the form. It is a small act, and a large one.
{npc} stamps it, unwillingly, with a faint sigh. Or perhaps not. You do not stay to see.

events.text: The rule is struck from the book with a line of ink, and the rogue's lamp is first among a thousand to float over the lake. {npc} says nothing, and stamps every new licence, rogue or not. A year later {he} gives you the old stamp as a keepsake. It is tarnished, heavy and quite useless.
events.arc: The Clerk Who Licensed Lamps

choices.text: Keep the stamp on your desk

effects.log: It sits among your papers like a small brass conscience.
{npc} smiles at this and hangs it on a nail in the office, among others like it.

events.text: Your sponsorship holds, and the rogue's lamp floats on, though the rule stays in the book. {npc} says that rules are like roots: you can lift one tree and it will grow back. Still, there is now a lamp on the lake that is yours and a stranger's together, and on festival nights it burns slightly brighter than the rest.
events.arc: The Clerk Who Licensed Lamps

choices.text: Visit the lamp at festival time

effects.log: The rogue is there, grinning. Two chairs have been brought down to the water.

choices.text: Say nothing about the lamp to anyone

effects.log: The kindest acts are quiet. This one is among them.

events.text: Every tribute of tea sent up to the Ministry must be tasted before it is accepted, and {npc} has tasted every cup for a thousand years. {He} has a palate that can tell the isle, the season and the mood of the picker. {He} sets a cup before you, unlabelled, and asks you to say where it came from.
events.arc: The Tea-Taster of the Ministry of Tribute

choices.text: Guess the isle by the taste

effects.log: You are wrong about the isle and right about the mood. {npc} says that is the harder half.

choices.text: Say the tea tastes of home

effects.log: {npc} is quiet for a moment. "It does," {he} says. "They always do."
The tea is good all the same. {npc} nods approvingly at the honesty.

events.text: A cup of tribute from the Mist Isle tastes of grief, and {npc} cannot accept it for the banquet, though the Mist Isle has sent it as a gift. The picker was widowed in the spring, and the tea carries it. {He} asks for your advice: send it back politely, or accept it as a true tribute, sorrow and all.
events.arc: The Tea-Taster of the Ministry of Tribute

choices.text: Accept it as a true tribute

effects.log: The cup goes to the banquet, untouched. A silence falls over the table, and it is the right silence.

choices.text: Send it back with a note of thanks

effects.log: The Mist Isle receives it, and the picker writes a long letter in reply.

choices.text: Mix it with a lighter tea

effects.log: {npc} flinches visibly. You are not asked again.

events.text: The tea is placed on the banquet table in its own cup. The Minister, after a long pause, bows to it. The Mist Isle picker, informed of this, sends the next season's tea with a note: “I will pick it with a lighter hand.” {npc} writes back, in a letter of {his} own, that no hand should be lighter than it has to be.
events.arc: The Tea-Taster of the Ministry of Tribute

choices.text: Carry the note to the Mist Isle

effects.log: The picker meets you at the dock, thin and kind. You drink together in silence.

choices.text: Keep a cup of that tea for yourself

effects.log: It tastes of a long afternoon in the rain. You are glad of it.

events.text: The tea is returned, and the Mist Isle picker, relieved, writes to {npc} for the first time. They correspond for decades, always about tea, never about grief. Their letters are stored in the Ministry archive under Tribute Correspondence, and a clerk, in a century, reads them aloud on a rainy afternoon. It is the gentlest reading the Ministry has ever heard.
events.arc: The Tea-Taster of the Ministry of Tribute

effects.log: Nobody speaks after. The rain fills the quiet.

choices.text: Add a letter of your own to the file

effects.log: It is a short one. It is kept.

events.text: At the Edge Post, letters that reach no one are kept in a long room that smells of dust and rain. {npc} keeps the dead-letter room and reads none of them. {He} says it is a rule of the trade. Today a letter has arrived for you that is a hundred years old, addressed in a hand you almost recognise, and {he} sets it before you without a word.
events.arc: The Dead-Letter Room of the Edge Post

effects.log: It is a short note from a friend you lost touch with. It says, simply, "I looked for you."

choices.text: Hold the letter a while before opening it

effects.log: You hold it for a day. Some letters need their time.
{npc} takes it back, gently. "It will keep," {he} says.

events.text: The friend, you find, still lives, on a far isle. {npc} offers a small spirit-skiff, the kind used for letters, to carry a reply. {He} says the Post has never delivered anything back to a friend after a century, but nothing in the rules forbids it. The skiff waits, with its little lamp, on the edge.
events.arc: The Dead-Letter Room of the Edge Post

choices.text: Write a long reply and send it

effects.log: You write a page, then three. The skiff leaves, small and quick.

choices.text: Write only a line: “I am here.”

effects.log: It is quicker, and perhaps truer. The skiff bobs away.

choices.text: Keep the old letter as it is

effects.log: You let it be. Some old things are best left open.

events.text: A reply returns within the season: an invitation to tea, a hundred years late and just on time. The friend's hair is white, and their eyes are the same. You sit on the porch of a small isle, and the dead-letter room, you learn, was how they found the courage to write. {npc} receives a gift of tea from them both, and keeps it for the quiet hours.
events.arc: The Dead-Letter Room of the Edge Post

effects.log: It passes like an afternoon. You promise to write again, and mean it.

choices.text: Bring {npc} a pot of the tea

effects.log: {He} drinks it with the door ajar, as if listening for a delivery.

events.text: Your line reaches the friend, who replies with one of their own: “So am I.” That is all. It is kept, with the first, in a drawer at the Post. {npc} says it is the shortest correspondence the room has ever recorded. In the years after, you both send a line each spring, nothing more, and it is plenty.
events.arc: The Dead-Letter Room of the Edge Post

effects.log: It is a small ritual, and a true one.
The tea is better than the letters, and the letters better than silence.

events.text: At the foot of the Hot Spring terraces, {npc} sells tonics from a wheeled cart: a pink one for the afternoon, a green for the morning, a cloudy one for no purpose in particular. All are mild. {He} says strong tonics make strong customers, and strong customers are never grateful. {He} offers you a sample of the cloudy one.
events.arc: The Tonic-Seller Who Sold Nothing Strong

effects.log: It tastes of nothing, and of the afternoon. You feel entirely fine.
"Hot water," says {npc}, "and attention." {He} does not smile.
"No," says {npc}. "Come back when you want something kinder."

events.text: A Minister's secretary arrives, annoyed. The tonics have been described in a report as “suspiciously mild”, and an inspection is due. {npc} is nervous, since mildness is difficult to prove. {He} asks if you would accompany the inspector to the cart, as a character witness to a lack of effect.
events.arc: The Tonic-Seller Who Sold Nothing Strong

choices.text: Stand as witness to the mildness

effects.log: The inspector sips, frowns, and writes "harmless". {npc} could kiss you.

choices.text: Praise the tonic's subtlety to the inspector

effects.log: The inspector, who has never been praised, softens and buys a flask.

choices.text: Say you barely know the cart

effects.log: {npc} stiffens. The inspection goes poorly.

events.text: The inspector writes a short glowing report, which {npc} frames above the cart: “Does what it says: nothing, kindly.” The inspector becomes a regular, and on slow afternoons you can see two figures sipping and not speaking at the cart. It is, you suspect, a quiet romance.
events.arc: The Tonic-Seller Who Sold Nothing Strong

effects.log: Some things are best left to the cloudy tonic.
They look up, startled and pleased. The cup is accepted.

events.text: The inspection goes poorly, and the cart is licensed with a restriction: no more than half a ladle per customer. {npc} accepts it with a shrug. “A half-ladle is plenty for what I make,” {he} says, and stirs the pot. The line grows longer, since the half-ladle has become a thing people value, rare and small.
events.arc: The Tonic-Seller Who Sold Nothing Strong

effects.log: It tastes the same, and somehow better.
{npc} lets you ladle half-ladles for an hour. It is delicate work.

events.text: A clerk of the Ministry of Registers has, after three hundred years, run out of blank forms. The shelf is empty. The Ministry does not make them: it only fills them in. The clerk stands in front of the shelf in an attitude of calm despair and asks if you have ever seen a form with nothing on it.

choices.text: Offer a sheet of your own paper

effects.log: The clerk draws the lines by hand. The form is accepted as irregular and beautiful.

choices.text: Suggest the clerk simply invent a form

effects.log: The clerk gasps, then smiles, and sits down to write one. It runs to forty lines.

choices.text: Say you have never seen one

effects.log: The clerk nods. The Ministry, you suspect, has never seen one either.

events.text: Once a decade the Ministry of Precedence renews its ink: a ritual of grinding ten thousand ink-sticks and pouring them together in a hall that smells of pine and old rain. A junior clerk offers you a brush and says the first stroke of the new ink is traditionally made by a guest.

effects.log: You paint one character, slowly. The hall applauds a single stroke.

choices.text: Decline and let the clerk do it

effects.log: The clerk blushes, paints, and the day is theirs.

choices.text: Ask what the stroke should be

effects.log: "A line," says the clerk. "Just a line." It is the best answer you hear all year.

events.text: The Ministry of Weather takes a census of clouds every hundred years, by hand. A cheerful clerk with a counting-stick stops you on the quay and asks how many clouds you can see. “Be honest,” says the clerk, “I count what people say, and then I divide.”

effects.log: You settle on a number. The clerk writes it in the book and halves it, mysteriously.

choices.text: Say there are too many to count

effects.log: The clerk beams. "That is the most useful answer I have heard."
The clerk notes them in the margin with names. The Ministry has never known clouds with names.

events.text: At the edge of the Pasture Isle a small herding-dog made of mist watches the flock. It has no bark: it only presses against the clouds until they move. The shepherd says the dog is eleven hundred years old. It comes to you and sits, and looks at you in the way of one waiting to be told.

choices.text: Say something kind to the dog
