effects.log: It wags, and for a moment its tail makes a small fog in the air.
Your hand comes away damp and cool. The feeling lasts all afternoon.

choices.text: Whistle for it to herd you

effects.log: It herds you gently to a bench and sits beside you.

events.text: The root-pruners hold a yearly picnic under the Orchard Isle, on hanging seats arranged in a circle around a huge, slow-turning root. Plates are passed by rope. A pruner insists you must try the pickled root, which is considered bad luck to refuse and worse luck to like.

effects.log: It is sour, earthy and unexpectedly good. The pruners cheer, since you have risked the worse luck.
You are given tea, and it is accepted that you are cautious.

choices.text: Trade a story for the pickle

effects.log: The tale you tell is a poor one. You are forgiven by the second helping.

events.text: A star-polisher's rag is left on a bench on the observation terrace: grey cloth, soft as a petal, warm to the touch. It smells of starlight. A note beside it says “for whoever needs it”. You wonder who has left it, and whether anyone has ever used it more than once.

effects.log: It cleans the lamps in your house to a polish nothing else will give.
Someone takes it by evening. The bench is empty, and you feel kind.
The bench shines with a faint blue gleam. People sit longer on it than they should.

events.text: Pet day at the heaven-born school: each child brings a creature to show. There is a hound of mist, a baby thunder sparrow in a hat, and a small tortoise that has been a teacher's secret for centuries. A child asks you to judge. The only rule is that no pet may be called the best.

choices.text: Give each a ribbon for a different thing

effects.log: The ribbons are for Loudest, Shyest, Most Likely to Outlive Us All. All are delighted.

choices.text: Say you cannot judge such lovely creatures

effects.log: The child says that is exactly what the last judge said, and hands you cake.

choices.text: Ask the pets to judge each other

effects.log: The result is chaos and a very happy afternoon.

events.text: It is exam season, and the Seven Stairs are choked with rumours: the exam has moved to the Ninth Stair, the proctor has been replaced by a goose, the questions are all in verse. A nervous student catches your sleeve and asks whether any of it is true.

choices.text: Tell the truth as you know it

effects.log: The exam is where it has always been. The student sighs with relief and falls over the first stair.
The student blanches. You decide not to explain.
The breath goes through the whole queue. The Stairs are quiet and calm.

events.text: At a Low Market stall a rogue is selling a small purse with a clever lining that can hold ten stones and looks empty even to a thief. “Every rogue needs one,” the seller says. “Not for the stones. For the look of having none.” The price is two stones, which is, in itself, a joke.

effects.log: It sits empty in your sleeve and heavy in your thoughts. It is the best thing you ever bought.
The seller grins, taps the purse, and agrees to a stone and a story.
A rogue with stones in a plain pouch is a rogue easily robbed. You walk on, a little lighter.

events.text: A smiling collector of the Cloud-Merchants' Guild finds you at the Low Market with a ledger and a list of debts, some of which are yours, some of which belong to people who have the same name. The collector is polite. The collector is entirely certain of the numbers.

choices.text: Pay what you owe (3 spirit stones)

effects.log: The collector blots the line, thanks you, and moves on. The sky seems briefly cleaner.
You show a receipt. The collector crosses out a debt, grumbling, and the rest hold.

choices.text: Say you will pay next market

effects.log: The collector writes "promised". It is a word that follows you.

events.text: The canteen of the Ministry of Tribute serves the same soup every day, and has done for six centuries. A clerk sits beside you and, with great shyness, says today it is different. You taste it. It is the same. You say so. The clerk nods, relieved, and asks you not to tell the cook.

effects.log: The cook never learns. The soup is the soup, and everyone is content.
The cook looks into the pot a long time and says, "Ah." The soup is different the next day.

choices.text: Ask the clerk how they knew

effects.log: "I tasted it every day," says the clerk. "It is the only thing I do."

events.text: In the Map Room a loose map has been left unfolded on a table: an old chart of an isle that no longer exists. The creases are soft with age. A note says: “To be refolded by someone with a steady hand.” Its owner is nowhere to be seen. The room smells of paper and warm tea.

effects.log: The creases fall into place. The room feels briefly satisfied.
The isle was beautiful. You wonder where it went.
It is still there next week, patiently unfolded.

events.text: On the Long Bridge a bench has appeared, with a plaque that reads “Sit as long as you like”. There is no sign of who built it. Immortals pass it all day with a faint, guilty look, as if they ought to sit and cannot spare the time. A child is already on it, swinging both legs.

effects.log: You sit in silence. The bridge goes by like a river.

choices.text: Join the guilty crowd and walk on

effects.log: You promise yourself you will return. You do not.

choices.text: Leave a cushion on the bench

effects.log: The cushion is gone by evening. A new one, bright, has taken its place.

events.text: At the Ministry of Lights, the queue for new lamp-oil winds three times round the building. A cheerful clerk walks along it with a trolley of tea, and a notice that says: “Your turn will come, but not soon.” The woman ahead of you has been in the queue for nine years and has knitted a scarf.

choices.text: Join the queue with a book

effects.log: You read through half a library. The queue moves, in its fashion.
She gives you the scarf. It is far too long, and very warm.
You leave. The queue, you hear, is still there.

events.text: On Reed Lake the cutting of the reeds is a day of rest for no one and work for all. Skiffs drift in a line with long hooks and green sleeves. A chubby cutter hands you a hook and a hat, and says if you cut one you may keep a bundle for your roof, and if you cut none you may keep the hat.

choices.text: Cut a bundle for your roof

effects.log: The reeds smell of summer. Your roof is the lighter for it.
The hat is large and shady. You are comfortable.

choices.text: Cut two and give one away

effects.log: A passing skiff receives a bundle, with thanks.

events.text: The cloud-shepherd's yearly sale: bundles of cloud-wool, spun fine and grey, sold by the armful at the Pasture Quay. The wool is soft as breath and, when worn, keeps off the colder winds. A bundle costs two stones, though there is always a story to be told for a discount.

choices.text: Buy a bundle of cloud-wool (2 spirit stones)

effects.log: It becomes a scarf, then a coat, then a thing you wear for centuries.

choices.text: Offer a story for a discount

effects.log: The shepherd laughs and hands you a half bundle.

choices.text: Just feel the wool and move on

effects.log: The softness stays on your fingers for an hour.

events.text: The wind-miller of the High Quay is mending the sails of the mill, a hundred ells of grey cloth, by hand, in a gale. The wind, named Hollow Pell, is not in season, but a lesser breeze keeps pulling the cloth from the mender's fingers. A nearby child holds one end and looks proud and terrified.

effects.log: The three of you work till dusk. The mill has new sails.

choices.text: Whisper to the breeze to be still

effects.log: It sulks, but lets the cloth rest.
The mender thanks you with a mouthful of pins.

events.text: The Guild of Isle Trades holds its yearly meeting in a barn on a neutral isle. Cloud-shepherds, root-pruners, star-polishers, ferry-oilers: all in their working clothes, none in their finery. The agenda is long and the tea is short. A grey pruner asks you to second a motion about the price of rope.

effects.log: It passes, amid the groans of people who cannot afford rope. You are thanked and cursed.

choices.text: Ask what the motion actually is

effects.log: It takes an hour to explain. The answer is "more rope, less price".

choices.text: Offer tea to improve the mood

effects.log: The meeting is shorter by an hour. The rope price is decided in good humour.

events.text: A very young apprentice runs her master's stall at the market for the day, while the master sleeps behind the counter. She is selling jars of starlight at the wrong price, a stone each, and she does not know. A queue of cheerful immortals has formed. They know.

choices.text: Warn her quietly of the price

effects.log: She turns pink and fixes it. The queue sighs. The master snores on.

choices.text: Buy a jar at the wrong price

effects.log: A stone for a jar worth five. You will be paying for it in gratitude.
She learns, expensively. She comes out of it very wise.

events.text: The healer of sky beasts hangs a bell at the quay for every creature that gets well. There are, by now, thousands, and the quay rings like a field of tiny spoons in any wind. A newcomer has just been added: a very small bell, with a ribbon of green, for a cloud carp that recovered from a cold.

choices.text: Stand and listen to the bells

effects.log: There is a note in them you can almost name. You stay for an hour.

choices.text: Add a bell of your own for a lost pet

effects.log: It chimes next to the others. It is the sweetest one.
The bells ring after you. You carry them for a while.

events.text: A clerk of the Ministry of Registers has fallen asleep at the stamp. The pad is still wet, and the page beneath is a perfect set of marks, one hundred of them, side by side, as neat as stars. The clerk's head is on the desk. The Ministry is quiet. A bell will ring in an hour.

choices.text: Put a cushion under the clerk's head

effects.log: The clerk sleeps on. The stamp, you note, goes on stamping in the dream.

choices.text: Wake the clerk before the bell

effects.log: The clerk blinks, grateful and embarrassed, and finishes the page.
Your stamp is a little crooked. No one notices.

events.text: The tonic-seller's cart, which usually sits at the foot of the springs, has been moved to a spot beneath a cloud-pine. The seller says the cart wants a rest. There is a hand-lettered sign: “Today’s tonic is a nap”. A line of customers lies on the moss, eyes closed.

effects.log: You sleep deeply for an hour. You wake to the clink of the cart wheels.

choices.text: Buy a nap for a friend

effects.log: The seller hands you a leaf-wrapped dream, not for sale.

choices.text: Sit by the cart and keep watch

effects.log: No one is robbed. The sleepers murmur.

events.text: A small mailbox has been nailed to a post on the Edge, with a sign that reads “Letters to nobody”. It is half full. A cleaner, tidy and pale, empties it once a year and burns the letters on a grate at dusk. The smoke drifts upward, out of the cloud sea, where no one lives.

effects.log: You write a page. It is the most honest page you have written in years.
The smoke curls up in many colours. You stay till the last ember.
A letter pokes out of the slot as you pass. It does not seem to mind.

events.text: The Ministries keep a day on the calendar called the Slow Morning, on which no petition may be opened before noon. The corridors are quiet. Clerks sit at their desks with tea, staring at the same spot of light. A tiny paper flag on every door says: “Not yet.”

choices.text: Sit in the light with a clerk

effects.log: No one speaks. It is companionable and strange.
The Ministry without noise is a different building. You see its bones.
A neighbouring clerk clears their throat. You close it.

events.text: At the Hall of Precedence the clerks lunch in order of rank, which means a clerk of the sixth desk waits until the fifth has finished, and so on. A very junior clerk beside you has been waiting since morning and has begun to hum the order backward to keep up their spirits.

choices.text: Share your lunch with the junior clerk

effects.log: The clerk eats it in four bites and thanks you by promising to remember you.
You are, together, quite good. A passing senior clerk taps their foot.

choices.text: Remind them that rank is only order

effects.log: The clerk looks at you with new, dangerous clarity.

events.text: The forecast board at the Weather Window is a large slate marked with chalk, and today it reads: “Fair, with one cloud who has opinions.” People gather beneath it to see which cloud. It is a small, bitter, nearly black cumulus above the tea-house, and it is scowling at no one in particular.

effects.log: You hold a cup aloft. It rains, quietly, in the cup.

choices.text: Ask the forecaster what it is cross about

effects.log: "A lost kite," says the forecaster. "From a century ago."
The cloud rains on your umbrella only. You are flattered.

events.text: The ferry timetable of the Leeward Isle has not been changed in six hundred years, and it is wrong. A skiff arrives each dawn three hours before the posted time, and the whole isle has adjusted, with gravity, to this. A new clerk, innocent and brave, has proposed to correct the board.

effects.log: The board is repainted. The isle finds it slightly offensive and, later, reasonable.

choices.text: Say the board is a monument

effects.log: It is kept as it is. A second board is added beside it, with the true times.

choices.text: Take the dawn skiff and say nothing

effects.log: You arrive early, and in time for breakfast.

events.text: The Ministry of Gardens inspects the orchards once every sixty years, and today is the day. A very small inspector, wearing a hat with a feather, examines every tree with a magnifying glass. The owner follows at a respectful distance, glaring at the leaves as if urging them to behave.

choices.text: Help the owner polish the leaves

effects.log: The leaves shine like jade. The inspector declares it excessive and gives full marks.

choices.text: Distract the inspector with a question

effects.log: The inspector spends an hour on the history of grafting. The trees survive unharmed.

choices.text: Join the inspection as a bystander

effects.log: You learn more about peaches than you wished.

events.text: In the corner of a tea-house a sample tray has been set out: eight cups, none labelled, each only a mouthful. A sign says: “Choose the one you like the most, and we shall tell you what you are.” A crowd debates the meaning of this, and drinks on.

effects.log: The sign says you are "patient, with a weakness for shortcuts". You cannot argue.
The sign says you are "greedy, but honest". The crowd cheers.

choices.text: Ask what the tea-house itself is

effects.log: "Open," says the owner. "Mostly."

events.text: Behind the Hall of Precedence a back stair goes down to a low cellar, unlisted in any plan of the Ministry. Every clerk knows of it, every clerk uses it, and every clerk, asked, denies it. A faint smell of baking rises from the dark. Someone whispers: “Third step, avoid the creak.”

effects.log: There is a tiny bakery, run by two old clerks, who feed you a hot bun and ask you not to tell.

choices.text: Mention the stair to the Ministry

effects.log: The Ministry sighs and does nothing. The bakery gets a plaque.
You can smell cinnamon for a mile.

events.text: On the roof of the Ministry of Tribute, past the beehives, a chair has been placed at the edge. A thermos of tea and a cup stand on the rail, with a note: “For the next person who needs the sky.” The view is the whole fleet, a spread of tiny lights like spilled sugar.

effects.log: It is exactly warm. You look at the fleet for an hour.

choices.text: Leave a second cup for the next

effects.log: The cup is gone by evening, and the note has a second line.

choices.text: Write your own note on the rail

effects.log: It says only "Thank you." It is enough.

events.text: The Elder Minister of Seasons has been due to retire for three hundred years. Each time, the Ministry prepares a farewell banquet, and each time {npc} arrives, eats the banquet, and returns to the desk at dawn. The younger clerks have begun to bring {him} their questions instead of the Minister's. {He} asks you, plainly, whether it is time.
events.arc: The Elder Minister Who Would Not Retire

choices.text: Say a banquet is a fine thing to repeat

effects.log: {npc} laughs until {he} coughs. "Then I will stay for the next," {he} says.

choices.text: Say the young clerks need room

effects.log: {npc} is quiet, then nods slowly. "That is the first honest answer in a century."
Tea is accepted. The question is left to hang.

events.text: The young clerks have been quietly doing all the work, and {npc} knows it. {He} confesses to you, on the long balcony, that {he} does not know what {he} would be without the desk. There is a retirement garden on the Willow Isle, offered every spring. {He} has never once looked at the map.
events.arc: The Elder Minister Who Would Not Retire

choices.text: Offer to walk the garden with {him}

effects.log: You go together on a clear day. The willows move like slow thoughts.
It takes a decade. The clerk becomes, in time, the best Minister of Seasons in a thousand years.

choices.text: Tell {him} the desk will always be there

effects.log: {npc} looks at the desk as at a fond, tired creature.

events.text: {npc} retires to the willow garden and keeps a small bell on the gate. Any clerk with a question may ring it. They do, at first daily, then monthly, then at last just to say hello. Sometimes {he} answers with a poem, sometimes with a flask of tea passed over the wall. It is, {he} says, the most useful retirement a person could have.
events.arc: The Elder Minister Who Would Not Retire

choices.text: Ring the bell with a question

effects.log: The answer is wise, and short, and comes with tea.

choices.text: Plant a willow of your own beside the wall

effects.log: It grows slowly, and shades both gardens.

events.text: {npc} trains the clerk, hands over the seal, and stays on in a small chair beside the desk. The clerk, wise enough, never asks {him} to leave. At the next banquet, the farewell is for no one in particular, and everyone raises a cup to the chair. {He} tells you it is the finest retirement a person could wish: to keep the room and lose the weight.
events.arc: The Elder Minister Who Would Not Retire

choices.text: Raise your cup to the chair

effects.log: The whole hall rises to its feet. {npc} waves a hand and blushes.
Some honours are best left unwitnessed. You let this one be.

events.text: At the Jade Void gate sits a gatekeeper who has outlived four sect-masters and expects to outlive the fifth. {npc} sweeps the same step each morning, and the sect calls {him} the Fifth Pillar. {He} asks every visitor the same question, which is “Have you eaten?” and listens to the answer as if it mattered.
events.arc: The Gatekeeper Who Outlived Four Masters

choices.text: Say you have not, and sit on the step

effects.log: {npc} brings rice in a wooden bowl. It is the plainest and warmest meal in the Void.

choices.text: Say you have, and ask about the masters

effects.log: "Four," says {npc}. "All good. All gone. The step remains."

choices.text: Say you are in a hurry

effects.log: {npc} nods and wishes you a swift return. The wishing is somehow a rebuke.

events.text: The new sect-master, young and eager, wants to replace the old gate with a grander one, carved with the Void's history. {npc} is asked to approve. {He} says nothing, which is the form of refusal that sect-masters find hardest to answer. You are asked to deliver the plans and may speak your mind.
events.arc: The Gatekeeper Who Outlived Four Masters

effects.log: The sect-master listens to a tale of four predecessors who each stepped over this threshold.
The master brightens. {npc} stiffens, but accepts it with a bow.
{npc} takes the plans without looking and puts them under the bowl.

events.text: The old gate is kept, and a small stone is added beside it carved with the names of the four masters and a blank space. “For the fifth,” the young master says, and does not look at {npc}, who is looking hard at the sweeping broom. The blank is left a long time. It is a good reminder, and a gentle one.
events.arc: The Gatekeeper Who Outlived Four Masters

effects.log: It is a strange honour, to bow to a space. You find it appropriate.

choices.text: Bring {npc} an extra bowl of rice

effects.log: "Have you eaten?" {he} asks you gravely. "Yes," you say, and for once it is true.

events.text: The new gate goes up, grand and dark, carved in dragons and dates. It is admired for fifty years. Then one morning it is found to be cracked, and {npc}, without a word, goes back to sweeping the old step, which is still there beneath the new foundation. The sect begins to speak of the first gate as a legend.
events.arc: The Gatekeeper Who Outlived Four Masters

effects.log: The two of you sweep for an afternoon. The step is as clean as a bowl.

choices.text: Tell the sect-master about the crack

effects.log: The master laughs ruefully and orders it left alone. Some mistakes are monuments.

events.text: Deep in the archive lives {npc}, who wrote one slim book six centuries ago and has been commenting on it ever since. The commentary is now four hundred volumes, the commentary on the commentary has reached ninety, and {he} is writing a note on a footnote. {He} welcomes you as a possible fresh pair of eyes.
events.arc: The Scholar Who Commented on Their Own Commentary

choices.text: Offer to read the first volume

effects.log: The first book is lovely, brief and sharp. {npc} is moved that someone has gone back to it.

choices.text: Ask why {he} does not just revise the original

effects.log: "Because it was true when I wrote it," {he} says, "and a true thing should be argued with, not changed."
The volumes have a way of leaning toward visitors. You are sensible.

events.text: {npc} asks you a favour: to pick one volume from the whole pile and tell {him} honestly where the argument has gone wrong. {He} has no one else who will say. The task takes you weeks. In volume two hundred and six, you find a small error that has been quietly carried through every volume since.
events.arc: The Scholar Who Commented on Their Own Commentary

effects.log: {npc} sits silent for a long hour. Then {he} laughs, and says it is the best news of the century.

choices.text: Hint at it gently over tea

effects.log: {npc} understands at once and goes pale, then thoughtful, then pleased.
The error goes on, harmlessly, through ninety volumes more.

events.text: {npc} begins an entirely new commentary on the error: one volume, a hundred pages, the shortest in years. It is, you realise, a love letter to being wrong. When it is bound, {he} dedicates it to you, in small gold characters, and the archive displays it in the front case. Scholars come to read it just for the preface.
events.arc: The Scholar Who Commented on Their Own Commentary

choices.text: Read the preface aloud in the hall

effects.log: The hall goes quiet. A dozen scholars find themselves nodding.
{He} insists. It stays.

events.text: You say nothing and the error goes on. Years later {npc} finds it by chance, in the last volume, and is delighted and wounded in equal measure. {He} sends you a note: “Why did you not tell me?” You have no good answer. The note sits on your desk, folded, for a century, and you answer it at last in person.
events.arc: The Scholar Who Commented on Their Own Commentary

effects.log: {He} waves it away. "The error was the best part," {he} says. It is a kind lie.

choices.text: Send the answer in a small book

effects.log: It is eleven pages. It is the first book you have ever written, and you hand it over with shaking hands.

events.text: A guest arrives at the Tea Pavilion without a card: tall, plain-coated, with a quiet voice and the unmistakable weight of a being from the Divine Realm. {npc} introduces {him}self only as “a traveller”, and asks for the oldest tea you have. The pavilion goes quiet. Even the kettle seems to stand a little straighter.
events.arc: The God Who Came to Tea Unannounced

choices.text: Serve the oldest tea without remark

effects.log: The tea is poured. The traveller drinks, and a crease of recognition crosses {his} face.

choices.text: Ask politely where the traveller is from

effects.log: "Far," says {npc}, with a smile. "And not far at all."
The traveller notices your bow and returns it, to everyone's alarm.

events.text: The traveller stays three days, asking small questions: how the isles are moored, what the children sing, where the best tea is grown. At last {he} says that the Divine Realm has forgotten how it feels to be a guest. {He} asks if you will teach {him} a custom of the Upper Realm, so that {he} can take something home.
events.arc: The God Who Came to Tea Unannounced

choices.text: Teach {him} how to share a pot of tea

effects.log: It is the simplest custom you know. {npc} learns to pour for another before pouring for {him}self.
The traveller sits in the light until noon without a word, and is changed.

choices.text: Say you have no customs worth giving

effects.log: {npc} looks at you gravely. "That is the first thing you have said that is false," {he} says.

events.text: The traveller leaves at dawn, and at midday a small, bright cup appears on the pavilion shelf that was not there before. It is of a white that does not belong to any kiln of the Upper Realm. Inside it, a message in light: “A cup, given back.” The pavilion treats it as a holy thing, and does not use it.
events.arc: The God Who Came to Tea Unannounced

effects.log: The tea in it tastes of the first day of the sky. It never happens again.

choices.text: Leave the cup on the shelf for guests

effects.log: It is admired by thousands, drunk from by no one, and loved.

events.text: The traveller leaves a bow and a promise to return, and the Slow Morning, it is told in later centuries, spreads upward into the Divine courts, where a god is rumoured to sit each year in the light until noon, saying nothing, with a bowl of tea. The pavilion keeps a chair for the traveller. It is never sat in, and is dusted daily.
events.arc: The God Who Came to Tea Unannounced

choices.text: Sit in the chair, once, as a gift to it

effects.log: The chair is warm. The room is very quiet.
You stand beside it in respect, and the afternoon is long and kind.

events.text: A gift has arrived from the Divine Realm for the Jade Court: a box of white wood, bound with a ribbon of dusk, with no lid, no hinge and no seam. {npc}, the Court's keeper of gifts, has stared at it for a year. Etiquette demands that it be opened in the giver's presence. The giver sent no word of when to come.
events.arc: The Gift from the Divine Realm Nobody Could Open

choices.text: Offer to sit with {npc} and the box

effects.log: You sit for an afternoon. The box is silent and, you feel, patient.

choices.text: Suggest sending a letter of thanks regardless

effects.log: {npc} thinks it pious, and slightly cowardly, and agrees.
{npc} looks horrified. The idea is withdrawn at once.

events.text: On the anniversary of its arrival, the box hums. The ribbon of dusk loosens by a knot. {npc} sends for you, trembling. “It is listening,” {he} says. “I think it was waiting for someone to sit beside it that did not want anything.” Nothing else happens. But the hum deepens.
events.arc: The Gift from the Divine Realm Nobody Could Open

effects.log: You do not ask. You do not want. By dawn the ribbon has come undone.

choices.text: Ask the box what it contains

effects.log: The hum falters. The knot tightens. You have asked too soon.
By the time one arrives, the box is silent. The Minister is disappointed in you.

events.text: The box opens like a flower at dawn. Inside is a single seed, white, no larger than a pea, with a note in unreadable script. {npc} plants it in the Court garden, in a spot that is no one's. Within the year a tree stands there that bears no fruit, only shade. People come from every faction to sit under it, and no one quarrels there.
events.arc: The Gift from the Divine Realm Nobody Could Open

effects.log: It is the quietest place in the Court. You think you can hear the box's hum in the branches.

choices.text: Water the tree on dry days

effects.log: You become, without trying, the tree's gardener. It is a gentle post.

events.text: The box tightens and goes cold. {npc} orders it placed in the vault, and written down as Unopened. Years pass, and each year on the anniversary you visit the vault and sit a while beside it. It does not hum. But the ribbon, you notice one year, is a little looser. You keep visiting. The box, you decide, is a patient friend.
events.arc: The Gift from the Divine Realm Nobody Could Open

effects.log: The knot loosens by a thread a decade. You have time.

choices.text: Leave a small gift beside it

effects.log: A cup of tea, left cold. The next year it is gone, and the box is humming.

events.text: A lesser god of orchards has come up from the Divine Realm to inspect the peach terraces of the Upper Realm, and {npc} is the most polite and most terrifying visitor the orchard-keepers have ever hosted. {He} counts peaches silently, bowing to each tree. The keepers hover behind, whispering. {He} turns and asks you whether the fruit is meant to be eaten.
events.arc: The Divine Guest Who Counted the Peaches

choices.text: Say yes, of course, with joy

effects.log: {npc} looks at the peach in {his} hand with mild astonishment. "Of course," {he} says, and takes a bite.

choices.text: Say it is meant to be admired first

effects.log: "Then I have done it right," says {npc}, and puts the peach back.

choices.text: Say you are only a visitor yourself

effects.log: {npc} nods. "We are both guests, then."

events.text: The god stays for the harvest. {He} cannot work the baskets, being unused to hands, but {he} sits among the pickers and listens to their songs. One evening {he} asks you to teach {him} a verse. The pickers go quiet. No one has ever taught a god a harvest song. The verse is only four lines.
events.arc: The Divine Guest Who Counted the Peaches

effects.log: {npc} sings them back flat. The pickers gasp, then laugh, then join in.

choices.text: Ask a picker to teach it instead

effects.log: The oldest picker does it, red-faced, in a whisper. It is the verse the orchard remembers.

choices.text: Say a god needs no songs

effects.log: {npc} says nothing. The next evening there is no singing.

events.text: The god leaves at harvest's end, and the next spring the peaches are twice as sweet. No one can say why. A small shrine appears on the terraces, built by the pickers without a word to anyone, no larger than a lantern. Inside it is a peach pit and four lines of a song. You leave a flower there every year.
events.arc: The Divine Guest Who Counted the Peaches

choices.text: Bring a flower to the shrine each spring

effects.log: It is a quiet pilgrimage. Others begin to join.

choices.text: Help the pickers keep the shrine

effects.log: It is a modest work. The shrine is never grand, which is correct.

events.text: The god leaves in silence and the orchard is just an orchard. The keepers are relieved, then uneasy, as if they had failed a test they did not understand. A year later a basket of divine peaches arrives at the gate with no note. They are eaten in secret, quickly, and with gratitude. The next year there is a basket again.
events.arc: The Divine Guest Who Counted the Peaches

choices.text: Ask the keepers what the basket means

effects.log: "A thank-you," they say. "And an apology." They do not say for what.

choices.text: Share a peach with a neighbour

effects.log: You carry it up the lane. The neighbour weeps, and does not explain.

events.text: Every ninth year the Stone Isle holds the Festival of the Returned Pebble, in which every resident brings a pebble they have kept for nine years and drops it off the edge. {npc}, the festival-master, has a list of who has brought one. {He} hands you a pebble from a bowl, a gift to be kept for the next festival.
events.arc: The Festival of the Returned Pebble

choices.text: Accept the pebble and promise to keep it

effects.log: It is warm and smooth. You tuck it into a sleeve like a small, serious thing.

choices.text: Ask what the pebble is for

effects.log: "To remember a nine years," says {npc}. "And then to forget them gracefully."
{npc} puts the pebble back in the bowl. It clicks like a small door closing.

events.text: Nine years on, you arrive at the Stone Isle with your pebble. It has been through a great deal. You tried to throw it away twice. You have slept with it, and lost it, and found it again. At the edge, {npc} asks what the pebble meant. The line behind you is patient and watching.
events.arc: The Festival of the Returned Pebble

choices.text: Say it was a promise you kept

effects.log: You drop it. It falls for a long time and makes no sound. The crowd claps once.

choices.text: Say you do not know yet

effects.log: {npc} nods. "Then keep it another nine," {he} says. You do.

choices.text: Say it was only a pebble

effects.log: The line chuckles. {npc} looks quietly pleased, as though that were the right answer too.

events.text: The pebbles fall in a long silver rain, and the Stone Isle goes quiet. {npc} turns to you at the end and presses a new pebble into your palm, unasked. “For the next nine,” {he} says. You realise, holding it, that you will be back. The festival is a way of making sure you do.
events.arc: The Festival of the Returned Pebble

effects.log: It is lighter than the last, and warmer.

choices.text: Offer to help organise the next festival

effects.log: {npc} is moved. You are added to the list.

events.text: You keep the pebble another nine years, and then nine more. By the third festival it has become something close to a friend: smooth, silent, dependable. {npc} has grown old, and the new festival-master is quiet and young and asks what the pebble was. You tell them, and they say it is the longest answer they have heard.
events.arc: The Festival of the Returned Pebble

choices.text: Keep it for the rest of your life

effects.log: It travels with you, a small grey companion, to every place you go.

choices.text: Drop it at last and watch it fall

effects.log: It falls silently. You feel, strangely, nothing and everything.

events.text: The Lantern Isle is famous for its lights, so its great festival is the one night each century when every lamp is put out. {npc}, the lamp-warden, goes from door to door with a snuffer and a gentle apology. {He} asks you to help put out the lanterns of the long street, and says the dark is a guest that visits seldom.
events.arc: The Festival of the Unlit Night

choices.text: Help put out the lamps one by one

effects.log: The street goes dark in a long soft wave. Stars come out above you, startled.

choices.text: Ask why the dark is invited

effects.log: "Because we have forgotten what the lamps are for," says {npc}.

choices.text: Keep one small lamp lit in your sleeve

effects.log: It glows, small and selfish. {npc} says nothing, which is generous.

events.text: In the dark, the isle behaves differently. Neighbours who never spoke begin to talk across fences. Someone plays a flute badly and everyone listens. Then the voice of a child, lost, drifts up the street. {npc} calls for a light, and for the first time in a century cannot decide whether to allow one.
events.arc: The Festival of the Unlit Night

choices.text: Light your one small lamp and lead the child home

effects.log: The lamp is the only light in the street. It is enough. The festival forgives you.

choices.text: Call out to the child in the dark

effects.log: Voices answer from the doors, and the child follows them home.
The child is found by a neighbour. The festival continues, a little shaken.

events.text: The festival ends at dawn with the first lamp relit by the child you led home. The street blazes, and the warden weeps openly. A new custom is born: the first lamp, every century, is lit by a lost child, or someone who was once lost. You are given a small brass lamp of your own to keep.
events.arc: The Festival of the Unlit Night

choices.text: Keep the brass lamp lit all your life

effects.log: It burns with a steady, homely glow. You are always found.

choices.text: Give the brass lamp to the next lost child

effects.log: It burns in a stranger's window for a thousand years.

events.text: The child is led home by voices, and in the dawn a hundred neighbours carry the child's name up and down the street, delighted, proud. The warden decides the festival will begin with a roll-call of lost things found, rather than lamps put out. You are asked to read the first name, and it is the child's.
events.arc: The Festival of the Unlit Night

choices.text: Read the name aloud to the whole street

effects.log: The street cheers. The child hides behind a lantern.
The warden does so with a thick voice. It is the gentlest dawn in memory.

events.text: Once in a lifetime the Hollow Isle holds the Great Sleep, a festival in which the entire population lies down at noon and wakes at dusk. Gates are left open, kettles are left unlit, and the only guard is a lazy cat. {npc}, the festival-organiser, asks you to be the one who stays awake and tends the quiet.
events.arc: The Isle That Slept for a Festival

effects.log: You sit at the crossroads while the isle breathes around you. The cat nods in approval.

choices.text: Politely refuse and join the sleep

effects.log: You sleep so deeply you dream of clouds. {npc} tucks a blanket over you.
You return to find the festival over, and a charming painted card on your pillow.

events.text: At the quietest hour, a ferry arrives with a traveller who needs the Hollow Isle's healer, urgently. The healer is asleep. So is the isle. {npc} left strict instructions that no one is to be woken. You are the only waking person, and you hold both the rule and the traveller in your hands.
events.arc: The Isle That Slept for a Festival

effects.log: The healer rises, grumbling and kind, and the traveller is saved. {npc} forgives you in the morning.

choices.text: Tend the traveller yourself till dusk

effects.log: You are no healer, but you are steady. The traveller lives, and the festival stays whole.

choices.text: Keep to the rule and wait

effects.log: The traveller waits, and the waiting is not easy. You will think of it for years.

events.text: The healer wakes, works, and returns to sleep within the hour, an astonishing performance that the isle claims later to have dreamed. {npc} tells you the festival will never be the same, and means it as a compliment. A new line is added to the custom: “One person stays awake, and one person may be woken.”
events.arc: The Isle That Slept for a Festival

choices.text: Accept the new custom with pride

effects.log: It is a small rule, wise and kind, and it is partly yours.

choices.text: Return the next Great Sleep as the watch

effects.log: The cat remembers you. It takes the seat beside you.

events.text: You tend the traveller till dusk, and when the isle wakes the traveller is sitting up, weak and smiling. {npc} never says a word about the rule. Instead the isle sends you a stack of folded blankets, one for each of its households, with notes: “For the one who stayed awake.” You keep them for centuries, and they are never quite cold.
events.arc: The Isle That Slept for a Festival

choices.text: Use the blankets on the coldest nights

effects.log: They hold the warmth of an isle that trusted you.

choices.text: Pass them on to those in need

effects.log: They go to a dozen strangers. Each sends a note.

events.text: The Small Willow Isle has strained at its moorings for a hundred years, the ropes humming each night with a note of longing. {npc}, its oldest resident, tells you the isle wants to go somewhere. Not far, not permanently. Just to see the other side of the fleet. The Steersman Ohwa has heard the rumour and does not like it.
events.arc: The Isle That Wanted to Drift Away

effects.log: The ropes tremble beneath your hand. They do seem to be pulling toward something.

choices.text: Ask the Steersman what harm it could do

effects.log: "It would leave a gap," says the Steersman, "and gaps get filled by weather."

choices.text: Say isles do not want things

effects.log: {npc} gives you a very long look and says, "Then you have never moored one."

events.text: The ropes snap one stormy night. The Small Willow Isle drifts, trailing a single frayed line, gently out of the fleet. People run to the edge. The Steersman rings the alarm. {npc} stands calmly at the willow with a pot of tea and says the isle will come back when it has seen what it needs to see. Everyone looks at you.
events.arc: The Isle That Wanted to Drift Away

choices.text: Fly out and escort the isle

effects.log: You ride beside it for three days. It drifts happily, a child out of its lesson.

choices.text: Help the Steersman cast a towline

effects.log: The line holds. The isle, hauled back, sulks for a week.

choices.text: Tell the residents to stay calm

effects.log: It is the right thing to say, and nothing more. The isle drifts on.

events.text: The isle travels to the far edge of the fleet, rests there for a season, and returns on its own, trailing a long line of mist that smells of other weathers. The ropes are mended with a new knot, loose and wide, that lets the isle swing a little further. The Steersman permits it with a sigh. Everyone says it is the happiest isle in the sky.
events.arc: The Isle That Wanted to Drift Away

choices.text: Visit the isle in its new mooring

effects.log: The willow sways. A little further out, the isle says nothing and means it.

choices.text: Teach the new knot to other isles

effects.log: It spreads through the fleet in a century. Isles sleep better.

events.text: The towline brings the isle home. It is moored again with the old knots and sits stiff and silent for years. {npc} says it is mourning, and the willows droop. A few residents begin to leave quietly for other isles. By the second century the Small Willow Isle is half empty, and its ropes no longer hum. The Steersman, passing, lowers a cap.
events.arc: The Isle That Wanted to Drift Away

choices.text: Stay on the isle and keep it company

effects.log: You are one of the last. The willows seem to lean closer.

choices.text: Argue for a looser mooring at the next Fleet Assembly

effects.log: The Assembly considers it, with groans. The matter is tabled for a century.

events.text: Two small isles, the Reed and the Heron, have shared a mooring for a thousand years. Lately they have begun to drift a little apart each night, and back each morning, in a kind of slow quarrel. {npc}, who lives on the narrow strip of cloud between them, asks if you can find out what is wrong.
events.arc: The Two Small Isles That Argued by Drifting

effects.log: The Reed folk say the Heron are loud. They say it very quietly.
The Heron folk say the Reed are dull. They say it very loudly.

choices.text: Sit with {npc} on the strip and listen

effects.log: {npc} says nothing is wrong that tea cannot discuss.

events.text: You come to a plain truth: the Reed folk are tired of the Herons' dawn songs, and the Herons are tired of the Reeds' silence at supper. Neither wants to say it. Each night the isles pull slightly apart, as if apologising. {npc} suggests a dinner on the strip between them. “Neutral ground,” {he} says, “where nobody has to be the first to speak.”
events.arc: The Two Small Isles That Argued by Drifting

choices.text: Arrange a dinner on the strip

effects.log: It takes three months of notes. The tables are laid over cloud, and both isles come.

choices.text: Write each isle a letter of the other's complaint

effects.log: Both read, flush and write back. The letters become a very fine correspondence.

choices.text: Tell them to settle it themselves

effects.log: They try, and drift further. {npc} sighs.

events.text: The dinner is long, funny and difficult. By the third course the Herons are singing a lullaby to the Reed children, and the Reeds are telling stories from their quiet suppers. The isles do not drift apart again. They drift together, a little, each night, like two people leaning into a conversation. {npc} claims the credit modestly.
events.arc: The Two Small Isles That Argued by Drifting

choices.text: Stay to the end of the dinner

effects.log: It ends at dawn with a chorus. The strip of cloud between them is renamed Supper.
The first Supper Day is held the following spring.

events.text: The letters pass back and forth for a hundred years, each isle courteous and exact. The correspondence is gathered into a book and read aloud on festival nights. The isles never fully reconcile, but they are never really apart, and {npc} keeps the strip between them swept and the post kept open.
events.arc: The Two Small Isles That Argued by Drifting

choices.text: Read a letter of the book aloud

effects.log: The audience laughs at the right places and is quiet at the others.

choices.text: Add a letter of your own

effects.log: It is a small one. The book makes room.

events.text: A rogue with no faction, no isle and no luck at the stalls, {npc} saves one spirit stone every ten years and keeps the lot in a clay jar under a floorboard. {He} has been doing it for six hundred years. {He} lets you hold the jar. It is surprisingly heavy and very warm. “It is not about the stones,” {npc} says. “It is about the decade.”
events.arc: The Rogue Who Saved a Stone a Decade

choices.text: Weigh the jar and say it is a fine sum

effects.log: "It is," {npc} says. "And it is nothing." {He} smiles at the paradox.

choices.text: Ask what the saving is for

effects.log: "A cup of tea," says {npc}, "on the day I stop."

choices.text: Hand the jar back and say nothing

effects.log: It is returned to its floorboard with care.

events.text: The market raises the licence fee for rogue stalls by twenty stones. It is the end of {npc}'s little trade in tea-leaves. {He} has the sum. It is exactly twenty stones: the jar, to the last coin. {He} does not weep. {He} asks, mildly, whether you think the decade was worth it.
events.arc: The Rogue Who Saved a Stone a Decade

choices.text: Say the decade was the point, not the sum

effects.log: {npc} looks at the jar and nods. "That is what I thought," {he} says, but {his} voice shakes.

choices.text: Offer to cover half the fee (10 spirit stones)

effects.log: {npc} refuses at first, and then accepts, on the condition of a share in the stall.

choices.text: Say rules are unfair, and leave

effects.log: {npc} sets the jar on the table. "They are," {he} says. "And here I am."

events.text: {npc} pays the fee from the jar, keeps the stall, and starts again with one stone in a new clay pot. “Six hundred years,” {he} says, “and I have learned to like beginning.” On the stall you notice a little sign: “Rogues welcome. Take what you need, leave what you can.” It is a different kind of saving.
events.arc: The Rogue Who Saved a Stone a Decade

choices.text: Leave a stone in the new pot

effects.log: The pot rings. {npc} pretends not to see, and nods once.

choices.text: Buy tea and sit a while

effects.log: It is the best tea of the day, and the cheapest.

events.text: With your ten stones the fee is paid and the jar is kept. The stall becomes a partnership: {npc} makes the tea, you carry the stock. Over the century the two of you earn the licence back many times over. In the end {npc} drinks the long-promised cup of tea beside you, and pours the last stone into the jar for the next rogue who needs it.
events.arc: The Rogue Who Saved a Stone a Decade

choices.text: Keep the jar for the next rogue

effects.log: It sits on your shelf, warm, waiting for the right hands.

choices.text: Leave the jar under the floorboard as it was

effects.log: The floorboard creaks happily. The jar waits.

events.text: At the Low Market, rogues who cannot borrow from any guild have made their own: a circle of twelve who each put in one stone a month, and each month one member takes the whole pot. {npc} runs it from a stool under a lamp. {He} invites you to sit in, on the grounds that rogues should help one another, and because the twelfth place is empty.
events.arc: The Rogues' Lending Circle

choices.text: Join the circle with one stone (1 spirit stone)

effects.log: The circle welcomes you with twelve nods. The pot is passed around with ceremony.

choices.text: Sit in as a guest and listen

effects.log: It is a kind of prayer. You learn names and troubles.

choices.text: Say you have no stones to spare

effects.log: {npc} nods and slides over a cup of tea. "Come back when you do," {he} says.

events.text: One month, the pot is due to a member who has secretly lost a job at the market. The member needs it more than anyone. Another, though, has a child to bury, and needs it as badly. The circle has never faced such a double claim. {npc} looks to the whole circle, and then to you, the newest member.
events.arc: The Rogues' Lending Circle

effects.log: The circle rumbles, then agrees. Each takes half, and each is grateful.

choices.text: Offer to give up your own turn

effects.log: A silence falls. Then the circle declines your offer, and insists you take it anyway, next month.

choices.text: Say the order is the order

effects.log: The rule holds. Nobody holds your eye for a month.

events.text: The circle splits the pot, and by the next month it has become its own small law: when two need, the pot is halved. {npc} writes it on the back of a tea-box and hangs it on the lamp. Rogues of other markets hear of it and start circles of their own. Within a century there are hundreds, tied by a thread of coin and trust.
events.arc: The Rogues' Lending Circle

choices.text: Help set up a new circle

effects.log: You take a stool in a stranger's market. It is a first stone in a large wall.
The lamp burns low. Twelve faces glow around it.

events.text: You give up your turn, and the circle, scandalised, makes you take it next month with interest. It is a strange sort of lesson. {npc} says wryly that a lending circle exists to teach rogues to take as well as give. You learn it slowly, and badly, and it does you good. By the year's end you are no richer, but you have eleven friends.
events.arc: The Rogues' Lending Circle

effects.log: The twelve of you take over a corner of the market. It is loud and generous.

choices.text: Quietly add another stone to the pot

effects.log: It is noticed. No one says a word.

events.text: At the back of the Silver Tea-House a rogue named in the books only as “the guest” has been washing dishes since the evening they could not pay their bill. It was a bowl of noodles and a pot of tea, ten coppers' worth, long ago. {npc}, the owner, has never given a date for the debt to end. The guest has stopped asking. You are served tea in a cracked cup.
events.arc: The Cook Who Worked Off a Dinner for a Century

choices.text: Ask the guest about the debt

effects.log: The guest shrugs. "It was good noodles," they say, and go on washing.
"When they ask," says {npc}. {He} says no more.

choices.text: Drink your tea and say nothing

effects.log: The cup is cracked, but warm. The dishes clink behind you.

events.text: One day you realise the arrangement is not what it seems: the guest could leave at any hour, and {npc} would let them go, but neither will say it. The guest has become the best cook on the street. {npc} has become unable to run the tea-house without them. The debt is a way of belonging that neither can name.
events.arc: The Cook Who Worked Off a Dinner for a Century

effects.log: You say what you have noticed. The guest is silent for a long time, then says, "I know."
{npc} goes pale. "I have been a coward," {he} says. "For a century."
The dishes keep clinking. The century goes on.

events.text: The guest asks to be released, and is, with a handshake and a small, strong tea. Then, without a pause, they ask for a job. {npc} laughs until {he} cries. The guest is made a partner, and a sign goes up: “The Guest’s Noodles”. The long debt is framed in the kitchen, stamped Paid, with a thumbprint of flour.
events.arc: The Cook Who Worked Off a Dinner for a Century

choices.text: Eat the first bowl of Guest's Noodles

effects.log: It is better than you remembered, and cost ten coppers.

choices.text: Frame a tiny note for the kitchen wall

effects.log: It says only "Thank you for the tea." It hangs there for centuries.

events.text: {npc} admits the truth to the guest, who stays anyway. The tea-house goes on exactly as before, but with a different air, and the dishes are washed with a lighter hand. The debt is never mentioned again. The cracked cup is kept for the guest alone. On festival days {npc} fills it first, and the guest drinks it, and neither says a word.
events.arc: The Cook Who Worked Off a Dinner for a Century

choices.text: Leave a good cup as a gift

effects.log: It sits beside the cracked one. The guest uses both.

choices.text: Bow to them both on your way out

effects.log: Neither returns it. Both smile.

events.text: A rogue ferryman, dying, has left a debt of seven stones owed to the Quay Guild to a child of nine who has no isle, no faction and one pair of shoes. {npc}, the guild's clerk, stands uneasy in the rain with the paper. {He} says the Guild's rules require the debt to pass, but the heart does not require it. The child looks at you.
events.arc: The Toll Left to a Child

choices.text: Ask {npc} what a kind clerk might do

effects.log: "Find a rule that forgives," says {npc}, "if there is one." {He} begins to look.

choices.text: Take the child to a warm tea-house

effects.log: The child eats three buns and says nothing. It is the best medicine.

choices.text: Tell the clerk rules are rules

effects.log: {npc} does not answer. The child watches you with grave eyes.

events.text: {npc} finds a rule: a debt owed by an orphan may be worked off in Guild service. It is not forgiveness. It is a place in the Guild for the child, with a bed and a bowl. The child would be an apprentice at a trade the child does not love. {He} asks you whether the child should accept.
events.arc: The Toll Left to a Child

choices.text: Say yes, a roof is a roof

effects.log: The child agrees. The Guild is surprised by how much it likes having a child about.

choices.text: Offer to pay down the debt (3 spirit stones)

effects.log: It is a start. The Guild, shamed, forgives the rest.

choices.text: Ask the child what the child wants

effects.log: The child wants to see a whale. {npc} blinks. That, at least, can be arranged.

events.text: The child grows up in the Guild, learning knots and tides. At forty, the child is the Quay's best harbour-hand, and on the day the old ferryman's skiff is finally retired, the child rows it out one last time at dusk with {npc} and you aboard. Nobody speaks. It is a funeral and a blessing.
events.arc: The Toll Left to a Child

effects.log: The skiff glides over the dark clouds. The Quay lights come on behind you.

choices.text: Say a few words for the ferryman

effects.log: You say very little. It is enough, and long remembered.

events.text: The debt is forgiven, with a note in the Guild's books that no such debt shall pass to a child again. It is the first new rule of the Guild in three centuries and the shortest. The child receives a pair of boots from {npc}, and a small, brass whistle from you. Years later the whistle rings out over the Quay at the start of a long day, in a grown voice.
events.arc: The Toll Left to a Child

choices.text: Listen for the whistle each morning

effects.log: It is a small happiness. It never stops.

choices.text: Tell {npc} the new rule is a good one

effects.log: {He} bows. "It was only a line," {he} says. "But it was the right line."

events.text: In a low town on the edge of the Demon Realm, {npc} keeps a barbershop with one chair and a mirror that does not lie. Customers from both realms sit there and are shaved, trimmed, braided and told the truth. {He} says it is the only honest business on the border. You are invited to take the chair for a trim.
events.arc: The Barber of the Border Town

effects.log: The mirror shows you plainly. You are a little older than you thought, and a little kinder.

choices.text: Ask the barber what the mirror says about the town

effects.log: "That it is tired," says {npc}, "and not at all unhappy."

choices.text: Say you like your hair as it is

effects.log: {npc} shrugs. "Everyone does, until they see it."

events.text: A young soldier of the Demon Realm comes in nervous, hair matted from the road, and asks for a cut that will make {him} look like a captain. {npc} says that cannot be done. The soldier looks to you, a stranger, for some reason. “Tell me honestly,” {he} asks, “do I look like a captain?”
events.arc: The Barber of the Border Town

effects.log: You say the soldier looks tired, honest and reliable. The soldier goes quiet, then sits straighter.

choices.text: Say the haircut makes the captain

effects.log: {npc} gives you a thin look, but allows it. The soldier leaves cheered.
The soldier laughs and sits for a plain trim. {npc} nods approvingly.

events.text: Years later a captain walks into the barbershop in a worn coat and sits in the chair without a word. The mirror shows a tired, honest, reliable face. It is the soldier. “I came back for the same cut,” the captain says. {npc} laughs and gets out the scissors. You watch from the window, tea in hand, and feel part of something small and complete.
events.arc: The Barber of the Border Town

effects.log: The captain remembers you, a stranger, and bows. It is a good morning.
Some reunions are better as a view through glass.

events.text: The soldier leaves cheered and oddly empty. The next year the barber hears the soldier has taken a post in the south, still wearing the cut. {npc} says nothing about it, but trims a little slower for the rest of the season. You wonder, privately, whether kindness and truth are as far apart as they seem.
events.arc: The Barber of the Border Town

choices.text: Say a good word for the soldier to the barber

effects.log: "They will be fine," {npc} says, and means it, a little.

choices.text: Ask for a cut yourself, honest this time

effects.log: The mirror shows a plain, honest face. It will do.

events.text: A tiny school on the border takes children from both sides, and {npc}, the schoolmaster, has been told by both sides that it is a mistake. The classroom has a line painted down the middle of the floor. Children sit on whichever side they like, and in practice move freely. {He} invites you to give a morning lesson on whatever you know best.
events.arc: The School at the Edge of the Demon Realm

effects.log: The children are rapt. They ask impossible questions and are delighted by the answers.
They learn to pour for each other. The line down the floor is ignored for an hour.

choices.text: Sit at the back and listen

effects.log: {npc} teaches a lesson on rivers. The children sing the names.

events.text: A letter arrives from both sides: the school is to be separated into two. The Court has demanded one half, and a Demon Realm elder the other. The letters are polite and clear. {npc} reads them twice and puts them in a drawer. {He} says no one has yet asked the children what they think.
events.arc: The School at the Edge of the Demon Realm

effects.log: They draw pictures. In every picture, the line on the floor is gone.

choices.text: Offer to speak to the Court and the elder

effects.log: It takes a season of tea and persuasion. Both listen.
{npc} nods. The school waits.

events.text: The children's pictures are sent to both letter-writers, framed. The Court and the elder, ashamed, withdraw the demand without apology and send a gift of chalk. {npc} accepts the chalk, and on the floor, where the line was painted, the children draw a wavy new one, and cross it constantly. The school is never threatened again.
events.arc: The School at the Edge of the Demon Realm

choices.text: Draw something on the floor with them

effects.log: You draw a cloud. It is bad. They treasure it.

choices.text: Frame one of the pictures for yourself

effects.log: It hangs on your wall for a thousand years, full of children and color.

events.text: You speak to the Court and the elder, and both listen. The school is allowed to stay as it is, though it is renamed, on paper, the School of the Neutral Zone, which no child ever says. {npc} thanks you, and cooks a pot of black-bean broth. The children eat it from the same bowl. It is not a victory. It is a Tuesday.
events.arc: The School at the Edge of the Demon Realm

effects.log: The broth is thick and warm. The line on the floor fades.

choices.text: Teach one more lesson before you go

effects.log: It is about leaving gracefully. The children are not impressed.

events.text: A low wall runs around the Demon Realm border town, built to keep out wind and the wrong kind of rumour. {npc} mends it daily with clay, stone and moss, working westward from the gate. By the time {he} has gone all the way round, the first stretch has crumbled again. {He} calls it the Long Job, and does not complain.
events.arc: The Wall-Mender of the Border Town

effects.log: You work a morning. The clay is cold, and the wall is warm in the sun.

choices.text: Ask {npc} why mend what will crumble

effects.log: "Because it is mended while I mend it," says {npc}. It is a fair answer.
The wall grows a hand's breadth taller while you rest.

events.text: A heavy rain begins to wash out a stretch of the wall near the market. The town shrugs, as it always does, but {npc} is out in the downpour with a bucket. {He} is no longer young. A group of soldiers from the Demon Realm and a group of Court merchants stand under the same awning, watching, saying nothing.
events.arc: The Wall-Mender of the Border Town

effects.log: You bail clay in the downpour. After a while the soldiers join, and then the merchants.

choices.text: Shout to the awning for help

effects.log: They look at each other. Then they come out in a clump, grumbling, and work.

choices.text: Wait for the rain to stop

effects.log: The wall washes out. {npc} mends it, alone, over a week.

events.text: The wall holds that night, patched by soldiers and merchants and one wet stranger. At dawn, there is a strange, brave quiet in the town, and a communal pot of broth on the gate. {npc} sits against the wall, mud to the knees. “I have mended it two thousand times,” {he} says. “Tonight it was done by a crowd. It felt different.”
events.arc: The Wall-Mender of the Border Town

effects.log: You eat broth together. The wall is warm behind you.

choices.text: Say the wall is a good one

effects.log: "It will fall again," says {npc}, delighted. "That is what makes it good."

events.text: The merchants and soldiers join forces and shout at the awning for more helpers, and by morning the whole town is bailing. {npc} is a cheerful ghost at the edge, directing from a chair. The wall holds. It is the only time anyone remembers the town acting as one body, and it has never repeated, though the chair, you notice, stays at the gate.
events.arc: The Wall-Mender of the Border Town

choices.text: Sit in the chair at the gate

effects.log: It is not a comfortable chair. It is an honest one.
It improves the chair and the town at once.

events.text: The Ministry is holding a retirement party for a clerk who has been retiring for two hundred years. The cake is old and the speeches are older. The clerk, seated at the head of the table, is quietly sorting the minutes of the party into folders. A tiny flag on the cake reads: “See you tomorrow.”

effects.log: You praise the filing. The clerk looks up, startled, and holds the folder like a prize.

choices.text: Eat the cake and say nothing

effects.log: It is excellent. It has been baked many times.

choices.text: Offer to help with the folders

effects.log: The clerk gives you the minutes of the speeches. They are very long.

events.text: An immortal elder of the Jade Void has taken to napping in the great hall at noon, in a chair too small for the hall and too grand for a nap. Students tiptoe around. Today the chair is occupied and a fly has landed on the elder's nose. The whole hall is watching to see who dares.

effects.log: The elder smiles in sleep. The hall exhales, and a student whispers, "Hero."
The fly walks to the elder's forehead, thinks better of it, and leaves. The hall applauds silently.

choices.text: Fan the elder with your sleeve

effects.log: The elder sleeps the better for it, and dreams, perhaps, of you.

events.text: An elder in the archive refuses to use the new catalogue, and carries a lifetime's worth of locations in their head. When a young archivist asks where a certain slip is, the elder shuts their eyes and answers: “Third hall, left shelf, behind the slip about weather.” It is correct. It is always correct.

effects.log: The elder produces it in a breath. The young archivist faints, politely.

choices.text: Offer to help write the elder's memory down

effects.log: The elder says it would be a waste of good forgetting.
The elder nods. Their slips will outlive them.

events.text: The keeper of the weathervane on the Ministry roof is two thousand years old and refuses to be replaced by a newer, quieter device. The vane screeches in the wind like a goose. The Ministry has put in four requests. The keeper has put in none, and oils the vane every evening with a rag and a murmured compliment.

choices.text: Offer to oil the vane with them

effects.log: It stops screeching and begins to hum. The keeper looks at you with real warmth.

choices.text: Tell the keeper the Ministry is complaining

effects.log: The keeper says the Ministry has been complaining for eight hundred years.
The keeper beams. "The only honest voice on the roof," they say.

events.text: A basket of visiting cards from the Divine Realm has been delivered to the Jade Court by a messenger who seems to have fallen out of the sky. Each card has a name, a title and a bored little scrawl: “Visiting. Will return.” Court clerks sort them with great reverence. One reads, in your own name, “Interesting.”

effects.log: It glows faintly on your wall. Visitors read it and say nothing.

choices.text: Ask the clerk who sent it

effects.log: The clerk checks. The sender is a name you do not know, in a hand of light.

choices.text: Pass it on to a friend as a joke

effects.log: The friend frames it and glows for a month.

events.text: A divine visitor, in a plain coat, is climbing the stairs of the Jade Void one at a time, counting aloud. They say it is a pilgrimage in reverse: they have come up from the Divine Realm to see what it is to labour toward something. They are on step nine hundred and two. They ask if you will count with them.

choices.text: Count a hundred steps beside them

effects.log: Your breath slows. The numbers become a kind of prayer.

choices.text: Carry their bag for a while

effects.log: It weighs nothing. They are very grateful anyway.
You nod. They nod. It is the shortest exchange you ever had with a god.

events.text: The Orchard Isle holds its Festival of the First Blossom, in which a single branch is allowed to flower early and the whole population stands under it, silent, for as long as the petals last. Children are given a petal each on a thread. The oldest resident holds a sprig and tells the year's riddle.

choices.text: Stand beneath the blossom in silence

effects.log: A petal lands on your sleeve. The silence is huge and soft.
You get it wrong, and the oldest resident is thrilled.

choices.text: Hang a petal on your door

effects.log: It lasts a week and perfumes the lane.

events.text: On the Lantern Isle's festival night a long line of paper lanterns is loosed off the edge, each carrying a name. Children write the names of those who have gone; adults write the names of those who have not yet come back. A woman beside you writes a name, crosses it out, writes it again, and sets it aflame.

choices.text: Write a name of your own and set it free

effects.log: It floats, small and orange, into the dark. You do not look away.
She does not look at you. She is grateful anyway.
They look like a slow fleet of stars. You think of nothing at all.

events.text: The Whale Isle has a festival at which the sky whales are asked to sing a single note together. The note is never the same. This year it is low and trembling, and the whole isle shivers pleasantly. A child tugs your sleeve and asks whether the whales know what they are singing. You find you do not know either.

choices.text: Say they know, and it is a prayer

effects.log: The child nods gravely. "Then I will answer," the child says, and sings a small, bright note.
The child frowns. "That is the best kind of song," the child decides.
A whale answers, or perhaps the wind does.

events.text: The Edge Isle keeps a festival of dawns, in which every resident climbs to the cliff and watches the sun come up in silence, then goes home to sleep the day away. Nobody works. The shops are shut. A neighbour who sleeps late is being gently pulled out of bed by children with blankets.

effects.log: The sky goes from black to rose to gold. You sit in it like a bath.

choices.text: Help the children with the blankets

effects.log: The neighbour is delivered in a wheelbarrow. All laugh.

choices.text: Stay in bed with the neighbour

effects.log: You both snore through the sunrise. The neighbour is quietly pleased.

events.text: A rumour goes round the quay that the Marsh Isle is planning to slip its moorings and drift off by spring. The isle has said nothing. Its folk go about their business in an unusually tidy way, mending everything, returning every borrowed pot. A visitor who asks about it is given three cakes and no answer.

effects.log: "Isles," says the elder, "do not leave. They merely go elsewhere carefully."

choices.text: Return a long-borrowed book, just in case

effects.log: The resident accepts it gravely and gives you a fourth cake.
The Steersman sighs. "I have heard," he says. "It happens each century."

events.text: A stall at the Low Market sells only second-hand items: a cracked lamp, a wedding sash, half a jade slip, an umbrella with a note saying “Rainy day, nine centuries ago”. The seller, a thin rogue, is honest about every flaw. A queue of other rogues wanders the stall, buying a little, smiling a lot.

effects.log: It keeps off no rain at all. It keeps a story, which is more.
The seller adds a wick for free and a joke at no cost.
The stall, full of other people's endings, gives you a slow, thoughtful hour.

events.text: A rogue ahead of you in line at the noodle stall is told their tab has run to forty stones. Everyone in the line tries not to look. The stall-owner is apologetic and firm. The rogue, in a tired voice, begins to offer payment in mending: roofs, chairs, a spoon. The owner has a roof in need of mending.

choices.text: Quietly pay five stones toward the tab (5 spirit stones)

effects.log: The owner notes it. The rogue never learns. The line breathes again.

choices.text: Offer to help carry the roof tiles

effects.log: You work an afternoon beside the rogue. The tab drops by a stone.

choices.text: Turn your face and wait for your noodles

effects.log: They are cold by the time they reach you.

events.text: A basket of letters hangs from a rope at the middle of the Long Bridge, with a sign: “For the person who will walk here at the end”. Nobody knows who put it there or when. The letters are in different hands, some faded, some new. A passing immortal reads one, folds it with care, and puts it back.

choices.text: Read one letter, and put it back

effects.log: It is a short note about a garden. You think about it for days.

choices.text: Add a letter of your own

effects.log: You write only: "It was worth it." The basket gains a small weight.
The basket swings in the wind behind you.

events.text: On Reed Lake a skiff goes by decorated with yellow ribbons, and everyone on the shore claps at once, because everyone knows two families have, after eighty years of feud, agreed to a wedding. The two grooms' mothers sit in the stern of the skiff, arms folded, glaring at each other in an almost friendly way.

choices.text: Clap and call out a blessing

effects.log: The mothers turn their glares on you for a moment, and soften.

choices.text: Ask a neighbour what the feud was about

effects.log: "A pot," says the neighbour. "Nobody remembers which pot."

choices.text: Watch from the shore with tea

effects.log: It is the best entertainment of the season.

events.text: On the thirteenth day the border town's market fills with Demon Realm stalls and Court merchants selling to each other as if there had never been an argument. Pickled ember-peppers, black-bean paste, bolts of dusk-silk. A fishmonger from the Upper Realm is selling cloud carp to a family of Demon Realm cooks, laughing over the price.

choices.text: Buy a jar of ember-pepper paste (1 spirit stone)

effects.log: It burns, sweetly and long. Your next three meals are remarkable.
The seller grins and halves the price for a joke. You leave with a ribbon and the joke.
Two languages mix in your ears, and the sum is a music.

events.text: In the border town of the Demon Realm, lanterns are black, with a single slit of red light, and they hang over doors to show who is home. A new lantern has appeared above a door that was always dark. Neighbours leave small gifts on the step: a bun, a candle, a folded cloth. Nobody has yet knocked.

choices.text: Leave a small gift on the step

effects.log: A bun, warm from your sleeve. In the morning it is gone, and a red thread is tied to the rail.
An old voice calls "Come in" and a very small kitchen smells of ginger. You are given tea.
No one knocks. The lantern burns all night. It is enough.

events.text: At dusk the border-town gate is closed by a watchman who does it very slowly, humming. He pauses to let the last cart through, looks at the stars, then closes it softly. A boy asks what he is humming. He says it is the gate's name. He says every gate has one, and that no one asks.

effects.log: The watchman smiles. "It will tell you, if you stay long enough," he says.
The two of you hum a few bars. The gate seems to listen.
You make it with a breath to spare. The watchman does not look up.

events.text: A very old cook is writing down a recipe for the first time. It is for broth that has been passed from cook to cook by voice for a thousand years. Every apprentice has added a word, some of them contradictory. The cook, with a stub of charcoal, reads them out loud and asks you to say which ones sound true.

choices.text: Pick the ones that sound like home

effects.log: The cook writes them down. The broth, later, tastes of nothing and everything.

choices.text: Say all of them sound true

effects.log: The cook writes them all. The recipe is a monster. The broth is a triumph.
The cook laughs. "That was my fear," they say, and write it down.

events.text: An elder on the Cloud Terrace has fallen asleep over a game of go, in the middle of a move, with the stone held between two fingers. The opponent, equally old, is waiting politely. They have been waiting eleven years. Visitors come to see the game and tiptoe past. The tea beside the sleeper is, mysteriously, still hot.

effects.log: Neither of you speaks. A cherry blossom lands on the board.

choices.text: Study the position on the board

effects.log: It is a brilliant position. You cannot find a winning move.
The sleeper smiles faintly. The stone does not move.

events.text: A pair of guests from the Divine Realm have come to sit on the cliffs of the Edge Isle and watch the sun set, because they have heard it is lovely. They sit very straight and take notes in tiny script. A child offers them a sweet. They look at it for a long time before eating, then ask for the recipe.

choices.text: Tell them it is just sugar and patience

effects.log: They note it down. They are enormously moved.
They accept with the joy of beings who rarely get seconds.
The sun goes down. They write one word, and cross it out.

events.text: At the Hot Spring Terrace an ancient immortal soaks in the same pool every morning at dawn and has done for four thousand years. They know every bather by the splash. Today a newcomer enters with a bang, and the elder, eyes shut, says: “Third time you have dived since spring. You are in love.” The newcomer sinks to the chin.

choices.text: Ask the elder to read your splash

effects.log: "You are tired," says the elder, "but pleased about it." It is exactly right.
The elder nods in approval. "An honest bather," they murmur.
The newcomer glows. The pool glows with them.

events.text: In the lee of a passing tribulation cloud, a very old immortal sets out a small table and pours tea for anyone who needs it. They have done so for a thousand years, they say, because someone once did it for them. The cloud rumbles overhead. The table does not shake. The tea is hot.

effects.log: You and the cloud both cool down. The old one says nothing, which is generous.

choices.text: Ask who poured the first cup for them

effects.log: "A stranger," says the old one. "I never saw their face."

choices.text: Offer to pour for the next passer-by

effects.log: The old one hands you the pot. You pour for a trembling disciple.

events.text: An apprentice has come to say goodbye to their master, who sits very still on the porch. The apprentice has outgrown the master in the matter of the sword, and both know it. The master says only, “Go, and be better than me, but not at tea.” The apprentice bows low, and the master turns the cup in their hand.

effects.log: The master does not speak. Their hand on the cup is steady.
The apprentice thanks you, eyes wet, and goes.

choices.text: Leave the porch to the two of them

effects.log: You walk away, and leave tea on the step.

events.text: A young elder who has just reached that rank, three hundred years old and very nervous, practises their stern face in a bamboo pool at dawn. They try disapproving, wise, mysterious. All of them look like someone with a stomachache. They notice you watching and stiffen.

choices.text: Say the stern face is quite convincing

effects.log: The elder glows, then catches your look, and laughs.

choices.text: Say they should just be themselves

effects.log: The elder thinks about it. "That," they say, "is terrifying."
The elder bows, grateful, and tries the face again after you leave.

events.text: An overdue slip has come back to the archive on the back of a small cloud-ferret, six centuries late. It is wrapped in a bit of cloth and smells of woodsmoke. The ferret, pleased, deposits it on the desk and sits. The archivist reads the borrower's note: “I meant to return it sooner. Please forgive me. I got caught up in the world.”

choices.text: Mark it returned with a kind note

effects.log: The archivist writes "Forgiven" in the margin. The ferret nods.

choices.text: Read the slip before it is reshelved

effects.log: It is a poem about a river. It was worth the wait.

choices.text: Give the ferret a small biscuit

effects.log: It eats the biscuit, bows, and leaves for another century.

events.text: A school on the Bamboo Isle has invited a retired immortal to talk about a long life. The children are sitting in rows. The immortal gets up and says: “I have nothing to tell you.
