Nap often. Be kind to cats. Learn one song.” Then they sit down. The children, deeply impressed, write it all down.

effects.log: The immortal bows, very pleased, and promptly falls asleep.
The immortal wakes: "Any. But learn it all the way to the end."
The questions go on without you. There are very few.

events.text: A bundle of letters has been caught in the cloud-pines, carried up from the world below by a long south wind. They are crumpled, wet, and in several hands. One says: “To whoever is up there, I hope you are warm.” A child reading it aloud asks if the writer is warm. Nobody can answer.

choices.text: Write a short reply and send it on the wind

effects.log: Seven words. They rise and vanish. You hope.

choices.text: Tell the child the writer is warm now

effects.log: The child nods, comforted. You hope it is true.

choices.text: Press the letter between jade slips

effects.log: It is kept in the archive under Unknown Well-Wishers.

events.text: The notice-board at the Quay lists the yearly hunts: thunder sparrows in spring, mist hounds in autumn, a sky whale to be turned once in a century. A very old hunter reads the list aloud to a very young hunter, who corrects the pronunciation. The old one is delighted at being corrected. The young one is mortified. Both are happy.

choices.text: Sign up for the sparrow hunt

effects.log: Your name goes under the old hunter's, in a sprawl. It is a good start.

choices.text: Ask the old hunter for a story

effects.log: The story is about a sparrow that outwitted a hundred hunters. It takes an hour.
The young hunter thanks you with an expression of deep relief.

events.text: In the back of an old tea-house there is a door that has never been opened, and a regular who sits beside it every day. When asked, the regular says there is a second tea-house behind it, empty and perfectly kept, and that they are on its guest list, waiting. They have been waiting for two centuries.

effects.log: You wait an hour. The door stays closed. The tea is warm.

choices.text: Ask who keeps the second tea-house

effects.log: "Someone kind," says the regular. "I think."
It does not move. The regular looks relieved, and a little sad.

events.text: Two old friends, {npc} on the Orchard Isle and another on the far Frost Isle, write to one another by the slowest post in the sky: a single carrier-tortoise that crosses the clouds between them in a century. {npc} has just received a reply to a question asked a hundred years ago. {He} reads it aloud to you and laughs: the question is no longer the question.
events.arc: The Letters That Took a Century to Cross

effects.log: "Whether I should leave the Orchard," says {npc}. "I left. I came back. The answer arrived just now."

choices.text: Offer to write a line in the next letter

effects.log: {npc} is delighted. Your line is small and formal and it will take a century to be read.

choices.text: Say the post is far too slow

effects.log: "Then it is exactly slow enough," {npc} says, and is not offended.

events.text: The tortoise returns with news that the friend on the Frost Isle has died, a few years ago. The last letter was written, it seems, with great care. {npc} cannot open it. {He} sets it on the desk and looks at it for a month, and asks you whether it is better to read a letter written by the dead or to keep it sealed and thinking.
events.arc: The Letters That Took a Century to Cross

choices.text: Say read it, they wrote it to be read

effects.log: {npc} opens it with shaking hands, and you leave {him} alone with it.

choices.text: Say keep it a while longer

effects.log: {npc} nods. The letter sits on the shelf, a held breath.

choices.text: Offer to read it aloud for {him}

effects.log: {npc} shakes {his} head, gently. "Mine," {he} says.

events.text: The letter is a single page about the Frost Isle's first snow. At the bottom, a sentence: “I am glad we wrote. You were always my best correspondent.” {npc} writes a reply, though there is no one to send it to, and sends it up with the tortoise anyway. “Someone will read it,” {he} says. “A letter always finds a reader.”
events.arc: The Letters That Took a Century to Cross

choices.text: Walk the tortoise to the quay

effects.log: The reptile carries the letter off into the cloud with a slow dignity. You wave until it is gone.
It takes you a year to finish, and {he} replies in a week, which is, for {him}, a miracle.

events.text: The letter stays sealed on the shelf. For years {npc} dusts it. Then, one evening, {he} says: “I am ready,” and opens it. It is the briefest note: “Dear friend, I have nothing to tell you but this: the snow is lovely and I am well.” {npc} laughs until the tears come. “Of course,” {he} says. “Of course.”
events.arc: The Letters That Took a Century to Cross

effects.log: You drink tea in the dusk. The note is read three more times.

choices.text: Frame the note for the wall

effects.log: {npc} hangs it above the desk. It outlasts the house.

events.text: A letter has come to you and a second to someone you have never met, both sealed with a single wax that will melt only when the two are held side by side. The sender, now dead, was apparently fond of puzzles. {npc}, the ferry clerk, hands you yours and a slip of paper with a name and an isle on it. “Good luck,” {he} says.
events.arc: The Letter That Could Only Be Opened Together

choices.text: Set out to find the other recipient

effects.log: The isle is far. The ferries are slow. The road is half the point.

choices.text: Send a note ahead to the name on the slip

effects.log: It travels a month, and a reply comes: "I have been waiting."

choices.text: Put the letter in a drawer

effects.log: It sits there, patient, for another decade.

events.text: The other recipient is a stooped, hard-eyed immortal who lives on a bare isle with only a goat. They have, it turns out, a long and unhappy history with the sender: a quarrel about a poem. They set their letter on the table with a click. “I will not open mine,” they say. “I know what it will say.”
events.arc: The Letter That Could Only Be Opened Together

choices.text: Say perhaps it says something else

effects.log: The immortal stares at the letter. "Perhaps," they allow. "Perhaps."
You break nothing, and read nothing, but your gesture is felt.

choices.text: Say you will leave them to it

effects.log: The goat watches you go with a long, level look.

events.text: The two letters are set side by side, the wax melts, and the pages open. Inside both is the same poem, the one they quarrelled over, now finished by the sender in a version neither would have written. The immortal reads it three times and then weeps. “He was right,” they say. “And so was I. Both. Both of us.”
events.arc: The Letter That Could Only Be Opened Together

choices.text: Sit with the immortal in silence

effects.log: The goat joins you. The afternoon goes quietly.

choices.text: Ask to hear the poem aloud

effects.log: The immortal reads it in a cracked voice, slowly, and it is lovely.

events.text: You ask to read yours first, and the immortal, reluctantly, lets you. Yours is only a line: “Persuade them.” The immortal laughs, a bitter bark. Slowly, over tea and with the goat as witness, you do. It takes a week. At the end the letters are opened, and the poem inside is both of theirs at once. You are mentioned in a footnote.
events.arc: The Letter That Could Only Be Opened Together

effects.log: It is a small, kind line. It is yours to keep.

choices.text: Take the goat as a gift

effects.log: The goat comes with a bell and a temper. You are very fond of it.

events.text: A scribe on the Reed Isle has a stack of unanswered letters from a friend who died before the replies could be written. {npc} answers them anyway, in the friend's style, each reply a little more cheerful. The post-carrier, a wind-sparrow, takes them off the isle at dusk and never returns. {He} confesses all this to you over a cup of cold tea.
events.arc: The Letter Answered by Someone Else

choices.text: Say it sounds like a lovely thing to do

effects.log: {npc} blushes and pours you more tea. The letters stack higher.

choices.text: Ask where the replies are going

effects.log: "To the wind," says {npc}. "It is a kind recipient."

choices.text: Say it is a strange habit

effects.log: {npc} straightens. "It is," {he} agrees, a little stiffly.

events.text: One evening a reply comes back. It is written in the dead friend's hand. {npc} turns the page over and over. It reads: “Thank you. You have it almost right.” {He} sits very still. The sparrow, perched on the sill, is eating a crumb. The handwriting is not quite the friend's. It is {npc}'s own, bent slightly.
events.arc: The Letter Answered by Someone Else

choices.text: Tell {npc} what you think it is

effects.log: "Perhaps it is," says {npc}. "Perhaps the wind writes back as one writes to it."
{npc} reads it aloud again and again. It does not seem to matter.
The sparrow trills once and flies off. You are none the wiser.

events.text: {npc} stops answering the old letters after that, and begins a new correspondence with the wind: a single page each evening, folded into a bird. Replies come irregularly. Some are bare. Some are warm. All are kept. {He} says it is the finest correspondence of {his} life, and that the wind is a better listener than most people.
events.arc: The Letter Answered by Someone Else

choices.text: Fold a bird of your own

effects.log: You write a line. The sparrow carries it off. No reply comes. It is enough.

choices.text: Visit {npc} at dusk to watch the birds go

effects.log: The sky fills with small white wings. You do not speak.

events.text: You let {him} believe. {npc} keeps the reply framed above the writing-desk, as proof of something {he} cannot name. For years the letters go on, and the replies come, and no one ever asks who writes them. Near the end of {his} life {he} says to you: “I do not think it matters who answers. I think it matters that someone is asked.”
events.arc: The Letter Answered by Someone Else

choices.text: Keep the framed reply when {he} is gone

effects.log: It hangs in your hall. Guests ask about it and you tell them, truly.

choices.text: Add your own reply to the pile

effects.log: Written in a hand that is almost the friend's. The wind takes it kindly.

events.text: At the Lantern Isle's oldest noodle shop, {npc} has taught an apprentice for a hundred years. The apprentice's broth, last month, was better than the master's. Everyone tasted it. Nobody said a word. {npc} stands behind the counter with {his} jaw tight and asks you to taste both bowls and tell {him} honestly which is the better.
events.arc: The Apprentice Who Cooked Better Than the Master

choices.text: Taste both and tell the truth

effects.log: You say the apprentice's is better. {npc} nods slowly, as though it were a diagnosis.

choices.text: Taste both and say you cannot tell

effects.log: It is a lie, and both of you know it. {npc} is grateful for it.
{npc} sets the bowls down side by side and says nothing.

events.text: The apprentice, noticing the silence, offers to leave. “I do not want to take your shop,” the apprentice says. {npc} stares. {He} has been waiting for the apprentice to take it for fifty years, and is afraid, now that it is offered, that {he} will not be able to let go. You are asked to sit with them both.
events.arc: The Apprentice Who Cooked Better Than the Master

effects.log: You say the shop is a gift to be handed on, not a prison to be guarded. {npc} lowers {his} head.
You say the apprentice owes the master nothing but gratitude, and should accept both gifts.

choices.text: Say nothing and pour the tea

effects.log: The tea steams. The silence between them is a long one.

events.text: {npc} hands over the shop in a quiet ceremony: the ladle, the sign, the key. The apprentice weeps. {npc} sits at the corner table with a bowl of the apprentice's noodles and eats them all, slowly, and says, “Not bad.” It is the highest praise {he} has ever given anyone. The shop is renamed, but {npc}'s chair is never moved.
events.arc: The Apprentice Who Cooked Better Than the Master

choices.text: Eat at the shop each week

effects.log: The noodles are the best in the sky. The corner table is warm.

choices.text: Say a few words at the ceremony

effects.log: They are well received. They are also, you notice, brief.

events.text: {npc} keeps the shop and the apprentice stays, cooking in the back, unacknowledged. The noodles are served under the master's name. Customers say they have never been better. {npc} receives the praise with a lowered head, and sends the apprentice a gift each festival: a ribbon, a knife, an extra day. It is not enough, and both of them know it. It lasts a century.
events.arc: The Apprentice Who Cooked Better Than the Master

choices.text: Quietly tell the apprentice the truth is known

effects.log: The apprentice smiles. "I know," they say. "It is enough."

choices.text: Tell {npc} the apprentice deserves the credit

effects.log: {He} is silent a long time. Then {he} puts the sign in the apprentice's hands.

events.text: The flute-master {npc} has taught a thousand pupils and has one left: a quiet child who plays the same four notes and nothing else. The other pupils graduated, wandered, taught or died. The child plays the four notes at dawn. {npc} listens from the porch with {his} eyes closed, and invites you to sit and say what the notes remind you of.
events.arc: The Flute-Master's Last Pupil

choices.text: Say they remind you of rain

effects.log: {npc} nods. "Rain is the master of the flute," {he} says.

choices.text: Say they remind you of waiting

effects.log: "Yes," says {npc}. "The child is waiting for the fifth note."

choices.text: Say you do not know music

effects.log: {npc} smiles. "Neither do I," {he} says. "Neither does the child."

events.text: The fifth note arrives on a morning in spring, and it is wrong. It is a cracked, strange note, like a bird trying to say a word. The child looks at {npc}, horrified. {npc} says nothing. {He} puts down {his} tea and stands. Not since the first day of teaching has {he} stood to listen. You are the only witness.
events.arc: The Flute-Master's Last Pupil

choices.text: Tell the child the note is right

effects.log: The child nods, cheeks wet, and plays it again, cracked and true.

choices.text: Tell the child to keep playing

effects.log: The child plays all morning. The note finds its place among the four.
{npc} has the matter in hand. You are a bystander to a miracle.

events.text: The child grows up and plays the five notes at the Jade Court, to a hall that falls utterly silent. {npc}, in the back, listens with closed eyes. At the end the child bows to the empty seat beside {him}, and then to {him}. “I have nothing more to teach,” {npc} says afterwards, and the child answers: “Then teach me to teach.”
events.arc: The Flute-Master's Last Pupil

effects.log: They bow to you, side by side. It is the best thing you saw all year.

choices.text: Slip away before the applause ends

effects.log: Some triumphs belong only to the people in them.

events.text: The child keeps the five notes secret, playing them only at dawn on the porch for {npc}, who dies the following year with the notes still in {his} ears. The child never plays them again in public. But the child teaches, and every pupil learns four notes and waits for the fifth. It is the strangest school in the sky, and the most patient.
events.arc: The Flute-Master's Last Pupil

effects.log: Four notes. Silence. You wait with the pupils for what does not come.

choices.text: Leave a flower on the old porch

effects.log: It is gone by morning. A fifth note drifts from somewhere in answer.

events.text: At the Star Sea Pavilion, {npc} has trained an apprentice in the art of charting, and the apprentice has begun drawing a sea that is not on any map. It lies, the apprentice says, in the gaps between the known stars. {npc} frowns. “The gaps are gaps,” {he} says. “That is why they are called that.” But {he} does not quite throw the chart away.
events.arc: The Navigator's Apprentice Who Drew a New Sea

choices.text: Ask to see the new chart

effects.log: It is strange and lovely. The gaps are filled with currents you have never imagined.

choices.text: Ask {npc} why {he} did not throw it away

effects.log: "Because it is wrong," says {npc}, "in a way I cannot name."

choices.text: Say the apprentice is wasting ink

effects.log: The apprentice lowers their eyes. {npc} gives you a cold look.

events.text: The apprentice asks to sail the new sea, alone, in a small skiff, for a year. {npc} says no. The apprentice asks again. {npc} says no again, and at night {he} sits with the chart unrolled, running a thumb along the gaps. {He} asks if you would go with the apprentice, to keep a steady hand at the tiller.
events.arc: The Navigator's Apprentice Who Drew a New Sea

effects.log: You and the apprentice set out on a skiff the size of a bathtub, into the dark between the stars.
{npc} starts. "I am too old," {he} says, and does not mean it.
{npc} nods heavily. The apprentice does not sail.

events.text: The year in the gaps shows you a sea of slow blue currents that carry the skiff gently from nowhere to nowhere. The apprentice charts it with trembling hands. When you return, the chart is a masterwork, and {npc} reads it standing, in silence, with tears. The Pavilion adds a new leaf to its atlas that night, titled with the apprentice's name.
events.arc: The Navigator's Apprentice Who Drew a New Sea

choices.text: Sign the chart as a witness

effects.log: Your name is a small mark in the corner. It is enough.

choices.text: Describe the voyage to the Pavilion

effects.log: You are a poor storyteller. The room hangs on every word.

events.text: {npc} goes. The old navigator and the apprentice set out together in the little skiff, and are gone for a year, then three. They return with a chart that has two hands on it, one steady, one trembling, and a note: “We are not finished.” They sail again. The Pavilion, in time, names the new sea after both of them, and no one asks whose name comes first.
events.arc: The Navigator's Apprentice Who Drew a New Sea

choices.text: Wave them off at the quay

effects.log: The skiff is a speck. The quay is empty after.

choices.text: Keep their chart in the Pavilion

effects.log: It hangs beside the great atlas. Visitors lean close.

events.text: {npc}, the master of tea of the Cloud Terrace, has taught only one thing for eight hundred years: how to wait for the water. Their apprentice has learned, and learned past it, and now the apprentice's tea is quieter than the master's, which no one thought possible. {npc} asks you to sit between them at the next tasting and say nothing.
events.arc: The Apprentice Who Outgrew the Master of Tea

effects.log: The tasting is the stillest hour of your life. The two cups steam in unison.

choices.text: Sit and sip, and say a word at the end

effects.log: You say "good". Both nod. It is, for once, enough.
{npc} nods. The tasting goes on without a witness.

events.text: After the tasting {npc} goes out onto the terrace and stands in the wind for a day. When {he} returns, {he} has decided something. “I am not the master of this tea any more,” {he} says to the apprentice. “I am the oldest student of it.” The apprentice, appalled, starts to protest. You are asked to keep the peace.
events.arc: The Apprentice Who Outgrew the Master of Tea

effects.log: You say it is the truest title in the Terrace. The apprentice goes silent.
You say a master cannot step down while a student still bows. Both laugh, ruefully.

choices.text: Say it is not your quarrel

effects.log: They work it out, awkwardly, over three weeks.

events.text: The apprentice becomes the master of tea and {npc} becomes the oldest student, sitting on the lowest cushion and learning new tricks. The tea is quieter than ever. A rumour goes round that on certain mornings you can hear nothing at all from the Terrace, and that this is the point. People climb up just to listen to the silence.
events.arc: The Apprentice Who Outgrew the Master of Tea

effects.log: The silence is full. You do not want to leave it.

choices.text: Bring the oldest student a gift of leaves

effects.log: {npc} receives them with a bow so deep you are embarrassed.

events.text: The apprentice refuses, and the two remain master and master, side by side, neither willing to lead. The Terrace has two heads and one teapot. It is a wonderful absurdity. Guests are served by both, in turn, with identical movements. After a century no one can tell who is who, and neither of them cares.
events.arc: The Apprentice Who Outgrew the Master of Tea

choices.text: Ask them which is the master

effects.log: "Yes," they say together, and pour.
It is the best tea you ever had, and no one claimed credit.

events.text: Two people from different isles are to be married, and the two isles have never agreed on anything. The wedding must take place on neutral cloud, with a menu both can eat, a song both can sing and a mooring both can reach. {npc}, the matchmaker, has been negotiating for a year. {He} hands you a list of fifty items and asks you to help with number thirty-one: the cake.
events.arc: A Wedding That Needed Two Isles to Agree

effects.log: It takes three bakers, two arguments and one compromise: a cake with a line down the middle.

choices.text: Offer to carry messages between the isles

effects.log: You are sent running back and forth for a month. Both isles come to like you.

choices.text: Say you are no good at weddings

effects.log: {npc} nods, unoffended, and finds someone else.

events.text: A week before the wedding, the two isles quarrel over the order of the toasts. One insists on speaking first; the other has never spoken second. The couple, young and tired, sit on the neutral cloud and watch the quarrel from a distance. {npc} tells you gravely that the wedding will not happen unless something is done.
events.arc: A Wedding That Needed Two Isles to Agree

choices.text: Propose that the toasts be given at the same moment

effects.log: It is chaos on paper and beauty in practice. Both isles agree, with groans.

choices.text: Propose no toasts at all, only a silence

effects.log: The isles are shocked, then moved. A silence it is.

choices.text: Leave the isles to settle it

effects.log: They settle it on the day, grudgingly and late.

events.text: The two toasts are given at once, in two voices that rise and fall and finally harmonise. The cake with its line is cut along the line, and each isle eats its half and then, shyly, a bite of the other's. The couple dances on the neutral cloud, and the two isles, for one evening, share a moon. {npc} weeps into the napkin and calls it the finest work of {his} life.
events.arc: A Wedding That Needed Two Isles to Agree

choices.text: Dance at the edge of the floor

effects.log: You are not good at it. No one minds.
{He} blushes. The cup is raised by everyone.

events.text: The silence is held, long and deep. When it ends, the two isles are looking at each other with a kind of astonished mildness. A child laughs. Then everybody does. The marriage lasts, and so does the peace, which is a smaller thing, and a more fragile one, kept up by yearly dinners on the neutral cloud. {npc} insists on being host.
events.arc: A Wedding That Needed Two Isles to Agree

effects.log: It is a small affair, warm, slightly awkward. You come every year.

choices.text: Send a gift of cake with a line down the middle

effects.log: It is received with great solemnity.

events.text: At a wedding on the Blossom Isle, an elderly immortal in a faded coat sits at the back, unannounced, eating nothing. {npc}, the groom's uncle, murmurs that no one knows who it is. The coat is a style from a thousand years ago, and the guest has brought no gift. {He} asks you to find out who the stranger is without causing a scene.
events.arc: The Uninvited Guest at an Isle Wedding

choices.text: Sit beside the stranger and make small talk

effects.log: The stranger talks of weather and nothing else, but with great charm.

choices.text: Ask a servant who let them in

effects.log: "The gate was open," says the servant, helpfully.

choices.text: Tell {npc} to ask the stranger directly

effects.log: {npc} goes pale. "I would rather not," {he} says.

events.text: The stranger, you learn, is the bride's grandfather, who was banished from the isle eight centuries ago for a quarrel long since forgotten. Nobody has told the bride. The old one came only to see the wedding from the back and leave. They say they will go at once, and ask you to say nothing. Their voice shakes.
events.arc: The Uninvited Guest at an Isle Wedding

effects.log: The bride crosses the hall at a run, silk and all, and embraces the old one in front of everyone.

choices.text: Persuade the old one to stay to the end

effects.log: They stay. They eat a single honeyed fig, and weep into it.
The old one leaves unnoticed. You feel the weight of it for decades.

events.text: The family is thrown into uproar, then into tears, then into a feast. The groom's uncle, {npc}, stands and offers the old one a seat at the head of the table. The quarrel, it turns out, was over a pot of paint. The bride's grandfather moves back to the isle in the spring and takes up painting, badly, at once.
events.arc: The Uninvited Guest at an Isle Wedding

choices.text: Visit the painter on the isle

effects.log: The paintings are terrible. You buy one. It hangs in your hall.

choices.text: Toast the family on its wedding day

effects.log: The old one raises their cup to you in return.

events.text: The old one stays to the end of the feast and then leaves quietly before dawn, with a kiss on the bride's sleeping brow. The family never learns who they were, though the bride, years later, finds a small painting in her chest, signed with a name she does not recognise, and puts it up in her kitchen. She says it feels like the cheeriest ghost.
events.arc: The Uninvited Guest at an Isle Wedding

choices.text: Say nothing about what you know

effects.log: Some stories keep best untold. This one hangs in a kitchen.

choices.text: Visit the bride and mention the painting

effects.log: She tells you it feels like a blessing. You nod.

events.text: Two siblings who were raised on the same small isle now live on opposite ends of the fleet. They have not spoken in a century. Neither will say why. {npc}, a neighbour of the elder, asks if you would carry a basket of dried plums from one to the other, as a favour. “No message,” {he} says. “Just plums.”
events.arc: The Siblings Who Drifted to Opposite Isles

choices.text: Carry the plums to the other sibling

effects.log: The younger takes the basket and stares at it for a long minute. "These are Mother's," they say, and say nothing more.

choices.text: Carry the plums and a word of greeting

effects.log: The younger refuses the word and accepts the plums. Both are communications.

choices.text: Say a favour is a favour, but not this one

effects.log: {npc} nods and carries the basket {him}self. It takes a year.

events.text: A reply returns: a jar of pickled ginger, with no note. The elder looks at it for a long time, then laughs, a short rough sound. They begin, by baskets and jars, a slow correspondence in food. Years pass. At last the younger sibling sends a message in words: “Come to the harvest.” The elder cannot decide whether to go. {npc} asks you to help decide.
events.arc: The Siblings Who Drifted to Opposite Isles

effects.log: The elder packs a bag. It takes three days to close it. They go.

choices.text: Say it is the elder's own choice

effects.log: The elder sits with the invitation for a season and then, quietly, goes.

choices.text: Say a century of silence is fine

effects.log: {npc} says nothing. The elder stays home. The jars stop.

events.text: The siblings meet in the harvest field. For an hour they simply stand a step apart, looking at the rows. Then the younger holds out a plum. The elder takes it, eats it, and says: “Too sour.” They laugh till they weep. The quarrel, it transpires, was about a swing in the garden of their youth. It is still hanging, and they ride it together.
events.arc: The Siblings Who Drifted to Opposite Isles

choices.text: Watch from the edge of the field

effects.log: It is a private joy, and you are glad to be near it.

choices.text: Bring a flask for the harvest feast

effects.log: It passes round the whole field. Both siblings drink.

events.text: The elder goes, and the visit is polite and brief, with long silences. They part on the third day with a stiff handshake and the promise of a basket. It is not a reconciliation. It is a thread. Years later the thread is still there: a jar here, a plum there, and a swing, somewhere, hanging empty in a garden that neither has the heart to visit.
events.arc: The Siblings Who Drifted to Opposite Isles

effects.log: The siblings take it, and for once, in the same week, thank you.

choices.text: Visit the garden and push the swing

effects.log: It creaks. It is enough.

events.text: On the Reed Isle, two houses stand side by side, and the neighbours in them have not exchanged a word in two hundred years. They are polite: a nod at the well, a wave over the fence. No one remembers the quarrel. {npc} is the elder of one house, and has begun to feel, privately, that the silence has become the house's tenant. {He} asks you to help break it.
events.arc: The Two Neighbours Who Had Not Spoken in Two Hundred Years

choices.text: Carry a message to the other neighbour

effects.log: The other neighbour hears it, shrugs, and says, "Tell them it is going to rain." It does.

choices.text: Sit between them at the well

effects.log: The two never look at each other. Your presence is a bridge.

choices.text: Say a silence that old is a monument

effects.log: {npc} glares at you, then at the fence. You are not asked back.

events.text: The rain comes. Both neighbours bring in washing at the same hour and, flustered, drop a basket each. The baskets mingle in the mud. For a moment the two stand on either side of a heap of laundry. Neither speaks. {npc} looks at you from the window, white-knuckled, and mouths: “What do I say?”
events.arc: The Two Neighbours Who Had Not Spoken in Two Hundred Years

effects.log: {npc} says it, aloud, through the window. The other neighbour looks up and nods.

choices.text: Mouth back: “Help them with the laundry”

effects.log: {npc} goes out into the rain and kneels in the mud. The other joins.
{npc} shrugs back, helplessly. The baskets are sorted in silence.

events.text: They sort the laundry together without speaking, and when it is done the other neighbour hands over a single sock, held up with a puzzled air. {npc} laughs aloud. The other laughs. It is the first sound either has made to the other in two centuries. By evening they are on the porch drinking tea and not discussing the quarrel, which remains a mystery.
events.arc: The Two Neighbours Who Had Not Spoken in Two Hundred Years

effects.log: You walk home slowly through the wet, pleased.
"A fence post," they say together, and laugh again.

events.text: The sorted laundry is exchanged silently, with a nod, and the silence resumes, but changed. The porch light is left on at night, on both sides. A pot of soup, left on the fence, is returned empty. Silent neighbours, you reflect, are not silent at all. They have a whole language of things placed on fences.
events.arc: The Two Neighbours Who Had Not Spoken in Two Hundred Years

choices.text: Leave a small gift on the fence for both

effects.log: It is claimed within the hour. A thank-you is left in its place.

choices.text: Add a bench to the well for them

effects.log: They sit on it, at opposite ends, and share the view.

events.text: A newly married pair of immortals have registered their marriage at the Ministry of Lamps instead of the Ministry of Registers. The clerk there, {npc}, took the form with a smile and stamped it, then realised the error. By then the couple had left on a honeymoon. {He} asks you in a whisper if the marriage counts.
events.arc: The Marriage Registered at the Wrong Ministry

choices.text: Say that love is love, and forms are forms

effects.log: {npc} writes this on a slip. It is quoted in the Ministry for years.

choices.text: Say you will check with the Ministry of Registers

effects.log: You are sent through three offices and a courtyard. The answer is "possibly".
{npc} pales and leaves for a long walk.

events.text: The couple returns from their honeymoon to find that the Ministry of Registers has no record of them. They are, on paper, unwed. They find this unbearably funny, but the pair's families do not. A great-aunt arrives demanding a correction. {npc} hides behind the counter. The clerk begs you to speak for the error.
events.arc: The Marriage Registered at the Wrong Ministry

choices.text: Explain the error to the great-aunt with calm

effects.log: The great-aunt, silenced by your civility, demands only tea and gets it.

choices.text: Offer to carry the form to the right Ministry yourself

effects.log: You do. It takes six weeks and a lot of stamps. It is done.

choices.text: Tell the clerk to confess to the Minister

effects.log: {npc} does, and is gently scolded.

events.text: The marriage is entered in both Ministries, with a note that it was “first registered by lamp”. The couple frames the Lamps form on their wall. Whenever they quarrel, they look at it and remember that they were once married by accident and decided to stay that way on purpose. {npc} receives a card every year. It always says: “Thank you for the mistake.”
events.arc: The Marriage Registered at the Wrong Ministry

choices.text: Visit the couple on their anniversary

effects.log: The lamp form hangs in the hall. They toast it with cloud-wine.
{He} blushes. "It was," {he} says, "and I will never make one like it again." {He} will.

events.text: You carry the form through the Ministries. At each desk a clerk looks at it with the same startled expression and then stamps it as if afraid not to. By the end it is a thing of beauty, a hundred stamps deep. The couple keeps it in a case, and the Ministry of Registers quietly adds a new rule: marriages registered elsewhere are valid if the stamp is genuine.
events.arc: The Marriage Registered at the Wrong Ministry

choices.text: Accept the thanks of the Ministry

effects.log: The new rule is called the Lamp Clause, and your name is attached to it in a footnote.

choices.text: Attend the next wedding at the Ministry of Lamps

effects.log: It is a very bright occasion. The clerks wear their best.

events.text: Two long-married immortals on the Cedar Isle have decided, after eight hundred years, to part. There was no quarrel. They simply no longer wish the same things. They have invited the neighbours to a farewell dinner, to say so plainly and to thank everyone. {npc}, a close friend, is anxious and asks you to sit beside {him}.
events.arc: The Couple Who Parted Politely After Eight Centuries

effects.log: The food is lovely. The silences are not. {npc} takes your arm under the table.

choices.text: Bring a gift for each of them

effects.log: Two small, identical cups. They are both moved.
{npc} goes alone. You hear it went well.

events.text: At the dinner they stand together and give a short, kind speech. They are not angry. They have simply grown in different directions. They say they will remain friends, and that the house will be shared for a year, in separate rooms, while they decide who keeps what. A guest begins to cry. {npc} whispers to you: “Is this how it is done? Can this be done well?”
events.arc: The Couple Who Parted Politely After Eight Centuries

choices.text: Say yes, when it is honest, it can

effects.log: {npc} lets out a breath. "Good," {he} murmurs. "Good."

choices.text: Say it is sad but not wrong

effects.log: {npc} nods. "That is what I think too," {he} says, "and I am not certain."
{npc} squeezes your arm. "Nor do I," {he} says. It is a comfort.

events.text: After the year, they part with a handshake on the quay, one going to the Frost Isle, the other staying. A small package arrives for you a decade later, containing two cups that are identical, and a note: “To the one who sat with us.” You use them for tea with {npc}, and the three of you, sometimes, speak of the dinner and what it taught.
events.arc: The Couple Who Parted Politely After Eight Centuries

choices.text: Invite them both to tea, separately

effects.log: Each comes, and each brings the other's regards.

choices.text: Keep the cups on a shelf together

effects.log: They sit side by side, never to be separated again.

events.text: They stay in the same house for ten years, in separate rooms, passing in the hall with a nod. In time one of them leaves and the other remains. There is no ceremony. They simply stop passing in the hall. {npc} says, years later, that it was the loneliest parting {he} had ever seen, and the politest. You say it was both of those things. The cups are still on the shelf.
events.arc: The Couple Who Parted Politely After Eight Centuries

effects.log: The house is quiet. They have kept both cups.

choices.text: Write to the one who left

effects.log: The reply is warm and short. They are well.

events.text: In the border town of the Demon Realm, a wake is held for an old gate-watcher who died in their sleep, and the whole town comes, both sides, in black. {npc}, the dead one's sister, passes out bowls of soup and asks each guest to say one thing the watcher said that they remember. When it is your turn, you realise you barely knew the dead.
events.arc: A Wake in the Border Town

effects.log: You say that the gate was always shut gently. {npc} nods, moved.
A hundred voices, a hundred small anecdotes. The watcher comes alive in them.

choices.text: Stay at the back and eat your soup

effects.log: It is thick and hot. {npc} brings you a second bowl without a word.

events.text: Late in the evening an old soldier of the Court appears at the door in full dress, medals and all. The watcher once spared the soldier a night in the cold, sixty years ago, and the soldier has come to say so. A hush falls. The town is divided about whether the soldier should be admitted. {npc} looks across the room at you.
events.arc: A Wake in the Border Town

choices.text: Open the door wider for the soldier

effects.log: The soldier steps in, and the room gives way, one body at a time.
{npc} takes the soldier's hand and leads the way to the table. The town breathes.
The soldier waits at the door for a long time before being let in.

events.text: The soldier says his piece, simply, to the empty chair where the watcher used to sit. There is no applause. After a while the soldier is given soup, and a place by the fire, and a bed for the night. In the morning he leaves a medal on the table. It is hung beside the watcher's lantern, a tiny bright thing among the black and red.
events.arc: A Wake in the Border Town

effects.log: It catches the light. The lantern glows a little warmer.

choices.text: Walk the soldier to the gate at dawn

effects.log: The gate swings shut behind him, softly, as the watcher would have done.

events.text: You leave the soldier to fate, and the soldier is eventually let in, but late. By then the soldier has said a piece to the door and gone, unrecognised. {npc} finds the medal on the step in the morning and hangs it by the lantern, without comment. Nobody ever says whose it was. The town learns, quietly, to open the door sooner.
events.arc: A Wake in the Border Town

choices.text: Say a word to {npc} about the medal

effects.log: {He} nods. "We will open sooner," {he} says. "Next time."

choices.text: Hang another lantern beside the first

effects.log: Two lights burn at the gate. The town calls it the Welcome.

events.text: Once a year the border town bakes a great loaf the length of a street, black on one side and white on the other, to be broken by the whole population. {npc}, the head baker, has made it for three hundred years and is in despair this spring: the black flour has failed and the white is thin. {He} asks if you know a merchant who might sell fine flour on trust.
events.arc: The Festival Bread of the Border Town

choices.text: Ask around the market for flour

effects.log: It takes three days and a great deal of charm. Two merchants agree.

choices.text: Offer to help with the baking itself

effects.log: You knead a dough the size of a boat. Your arms ache for a week.

choices.text: Say you have no head for flour

effects.log: {npc} goes back to the oven with a heavy sigh.

events.text: The flour arrives, a dark grey and a pale cream, neither quite right. The loaf comes out of the oven mottled, with a swirl through the middle that nobody planned. The town looks at it in doubt. A child says it looks like a storm cloud. {npc} says it is a failure. You are asked to say whether the loaf is fit to be broken.
events.arc: The Festival Bread of the Border Town

choices.text: Say it is the finest loaf you have seen

effects.log: It is broken, and it is delicious. The swirl is hailed as a design.

choices.text: Say a loaf is for eating, not for looking

effects.log: The town agrees heartily. The storm-cloud loaf is eaten in an hour.

choices.text: Say it is not what you expected

effects.log: {npc} goes pale and walks off to the oven. The town eats anyway.

events.text: The mottled loaf is remembered. For years afterward the town bakes it on purpose: grey and cream, swirled like a storm. {npc} sets up a plaque in the bakery: “Mistakes of the first rank.” You are given the heel of the loaf each spring, which is the best part, and a small cloud of flour on your sleeve that refuses to brush off.
events.arc: The Festival Bread of the Border Town

effects.log: It is crisp and sour and wonderful. You eat it on the gate step.
The dough remembers your hands.

events.text: The loaf is eaten in an hour and forgotten, though {npc} keeps the recipe of the failure in a drawer. Years later, when the black flour fails again, the drawer is opened and the failure is baked again, deliberately. It is a success. The town, unaware of the history, pronounces it the best the baker has made.
events.arc: The Festival Bread of the Border Town

effects.log: It is a small secret that does no harm.

choices.text: Tell the baker the first time was better

effects.log: {He} laughs, and slices the heel for you.

events.text: In the Demon Realm border town the post is carried at night, because by day the road is too crowded with two realms' worth of traffic. {npc} walks it with a black lantern and a satchel, knocking on doors that never answer. {He} says the best letters arrive when no one is awake to take them, and that the sleeping know it. You are invited to walk the round.
events.arc: The Night Postman of the Border Town

effects.log: The town is quiet. The doors seem to breathe. {npc} hums and knocks and leaves each letter on the sill.

choices.text: Carry the satchel for part of the way

effects.log: It is heavy with other people's news. You do not read any.

choices.text: Say you prefer to sleep at night

effects.log: {npc} nods kindly. "Most do," {he} says.

events.text: One door answers. An old neighbour in a worn gown stands in it, awake, and holds out a hand for a letter that is not there. {npc} says there is none tonight. The neighbour nods, takes it well, and closes the door. {npc} stands in the street with the lantern a long time. “They have asked every night for forty years,” {he} says. “There has never been one.”
events.arc: The Night Postman of the Border Town

choices.text: Suggest writing the neighbour a letter yourself

effects.log: {npc} looks at you sharply. Then, slowly, nods. The idea has never occurred to {him}.

choices.text: Suggest asking the town to write to the neighbour

effects.log: {npc} blinks. "All of them?" {he} says. "Yes."

choices.text: Say it is not the postman's business

effects.log: {npc} is silent. The lantern burns low.

events.text: The letter is a brief one, written in your best hand: “Dear neighbour, I hope you are well. I hope the nights are kind.” {npc} delivers it the next night and the door opens. The neighbour reads it on the step by the lantern and says nothing. Then: “Thank you.” The next night the neighbour sleeps, and a reply lies on the sill.
events.arc: The Night Postman of the Border Town

effects.log: It is a quiet, years-long correspondence between strangers. You love it.
The postman does, gladly, and begins writing a letter each night.

events.text: The town writes to the neighbour, in dozens of small hands: a child, a soldier, a baker, a barber. The letters arrive in a heap. They are read one by one, each night, by lantern-light on the step. By spring the replies come, and they are the best-loved letters in the town. {npc} says it is the finest thing the post has ever done, and takes no credit.
events.arc: The Night Postman of the Border Town

choices.text: Read a reply on the step

effects.log: It is witty and wry and kind. You laugh in the dark.
It becomes a custom: one letter a week to someone who is alone.

events.text: A clerk of the Ministry of Lamps, {npc}, has lit the lamps of the wrong bridge for three hundred nights. The Long Bridge, which needed them, has been dark; the Little Bridge, which did not, has been blazing. {He} found out only this morning, when a ferry-pilot complained. {He} stands now at the Ministry door, ashen. {He} asks you what to do.
events.arc: The Clerk of Lamps Who Lit the Wrong Bridge

effects.log: {npc} nods and begins composing a letter in {his} head. {His} hands shake.

choices.text: Say light both bridges and say nothing

effects.log: {npc} brightens, and then thinks better of it.

choices.text: Say it is a mistake anyone could make

effects.log: {npc} says it is a mistake exactly one person could make.

events.text: The Little Bridge, it turns out, has loved its three hundred nights of light. The residents of the Little Bridge have held dinners under the lamps, and a small festival has grown up there. They send a petition: please do not take away the lamps. The Long Bridge residents send another: please put back ours. {npc} holds both and sits down on the Ministry steps.
events.arc: The Clerk of Lamps Who Lit the Wrong Bridge

effects.log: The Ministry budget gasps. The clerk grins.

choices.text: Suggest asking each bridge to share

effects.log: A conference of bridge-dwellers is called. It takes a year and ends in mutual nonsense.

choices.text: Say the Long Bridge comes first

effects.log: {npc} nods dutifully, and the festival on the Little Bridge ends.

events.text: Both bridges are lit. The Ministry sighs, and then, impressed with the festival, issues a new lamp-licence for every bridge in the sky, with a provision for “joy”. {npc} is promoted to something with a title. {He} says it was all a mistake. You agree. It was the best mistake of the century.
events.arc: The Clerk of Lamps Who Lit the Wrong Bridge

effects.log: Two bridges shine across the gap, and a thousand people wave across it.
{He} thanks you with the nervous air of one who is still checking the map.

events.text: The two bridges confer for a year, and the result is a rota: the Little Bridge lit on odd nights, the Long on even, with both on feast days. Neither is perfectly satisfied. Both are, in a way, content. {npc} writes the rota out in a firm, clear hand, framed on the Ministry wall, headed: Resolved, Imperfectly.
events.arc: The Clerk of Lamps Who Lit the Wrong Bridge

choices.text: Visit the Little Bridge on an odd night

effects.log: The lamps burn gold. The dinner goes on.

choices.text: Visit the Long Bridge on an even night

effects.log: The lamps burn steady. A hush falls on the crossing.

events.text: On the dyers' row of the Cloud Market, {npc} dyes silk the colours of dawns and moods. Customers bring a memory and {he} matches it. Today a customer asks for the colour of the sky on the last day of a marriage. {npc} falls silent. {He} has never been asked for a colour like that, and cannot find it among the vats. {He} turns to you.
events.arc: The Cloud-Silk Dyer Who Could Not Match a Colour

choices.text: Describe the sky of an unhappy day

effects.log: You say it was white, flat, and slightly warm. {npc} nods and begins to mix.

choices.text: Ask the customer to describe it

effects.log: The customer does, haltingly. The dye comes slowly to match the words.
{npc} frowns. "I have never failed a colour," {he} says.

events.text: The dye comes out a pale, tender grey, with a thread of gold. The customer holds it to the light and weeps, pays, and leaves it on a chair at the edge of the market, where a stranger picks it up and walks away with it. {npc} runs after them. “That is not yours!” {he} cries. The stranger shrugs: “It is the colour of everybody's sky.”
events.arc: The Cloud-Silk Dyer Who Could Not Match a Colour

effects.log: You chase it across three stalls and a bridge. At the end, the stranger is the woman's sister.
{He} sags, then nods. "Perhaps it is meant to travel," {he} says.
The silk is lost. The tea is hot and sweet.

events.text: The silk is returned. The sister and the woman sit on the market step, with the silk across their knees, sharing a flask. Later the sister commissions the dyer to make a second bolt in the colour of the first day, and the two silks are woven together into a single shawl. {npc} says it is the finest piece to leave the row. It has no price.
events.arc: The Cloud-Silk Dyer Who Could Not Match a Colour

effects.log: It is grey and gold and rose, and warm to the eye.

choices.text: Tell the sisters they are lucky

effects.log: They smile at you through tears. The shawl goes home between them.

events.text: The silk travels. Years later you see a scrap of it in a cloud-market stall on a far isle: a pale, tender grey with a thread of gold, hanging as a banner. The seller says it is of unknown origin and brings good luck. You do not correct them. You buy a handspan for a stone and tie it to your sleeve, where it stays.
events.arc: The Cloud-Silk Dyer Who Could Not Match a Colour

choices.text: Keep the scrap on your sleeve

effects.log: It is soft, and mysteriously warm.
{He} laughs until the tears come. "Good," {he} says. "Let it be good luck."

events.text: On a high pasture, {npc} keeps a herd of wind-serpents: long, pale creatures that braid through the air and give a smooth, clean wind that the Ministry buys by the season. They do not like strangers, and they like each other less. {He} invites you to help move the herd to the lee side before the storm season.
events.arc: The Rancher of Wind-Serpents

effects.log: You wave a long pole and sing. The serpents flow ahead, a river of white in the air.

choices.text: Stay with {npc} and watch from the rise

effects.log: The herd moves in loops. It looks like a handwritten letter.

choices.text: Say serpents are best left alone

effects.log: {npc} nods. The herd moves without you, only slower.

events.text: One young serpent will not move. It coils around a fence-post and stares at nothing. {npc} says it has done this before: it is mourning, in the way of its kind, a mate that was caught in a storm. The herd will go on without it. {npc} asks whether to leave the creature or to try to coax it, and whether either is kind.
events.arc: The Rancher of Wind-Serpents

choices.text: Sit with the serpent a while

effects.log: You sit three hours. The serpent uncoils slowly and rests its head on your boot.
It takes a morsel. It follows, grudgingly.
{npc} nods. The herd moves on without it.

events.text: The serpent, calmed, rejoins the herd in the lee of the isle, and the storm season passes with no loss. The following spring, it brings a young serpent of its own to the pasture, a thin pale thing with a bright eye. {npc} names the youngster after you. You are embarrassed and delighted. It flies in loops around your head whenever you visit.
events.arc: The Rancher of Wind-Serpents

effects.log: It winds around your arm like a scarf, a small cold friend.
You learn the names of all forty serpents and some of their moods.

events.text: The serpent follows the herd and is quiet for a year. Then, one windless dawn, it leaves the pasture without a sound and is not seen again. {npc} says it went to find its mate in the wind. The pasture sings a little differently after that: a low note under the rest, like a held breath. You hear it sometimes on still mornings.
events.arc: The Rancher of Wind-Serpents

choices.text: Stand in the pasture on a still dawn

effects.log: The low note comes. You hold your breath, and the note holds with you.
{He} smiles. "So can I," {he} says. "I thought I was alone."

events.text: At the foot of the Storm Isle a glass-blower catches lightning in bottles. {npc} calls it storm-glass: clear, with a vein of blue at its heart that hums faintly in a storm. The Ministry of Weather buys it to predict the winds. {He} blows a bubble and lets you hold it. It trembles in your palm like a sleeping bird.
events.arc: The Storm-Glass Blower

effects.log: It hums a little louder and then quiet. {npc} nods with approval.

choices.text: Ask how the lightning is caught

effects.log: "Gently," says {npc}. "It is the only way."

choices.text: Hand the bubble back at once

effects.log: {npc} laughs. "Most do," {he} says.

events.text: A single piece of storm-glass in the shop begins to hum at midday, loudly, out of season. {npc} hushes the shop. The humming rises. Outside the sky is clear. {He} looks at the clock, at the glass, at you. “It is predicting something,” {he} says. “Not a storm. It is predicting something else. I do not know what it is.”
events.arc: The Storm-Glass Blower

choices.text: Take the glass to the Ministry of Weather

effects.log: The clerks consult a hundred charts. The reading is a mystery.
You sit in the shop all afternoon. The hum fades at dusk.

choices.text: Say it is a faulty piece

effects.log: {npc} bristles. "It has never been faulty," {he} says.

events.text: At dusk a wedding procession comes up the lane, unexpected, two isles' worth of people in red and gold, and a bride and groom who stop at the glass-blower's door and ask for a wedding-glass. {npc} stares at the humming piece. “That is what it was predicting,” {he} says, and begins to laugh. It is a glass for a marriage, and it sounds like a song.
events.arc: The Storm-Glass Blower

effects.log: You hold the piece as the couple touch it together. It rings, once, clear.
The lane is full of bright cloth. You are glad to be in it.

events.text: The piece is sent to the Ministry, and after a year the clerks conclude it was predicting a lull in the storms. The lull arrives on schedule. Nobody remembers the afternoon in the shop. {npc} keeps a copy of the reading framed, with a note: “Correct, as far as it goes.” The hum, on certain still days, comes back for a moment, and {he} says it is saying hello.
events.arc: The Storm-Glass Blower

choices.text: Visit the shop on a still day

effects.log: You hear it, faint and sweet. {npc} offers you tea.

choices.text: Buy a small piece of storm-glass

effects.log: It hums when you are sad. You keep it in a drawer. It rarely needs to.

events.text: On the Seven Stairs, a young heaven-born who tested as a prodigy at the sword has quietly requested a post as a clerk in the Ministry of Registers. {npc}, their master, is appalled. The young one explains, mildly, that they love the filing: every slip a small life, every drawer a little country. {npc} asks you to talk some sense into the youngster.
events.arc: The Heaven-Born Who Chose to Be a Clerk

choices.text: Talk to the young one over tea

effects.log: They speak of drawers with the glow of a poet. You find yourself unconvinced and then convinced.

choices.text: Talk to the master about letting go

effects.log: {npc} sags. "I had plans," {he} says. "They were mine, not theirs."

choices.text: Say talent should not be wasted

effects.log: {npc} nods and glows. The young one looks away.

events.text: The young one begins as a junior clerk, and is brilliant, quiet and gentle. Within a decade they have reorganised a drawer that no one had touched in four centuries and found, in it, an unpaid pension owed to eighty widows. The Ministry is stunned. The master is silent. Then {npc} writes you a long, awkward letter: “Was I wrong?”
events.arc: The Heaven-Born Who Chose to Be a Clerk

choices.text: Answer: no, but you were not alone

effects.log: Your reply is kind. {npc} frames it.

choices.text: Answer: they have found their sword

effects.log: {npc} reads it three times. "The drawer is the sword," {he} says.

choices.text: Answer: it is not for me to say

effects.log: {npc} does not write again for a year.

events.text: The master visits the clerk at the Ministry, bringing a gift of an old sword in a plain scabbard. “For the drawer,” {he} says, and the clerk laughs. The sword hangs on the filing room wall. It has never been drawn. Clerks come to look at it and murmur, “Ah, the sword of the Ministry.” It is the best-guarded weapon in the sky.
events.arc: The Heaven-Born Who Chose to Be a Clerk

choices.text: Attend the hanging of the sword

effects.log: It is a small ceremony. The master wipes {his} eyes.
They bow, shy and glad. The drawer, open, is full of light.

events.text: The master and the young one speak little for years. Then, one winter, the young one finds a reason to visit the Stairs and asks to be taught a single sword form, for no purpose but to know it. The master teaches it in an afternoon. They part in silence, content. The form is never used, but the clerk keeps it, in the way of some things, as a comfort.
events.arc: The Heaven-Born Who Chose to Be a Clerk

choices.text: Watch the single lesson from the edge

effects.log: The form is plain and perfect. Neither speaks.
It is taken without a word. The cups are set down together.

events.text: In the dead-letter drawers of the Edge Post you find a bundle tied with green thread. Each letter bears the same stamp, a tiny crane, and every one is addressed to the same person at the same address, written eleven centuries apart. The clerk says no one has claimed any of them. The address is a house that fell into the cloud sea long ago.

choices.text: Read one letter, and leave it open

effects.log: It is a short note of greeting. The writer hopes the recipient is well. Eleven centuries is a long hope.

choices.text: Ask the clerk to keep the bundle together

effects.log: The clerk ties the thread again, tighter. "We do," she says.

choices.text: Add your own letter to the bundle

effects.log: It is addressed to the same house, with no message but your name.

events.text: A courier on the Wind Isle delivers letters at a pace that is considered rude, strolling from door to door with a flask of tea and a book. He is never late: the letters are slow letters, written to be received in a century or so. He has a satchel of a thousand and a gentle air. A child asks him if he ever gets bored. He says he has never been bored in his life.

choices.text: Walk a lane of the round beside him

effects.log: The lane is long and shaded. You have never been so unhurried.

choices.text: Give him a slow letter to carry

effects.log: It is addressed to yourself, in a hundred years. He nods and puts it deep in the satchel.
He tips his hat. It is two hours before he is out of sight.

events.text: A master potter has kept, for a thousand years, the very first cup her teacher made, chipped and ugly, on a high shelf. Today a visitor asks to see it. The potter takes it down, holds it a moment, and says that it has never been used, because the teacher said the best cup is the one you save. The visitor asks whether the teacher would mind if it were used now.

effects.log: She pours tea into it, hands trembling. It holds. She drinks, and sets it back on the shelf, used.

choices.text: Suggest she save it a little longer

effects.log: She nods and puts it back, content. The shelf keeps its secret.

choices.text: Say a cup is a cup

effects.log: She laughs and offers you tea in a different one.

events.text: On the mountain a former pupil returns to visit a master after four hundred years. The master does not remember the pupil. The pupil does not mind. They sit and drink tea together and talk of weather. At the end the master says: “You were a good pupil, I think.” The pupil bows. “I was a very bad one,” she says. Both are pleased.

choices.text: Pour another round of tea for them

effects.log: The tea steams between two people sharing a quiet that has taken four centuries to earn.
You close the door on a rare and gentle thing.

choices.text: Tell the master the pupil had a gift

effects.log: The master looks pleased. "Of course," they say. "Of course."

events.text: A wedding procession crosses the Long Bridge, and the bridge-toll clerk, who has seen eleven thousand weddings, stops the line to check the groom's papers. A hush falls. The clerk, solemn, holds up the form to the light, then to the bride, then to the sky. Then he stamps it, with a flourish, and shouts: “Pass, with joy!” The bridge erupts.

effects.log: You are thrown a handful of petals. They stay in your hair for days.

choices.text: Pay the couple's toll as a gift (1 spirit stone)

effects.log: It is a lovely small gesture. The couple never knows who.
You walk through a carpet of blossom and think of old festivals.

events.text: On Reed Lake two skiffs always row to opposite shores in the morning, the same two, and pass in the middle of the lake without looking at each other. Locals have a habit of calling out as they pass: one cries “fair weather” and the other answers “foul”, a ritual from some old quarrel. No one remembers which of them first said which.

choices.text: Call out “fair weather” from the shore

effects.log: Both skiffs hesitate. One of them answers "fair". The other almost smiles.

choices.text: Call out “foul” and see what happens

effects.log: Both skiffs turn and stare. You are quickly forgotten.

choices.text: Row out and sit between them

effects.log: They both stop. An hour of silence passes. It is oddly pleasant.

events.text: A dumpling-master of the Silver Quarter has trained forty apprentices in sixty years, and all of them make a dumpling subtly different from hers. She says she cannot tell which is better, only which are hers. A visitor asks her to name her best student. She says: “The one who is no longer in my kitchen.”

effects.log: "That would be telling," she says. "And they are not here to hear it."

choices.text: Try a dumpling from each of the forty

effects.log: It takes an evening. Each is remarkable. None is the same.
She bows and offers you a dumpling for the road.

events.text: In the Hall of Registers a master clerk and their former apprentice, now their superior, work at adjoining desks and never mention the change. When the apprentice needs something filed, they place it on the master's desk with a note: “If it would not trouble you.” The master files it, perfectly, with a small mark of approval. Neither says a word.

effects.log: It is set between the desks. Both reach for it at once and laugh.

choices.text: Say nothing and file your own papers

effects.log: The room hums with unspoken kindness.
The master reddens. "It is an old habit," they say.

events.text: On the observation terrace a young navigator is learning from an old one how to read the sky. The old one says the stars are not fixed, only slow. The young one asks which star is the slowest. The old one points to a faint point and says that star is the oldest friend she has, and that she has been waiting for it to move for six hundred years.

choices.text: Wait with them for the star to move

effects.log: It does not. The night is cold and glittering. You are glad of the company.
The old one smiles. "That is what I tell myself," she says.

choices.text: Ask the young one what they see

effects.log: "A very small light," the young one says. "That is enough."

events.text: A couple is married in the middle of the Long Bridge because neither isle will concede the other's shore. Guests stand in two crowds, one on each side, craning to hear. The bridge sways with the weight of three hundred well-wishers, and the clerk who performs the ceremony says the vows twice so that both sides can hear.

choices.text: Cheer from your own side of the bridge

effects.log: A cheer returns from the far side. It is the best echo of the year.

choices.text: Walk to the middle and stand with the couple

effects.log: You are given a flower and a small seat on a plank. The vows are lovely.

choices.text: Watch from the shore with tea

effects.log: The whole bridge glows in the evening sun. You think of nothing at all.

events.text: At dusk in the border town the lanes fill with people strolling in the red light of the lanterns, nodding at one another, buying roasted chestnuts, stopping to talk. A Demon Realm soldier and a Court scholar walk side by side, arguing cheerfully about whether the moon looks larger from the east or the west. Nobody is in a hurry.

effects.log: The chestnuts are hot. The argument gets better as you add your own.
They accept with the equanimity of the well-fed.

choices.text: Sit on a bench and watch

effects.log: The lanterns come on one by one. You feel at home.

events.text: At a tea-house in the border town of the Demon Realm, a sign says: “A guest may not leave until the cup is empty, and the cup may not be empty until the guest is ready.” A newcomer reads this three times and sits down, perplexed. The old owner pours without comment. An hour later the newcomer is still there, calm, and the cup is still full.

choices.text: Sit with them in the quiet

effects.log: The hour passes. The cup stays full, and you do not mind.

choices.text: Ask the owner what the rule means

effects.log: "What it says," the owner replies, and refills the cup.

choices.text: Leave a coin and slip out

effects.log: The cup is empty by the time you reach the door. You are not sure how.

events.text: At the Edge Post a long queue forms for the daily departure of the evening skiff. A woman is saying goodbye to her old friend with a very formal bow, the sort given at funerals, and then a quick hug that surprises both of them. The skiff pulls away. The friend on the quay stands for a long time with a hand half-raised.

choices.text: Stand beside the one who stayed

effects.log: You say nothing. They nod, eyes wet, and thank you with a look.
A hand waves back. It is hard to say whose.

choices.text: Offer tea at the quay-side stall

effects.log: It is a quiet cup, shared, and the dusk comes down.

events.text: A notice has been pinned on the Cedar Isle's board: “Two households have decided to become one house again after a long quarrel. All are invited to dinner, and no explanation is offered or required.” The board is surrounded by people reading it three times and then quietly smiling. A child asks why it is a notice. A grandmother says it is a small miracle.

effects.log: It is a noisy, laughing, forgiving evening. You are glad you came.
It arrives with a note: "To the house that is one." They write back.

choices.text: Read the notice again and smile

effects.log: You pin a small flower beside it. By morning it is gone.

events.text: A wind-serpent has taken to wearing a hat. The hat was dropped by a passing immortal, and the serpent, long and pale and solemn, wears it perched on its head, wherever it goes. The rancher says the creature is quite vain. When people laugh, the serpent lowers its head and looks wounded. When people bow, it preens.

effects.log: It lifts its head and the hat tips. A friendship is struck.

choices.text: Tell it the hat suits it

effects.log: It coils with pleasure. You are rewarded with a ribbon of cool wind.

choices.text: Offer to buy it a better hat

effects.log: It declines, turning away. Some loves are particular.

events.text: A young storm-chaser is learning the trade from an old one by following her from storm to storm. The old one stands in the rain with her arms wide and tells the young one to stop flinching. The young one flinches. The old one laughs, shields her with a coat, and says: “Not yet, then. But soon.” The rain falls on both.

choices.text: Stand with the old one and open your arms

effects.log: The rain is cold and surprisingly kind. The young one watches, and learns.

choices.text: Hand the young one a dry cloth

effects.log: It is taken gratefully. The trade, you suspect, is mostly cloths.
You are dry, and a little envious.

events.text: At the market a stall sells letters. Not paper, but written ones: a letter of thanks, a letter of apology, a letter of long-delayed love, composed by a silver-haired scribe at a modest price. The line is long. People come out looking lighter. A rogue ahead of you buys three, and holds them against their chest as they walk away.

choices.text: Buy a letter of thanks (1 spirit stone)

effects.log: It is addressed to nobody. You carry it for a year, and then you know whom to give it to.

choices.text: Ask the scribe how she writes them

effects.log: "I listen," says the scribe. "And then I write what is left."

choices.text: Watch the line and walk on

effects.log: It moves very slowly, which seems to be the point.

events.text: A master of the bamboo-sword is teaching on the lawn when she falls asleep standing up, blade in hand. The pupils freeze. Sunlight lies over the lawn. A sparrow lands on her sleeve. One pupil, very quietly, takes a step forward and practises the form beside her. Then another. Soon the whole class is practising around her, in silence.

choices.text: Join the class in silent practice

effects.log: The form is steady and beautiful. The master smiles in her sleep.

choices.text: Take the sparrow gently from her sleeve

effects.log: It chirps once and returns to her shoulder. Lesson learned.

choices.text: Stand guard at the edge of the lawn

effects.log: No one disturbs the class. You feel oddly proud.

events.text: A dinner on the Cedar Isle gathers six old friends who have not met in a century. They are all quite changed. One is a hermit, one a clerk, one a rogue, one a master of tea, one a retired general and one a child again by some trick of cultivation. They stare at each other over the soup and burst into laughter at the same moment.

choices.text: Pour the wine for them all

effects.log: The evening is long and warm. They toast absent friends.

choices.text: Listen to their stories at the edge of the table

effects.log: You learn of a hundred years of small things in an evening.
The door closes on laughter. It is a good sound.

events.text: Under a loose floorboard in a rented room you find a box of letters never sent, all addressed to the same name and all unfinished: a few words, a line, a half page. The last one says only “Dear friend, I wanted to tell you that”. The ink has faded. You do not know the name. The landlord says the last tenant left a hundred years ago.

choices.text: Finish the last letter and send it

effects.log: You write what you hope the writer meant. It goes into the wind.

choices.text: Put the box back under the board

effects.log: Some silences are best left where they were found.

choices.text: Take the box to the Edge Post

effects.log: The clerk files it with reverence, in the long room of unanswered things.

events.text: Two old singers, a duet for six hundred years, have not sung together since a falling-out over a harmony. Today one of them sings alone on the cliffs, and the wind carries the song. After a time, from the far cliff, the other voice joins in, a third lower, exactly where the harmony should be. Neither looks at the other. The song is perfect.

choices.text: Listen from the middle of the gap

effects.log: The two voices meet over your head. You hear what it was that they had.
Both turn. Neither bows. Both are, you think, a little undone.

choices.text: Say nothing, and let it rest

effects.log: The cliffs are silent again. Something in you is warmer.

events.text: In the hot spring pools it is customary to confess one small thing to the water, which is said to forgive. A child beside you confesses to eating the last dumpling. An old man confesses to doing the same, thirty years ago. A woman confesses she does not like her mother's tea. The water bubbles with what looks like patient amusement.

choices.text: Confess something small of your own

effects.log: The water warms around you. Something loosens in your chest.
You are privy to a hundred small honesties. They are beautiful.

choices.text: Soak quietly and keep your sins

effects.log: The water, polite, does not press.

events.text: In the ruins of an old watchtower a letter has been pinned to the wall under a stone, addressed “To whoever holds this post next”. It is dated nine hundred years ago. It says only: “It is quiet here. Do not be afraid of the quiet. It was a good companion.” Someone has added in a different ink: “Still true.” And another: “Still true.”

effects.log: You write it with a nail. The wall holds the words a little longer.

choices.text: Sit in the quiet for an hour

effects.log: It is a good companion. It does not ask for anything.

choices.text: Copy the letter to carry with you

effects.log: You keep it in your sleeve. It is lighter than most books.

events.text: A grotto in the cliffs turns out to be a practice-room, secret from the school above it, where a pupil goes in the evenings to practise a form the master has forbidden. The pupil is startled to see you. The form, in the half-light, is beautiful. The master must have known; the cave smells of the master's tea.

effects.log: The pupil bows, grateful. The form begins again, even more graceful.

choices.text: Watch the form to its end

effects.log: It is a fine and strange sequence. You do not forget it.

choices.text: Leave a cup of tea at the cave's mouth

effects.log: In the morning the cup is empty, and another has been left beside it.

events.text: A tree on the Blossom Isle that has not flowered in two hundred years blooms the morning of a wedding between its two oldest caretakers, who have been silently in love for just that long. The petals fall on the guests like a slow pink snowfall. The couple look at the tree with matching astonishment. Then at each other.

choices.text: Throw a handful of petals back into the air

effects.log: The wind takes them. A child shrieks with joy.
A branch dips. A petal lands in your cup.

choices.text: Slip away to leave them their moment

effects.log: The petals follow you down the lane like confetti.

events.text: On the Willow Isle there is a ward for those who caught the Long Fever from a badly passed tribulation. They cannot die of it and cannot be rid of it. {npc}, the healer, has tended them for six centuries and asks you to sit a watch, because the patients, {he} says, are tired of the same few faces.
events.arc: The Ward of the Long Fever

choices.text: Sit the watch and talk with them

effects.log: They ask about weather, about prices, about anything that moves. You leave hoarse and oddly glad.

choices.text: Bring a bolt of fresh mist for the beds

effects.log: The mist keeps the ward cool. {npc} notes the gift in a ledger kept for a hundred years of small mercies.

choices.text: Say you are no healer and leave

effects.log: {npc} nods as though {he} has heard it before, and goes on folding sheets.

events.text: One patient, an old lute-maker, asks you to take a message to a sister on the Cinder Isle, who has not answered a letter in two hundred years. {npc} warns you gently that the sister may have died, or may only have grown tired. "Either way," {he} says, "someone should ask."
events.arc: The Ward of the Long Fever

effects.log: You cross the fleet in a hired skiff. The journey teaches you how far two hundred years can be.

choices.text: Write to the sister and wait for the reply

effects.log: You wait. The wait is its own kind of sickness. You learn what the ward learns.

choices.text: Tell the lute-maker it is not worth the trouble

effects.log: The old patient turns to the wall. {npc} pulls the blanket up without a word.

events.text: The sister is alive, bent over a loom, and has been writing to the lute-maker for two centuries in letters never sent. "I could not post them," the sister says. "I did not want to hear that the lute-maker was well." You carry the whole stack back in a basket.
events.arc: The Ward of the Long Fever

choices.text: Read them aloud to the lute-maker

effects.log: The reading takes a month. Somewhere in the second week the patient stops hurting, a little, and does not say why.

choices.text: Leave the basket on the bed and go

effects.log: You hear the rustle of pages from the corridor all night. {npc} says nothing, which is thanks.

events.text: The reply comes at last in a stranger's hand: the sister died a century ago, and the loom has been run by a niece, who found your letter and wrote back kindly. The lute-maker listens to it twice and asks to hear it again. {npc} sits with you in the corridor and says some patients are made well by news, and some by company.
events.arc: The Ward of the Long Fever

choices.text: Keep writing to the niece for the lute-maker

effects.log: The letters go on for decades. The lute-maker never recovers, and never finishes being cared for.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to teach you the ward's routines

effects.log: You learn to turn a bed without waking the dreamer. It is skill you will use for the rest of your life.

events.text: Beneath the Orchard Isle is a cellar of cots where immortals sleep out a century each, cured by dreaming of an illness the waking cannot reach. {npc} keeps the keys and turns the sleepers monthly. A new cot has been made up, and the name on it is yours, though you do not feel unwell.
events.arc: The Sleepers Under the Orchard

choices.text: Ask {npc} what the cot has seen in you

effects.log: "A tiredness older than you know," says {he}. "Come back when it grows teeth."

choices.text: Take the cot out of sheer curiosity

effects.log: You wake an afternoon later, rested in a way that shames the long nights of your cultivation.

choices.text: Strike the name from the cot

effects.log: {npc} leaves the cot made, in case you change your mind.

events.text: {npc} is turning sleepers when one of them, a navigator, speaks in {his} sleep: a chart of shoals, a name, a date. The date is next week. The shoals are real, and a fleet is due to cross them. {He} asks whether a sleeper's dream should be heeded.
events.arc: The Sleepers Under the Orchard

effects.log: The fleet reroutes with grumbling. The shoals are exactly where the sleeper said.

choices.text: Wait and watch the shoals yourself

effects.log: You sit at the edge of the reef through a night of wind and see the first hulls scrape. Nobody is hurt, because you have signalled early.

choices.text: Say a dream is only a dream

effects.log: {npc} looks at you for a long moment. Next week a skiff runs aground.

events.text: The navigator wakes in spring, thin and puzzled, and is told that a fleet was saved by the dream. {He} asks to meet the one who heeded it. When you come, the navigator takes your hand and says only: "Then it was not wasted." Fleet-folk begin to leave small gifts on the sleepers' steps.
events.arc: The Sleepers Under the Orchard

choices.text: Accept the gifts for the ward, not for yourself

effects.log: {npc} puts them to use in the cellar: cleaner linen, better lamps.
