choices.text: Ask the navigator to draw what else was seen

effects.log: The drawing is a map of nothing you can place. You keep it, and it begins to make sense in a decade.

events.text: You keep your watch at the reef and learn how many skiffs there are on a bad night. At dawn the navigator, still asleep, speaks one more word: your name. {npc} says the ward takes its debts seriously. A new cot is made up, and this time it is for a friend.
events.arc: The Sleepers Under the Orchard

choices.text: Sit by the friend's cot a season

effects.log: You keep a lamp on the pillow. The friend wakes smiling and does not say why.

choices.text: Offer to fund a second ward

effects.log: It takes a decade of fund-raising among fleets that remember the shoals.

events.text: In the Reed Lake infirmary, {npc} is the healer of a rare complaint: immortals who forget nothing. Their patient, an aged archivist, can recall every raindrop of nine thousand years and cannot sleep for the noise of it. {npc} asks if you will come and talk of something new.
events.arc: The Patient Who Remembered Too Much

effects.log: The archivist listens as if hearing of a foreign country. The ward is quiet an hour.

choices.text: Bring a puzzle the archivist has not seen

effects.log: It takes two days to solve. The archivist laughs for the first time in a century.
{npc} notes the refusal in the book of visits.

events.text: The archivist asks a strange favour: to be allowed to forget one thing, a quarrel with a friend long dead. {npc} says there is a draught from the lake's reeds that dulls one memory for good, but never the memory one chooses. The patient wants you to say whether it is worth the risk.
events.arc: The Patient Who Remembered Too Much

choices.text: Say the draught is worth trying

effects.log: The patient drinks it and weeps for an hour. The next morning the quarrel is gone, and so is something else.

choices.text: Say a memory is a friend, even a painful one

effects.log: The patient puts the cup down. {npc} nods, relieved, and no one speaks.

choices.text: Say you cannot answer for another

effects.log: The archivist smiles thinly. "No one can," the patient says. "Thank you for not pretending."

events.text: The draught takes the quarrel and, along with it, the friend: the archivist cannot remember the friend at all. A grave in the lake garden goes unvisited. {npc} asks you to visit it with fresh flowers each year, in the patient's stead.
events.arc: The Patient Who Remembered Too Much

effects.log: You do. The patient never knows, and is, you hope, a little lighter for it.

choices.text: Tell the patient of the friend, gently

effects.log: The archivist listens, politely, as to a story told of strangers. Then asks to hear it again.

events.text: The patient keeps the quarrel and, over the years, learns to carry it. When the friend's old letters are found in a trunk, the patient reads them aloud to the lake, a page a day. The quarrel is not forgiven so much as befriended. {npc} calls it the best cure of the infirmary's history.
events.arc: The Patient Who Remembered Too Much

effects.log: The last page is one line: "I was wrong, and so were you." The archivist laughs like a young person.

choices.text: Write down the cure for the infirmary's book

effects.log: The note is read by healers for a thousand years.

events.text: Only the attendants may draw from the Jade Spring: twelve of them, each wearing a pale sash and taking an oath of silence at the rim. {npc}, the eldest, has not spoken in nineteen hundred years. {He} stops you at the steps with a raised hand, then points to a bucket, then to you.
events.arc: The Attendants of the Jade Spring

effects.log: You carry water for a whole day, and nobody speaks. The silence is unexpectedly restful.

choices.text: Ask what the bucket is for

effects.log: {npc} only looks at you. Eventually you take it up anyway.
The attendant bows, as though you had passed some other test.

events.text: The attendants have a custom: on the last night of the year, each speaks one word to the spring, and the word is never told. {npc} hands you a slip of jade with a blank line. "Choose," the slip says, in a hand like water.
events.arc: The Attendants of the Jade Spring

effects.log: You write it and drop the slip in. The water takes it down without a ripple.

choices.text: Write a word for the one you miss

effects.log: The slip sinks. For some days afterwards you feel the water in your sleeves.
The attendant accepts the blank slip with a small, approving nod.

events.text: On the first morning of the new year the spring runs a shade clearer. {npc} looks at you, then at the water, and speaks aloud for the first time in nineteen hundred years: "Thank you." The twelve attendants all turn their heads. It is the loudest sound in the Heavens.
events.arc: The Attendants of the Jade Spring

effects.log: Silence returns, richer than before.

choices.text: Reply with the word you wrote

effects.log: The word echoes once off the rim. The attendants smile, each in a different way.

events.text: {npc} reads your slip at dawn, as the attendants do not, and says nothing for a day. Then, quietly, the eldest brings the person you miss a bowl of water from the spring, with a note: "Someone drew this for you." It is the nearest the spring can come to speaking.
events.arc: The Attendants of the Jade Spring

choices.text: Drink the water and keep the note

effects.log: It tastes like the first morning of something.
The attendant only points to the water. You think about that for years.

events.text: As a member of the Celestial Ministries you are sent to audit the Jade Spring's dues. Every jar drawn must be written down, and {npc}, the quartermaster, has kept a record so neat it is suspicious. "It is not that I fear audit," {he} says. "It is that I fear being understood."
events.arc: The Inspector of the Jade Spring's Dues

effects.log: They are flawless. Too flawless: a month in the year is written in a second hand.

choices.text: Walk the spring first and read later

effects.log: The attendants tell you nothing, which is itself a clue.

choices.text: Sign it as correct and go home

effects.log: It is done in an hour. The quartermaster seems more troubled by this than by any audit.

events.text: The second hand turns out to belong to a retired attendant who, in the worst winter, let the isle's poor draw a few jars they could not afford, and wrote the dues as paid from {npc}'s own purse. It has gone on for forty years. {He} watches you read it and says, "I will accept the penalty."
events.arc: The Inspector of the Jade Spring's Dues

choices.text: Quietly mark the dues as met

effects.log: You stamp the book. The quartermaster stares as though the stamp might leave.

choices.text: Report it as the Ministry requires

effects.log: The Ministry fines the quartermaster. Fame goes to you, and a chill goes with it.

choices.text: Ask for a month to think

effects.log: The month goes quickly. {npc} waits like a rock at the edge of a tide.

events.text: You close the books and enter "correct." Years later you learn that the isle's poor draw their jars without writing anything, and the spring has never been poorer or richer. {npc} sends you a jar of the water, with a note in two hands.
events.arc: The Inspector of the Jade Spring's Dues

effects.log: It keeps well. You drink a mouthful on hard days.

choices.text: Send a fresh seal of the Ministry to the spring

effects.log: The seal hangs by the rim. The Ministry later recalls the favour as an "administrative decision."

events.text: The fine falls on the quartermaster, who pays it in full, a stone at a time. The poor of the isle go without water one hard winter. By spring {npc} has quietly resigned, and no one remembers who drew what. You are praised for your thoroughness, and the praise sits badly.
events.arc: The Inspector of the Jade Spring's Dues

choices.text: Pay a portion of the fine yourself

effects.log: It is a small act, and there is no one to thank you for it.

choices.text: Accept the praise and say nothing

effects.log: It goes into your file. It is not a happy line.

events.text: Every isle has a bell, and {npc} tunes them all, flying from isle to isle with a fork of star-iron in a case. The Ropewalk Isle's bell has been flat since a collision in the Season of Drift, and the whole isle has quietly stopped noticing. {He} asks you to hold the fork while {he} listens.
events.arc: The Tuner of the Isle Bells

effects.log: The fork hums in your palm. You feel the note go through your arm and into the bones of the isle.

choices.text: Ask what is wrong with the bell

effects.log: "The crack is in the people," {npc} says, "not the bronze."

choices.text: Say the isle is used to it

effects.log: {npc} says that is the problem, and walks on.

events.text: The bell is not cracked. What sounds flat is a hundred small things: a loose rope, a door that sticks, a quarrel nobody mended since the collision. {npc} proposes to tune the isle, not the bell, and needs your help to talk the neighbours into mending what they have let lie.
events.arc: The Tuner of the Isle Bells

choices.text: Go door to door asking after the quarrels

effects.log: You hear a century of grievances. By the end, a few have been laughed off.

choices.text: Mend the rope and the door yourself

effects.log: The easy fixes are done by evening. The quarrels are harder, but the bell sounds a half-tone higher.
{He} takes it up with a sigh, and you hear nothing for a year.

events.text: The neighbours, one by one, speak to one another for the first time in a century. When the bell is rung at the next festival, the note is true, and the whole isle goes quiet to hear it. {npc} stands in the crowd, not in the front, and wipes the fork on a sleeve.
events.arc: The Tuner of the Isle Bells

effects.log: You hear the note with one who has made it a lifetime.
The note rolls out over the cloud sea, and the neighbouring isles ring back.

events.text: The ropes and doors are mended and the bell sounds a half-tone better, but the quarrels remain, and the note never quite settles. {npc} says that is how some isles are, and tunes it a little flat on purpose, with a smile: it is the sound of home.
events.arc: The Tuner of the Isle Bells

effects.log: {npc} laughs. The isle sounds like itself again.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to teach you the fork

effects.log: It takes a decade. You learn to hear what an isle is saying, a little.

events.text: Out on the cloud-reefs hang forty thousand chimes of cloud-glass, tuned by the wind and nothing else. {npc}, the choirmaster, has spent a lifetime learning which chimes ring together on which wind. Tonight a wind has come that no one has heard before, and {he} wants an ear to witness it.
events.arc: The Choirmaster of the Cloud-Reef Chimes

choices.text: Climb out on the reef to listen

effects.log: The reef sways. The chimes begin, one at a time, then all together, a sound with no instrument anywhere.

choices.text: Stay in the hall and listen from there

effects.log: The sound reaches you faint and strange, like a story heard through a wall.

choices.text: Say the wind is not worth the chill

effects.log: {npc} goes out alone and returns at dawn, silent.

events.text: The new wind plays a tune. It repeats every night, always the same eleven notes, as though someone were trying to say something. {npc} writes the notes and asks you to take them to the Ministry of Weather, where a clerk might say whose wind this is.
events.arc: The Choirmaster of the Cloud-Reef Chimes

choices.text: Take the notes to the Ministry

effects.log: The clerk looks at the notes for a long time and says it is the wind of a sunken isle, one that lost its song.

choices.text: Listen another month and write down more

effects.log: The tune lengthens. It is a lullaby, and it is slowly being sung in reverse.

choices.text: Say a wind has no meaning

effects.log: {npc} keeps the notes in a drawer, and keeps listening.

events.text: The sunken isle, the clerk says, is a place the Weather Ministry lost a thousand years ago, and the wind is its last child, looking for the way back. {npc} and you rehearse the lullaby on the chimes for a season. On a still night the wind comes to the reef, hears it, and goes quiet at last.
events.arc: The Choirmaster of the Cloud-Reef Chimes

choices.text: Say a word to the wind as it leaves

effects.log: It takes the word with it. For months you feel a small, warm absence.

choices.text: Ask the choir to play it every year

effects.log: {npc} agrees. It becomes the reef's longest-running tune.

events.text: You and {npc} write down the lullaby backward, the way the wind sings it, and play it forward on the chimes. The wind stops, startled. The next night, it plays something new, and cheerful, and fast, the tune of a creature who has been told it may stay.
events.arc: The Choirmaster of the Cloud-Reef Chimes

effects.log: The pair of you spend a winter on it. The wind answers in kind.
It sings on the reef each night, and no one writes it down.

events.text: The Hushed Isle has a rule: no singing, no humming, no whistling. It was passed after a famous singer's voice shattered a mountain, and nobody has repealed it since. {npc}, a visitor like you, is caught humming at the quay and fined a stone. {He} says the fine is not what hurts, but the shame.
events.arc: The Isle Where No One May Sing

effects.log: {npc} accepts it with a stiff dignity, and later returns the stone with interest in the form of a very good rumour.

choices.text: Ask why the rule is still kept

effects.log: The harbour clerk says it was kept because no one ever asked.
{npc} gives you a flat look, and hums, very faintly, as you walk away.

events.text: The clerk proposes a petition to the isle's council, and asks you to carry it. The old singer who started it all is still alive, living in a cave under the Hushed Isle, and has not been asked in nine hundred years whether the rule should stand. {npc} wants you to go see {him}.
events.arc: The Isle Where No One May Sing

effects.log: The cave is cold and lovely. The singer, bent over a ladle, tells you the rule was a joke that went too far.

choices.text: Take the petition to the council first

effects.log: The council listens with a stern face, and the vote is closer than anyone expected.

choices.text: Wait and see what the isle decides

effects.log: The isle decides nothing for a year. That is what isles do.

events.text: The singer gives a single note, in the cave, to prove a point. It is the most beautiful sound you have heard and it does no harm to anyone. The council, hearing the report, repeals the rule that spring. The first song on the quay is by a child, off key, and it is wonderful.
events.arc: The Isle Where No One May Sing

choices.text: Join the child in the next verse

effects.log: The quay fills with voices badly out of tune. {npc} sings the loudest.

choices.text: Record the singer's note for the archive

effects.log: The jade slip holds a sound that makes the reader sit down quietly.

events.text: The council refuses to repeal, but permits one hour of song a year at the new moon. The first hour is chaotic and moving. {npc} sings a hymn so thin and wavering that the whole quay weeps. You realise the rule has made music more precious than it could ever have been before.
events.arc: The Isle Where No One May Sing

effects.log: It is the shortest and most complete hour of your life.

choices.text: Teach a few of the young to hold a tune

effects.log: The hour grows louder every year.

events.text: {npc} planted a garden when the isle was young, and has tended it a thousand years. The garden has become the isle: its paths are the isle's streets and its wall is the isle's edge. {He} asks you to walk it with {him}, because the garden has never had a guest who was not a gardener.
events.arc: A Garden Over a Thousand Years

effects.log: The garden takes a day to cross. Every tree has a story, and they are all about someone {he} loved.

choices.text: Ask which tree is the oldest

effects.log: {npc} laughs. "The weed in the corner," {he} says. "It was here first."
{npc} watches you go with a small wave.

events.text: A blight has come to the western terrace. The gardener has fought it for ten years and is tired. {npc} asks whether the garden may simply be allowed to change, to let the old trees go and the new weeds come. It is a hard question for someone who has planted every leaf.
events.arc: A Garden Over a Thousand Years

choices.text: Say let the garden go where it goes

effects.log: {npc} breathes out slowly, and for the first time in decades, sits down.

choices.text: Offer to help fight the blight

effects.log: You work for a season, pulling roots and carrying water. The blight retreats but not for long.
{npc} nods. "That is what I say too," {he} says.

events.text: The western terrace turns to a tangle of unplanned flowers. Birds you do not recognise arrive. {npc} spends the spring on a bench, watching them, and says the garden has never been so busy. At dusk {he} brings you a seed from the new growth and asks you to plant it somewhere that is not here.
events.arc: A Garden Over a Thousand Years

choices.text: Plant it on your own isle

effects.log: It grows quickly into a tree no one can name. You water it every day.

choices.text: Plant it at the edge and let it spread

effects.log: By the next century it is a hedge nine miles long. {npc} considers this overdone.

events.text: You and {npc} fight the blight to a draw: the old trees live, a little thinner, and the garden is smaller. {He} accepts this. At the next festival {he} opens the garden to the isle, no longer a private thing, and the paths fill with children running between the thousand-year trunks.
events.arc: A Garden Over a Thousand Years

effects.log: The children are loud. The trees do not mind. It is the happiest festival in memory.

choices.text: Plant a seedling for each child

effects.log: In a century the isle has a forest. Each tree is named.

events.text: A weed grows in a crack of a ruined garden wall on the Fallow Isle. The garden has been gone eight hundred years, and the weed keeps flowering, a small white thing no one can name. {npc}, a travelling botanist, has come to see it and asks if you will help dig around the roots.
events.arc: The Weed That Outlived the Garden

effects.log: Under the wall lies a stone box. It is full of seeds.
{npc} says it is the last of a family of plants the Heavens lost. Nobody had noticed.

choices.text: Say a weed is a weed

effects.log: {npc} gives you a look and kneels on the ground without you.

events.text: The seeds are old, and they are not weeds: they are the cultivated line of an extinct orchard, kept in secret by the gardener who walled them in. A note in the box says: "For whoever is patient." {npc} proposes to grow them out and asks your help in keeping it quiet, so the Ministry of Orchards does not claim them.
events.arc: The Weed That Outlived the Garden

choices.text: Keep the secret and help plant them

effects.log: You hide a nursery in the back of an old cellar. The seedlings come up unnaturally green.

choices.text: Report the find to the Ministry

effects.log: The Ministry sends a clerk with a seal and a wagon. The seeds are archived, never planted.

choices.text: Ask for a share of the seeds

effects.log: {npc} gives you a small packet, and a warning to be patient.

events.text: The orchard blooms in the seventh year: small white flowers, like the weed, followed by fruit with a taste older than any peach. {npc} cuts one in four and shares it with you on the old wall. "To the patient," {he} says. A seed in the stone box is saved for whoever comes next.
events.arc: The Weed That Outlived the Garden

choices.text: Plant the saved seed in the old wall

effects.log: It sprouts in the crack the weed grew from. You smile at the symmetry.

choices.text: Carry a cutting to the Ministry as a gift

effects.log: The Ministry thanks you coldly and files it under "miscellaneous."

events.text: The Ministry takes the seeds. {npc} says nothing for a day, then bows to the weed. "At least the weed is not archived," {he} says. The weed goes on flowering. In the Ministry's vault, in the dark, the seeds do not.
events.arc: The Weed That Outlived the Garden

choices.text: Plant a cutting of the weed on your own isle

effects.log: It thrives. You think of the wall often.

choices.text: Argue the Ministry's case before the Jade Court

effects.log: You lose, but the Court agrees to let the weed be.

events.text: {npc} makes charts of isles that will not stay put. The charts are redone every season, and by the next they are wrong, and {he} says this is exactly why they are the best charts in the Heavens: they are honest about being temporary. {He} hands you a pen and asks you to draw the coast of the Quiet Isle from memory.
events.arc: The Cartographer of Moving Coasts

choices.text: Draw it as you remember it

effects.log: Your coast is a bit wrong. {npc} praises it as a "personal" chart.
{npc} hands you an easier isle.
You watch for an hour. The pen moves like a swimmer.

events.text: A new rule from the Ministry says all charts must be fixed and certified. A chart that moves, the Ministry says, is not a chart. {npc} is ordered to stop drawing seasonal sheets or lose the licence. {He} asks whether you would speak for the old way before the Hall of Weights and Measures.
events.arc: The Cartographer of Moving Coasts

effects.log: You describe the sky as a thing that does not hold still. A few officials seem to hear.

choices.text: Help {npc} draw a fixed chart that quietly updates

effects.log: The chart is a clever trick of overlays. It satisfies the rule and the sky.

choices.text: Say the rule is the rule

effects.log: {npc} bows to it with a stiff back.

events.text: The Hall relents: charts may move, so long as each sheet carries the date it is wrong. {npc} adds, in small letters on every chart, "Wrong as of this morning." It becomes the custom of the trade. Navigators trust the sheets more for the confession.
events.arc: The Cartographer of Moving Coasts

choices.text: Draw the first dated chart with {npc}

effects.log: The date is written in your hand.

choices.text: Frame the Hall's decision for the wall

effects.log: It hangs where chart-makers can see it.

events.text: The overlay chart is a marvel and a fraud, and {npc} loves it. For a decade it serves; then a skiff trusts it too much and strikes a reef. The trade passes a rule of its own: every chart must warn its reader. The warning is written by {npc}, who has never forgiven the trick.
events.arc: The Cartographer of Moving Coasts

effects.log: It reads: "Trust the sky, not the sheet." It sticks.

choices.text: Defend the overlay to the end

effects.log: You are right in part. The trade remembers you as a clever, careless voice.

events.text: {npc} is a chart-maker's apprentice with a habit: at the edge of every map {he} draws a small door. The master has asked {him} to stop. "A map is a thing that is true," the master says. "A door is a wish." {npc} comes to you after, and asks whether a wish can be true.
events.arc: The Apprentice Who Drew a Door

choices.text: Say a wish can be a direction

effects.log: {npc} lights up. "That is what I think," {he} says.
{npc} lowers {his} pen. The next chart has no door, and no life.

choices.text: Ask to see one of the doors

effects.log: {npc} shows you a chart full of small black doors, all open.

events.text: One of the doors on an old chart matches something real: a tiny gap in the reef that no one had known was passable. The master is furious, then silent. {npc} wants to take a skiff and see whether the gap is real. The master wants to burn the chart. Both ask for your advice.
events.arc: The Apprentice Who Drew a Door

effects.log: You row through the reef at slack tide and find the gap, narrow and perfect.

choices.text: Persuade the master to come too

effects.log: The master comes, grumbling. The gap is real. The master says nothing for an hour.

choices.text: Keep the chart safe from the fire

effects.log: You hide it in your sleeve. It smells of salt.

events.text: The gap becomes the fastest route from the Windward Isle to the Reed Lake, and the chart is copied to the fleet with the door marked in red. {npc} is credited as the discoverer. The master, still stubborn, adds a line: "The door is a wish. The wish was correct."
events.arc: The Apprentice Who Drew a Door

choices.text: Say the credit should be shared

effects.log: {npc} insists the master get half. The master pretends to be embarrassed.
The two of you spend a decade finding wishes that were true.

events.text: The master and {npc} sail out together. The gap is real, and in the middle of it is a small, strange isle that appears on no chart. The master says nothing. After a long time, {he} reaches out and draws, in the corner of the master's own chart, a very small door.
events.arc: The Apprentice Who Drew a Door

effects.log: The silence in the skiff is the warmest you have known.
The name is "The Door." It stays on charts forever.

events.text: You are a rogue with no faction, and the surveyors of the Star Sea Pavilion will not sell you a chart at any price. {npc}, a back-lane map seller, will. {He} charges double and says the charts are almost accurate. "Almost," says {he}, "is a friend of the poor."
events.arc: The Rogue Who Sold Maps of Isles That Move

choices.text: Buy a chart at the doubled price

effects.log: It is not quite accurate. You learn to read between the lines.
{npc} drops by one stone and asks if you have any tea.
You travel blind for a season. The lessons stay.

events.text: {npc} confesses that the charts are copied from the Pavilion's own, sold by a clerk who sees rogues treated shabbily and quietly pays them back. The clerk is about to be discovered. {He} asks you to carry a warning to the clerk, because you look unthreatening and the Pavilion's guards do not stop rogues.
events.arc: The Rogue Who Sold Maps of Isles That Move

choices.text: Carry the warning and mind your business

effects.log: The clerk reads it and goes pale, and smiles. "Thank you," the clerk says.

choices.text: Ask the clerk to give the rogues free copies

effects.log: The clerk laughs, and agrees to leave a trunk at a specific quay each month.

choices.text: Say it is none of your concern

effects.log: {npc} nods, hurt, and looks away.

events.text: The clerk is dismissed, but not before leaving a trunk of charts by the quay. {npc} distributes them free to rogues across the fleet. The Pavilion never learns who did it. A month later, a map arrives at your door with only a note: "For the one who did not flinch."
events.arc: The Rogue Who Sold Maps of Isles That Move

choices.text: Use the map, and share it

effects.log: Your route is clean and fast. You pass the chart to the next rogue you meet.

choices.text: Frame the note and use the chart quietly

effects.log: It hangs on your wall as a quiet honour.

events.text: The clerk keeps the trunk running for years, and rogues the fleet over sail by charts that nobody admits to making. {npc} retires, rich in goodwill and little else, and gives you the last blank sheet in the shop. "Draw what you find," {he} says. "Charge double for the truth."
events.arc: The Rogue Who Sold Maps of Isles That Move

effects.log: You draw your first coast with a shaky hand. It is almost accurate.

choices.text: Give the sheet to a younger rogue

effects.log: The youngster looks at it as though handed a star.

events.text: {npc} was once Third Clerk of Precedence, until a seating error at a state banquet ended in a decree of exile to the Ropewalk Isle. {He} now runs a stall selling second-hand seals, and bows to every customer in the exact order the Ministry prescribes. {He} asks if you know anyone who needs a clerk.
events.arc: The Exile from the Ministry of Precedence

choices.text: Say you might, and mean it

effects.log: {npc} writes your name in a tiny ledger, headed "Hope."

choices.text: Buy a seal to be polite

effects.log: It is a perfectly good seal, and absolutely useless.

choices.text: Say the Ministry is not hiring

effects.log: {npc} bows to you, correctly, and does not smile.

events.text: Word reaches the isle that the Ministry has lost a seat-plan for a visiting embassy, and no one can reconstruct it. {npc} is the only living clerk who knew the old plan. {He} could return in glory, but the plan would also reveal that {his} exile was a mistake the Ministry made. {He} asks you what to do.
events.arc: The Exile from the Ministry of Precedence

choices.text: Say do it, and let them be embarrassed

effects.log: {npc} considers this for a night and goes.

choices.text: Say rebuild a life here and let it go

effects.log: {npc} decides to keep the stall and send the plan anyway, anonymously.

choices.text: Say you cannot decide this for {him}

effects.log: {npc} thanks you for the honesty.

events.text: {npc} returns to the capital, draws the plan from memory in an afternoon, and is offered a post. {He} declines it, and takes instead the Ministry's acknowledgement of the error, written, sealed and framed. On the Ropewalk Isle {he} hangs the frame on the stall. "The best seal I ever sold," {he} says.
events.arc: The Exile from the Ministry of Precedence

effects.log: The stall closes early. You drink the tea on the quay.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to teach you the order of the seats

effects.log: It takes a year. You come away understanding the nature of courtesy.

events.text: The plan arrives at the Ministry without a name. A grateful official finds the author a month later and sends a letter of thanks, and an offer. {npc} writes back, politely: the stall is doing well. The Ministry sends an apprentice. By decade's end the stall has three clerks and a long queue.
events.arc: The Exile from the Ministry of Precedence

choices.text: Send your own errands to the stall

effects.log: You bring {npc} a steady trickle of customers.

choices.text: Take a seal of your own from the shelf

effects.log: It is old, plain and sound. You use it for decades.

events.text: The Ministry of Weather exiled {npc} for predicting rain on a day of state procession. {He} now lives on a cold rock called the Last Terrace and has planted a hedge around the only patch of soil. {He} does not speak of the Ministry. {He} speaks of the hedge, in great detail, and asks you to prune it.
events.arc: The Exile Who Planted a Hedge

effects.log: You work together all afternoon. The hedge looks better than the exile looks.
{npc} goes silent for an hour, then says, "It was only rain."

choices.text: Say the hedge is fine as it is

effects.log: {npc} looks relieved and a little insulted.

events.text: An envoy of the Ministry arrives, polite, with a pardon in hand. The pardon is conditional: {npc} must publicly apologise for the forecast. The rain, the envoy admits, did fall, and the procession was ruined, and the Ministry still cannot forgive it. {npc} looks at the hedge for a long time, then at you.
events.arc: The Exile Who Planted a Hedge

effects.log: {npc} bows to the envoy, stiffly, and reads the apology in a flat voice.

choices.text: Say the hedge is home now

effects.log: {npc} tears the pardon in half with great politeness.
{npc} weighs the choice with the shears in hand.

events.text: {npc} goes back and is restored to the Ministry, a year's apology read, a lifetime's grievance carried. {He} keeps a cutting of the hedge in a pot on the desk. When the next forecast of unseasonable rain comes, {he} announces it plainly, and is, for once, thanked.
events.arc: The Exile Who Planted a Hedge

effects.log: The pot of hedge is beside a seal of office. {He} says it keeps {him} honest.

choices.text: Send {npc} a new cutting every spring

effects.log: The pot becomes a small forest on the Ministry desk.

events.text: {npc} stays. The hedge grows, the rock warms, and a few birds nest. Rain falls on the Last Terrace whenever {he} predicts it, and not otherwise. The Ministry of Weather sends a scholar to study the effect, and the scholar stays too. The terrace has a population of two and a hedge.
events.arc: The Exile Who Planted a Hedge

choices.text: Visit once a year with seedlings

effects.log: The terrace grows green year by year.

choices.text: Write the effect up for the archive

effects.log: It is filed under "Inexplicable." It is read, a thousand years later, by someone who needs it.

events.text: {npc} was born in the Heavens and has never seen the ground. {He} has studied it for years from books, sketched it from rumours, and now declares {he} is going to walk on it. "It is mine," {he} says, "my birthright, the thing my parents left." {He} asks you whether it is allowed.
events.arc: The Heaven-Born Who Wanted to Go Below

choices.text: Say it is allowed, with conditions

effects.log: {npc} writes the conditions on {his} sleeve.

choices.text: Say it is not, and give reasons

effects.log: {npc} listens carefully, and does not agree.

choices.text: Say it is none of your business

effects.log: {npc} says it is somebody's business, and goes to find them.

events.text: {npc}'s parents learn of the plan and forbid it. They were exiles from the world below, and they chose to forget it. {He} asks you to help find out why. The answer, apparently, is in an old trunk in the attic, which the parents will not open.
events.arc: The Heaven-Born Who Wanted to Go Below

effects.log: Inside are a child's drawings of a green hill, a pair of worn shoes, and a letter never sent.
They are quiet, tired people who do not want their child to be hurt. You listen.

choices.text: Step back from the family quarrel

effects.log: You make tea for whoever comes to the door.

events.text: The letter is to a sibling left below, and was never sent because the parents could not bear the answer. {npc} reads it aloud to them. Then, together, they decide to send it. The Descent Office lets a letter pass. {npc} does not go below, this year: but {he} has a sibling to write to now.
events.arc: The Heaven-Born Who Wanted to Go Below

effects.log: It falls like a feather through the clouds. You watch it go.

choices.text: Promise to look for a reply

effects.log: You watch for a letter for a decade. One comes, in a child's hand.

events.text: The parents at last agree, on one condition: that {npc} comes home within a year. {He} goes down, on a rope of cloud-silk, and walks on grass for three days. {He} returns changed, quieter and brighter, with a leaf pressed in a book. "It is not mine," {he} says. "But it is real."
events.arc: The Heaven-Born Who Wanted to Go Below

effects.log: The tale takes a night, and the leaf is passed round.
It is small and brown and crumbling. You hold it very carefully.

events.text: Every Falling Season, the young of the Heavens leap from the isle edges on gliders of cloud-silk, plunging through the clouds and catching a wind at the last moment. {npc}, a heaven-born, has failed the catch for three years. {He} asks if you will teach {him}, because nobody else will say a true word about the wind.
events.arc: The Cloud-Divers of the Falling Season

effects.log: You spend a season on the edge teaching how a wind feels before it arrives.

choices.text: Take {him} to watch the old divers

effects.log: The old divers fly like leaves. {npc} learns more from watching than from any word of yours.
{npc} dives anyway, a week later, badly, and lands in a net.

events.text: The day of the Great Dive arrives, and the club's leader insists no one may jump who has failed before. {npc} stands at the edge with a glider and shaking hands. The leader looks at you. "Vouch for the youngster," the leader says, "or take the blame."
events.arc: The Cloud-Divers of the Falling Season

effects.log: The leader nods curtly. {npc} steps off the edge.
{npc} is angry, then relieved, then sulks charmingly through a spring.
You both jump. The wind is fine.

events.text: {npc} drops through the clouds in silence and catches the wind in the last breath of cloud, a long, slow turn, and glides home on a thread of gold. At the edge the old divers stand and bow. {He} lands badly and laughs. "It was nothing like I imagined," {he} says. "It was better."
events.arc: The Cloud-Divers of the Falling Season

effects.log: The two of you roll on the edge, laughing, while the leader pretends not to notice.

choices.text: Say you knew {he} would catch it

effects.log: You did not. {He} accepts the lie with grace.

events.text: You wait a year, and {npc} dives again, alone, at dawn with no audience. {He} catches the wind on the first try. When you ask why not the Great Dive, {he} shrugs: "Because then it would have been theirs. This one is mine." {He} carries the glider home on {his} shoulder and does not dive again until old age.
events.arc: The Cloud-Divers of the Falling Season

effects.log: You say nothing, and share a flask of cloud-tea.

choices.text: Tell the leader how it went

effects.log: The leader writes the dive in the book, in a small, careful hand.

events.text: The Star Sea Pavilion keeps a single night-bloom that opens once every ninety years, for one hour, under the right star. {npc}, the gardener, has been waiting two years for this one. {He} asks you, as a member, to stand watch at the greenhouse door against the visitors who will wish to gawk.
events.arc: The Night-Bloom of the Star Sea Pavilion

choices.text: Stand the watch and turn visitors away

effects.log: It is cold and quiet. Visitors grumble. {npc} is grateful.

choices.text: Let a few visitors in, in silence

effects.log: The few are quiet. The bloom does not notice.

choices.text: Say you have a lecture to give

effects.log: {npc} finds someone else.

events.text: The star is late. The bloom is opening, the hour is passing, and the star has not arrived. {npc} lights a lamp to stand in for it, but the bloom flinches. A visiting astronomer offers a lens, a trick that might bring the starlight down. {He} asks if you trust the astronomer.
events.arc: The Night-Bloom of the Star Sea Pavilion

effects.log: The astronomer focuses a thread of starlight on the bloom, and it opens fully, white and enormous.

choices.text: Say wait for the real star

effects.log: You wait. The star arrives with seven minutes to spare. The bloom opens slowly, perfectly.

choices.text: Say it is {his} bloom to decide

effects.log: {npc} decides slowly. The decision takes the whole hour.

events.text: The lens bloom is a little too bright, a shade strange. The Pavilion records it as the first "lens-bloom" in history, and {npc} is both proud and ashamed. {He} saves a petal in a book, and says that, in ninety years, someone will have to decide whether to use the lens again.
events.arc: The Night-Bloom of the Star Sea Pavilion

effects.log: It dries to a curl of silver. You carry it for centuries.

choices.text: Write the account for the Pavilion's record

effects.log: The entry is read, a century later, by the next gardener.

events.text: The bloom opens true, with the true star, in the true hour. {npc} cries silently into a sleeve. The Pavilion holds a small, private feast. You are given the first seed, and told to plant it somewhere, in ninety years, when the star is on its way again.
events.arc: The Night-Bloom of the Star Sea Pavilion

effects.log: You mark the date on a calendar that will not be needed for ninety years.
The apprentice is awed. {npc} nods.

events.text: The Jade Spring has always run. This year it runs a finger lower each month, and the attendants, who are silent, begin to write notes on slips. {npc}, the youngest attendant, brings one to you at the rim: "Someone is taking water from below." {He} asks you to help find where.
events.arc: The Year the Jade Spring Ran Low

effects.log: The underside of the isle is a tangle of roots and mist. You find a hollow, and a bucket.

choices.text: Ask the Ministry of Weather for a reading

effects.log: The reading is polite and unhelpful.
{npc} stares at you in the manner of one who has taken an oath not to argue.

events.text: The hollow holds a hidden pipe. It leads along the isle's underside to a small garden on a neighbouring rock, tended by an old immortal who has been drawing water, a thimbleful at a time, for a hundred years. {npc} says the old immortal could be reported or visited. {He} asks which.
events.arc: The Year the Jade Spring Ran Low

effects.log: The garden is lovely and failing. The old immortal bows and offers tea.
The Ministry arrives with an inspector and a deputy and a form.

choices.text: Say you will think about it

effects.log: {npc} waits on the steps with the kind of patience that cannot be hurried.

events.text: The old immortal is a retired attendant who left the spring in a quarrel and never came back, and who took water because the garden is all that is left of the person {he} once loved. The tea is plain and good. {npc} listens to the story and says nothing for a long time.
events.arc: The Year the Jade Spring Ran Low

choices.text: Ask the old immortal to come back to the spring

effects.log: The old immortal looks at the spring, and at the rim, and cannot speak.

choices.text: Offer to carry water to the garden instead

effects.log: The old immortal laughs. "That would be fair," {he} says.

choices.text: Drink the tea and keep silent

effects.log: You carry the story with you down the stair.

events.text: The old immortal returns to the spring and takes the sash again. The pipe is capped. The spring slowly recovers, a finger a month. At the rim, the two attendants, old and new, stand shoulder to shoulder, and for one morning they speak aloud to one another, loudly, about nothing at all.
events.arc: The Year the Jade Spring Ran Low

effects.log: The conversation lasts all morning. It is the best you have heard.
You leave them to it.

events.text: You carry water to the garden each week, two buckets, up the root-stair and down. It becomes a ritual. The spring recovers, in time, with the pipe capped and the garden fed by hand. {npc} says the spring prefers it. The old immortal says the garden does.
events.arc: The Year the Jade Spring Ran Low

choices.text: Keep carrying for the rest of the century

effects.log: The stair is worn smooth by your feet.

choices.text: Teach the youngest attendant to carry

effects.log: The attendant takes the buckets with solemn pride.

events.text: {npc} makes flutes from the reed that grows at the edge of the Reed Lake, and sells them to anyone who can make them sing. Nine flutes in a rack were made one for each wind that visits the isle, and none has ever been played. {He} asks if you would try the first.
events.arc: The Flute-Maker and the Nine Winds

effects.log: It sounds a thin, bright note like a lark pretending to be a drum. {npc} smiles.

choices.text: Ask why none has been played

effects.log: "The winds would answer," says {npc}. "I am not sure I am ready for that."

choices.text: Say music is not your talent

effects.log: {npc} sets the flute down without a word.

events.text: The first wind answers: a soft tap on the window, a rustle in the reed. {npc} is delighted and a little afraid. {He} proposes that you play the second, in the evening, and let the second wind answer. The third, {he} says, will probably want a choir.
events.arc: The Flute-Maker and the Nine Winds

choices.text: Play the second flute that evening

effects.log: The second wind arrives like a shy cat. It wraps itself around the flute.
You rehearse for a season. The winds wait with the patience of the weather.
{npc} refuses so politely it hurts.

events.text: By the sixth flute the winds have learned your name. By the ninth they come to the window together, and {npc} stands in the middle of the isle with a flute and the whole sky listening. The ninth wind, the oldest, takes the last note and carries it off over the lake.
events.arc: The Flute-Maker and the Nine Winds

choices.text: Stay till the last note fades

effects.log: The silence after the ninth wind is a whole afternoon long.

choices.text: Write the tune down for the isle

effects.log: It becomes the isle's evening song.

events.text: You rehearse for a season and return, calmer. The winds respond, one at a time, over years. {npc} says that nine flutes in nine winds, played well, would take about three centuries, and that is exactly right for a thing worth doing. You nod.
events.arc: The Flute-Maker and the Nine Winds

effects.log: It takes a long time, and it is worth it.

choices.text: Take one flute home to practise

effects.log: It hangs on your wall and hums in your sleep.

events.text: On the Willow Isle, a healer tells you that the hardest part of tending the sick who cannot die is knowing there will be no last day. "You do not heal them," she says. "You keep them company."

choices.text: Offer to help for a morning

effects.log: You turn beds and fill cups. The patients remember your name.

choices.text: Sit and listen to the healer

effects.log: She talks for an hour about the shape of patience.

events.text: A bedside tea cart rolls the ward of the Long Fever each afternoon. The patients choose a cup by the stories on its rim. A bright cup is brought to you, with a note: "For the visitor with the kind face."

choices.text: Drink the tea and read the rim

effects.log: It tells a tale of a boat. You finish it as the patients nod.

choices.text: Refill the cups for the ward

effects.log: You pour for an hour. The ward quietens.

events.text: A sign at the Jade Spring says: "Draw only what you will drink today." A pilgrim has taken three jars and is arguing with the attendant, who is silent, using the long gestures of an old argument.

choices.text: Settle it with a small gift

effects.log: You press two stones into the attendant's palm for the spring-box. The pilgrim puts two jars back.

choices.text: Say nothing and watch the argument

effects.log: It is as eloquent as a play.

events.text: The Jade Spring's attendants have the cleanest hands in the Heavens and the most careworn faces. One of them presses a small cup of water into your hands as you pass and does not look up.

effects.log: The water tastes of stone and light. You walk the rest of the day lighter.

choices.text: Pour a drop back into the spring

effects.log: The attendant looks up, for the first time, with a faint smile.

events.text: At dusk every isle in the fleet rings its bell once, in order of precedence. The sound passes across the sky like a rumour. You are on a quay with a view of seven isles and a clock, and you can tell by the pause which of them is in a mood.

choices.text: Count the bells and guess the moods

effects.log: You are right about four. It is a small, secret pleasure.

choices.text: Ring the quay's hand-bell in answer

effects.log: The quay-keeper winks at you. The other isles do not hear.

events.text: A cracked bell hangs in the market hall, kept because it was the first bell the Cloud Market ever cast. A bell-founder offers to recast it for ten stones. The stall-keepers say the crack is the bell's voice.

choices.text: Pay ten stones to recast it

effects.log: The new bell is bright and thin. The stall-keepers stop speaking to you for a year.

choices.text: Say the crack is the voice

effects.log: The stall-keepers buy you a bowl of noodles.

events.text: A street organ stands at a crossing of two cloud-bridges, driven by the wind, played by no one. It plays a different tune on every wind. A boy sits beside it taking notes on a slate.

choices.text: Ask the boy what he is writing

effects.log: He is making a book of every tune the organ plays. He is on volume forty.

choices.text: Leave him a few stones for chalk

effects.log: He looks up and says thank you as though it were a speech.

events.text: A choir of lamplighters sings as they light the bridge lamps at dusk. The song is old, and each verse is for a different lamp. By the last verse, the bridge is full of listeners.

choices.text: Join in at the last verse

effects.log: The choir moves over to make room, and the song is better for it.
The verses fade and the lamps stay lit. You walk on slowly.

events.text: The night nurse of the Sleeper Ward keeps a single candle burning at the end of the aisle, and reads poems aloud, low, to those who dream. She says they dream better with company.

choices.text: Ask for a poem to be read to you

effects.log: The poem is short. You sleep better for a month.

choices.text: Bring a candle of your own

effects.log: The nurse puts it beside hers. The aisle looks warmer.

events.text: A gardener on the Orchard Isle is grafting a peach onto a plum, and the old trunk frowns. "A thousand-year-old plum is not easily persuaded," the gardener says. "Hold the bandage."

effects.log: The graft takes, in a decade. The fruit is peculiar and fine.
The gardener tries it. It fails. You were wrong, and the gardener forgives you.

events.text: A small iron gate at the foot of a garden is locked and rusted shut. A card hangs on it: "Please go away." A snail on the lock looks at you expectantly.

effects.log: You bow to the gate. The snail seems to approve.

choices.text: Slip a note under the gate

effects.log: A week later a reply is slipped back: "Thank you for your concern. Please go away."

events.text: At the Survey Post on the Windward Isle, a chart-maker is drawing the horizon line by line. The clerk says the horizon has moved a hand-breadth since morning and the sheet will have to be redone.

choices.text: Hold the clerk's ink for the redraw

effects.log: The horizon moves again. The clerk sighs and redraws.
The clerk says nobody knows, but it never moves toward you.

events.text: A surveyor's card pinned to a lamp-post says: "Wanted: any record of the Foam Isle, lost, c. nine hundred years ago." Beneath it, in another hand: "It was never lost. We just stopped writing to it."

effects.log: You write: "I will look." The card collects other notes over the year.
You carry the phrase with you for weeks.

events.text: A slip of paper falls from a clerk's sleeve in the Hall of Precedence: a list of seats for a banquet that never happened, in an exile's hand. Someone has pencilled "Still waiting" beside the last place.

choices.text: Hand the slip back with a nod

effects.log: The clerk blushes and tucks it away.

choices.text: Keep the slip and ask around

effects.log: You learn about a long quarrel and a missing guest.

events.text: An exile's stall at the foot of the Jade Court steps sells scrolls, seals, and second chances. The sign over the door says: "Prices like the weather: they change when you aren't looking."

effects.log: It is a reprint of an old regulation, annotated. You keep it for decades.

choices.text: Talk with the stallholder a while

effects.log: You hear about a loss, and a beginning.

events.text: A heaven-born child is practising on a cliff with a glider far too big for them. The child falls on the third try and sits up grinning. "I am going to be the best at this," the child tells you gravely, "in about nine hundred years."

choices.text: Hold the glider while they try again

effects.log: The child makes it to the end of the cliff, and cheers.

choices.text: Show the child a breeze to ride

effects.log: You point at a pocket of warm air. The glider lifts. The child shrieks.

events.text: A heaven-born youth is lowering a letter on a thread over the edge of the cloud sea. "For below," the youth says. "Someone must be up here to read it." The thread runs out and the letter vanishes.

effects.log: The thread is long. The letter goes further. The youth thanks you in a wobbly voice.
It says only: "Hello. I am up here."

events.text: A slip in the archive is misfiled under "Bells, Cracked." It describes a chart of the sea of clouds, signed by a surveyor who is now two thousand years dead. The back of the slip holds a recipe for noodles.

choices.text: Copy the recipe and the chart

effects.log: The noodles are good. The chart turns out to be remarkably accurate.

choices.text: Return the slip to the right shelf

effects.log: The shelf where it belongs is a hundred shelves away.

events.text: A rogue chart-seller on the market bridge says her charts are "mostly accurate." A second stallholder beside her charges triple for "fully accurate" ones. The two have been arguing about accuracy for three centuries.

effects.log: You get where you are going, with detours. Both sellers are satisfied.

choices.text: Ask them to settle it by a test

effects.log: They agree. The test takes a week and ends in a draw.

events.text: Two apprentices of the Star Sea Pavilion, {npc} and a rival, have each been told to chart the same faint star, and neither will share a lens. {npc} comes to you at dusk with a smudged sheet. "Mine is better," {he} says. "Say so."
events.arc: The Apprentices Who Drew the Same Star

effects.log: The chart is careful and cramped. It is good, not perfect.

choices.text: Say you cannot judge without the other

effects.log: {npc} hands you the sheet and stalks off to fetch the rival.
{npc} says "fine" is the cruellest word in the language.

events.text: The two sheets are laid side by side. They disagree about the star by half a finger. The master of the Pavilion, a patient figure, says one of the two apprentices has made a mistake, and will not say which. {npc} asks you to find the error before the master does.
events.arc: The Apprentices Who Drew the Same Star

choices.text: Re-chart the star yourself on a clear night

effects.log: You find the star has moved. Neither chart was wrong.
One lens has a flaw. It is the rival's. You hesitate about telling.

choices.text: Leave the apprentices to settle it

effects.log: They argue until dawn, and you hear nothing more for a season.

events.text: You show the master the moving star. The two apprentices stare at one another across the table, then burst out laughing. They add the star's drift to the chart together, and the master, for once, praises both. {npc} comes to thank you with a very small, very hard pastry.
events.arc: The Apprentices Who Drew the Same Star

effects.log: It is rock-solid and delicious.

choices.text: Ask to see the new joint chart

effects.log: It is a finer thing than either one made alone.

events.text: The flawed lens is the rival's, and the rival knew. {npc} is outraged; the rival is ashamed. The master suspends them both. You are asked to speak for one. It is the hardest speech you have given. When it is over, the two shake hands over a broken lens, with the grim courtesy of the Pavilion.
events.arc: The Apprentices Who Drew the Same Star

choices.text: Say the lens was an honest flaw

effects.log: It was, in part. The rival keeps the post.

choices.text: Say the rival must answer for it

effects.log: The rival does, and later thanks you for it. Slowly.

events.text: {npc}, an apprentice at the Star Sea Pavilion, has logged a comet as a new star and sent the report to the Jade Court. The Court has already struck a medal. {He} has just worked out the error and begs you, as a trusted member, to say how to tell the Pavilion before the medal is cast.
events.arc: The Apprentice Who Mistook a Comet

choices.text: Go with {npc} to the master at once

effects.log: The master listens to the whole confession without blinking.
It takes a month to prepare. The medal is almost ready.

choices.text: Say the error is the Court's to find

effects.log: {npc} shakes {his} head, but does not argue.

events.text: The medal is cast and the Court has declared a festival of the "new star." The master asks {npc} what to do. {He} looks at you. Telling the Court now will embarrass the Pavilion and the Court. Keeping silent will let the festival go on. The comet will be gone in a month, and the error with it.
events.arc: The Apprentice Who Mistook a Comet

effects.log: The master drafts a letter. The Court answers with a stiff silence.

choices.text: Say let the festival run its course

effects.log: The comet fades. The Court notices quietly and says nothing.

choices.text: Say you cannot choose for them

effects.log: {npc} chooses the letter, shakily.

events.text: The Court reads the letter and, to everyone's surprise, praises the honesty. The medal is recast as the Medal of the Honest Comet. {npc} wears it on a hook behind the door and says it is the best thing {he} ever got for being wrong.
events.arc: The Apprentice Who Mistook a Comet

effects.log: The evening is long and kind.

choices.text: Write the story for the Pavilion's record

effects.log: It is read by apprentices for a thousand years.

events.text: The comet fades, the festival ends, and {npc} becomes quieter. Years later the Pavilion finds the old record and the quiet correction beneath it. The master does not scold. {npc} is made Keeper of Errata, which the master says is the most important post in the house.
events.arc: The Apprentice Who Mistook a Comet

effects.log: The records are in good hands.

choices.text: Ask {npc} how errors are best remembered

effects.log: The answer takes a whole evening.

events.text: The Great Slip Library has two shelf-keepers who have not spoken in four hundred years, and who communicate by moving slips an inch at a time. {npc} asks you to find a slip on the east wall. When you reach for it, a note falls out: "Please do not touch it. - The Other Keeper." The other keeper has left no note.
events.arc: The Feud of the Two Shelf-Keepers

effects.log: {npc} sighs and writes a short, bitter note to the rival.

choices.text: Ask {npc} what the feud is about

effects.log: "A catalogue," {he} says. "A very small matter of a catalogue."

choices.text: Go to the north wall instead

effects.log: The north wall has no notes, and no slips of use.

events.text: {npc} confesses it began as a quarrel over whether "Weather" came before "Winds." The other keeper, fiercer, has since reorganised the whole library to prove the point. Readers can no longer find anything. The Ministry is threatening an inspection. {He} asks if you will carry a note of truce.
events.arc: The Feud of the Two Shelf-Keepers

effects.log: The other keeper reads it standing up, and tears it neatly, and writes a reply.
You work for a month and the library is orderly, and both keepers are annoyed.

choices.text: Say you will stay out of it

effects.log: {npc} files a complaint against neutrality.

events.text: The reply is a poem. It is a very bad poem about a catalogue, and it ends: "Perhaps Winds before Weather, after all." {npc} reads it aloud three times, laughing. The two keepers meet in the middle of the library, bow, and swap a slip each. The reorganisation takes one night.
events.arc: The Feud of the Two Shelf-Keepers

effects.log: The two work side by side. By dawn, the library is shorter by an argument.

choices.text: Save the bad poem for the archive

effects.log: It is catalogued under "Reconciliation, Examples of."

events.text: Your reordering pleases the Ministry and no one else. The keepers stop quarrelling to quarrel with you. After a month, the three of you drink tea together and discover that the library is, in fact, in the best order it has been in for a century. Nobody admits who is responsible.
events.arc: The Feud of the Two Shelf-Keepers

effects.log: The Ministry sends a stamp. You hang it on the door.

choices.text: Give the credit to the keepers

effects.log: They are quietly delighted and refuse to say so.

events.text: In the Jade Void library a single slip sits in a locked case, with a card: "Not for lending. Not for reading. Not for discussion." {npc}, the junior librarian, polishes the case daily and will not say what is on the slip. {He} has been polishing it for sixty years.
events.arc: The Slip Nobody Would Lend

choices.text: Ask what is on the slip

effects.log: {npc} goes pale. "I do not know," {he} says. "No one does."
{npc} lets you hold the cloth. The case is warm.
You pass it every day for a year and never feel quite at ease.

events.text: The slip, {npc} finally admits, was placed by a founder whose will forbids its use until the library is "ready." Nobody knows what that means. {He} is certain the day is near: the case has begun to hum. {He} asks if you would be a witness when it is opened.
events.arc: The Slip Nobody Would Lend

effects.log: The hum rises. The case unlocks itself.

choices.text: Say it is dangerous to open it

effects.log: The hum falls. {npc} agrees to wait, with some relief.

choices.text: Say you are not the right witness

effects.log: {npc} nods, a little hurt.

events.text: The slip, when read, is blank. At its foot, in small letters: "You were ready. Thank you for waiting." {npc} laughs and cries at once. Then, quietly, the librarian takes a fresh slip and writes, at the head: "For the next who is ready."
events.arc: The Slip Nobody Would Lend

choices.text: Help {npc} lock the new slip in

effects.log: The case is re-sealed with a very small, very proud click.

choices.text: Take a rubbing of the blank slip

effects.log: The rubbing is blank too. You keep it, nonetheless.

events.text: You wait, and the hum fades. {npc} goes on polishing the case, but lighter now, as though it were a friend's grave. Years later the case unlocks itself on a night nobody expects, and the slip is read by a child, who reads it aloud, and nobody is ever sure what it said.
events.arc: The Slip Nobody Would Lend

effects.log: You hear the first line. It is perfect, and you forget it by morning.
You take the cloth. It is warm.

events.text: At the Great Slip Library a clerk will not let a rogue without a seal past the first hall. {npc}, the old doorkeeper, watches you argue. "I wrote the rule," {he} says quietly. "I regret it every day. I cannot repeal it. Would you carry a request to the Jade Court?"
events.arc: The Rogue at the Slip Desk

effects.log: {npc} gives you a sealed slip. You feel it grow warm in your sleeve.

choices.text: Ask how to read in the first hall

effects.log: "Stand where I cannot see you," says {npc}, and looks at the ceiling.
You do. It is not as good.

events.text: The Court's clerk takes the request with cold courtesy and says it must pass nine desks. At the fourth desk it is lost. At the seventh it is found, folded into a bird. {npc} has told you, with a small smile, that the Court's paper is an art. You go through the nine desks with a patience you did not know you had.
events.arc: The Rogue at the Slip Desk

choices.text: Fold your own request into the bird

effects.log: It flies. The clerks pretend not to notice.

choices.text: Persuade the ninth clerk by reasoning

effects.log: The clerk listens, to your surprise, with real attention.

choices.text: Give up at the seventh desk

effects.log: You go home, and the request goes on without you.

events.text: The rule is repealed in a short, odd decree: "Rogues may read in the first hall, the second hall, and the garden, provided they return the slips in the order found." {npc} reads it twice, bows to the paper, and gives you the first slip: a poem, ironically, about doors.
events.arc: The Rogue at the Slip Desk

effects.log: The old doorkeeper listens with closed eyes.
Rogues begin to read in the library, quietly, and carefully, and thank no one.

events.text: The ninth clerk is persuaded, and in a week the rule is softened: a rogue may enter with a sponsor. It is not what {npc} hoped. {He} sponsors you, grimly, and later says that half a repeal is better than none, and that the rest will take a century.
events.arc: The Rogue at the Slip Desk

effects.log: You read in the first hall for decades.
You spend years at it, and are remembered as stubborn.

events.text: At the Rusted Quay a mechanic named {npc} fixes cloud-skiffs by listening to them. {He} lays an ear to the hull, hums, and names the fault in a single word. A skiff you are about to board is humming something {he} does not like. {He} says, "Do not go out on that. Come and have tea."
events.arc: The Skiff Mechanic of the Rusted Quay

effects.log: The skiff is held back for repairs. A storm comes out of nowhere an hour later.
The skiff gets across. It does not get back.
"It is homesick," says {npc}. "They get that way."

events.text: {npc} has fixed skiffs for four hundred years with a set of tools made by a master now gone. The tool-box has one empty slot, for a piece no one can find. A customer has offered a fortune for the box. {He} will not sell, but is tired. "Tell me what to do," {he} says. "I mean it."
events.arc: The Skiff Mechanic of the Rusted Quay

choices.text: Say keep the tools, and find the piece

effects.log: You help look. The piece is found in a skiff's hold, wrapped in a child's sock.

choices.text: Say sell the tools and retire

effects.log: {npc} sits in silence. Then {he} takes the offer, and cries.

choices.text: Say it is {his} life to decide

effects.log: {npc} thanks you and does not decide for a year.

events.text: The missing piece is a small bronze key. When it is set in the slot, the tool-box hums in a voice like {npc}'s old master. {He} sits on the quay, holding it, for an hour. Then, wiping {his} face, {he} gets up and fixes the nearest skiff.
events.arc: The Skiff Mechanic of the Rusted Quay

effects.log: You pass wrench after wrench until dusk.
It is the right thing, and you know it.

events.text: {npc} sells the box, retires, and takes a small cottage on an isle that has no skiffs. For the first year {he} listens to nothing. In the second {he} begins to hum along with the wind. In the third, a skiff arrives in need of help, and {he} fixes it with a borrowed spoon.
events.arc: The Skiff Mechanic of the Rusted Quay

effects.log: The tea is good. The hum is back.
It is a simple job. It takes all day, with great joy.

events.text: Unsealed skiffs may not moor at the main quays of the Reed Lake, so a chandler named {npc} runs a floating shop out in the reeds. The prices are fair, the rope is honest, and the Ministry of Quays would like it gone. {He} asks you, as a fellow without a seal, to sign a petition in its favour.
events.arc: The Rogue Chandler of the Reed Lake

effects.log: The paper goes round forty skiffs by sundown.

choices.text: Offer to buy a rope as a show of faith

effects.log: {npc} sells it at cost and refuses payment for the second.

choices.text: Say the Ministry is within its rights

effects.log: {npc} is sorry for you, and says so.

events.text: A Ministry inspector arrives at the floating shop with a notice of closure. {npc} offers tea. The inspector, to everyone's surprise, accepts, and spends an hour inspecting every rope. The inspection ends with a single remark: "These are good." {He} asks you to help draft the response.
events.arc: The Rogue Chandler of the Reed Lake

choices.text: Draft a plain statement of fair dealing

effects.log: The statement is short and true. The inspector reads it twice.

choices.text: Gather the skiff-owners to speak for the shop

effects.log: Thirty skiffs crowd the reeds. The inspector looks overwhelmed.
{npc} speaks well. The inspector listens.

events.text: The Ministry grants the shop a licence to float: a licence for a thing that already floated. A small ceremony is held on a raft. {npc} keeps the licence in a jar of rope-oil and says it will outlast the Ministry. It is, in the opinion of the reeds, the most honest piece of paper on the lake.
events.arc: The Rogue Chandler of the Reed Lake

choices.text: Hold the other end of the ribbon

effects.log: The ribbon is cut by a child. The shop becomes a landmark.

choices.text: Buy the first rope under the licence

effects.log: It is sturdy. It lasts for ever.

events.text: The skiff-owners' chorus wins the shop its licence, and the Ministry's inspector is promoted for the "community response." The shop is soon crowded, noisy and beloved. {npc} grumbles that fame is the death of a good trade, and sells even more rope.
events.arc: The Rogue Chandler of the Reed Lake

effects.log: A second raft is lashed on. It leaks happily.

choices.text: Keep the old corner for rogues

effects.log: The corner has a bench, a stove, and a bowl of tea.

events.text: The kitchen of the Nine Clouds Palace has eleven hundred cooks and one head, {npc}, who is a terror. On the eve of the Banquet of the Long Noon, {he} hands you an apron without a word. "Thin-slice the moon-radish," {he} says. "Nobody will thank you. Do it perfectly."
events.arc: The Kitchen of the Nine Clouds Palace Before a Banquet

effects.log: Your hands remember forgotten patience. {npc} tastes one slice and says nothing, which is high praise.

choices.text: Ask what the radish is for

effects.log: "For the sauce that will not be eaten," says {npc}, "but without which nothing else works."
{npc} takes the apron back, politely, and the kitchen goes on.

events.text: Mid-banquet the sauce curdles. Eleven hundred cooks go quiet. {npc} stares at the pot like a general at a lost field. {He} asks your opinion, brusque, public. Everyone looks at you. The sauce is the thing the whole banquet rests on, and nobody dares say what is wrong.
events.arc: The Kitchen of the Nine Clouds Palace Before a Banquet

choices.text: Say it needs less heat and more patience

effects.log: You turn the flame low. {npc} nods once. The sauce comes back.

choices.text: Say the radish was sliced too thin

effects.log: It was your radish. {npc} says nothing, and starts again.
The kitchen sighs. {npc} fixes it alone.

events.text: The banquet is a triumph. No one thanks the radish. In the dim kitchen afterward, {npc} sets a small bowl before you and says: "The thanks of the kitchen." It is the sauce, plain and perfect, and the best thing you have ever eaten.
events.arc: The Kitchen of the Nine Clouds Palace Before a Banquet

effects.log: It tastes of patience and warm stone. You sleep soundly for three days.
"There is no recipe," says {npc}. "There is a radish."

events.text: You confess the thin radish. {npc} says nothing for a long time, then hands you a second knife. "Slice it again. This time, I will watch." The two of you stand in the empty kitchen at midnight, and the radish goes slowly, perfectly, one slice at a time. You are offered a post. You decline, and are offered tea.
events.arc: The Kitchen of the Nine Clouds Palace Before a Banquet

choices.text: Take the tea and the lesson

effects.log: You drink it on a flour sack, glowing with unaccustomed humility.

choices.text: Accept the post for a season

effects.log: You cook for the Palace for a hundred days. It is the hardest labour of your life.

events.text: {npc} has washed pots in a palace kitchen for three hundred years and never been let near the fire. {He} tastes every dish that leaves and is, in a quiet way, an artist. One night, when the cook is ill, {npc} asks you to stand beside {him} at the stove, because nobody else will.
events.arc: The Scullion Who Became Cook

effects.log: The pot, the knife and the flame all behave. {npc} cooks without a word.

choices.text: Tell the head cook {npc} is ready

effects.log: The head cook is annoyed and curious.

choices.text: Say a scullion should stay a scullion

effects.log: {npc} bows and returns to the pots.

events.text: The dish is a clear soup of cloud-leek and a single egg, and it silences the room. The head cook demands to know who made it. {npc} is frozen. The kitchen waits. You could say it was you, or name {npc}, or let it be lost. {He} looks at you, not begging, but ready.
events.arc: The Scullion Who Became Cook

effects.log: The head cook stares. The kitchen applauds, quietly, with spoons.

choices.text: Say it was a joint effort

effects.log: {npc} protests. Gently, you hold the line.

choices.text: Say nothing and let the cook guess

effects.log: The cook guesses wrong. {npc} sighs.

events.text: {npc} is promoted to line cook, the first scullion in the palace's history. The pots are given to a younger hand. On the first night at the stove, {he} cooks the soup again, and the egg comes out perfect, and {he} laughs, startled, at {his} own hands.
events.arc: The Scullion Who Became Cook

choices.text: Sit at the kitchen table with {npc}

effects.log: You eat the soup together, at midnight.
It was your teacher's. {npc} treasures it.

events.text: The head cook credits the dish to both of you, and {npc} is made an assistant at the stove. It is not what {he} wanted. But {he} cooks, and the kitchen is full of the smell, and on slow nights {he} sets a small bowl of the soup for the dishwasher. "Somebody should be tasted," {he} says.
events.arc: The Scullion Who Became Cook

choices.text: Taste the soup with the dishwasher

effects.log: The three of you sit by the washing-up. It is the best supper of the season.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to teach you the egg

effects.log: It takes a year. You never do it as well.

events.text: A tenant in an old cloud-house on the Lantern Isle has been dead for three hundred years and still leaves the rent each month on the sill: three stones in a wrapper. The landlord, {npc}, has never touched them. {He} asks if you will help find out what the ghost wants.
events.arc: The Ghost Who Kept Paying Rent

choices.text: Sit up a night and watch the sill

effects.log: At the third bell a soft grey form sets down the wrapper and stands, looking at the door.
You find an unfinished letter in a drawer.

choices.text: Say the ghost is a pest

effects.log: {npc} flinches and shows you out.

events.text: The ghost is courteous but silent. The letter is addressed to a landlord from three centuries earlier, and says: "I could not pay the last month. I will leave it when I can." The landlord was {npc}'s grandparent. {He} did not know. The ghost has been paying a debt that was forgiven long ago.
events.arc: The Ghost Who Kept Paying Rent

choices.text: Read the letter aloud to the ghost

effects.log: The ghost listens with its head tilted. The wrapper is not set down that night.

choices.text: Tell the ghost the debt was forgiven

effects.log: The ghost shimmers uncertainly. It does not believe you, quite.

choices.text: Take the stones for the isle's fund

effects.log: The stones are warm. You hand them to the almoner.

events.text: The ghost dissolves slowly, like mist on a window. In its place, a few stones remain on the sill, and a very faint, formal thank-you in the air. {npc} takes the stones, at last, and puts them in a jar with the letter. The cloud-house is let that spring, to someone young.
events.arc: The Ghost Who Kept Paying Rent

effects.log: The air smells of rain. The cloud-house warms.

choices.text: Help {npc} plant a tree for the tenant

effects.log: It is a small cloud-pine. It thrives.

events.text: {npc} writes a receipt in the old landlord's hand: "Paid in full." The ghost reads it and slowly, awkwardly, bows. The rent is never left again. But on the first of each month a wrapper is found on the sill with nothing in it, folded very neatly, and tucked under a stone as a token.
events.arc: The Ghost Who Kept Paying Rent

choices.text: Keep the wrapper as a memento

effects.log: It sits on your shelf, a small forgiveness.

choices.text: Leave a stone in it for the next ghost

effects.log: The wrapper is gone in the morning.

events.text: The Council of Weights and Measures has a vacant seat, but the departed councillor, {npc}, still attends every session as a pale outline in the chair, and votes with a faint tap. Nobody has formally noticed. The chairman asks you quietly whether the Council may count the vote.
events.arc: The Immortal Who Died and Kept Attending the Council

choices.text: Say the vote may count, for now

effects.log: The chairman exhales. The tap is entered in the minutes.
The chairman deletes the tap. {npc} sighs audibly.

choices.text: Say you will research the precedent

effects.log: The precedent is extremely thin. It takes you a year.

events.text: The ghost has been voting against a bridge. The vote is close, and {npc} is the swing. The living councillors argue over whether to honour the tap or take the bridge by a technicality. The chairman asks you, as a person of standing, to settle it before the next session.
events.arc: The Immortal Who Died and Kept Attending the Council

choices.text: Honour the ghost's vote and reconsider the bridge

effects.log: The bridge is paused. The ghost nods.

choices.text: Move to strike the ghost's vote and build

effects.log: The motion passes. The bridge goes ahead. The ghost does not return.

choices.text: Ask the ghost why it voted so

effects.log: {npc} writes on the air: "Because of the children who play under it."

events.text: The bridge is re-planned, higher, wider, with a place under it for the children. {npc} smiles in the empty chair, and the next vote is a gentle, approving tap. At the end of the session, the ghost stands, bows to the Council, and faintly departs. The seat is formally vacated, and a plaque is set.
events.arc: The Immortal Who Died and Kept Attending the Council

choices.text: Attend the unveiling of the plaque

effects.log: It reads: "Voted for the children." The ceremony is short.

choices.text: Take the old chair for your own committee

effects.log: It creaks like the memory of a good argument.

events.text: The bridge goes ahead, and the ghost never attends again. The empty chair is left, as a custom, and the Council falls into an uneasy silence. A year later a child falls from the half-built span, and is caught by the net the ghost had demanded. You are not sure it was the net. You are not sure it was not.
events.arc: The Immortal Who Died and Kept Attending the Council

choices.text: Propose a plaque in the ghost's name

effects.log: The plaque is approved without comment.

choices.text: Say nothing, and carry the doubt

effects.log: It sits in you for a long while.

events.text: An invitation arrives, written in cold silver ink: the wedding of two ghosts on the Lantern Isle, a pair of immortals who died a thousand years apart and have, in death, discovered each other. {npc}, the officiant, is a living bard who insists on a living guest or two. {He} begs you to come.
events.arc: The Guest at the Ghost's Wedding

effects.log: The gift is a lamp. {npc} approves.
{npc} says that presence is the gift, and that nothing is the traditional wedding present.
{npc} sends a second invitation, slightly less cold.

events.text: The ghosts' wedding is lovely and chilly. The guests are a mix: three living, a hundred pale. The vows are read by candlelight. At the rite, the groom's ghost falters: the groom's family has not forgiven the match. {npc} looks at you in desperation and asks you to speak up for the groom.
events.arc: The Guest at the Ghost's Wedding

choices.text: Speak for the groom with feeling

effects.log: Your words fill the cold hall, and the groom's ghost brightens.

choices.text: Ask the hall to hold a minute of silence

effects.log: The silence is deep. Something shifts.
{npc} manages, cracking.

events.text: The groom's family, a row of pale and disapproving figures, softens, rises, and bows. The couple kisses, or the cold equivalent. Then the hall dims, the candles blow out together, and the ghosts, in pairs, drift out through the roof. You are left with the bard, a cup, and a silver ring that glows.
events.arc: The Guest at the Ghost's Wedding

effects.log: It sits on your finger like a promise.

choices.text: Return the ring to the couple's grave

effects.log: You carry it up the hill, and set it on the stone.

events.text: The silence works its slow magic. The groom's family does not soften, quite, but the toast goes on, and the bride, in the cold, takes the groom's hand. When the wedding is over, {npc} walks you to the quay. "Weddings of the dead," {he} says, "are the only ones that end exactly when they should."
