events.arc: The Guest at the Ghost's Wedding

choices.text: Ask {npc} to play at your next celebration

effects.log: {npc} laughs. "The living are harder," {he} says. "But yes."
The night is quiet and strange and almost kind.

events.text: A stallholder at the Cloud Market greets you warmly, asks about your cousin, and mentions the debt you owe. You have no cousin and owe nothing. {npc}, the stallholder, apologises: someone with your name and manner has been trading here for a year, in your style, with your seal. You ask to meet them.
events.arc: The Other You at the Cloud Market

choices.text: Stay and wait for the other you

effects.log: They arrive at dusk, carrying a basket, and are, uncannily, almost you.
The description is flattering and not quite right.

choices.text: Say it is none of your business

effects.log: {npc} gives you a puzzled look and goes back to the stall.

events.text: The impostor is cheerful and apologetic. They say they took your name because nobody listened to theirs, and they have been careful to be honest in it. The market likes them. You are not sure whether to be angry. {npc} asks which of you is "real" in the market's eyes. The impostor waits.
events.arc: The Other You at the Cloud Market

choices.text: Say the name may be shared, for now

effects.log: The impostor lights up. The market claps, awkwardly.

choices.text: Say the name is yours and they must stop

effects.log: The impostor goes quiet. {npc} sighs, and the market looks away.

choices.text: Ask them for their real name

effects.log: They tell you, shyly. It is a lovely name.

events.text: The matter of the name does not die. A season on, the impostor stands at the edge of the market with a bundle and a small, careful face, and asks one last thing of you: a version of your name to keep, or leave to you in peace. {npc} stands between you, saying nothing.
events.arc: The Other You at the Cloud Market

choices.text: Let them keep a version of the name

effects.log: The impostor beams. The market cheers.
The impostor nods, takes the bundle, and goes.

events.text: You and the impostor, now partners, stand at the stall as the lanterns go up. The name on the sign is half yours, half theirs, and no longer anyone's. A traveller asks which of you is the original. You and the impostor look at each other and say, at once: "Neither."
events.arc: The Other You at the Cloud Market

effects.log: The market has made its peace.

choices.text: Add a third name to the sign

effects.log: The sign grows. The stall grows. So does the joke.

events.text: You find the impostor on a remote isle, selling noodles under their own name, and quietly proud. They are astonished to see you. You eat a bowl together, and say nothing about the old business. When you leave, they press a bundle into your hand: your old seal, polished.
events.arc: The Other You at the Cloud Market

effects.log: It is the only thing they ever stole, and they gave it back.
They hold it as though it were a star.

events.text: A parcel lands on the Orchard Isle, wrapped in oiled cloth and tied with a mortal knot. It is addressed to a friend of {npc}'s who left the isle four hundred years ago. The label says it was sent by a student in the world below, who has since grown old and died. {npc} turns the parcel over, unsure what to do.
events.arc: The Parcel That Fell Four Centuries Late

effects.log: {npc} writes the address on the back in careful ink.
Inside is a book of pressed flowers and a letter.

choices.text: Leave it with the isle's warden

effects.log: {npc} frowns, and sighs, and takes it back.

events.text: The friend is found on a distant isle, ancient and sceptical. "I taught that student for a year," the friend says. "I never thought the student would remember." They read the letter in silence. Then they ask {npc}, quietly, whether the student died well, which neither of you can answer.
events.arc: The Parcel That Fell Four Centuries Late

choices.text: Say you will try to find out

effects.log: The friend looks at you gravely, and nods.

choices.text: Say the student died as all do, and well

effects.log: The friend takes it as a lie and a kindness.

choices.text: Say nothing and sit with them

effects.log: The silence is long and warm.

events.text: You go below on a pilgrim's errand, and find the student's grave on a green hillside, small and tended. Neighbours say the student told stories of "the teacher in the sky" until the end. You bring a handful of the grave's earth back in a jar. The friend takes it in both hands.
events.arc: The Parcel That Fell Four Centuries Late

choices.text: Plant the earth in the friend's garden

effects.log: A seedling comes up. It is called the Student.

choices.text: Ask the friend to write a reply to send down

effects.log: It falls like a leaf. You never learn if it arrives.

events.text: The friend plants the earth under the old peach, and for years a faint sapling grows beside it, odd and sweet. When the sapling blooms, the friend invites {npc} and you to tea under it. "It took four hundred years," the friend says, "and it arrived at exactly the right time."
events.arc: The Parcel That Fell Four Centuries Late

effects.log: The tea is pale and fragrant.
It lasts a hundred years in a jar.

events.text: The reply is written in a hand that has not held a pen for centuries. It is a simple thing: "Thank you for teaching me to look up." The friend sends it falling into the cloud sea, and then sits for a very long time at the edge. {npc} brings a blanket and says nothing at all.
events.arc: The Parcel That Fell Four Centuries Late

effects.log: The sea goes violet.
You are glad of it.

events.text: A small packet of apple seeds arrives at the Cloud Garden, sent up by a mortal grower on a kite-string, with a note: "In thanks for the rain." {npc}, the head gardener, has never grown anything from below. {He} is sure they will not take. The air is wrong, the soil is wrong. {He} asks if you will help try anyway.
events.arc: The Mortal Apple Seeds in the Cloud Garden

effects.log: You mix cloud-loam and star-dust. The bed smells of morning.

choices.text: Say the seeds will not take

effects.log: {npc} sets them aside, a little disappointed.

choices.text: Say it is a waste of good soil

effects.log: {npc} files the seeds under "Unlikely."

events.text: The seeds come up, to everyone's surprise, as pale and thin as a ghost's apple tree. They bloom once and drop a single small fruit, sour as winter. {npc} tastes it and sits down heavily. "It is what the mortal grower grows," {he} says. "It is not what we grow. Should we graft it?"
events.arc: The Mortal Apple Seeds in the Cloud Garden

choices.text: Say graft it onto a peach

effects.log: The graft takes, in a decade. The fruit is odd and good.

choices.text: Say keep it pure and sour

effects.log: {npc} nods. The tree stays, small and stubborn.

choices.text: Say taste it again before deciding

effects.log: The second fruit is sweeter.

events.text: The graft is a marvel: a peach with an apple's snap. The gardener calls it the Kite-String, after the way it came. Children of the isle race to the tree each autumn. A mortal grower, far below, goes on sending seeds, and the Cloud Garden goes on trying.
events.arc: The Mortal Apple Seeds in the Cloud Garden

choices.text: Send down a graft in reply

effects.log: It falls on a windy night. No one knows where it lands.

choices.text: Take a slip to your own garden

effects.log: It thrives in a corner.

events.text: The pure tree stays small, sour and stubborn, and that is why {npc} loves it. In autumn the gardener brings out a basket of its fruit and gives one to every passer-by, with a bow, and a warning. People pull faces and laugh. It becomes the Cloud Garden's oldest joke, and its best-loved.
events.arc: The Mortal Apple Seeds in the Cloud Garden

choices.text: Eat the sour fruit with a straight face

effects.log: You are applauded by a gaggle of children.

choices.text: Write to the mortal grower in thanks

effects.log: The letter will take years to arrive.

events.text: {npc} keeps a mist hound on the Cinder Isle who is older than the isle's name. The isle is breaking up, a rock at a time, as isles do at the end, and the neighbours are packing for a new mooring. {npc} cannot decide whether the hound will bear the move. {He} asks you to walk with them both one last time.
events.arc: The Hound Who Outlived the Isle

choices.text: Walk the isle with {npc} and the hound

effects.log: The hound sniffs every stone like an old acquaintance. {npc} says nothing at all.

choices.text: Offer to carry the hound's basket

effects.log: It is heavy and warm and smells of rain.

choices.text: Say a hound is only a hound

effects.log: {npc} looks at you for a long moment, and walks on alone.

events.text: The ferrymen say a hound that old cannot cross the cloud sea; the crossing is too long, and the hound will not eat. {npc} sits on the doorstep through the night. In the morning, the hound has gone to the isle's highest rock and lain down, facing the sky, and will not be moved. {He} asks you what to do.
events.arc: The Hound Who Outlived the Isle

choices.text: Say stay with the hound on the isle

effects.log: {npc} nods, and lays out a blanket on the rock.

choices.text: Say carry the hound onto the ferry

effects.log: It takes both of you and an hour to lift it.
{npc} agrees, and waits.

events.text: The isle goes down in the night, a rock at a time, into the cloud sea. {npc} and the hound are on a skiff you hired, a few hundred yards off, watching. In the grey light the hound lifts its head and howls once, a long clean note that rolls out over the clouds, and then lays its head on {npc}'s knee.
events.arc: The Hound Who Outlived the Isle

choices.text: Row for the new mooring in silence

effects.log: The sea is flat and gold. The hound sleeps.
The hound is soothed. {npc} weeps.

events.text: The hound lives out its years on the new isle, a brown shape on a doorstep. When it dies, {npc} buries it under a young cloud-pine, with a stone that says only: "Home." Years later, at the pine, a mist hound pup is found sitting quietly, watching the door.
events.arc: The Hound Who Outlived the Isle

effects.log: The pup is wary and then not. {npc} calls it by the old hound's name.

choices.text: Leave a bowl of milk at the pine

effects.log: It is empty each morning.

events.text: {npc} stays on the old rock with the hound until the end, and you stay with them. The isle breaks and settles, and for one night the old hound lies on a dwindling stone in the middle of the clouds, content. By dawn a ferry has arrived, drawn by the howl. It carries all three of you home.
events.arc: The Hound Who Outlived the Isle

effects.log: The ferryman says nobody could have ignored that howl.

choices.text: Write the night down for the isle's archive

effects.log: The account is read at the next mooring festival.

events.text: {npc}'s cloud-cat has lived on the Pine Isle for six hundred years and never once been seen to leave. Today it is on the quay with its tail in the air, looking at a ferry bound for a distant isle. {npc} is aghast. "It has never even liked the water," {he} says.
events.arc: The Cat Who Chose a New Isle

effects.log: The cat boards the ferry with an air of sublime unconcern.

choices.text: Pick up the cat and carry it back

effects.log: The cat looks at you with a stare that withers.

choices.text: Say cats go where they like

effects.log: {npc} sits on a bollard and stares at the sea.

events.text: You and {npc} follow the cat across the sea. It strolls down the gangway at the far isle, a small place with a leaning house and one lantern. A very old person sits at the door, and the cat sits in their lap. {npc} gasps. "That is the cat's first owner," {he} says. "I thought they were dead."
events.arc: The Cat Who Chose a New Isle

choices.text: Greet the old owner with courtesy

effects.log: The old owner, almost deaf, nods and offers tea.

choices.text: Hold back and let the cat settle

effects.log: The cat settles. The owner strokes it, slowly, without looking up.

choices.text: Ask the owner how long they have been alone

effects.log: "A while," they say, "and no longer."

events.text: The cat stays. {npc} walks back to the quay with an empty basket and a full heart, and a standing invitation to tea. Every season thereafter, the old owner sends a note: "The cat is well." {npc} has never been happier to be told so little.
events.arc: The Cat Who Chose a New Isle

effects.log: The tea is stout, the house leans, the cat purrs.

choices.text: Send a gift of fish with {npc}

effects.log: It is received with the gravest courtesy.

events.text: The old owner dies that winter, with the cat in their lap. {npc} brings the cat home, in the basket, past the lantern and the quay, and the cat steps out onto the Pine Isle as though it had never left. It never leaves again. {He} says it went and did what it had to do.
events.arc: The Cat Who Chose a New Isle

choices.text: Sit with {npc} and the cat by the fire

effects.log: The cat purrs like a small engine.

choices.text: Plant a pine on the far isle for the old owner

effects.log: The tree thrives.

events.text: A carver named {npc} works at the foot of the Long Stairs, cutting epitaphs for immortals who have chosen to rest. {He} asks each client for a single line, and says most want grandeur and settle, in the end, for a joke. {He} has a blank tablet and a chisel, and offers you a seat.
events.arc: The Epitaph Carver of the Long Stairs

choices.text: Sit and think about what to say

effects.log: The line you think of surprises you. {npc} writes it on a slip.

choices.text: Ask to see the oldest epitaph

effects.log: It reads: "Went out to look at the weather." It has been there nine thousand years.

choices.text: Say you do not plan to die

effects.log: {npc} smiles. "That is what they all say," {he} says.

events.text: A client has died, and the family cannot agree on the line. One wants "A great scholar," another "A fine cook," a third "Never did as told." {npc} lets them argue. At dusk, {he} asks you what you think the tablet should say.
events.arc: The Epitaph Carver of the Long Stairs

effects.log: {npc} chisels the three lines in a neat column. The family goes quiet.
It is chosen. The family laughs, and weeps, and thanks you.
{npc} agrees. "They usually do," {he} says, "in the end."

events.text: The tablet is raised on a windy day and the whole family comes. The wind catches the carved letters and hums them, faintly, in the voice of the deceased. {npc} stands at the back, wiping dust from the chisel. "I have never cut a line that sang before," {he} says.
events.arc: The Epitaph Carver of the Long Stairs

effects.log: The hum fades slowly.
The carver nods, shyly.

events.text: You and {npc} cut the third line first, and then, in a better hour, a second beneath it: "But kind." The family leaves it. The tablet is passed by pilgrims for ten thousand years and is read aloud, now and then, to children, who grin.
events.arc: The Epitaph Carver of the Long Stairs

choices.text: Order a tablet for yourself, someday

effects.log: {npc} writes your name on a slip. "No hurry," {he} says.

choices.text: Read the tablet to a child

effects.log: The child grins.

events.text: {npc} is the Palace's sweet-maker, and in four hundred years has made a single sweet over and over, a white square that tastes of quiet. A guest from the Star Sea Pavilion has demanded something new. {npc} is crushed. {He} asks your advice, in the manner of one who has not heard the question before.
events.arc: The Sweet-Maker of the Nine Clouds Palace

effects.log: It is as good as ever, which is a problem.

choices.text: Say the guest is a fool

effects.log: {npc} brightens a little.
{npc} blanches and thanks you for your honesty.

events.text: {npc} experiments for a season. The results are strange: a sweet that tastes of hail, a sweet that tastes of other people's weddings. The kitchen gathers to taste, and they are not unkind. {He} asks which of the new sweets, if any, is worth serving. Your hand hovers.
events.arc: The Sweet-Maker of the Nine Clouds Palace

choices.text: Choose the one that tastes of weddings

effects.log: It is a marvel. The kitchen sighs.

choices.text: Choose none, and say the old is enough

effects.log: {npc} nods slowly, and sets the new ones aside.

choices.text: Eat them all and keep quiet

effects.log: You regret it, a little, and enjoy it, a lot.

events.text: The guest from the Star Sea Pavilion tastes the wedding sweet and weeps. {npc} is made master of the sweet-room, and the white square is retired from the Palace table, reverently, into a glass case. It is displayed to guests who do not eat it. {He} refills it with a fresh one each week.
events.arc: The Sweet-Maker of the Nine Clouds Palace

choices.text: Eat the glass-case sweet in secret

effects.log: It is better than anything in the Palace.

choices.text: Bow to the case when you pass

effects.log: The kitchen smiles.

events.text: The old sweet stays. The guest from the Pavilion tastes it with a stern face, then softens, and quietly takes a second. "It is," the guest says, "very quiet." {npc} bows. The new sweets are given away at the kitchen door, to the dishwashers, who love them extravagantly.
events.arc: The Sweet-Maker of the Nine Clouds Palace

choices.text: Share the new sweets at the door

effects.log: The dishwashers stand in a line, delighted.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to teach you the old sweet

effects.log: It takes ten years. It is the hardest thing you have ever learned.

events.text: {npc}, a librarian on the Willow Isle, reads aloud each evening to the shelves. The slips, {he} says, were written to be heard, and have been lonely. The other librarians find it absurd, and a few find it unsettling. {He} asks if you would like to sit in the front row.
events.arc: The Librarian Who Read Aloud to the Slips

effects.log: The reading is a poem about fog. The shelves seem to lean in.
You hear the reading from a distance. It is different there.
{npc} nods and begins again, reading to the dark.

events.text: One evening, the slips answer. A faint hum rises from a shelf as {npc} reads a poem of a dead author, and the jade lights up in the author's hand. {He} stops. The library is silent. The head librarian demands to know what is going on. {npc} looks to you.
events.arc: The Librarian Who Read Aloud to the Slips

choices.text: Say the shelves are only resonating

effects.log: The head librarian looks unconvinced, but lets it pass.

choices.text: Say the poems are alive in their way

effects.log: The head librarian goes pale, and sits down.
{npc} does. The hum rises. The head librarian sits and weeps.

events.text: The library is rearranged, quietly, to leave space for readings. Every evening now a librarian reads to a shelf, and the shelf hums back. Visitors come from other isles to hear. {npc} reads the last poem of the evening in a voice that has grown larger than the library, and the whole building seems to breathe.
events.arc: The Librarian Who Read Aloud to the Slips

choices.text: Read a poem of your own

effects.log: The shelf is polite. Then, shyly, it hums.

choices.text: Sit in the dark and listen

effects.log: You do, for an hour.

events.text: The head librarian forbids the readings, then forbids the forbidding. The slips go on humming faintly in the dark, a murmur like a distant crowd. {npc} says the library has become, at last, a place that is read. The humming stops only when the building is empty. Then it starts again.
events.arc: The Librarian Who Read Aloud to the Slips

choices.text: Spend a night in the library to hear it

effects.log: The humming lasts till dawn. You have never been so well accompanied.

choices.text: Bring a lamp for {npc} to read by

effects.log: The lamp is small and steady.

events.text: A lens-grinder at the Star Sea Pavilion polishes one lens for forty years. When it is done she holds it up to a candle and the flame divides into seven. "That is not what I meant," she says calmly, "but I like it."

effects.log: You see a candle seven times over, and each is a little different.

choices.text: Suggest she keeps it as it is

effects.log: She laughs. "That is the only way I will keep it," she says.

events.text: The apprentices of the Star Sea Pavilion sleep in shifts, and a tray of tiny, severe sandwiches is passed between them at four in the morning. One of the apprentices sleeps with her face on a chart. A moth sits on the star it is lying on.

choices.text: Slip a blanket over the apprentice

effects.log: She sleeps on. The moth stays on the star.

choices.text: Take a sandwich and a watch shift

effects.log: You sit up with the stars until dawn. The sandwich is surprisingly good.

events.text: A slip in the Jade Void library is eight thousand years overdue. The borrower has left a note: "Still reading." The clerk adds a fine to the card, as she has every year, and sets the card carefully back.

choices.text: Ask how much the fine has reached

effects.log: It is a number so large the clerk has run out of ink.

choices.text: Offer to return the slip for the borrower

effects.log: The clerk looks at you with weary gratitude. You find the borrower reading under a tree, a very old figure.

events.text: Dust gathers on the highest shelves of the Great Slip Library, and no one dusts them. A librarian explains that the dust is itself catalogued: it is the dust of earlier slips, and has been indexed to the century.

choices.text: Ask to see the dust index

effects.log: It is a vast, beautiful, useless book. You read the first page twice.
The librarian faints, very quietly.

events.text: A skiff mechanic is oiling the bow of a cloud-skiff with something that smells of rain and old coins. "The skiff likes it," the mechanic tells you. "Never ask me what it is."

effects.log: The oil is warm. The skiff hums.

choices.text: Ask for a little for your own boat

effects.log: The mechanic fills a tiny bottle. Your skiff has never run smoother.

events.text: A new cloud-skiff has been launched at the Rusted Quay, and its owner cannot decide on a name. The mechanic holds the paintbrush. The owner tries "Dawn," "Brave Wind," "My Third Wife." The skiff itself is humming "Patience."

effects.log: The owner paints it on the bow. The skiff hums happily.
The owner paints it. The skiff sulks for a decade.

events.text: The head cook of a palace kitchen is said to hand an apron to anyone worth teaching. A scullion once told you that she kept hers twenty years in a drawer, unworn, and the head cook never asked for it back.

choices.text: Ask the head cook for an apron

effects.log: The head cook gives you a long look and hands you a ladle instead.
She goes pink. You make a friend for life.

events.text: In the palace kitchen at midnight, a pot of tea is left on the back of the stove for whoever is awake. The kitchen cats take their turn. On the table, a note: "If you are reading this, you are the night shift. Thank you."

choices.text: Pour a cup and sit with the cats

effects.log: The cats permit it. The tea is the best of the day.
In the morning, a second note: "You are welcome."

events.text: A cloud-house on the Lantern Isle has been let to the same ghost for six hundred years. The landlord says the ghost is no trouble, pays on time, and has never once complained about the draught.

choices.text: Leave a candle on the sill for the ghost

effects.log: The candle burns steadily. A cold hand passes over the flame.

choices.text: Ask the ghost how it likes the house

effects.log: A faint answer: "Quiet."

events.text: A ghost stands at the gate of the Jade Court every day, politely asking if the audience is still scheduled. The court clerk says it was scheduled eight hundred years ago and he has never had the heart to tell the ghost.

choices.text: Tell the ghost the audience is over

effects.log: The ghost bows deeply and drifts away, relieved.

choices.text: Take the ghost's petition to the clerk

effects.log: The petition is filed. The ghost is content.

events.text: In the Hall of Precedence a chair is set aside for an immortal who has been dead for a thousand years. The clerks bow to it as they pass. A visitor tries to sit in it, and the hall goes cold.

effects.log: The visitor mutters. The hall warms.
You feel an answering bow.

events.text: At the Cloud Market, a stall sells new names, of a quality said to be hard to tell from real ones. A banner reads: "Be anyone, within reason." The stallholder asks what name you would like to try.

choices.text: Try a name for the afternoon

effects.log: You are called by it all day. It fits oddly well.

choices.text: Say you are happy with your own

effects.log: The stallholder nods approvingly. "Rare," he says.

events.text: Someone has been using your seal at the Cloud Market, small purchases only: a bolt of mist, a jar of starlight. The merchants say the person was very polite. They have all assumed it was you.

choices.text: Pay the small bills and say nothing

effects.log: You pay a few stones. The merchants are relieved.

choices.text: Tell the merchants it was not you

effects.log: They are baffled and hurt, and they go quiet.

events.text: A parcel from below has come to rest on your doorstep: a bundle of dried persimmons, wrapped in a mortal's newspaper and tied with string. There is no note. They are good persimmons.

choices.text: Eat them slowly, one a day

effects.log: They last a month. The last tastes like autumn.
The whole row smells of fruit for a day.

events.text: A letter, a thousand years late, arrives on the evening wind addressed to a name you do not recognise. The postmaster squints and says it is yours, in a way. It was meant for the previous owner of your house.

choices.text: Read it aloud to the empty house

effects.log: The house creaks, as though listening.

choices.text: Seek out the previous owner's kin

effects.log: You find a descendant three isles away. They are delighted.

events.text: On the Pine Isle, a row of small stones marks the graves of pets, with names and dates. The oldest bears a date from before the isle had a name. A child is leaving a daisy chain on the newest.

choices.text: Leave a flower of your own

effects.log: The child nods approvingly.
There are four hundred of them. The wind carries them off.

events.text: A stooped immortal feeds forty-one stray cloud-cats each dusk from a basket, on the same bench, in the same coat. The cats wait in a line, and the sky blazes behind them. The immortal looks at you and says nothing.

effects.log: The cats take to you at once, and then less.

choices.text: Sit on the end of the bench

effects.log: You watch the sunset from among forty-one cats.

events.text: On the Long Stairs a carver has cut a hundred small jokes into the risers. Pilgrims laugh at one in four and glare at the rest. A new line is being cut as you climb: "Nearly there."

choices.text: Ask the carver if it is true

effects.log: "No," the carver says cheerfully. "But it helps."
You reach the top in better spirits.

events.text: A skiff has been tied to the Reed Lake quay for three weeks with its sail half-mended. The mechanic says the owner is a friend of a friend and has not paid. He mends it daily anyway, in case the owner turns up.

choices.text: Offer to pay for the repair

effects.log: The mechanic refuses, with dignity, and then accepts a stone.

choices.text: Wait for the owner with the mechanic

effects.log: The owner arrives in a week, and is sorry.

events.text: On the longest night, ghosts of the isle's former residents drift through the lantern-lit streets, pausing at doors where once they lived. The living leave doors ajar. The ghosts are polite, and their step is the sound of falling snow.

effects.log: Something enters, rests a moment by your fire, and goes.

choices.text: Walk with the ghosts to the end of the street

effects.log: They do not mind your company.

events.text: At the Cloud Market, {npc} lends spirit stones at an interest so low it is almost an insult, and collects with a patience that frightens the other lenders. {He} has a ledger of debts running back eleven centuries. A customer is two hundred years behind and {npc} sends you to ask, nicely, when they might pay.
events.arc: The Lender Who Forgave by the Century

effects.log: The debtor is a stooped tailor with a house full of cats. The conversation is long and awkward.

choices.text: Ask to read the ledger first

effects.log: The ledger is a history of the Cloud Market in numbers.
{npc} nods. "Few are," {he} says.

events.text: The tailor cannot pay. The tailor's partner died two hundred years ago and the shop went with them. {npc} knew this, and has kept the debt on the books as a way to keep a visit on the calendar. {He} asks you what a lender is for, if not for stones. It is a real question.
events.arc: The Lender Who Forgave by the Century

choices.text: Say a lender is for keeping people in the world

effects.log: {npc} writes this in the ledger margin.

choices.text: Say a lender is for being paid

effects.log: {npc} bows to the answer, and looks tired.
{npc} says that is the honest answer.

events.text: {npc} strikes the debt from the ledger in front of the tailor, with a flourish, and then, to everyone's astonishment, lends the tailor a hundred stones to reopen the shop. The tailor weeps. The cats are fed. The ledger gains a new page, headed "Beginnings."
events.arc: The Lender Who Forgave by the Century

choices.text: Order the first suit from the reopened shop

effects.log: It is a fine suit, and a little too long in the sleeve.

choices.text: Help the tailor hang the sign

effects.log: The sign is crooked. Both of you like it.

events.text: The ledger is closed on the debt. The tailor pays back what can be paid, in eggs and mended coats, over a century. {npc} never raises a voice. At the century's end, the tailor presses a perfect suit into {his} hands, and {npc} wears it to the market, with great and silent pride.
events.arc: The Lender Who Forgave by the Century

effects.log: {npc} smooths it. "I did not lend it," {he} says. "I invested."

choices.text: Say a debt can be many things

effects.log: The lender smiles, a rare event.

events.text: No lender in the Cloud Market will lend to a rogue without a seal. {npc}, an old stall-keeper, sells noodles on credit to anyone, and keeps a ledger of every hungry rogue {he} has fed. {He} sees you counting your stones and slides a steaming bowl across the counter without a word.
events.arc: The Loan Nobody Offered a Rogue

choices.text: Ask for a bowl on credit

effects.log: The noodles are hot. {npc} writes your name in the ledger without a word.
"It is a list of people who were hungry," says {npc}.
{npc} accepts the stones with the look of one robbed of an opportunity.

events.text: A rogue you know, desperate, borrows a hundred stones from a dark-lantern lender at ruinous interest. {npc} hears of it and is quiet for an hour. {He} asks whether you would go with {him} to the lender, to ask a favour that no one has asked. {He} is not sure it is wise.
events.arc: The Loan Nobody Offered a Rogue

effects.log: The lender listens, bored, with a lamp turned too low.

choices.text: Say the rogue must face it alone

effects.log: {npc} nods. The rogue does not forget.

choices.text: Offer stones of your own to the rogue

effects.log: The rogue refuses, and thanks you, and weeps.

events.text: The lender, startled by the old stall-keeper's plain courtesy, halves the interest and extends the term. The rogue pays it in forty years. {npc} takes no credit, and keeps no ledger of the matter. But the rogue brings {npc} a bowl of noodles every year, on the same day, and a flower.
events.arc: The Loan Nobody Offered a Rogue

effects.log: It is the most generous bowl you have had.

choices.text: Add your name to the credit ledger

effects.log: It is a short list, and a good one.

events.text: The rogue pays alone, the hard way, over a century. At the end they are free, thin, and fearsome. They come to the noodle stall and put a heap of stones on the counter. {npc} counts it, whistles, and pushes half back. "For the next hungry one," {he} says. The rogue nods slowly, and does.
events.arc: The Loan Nobody Offered a Rogue

choices.text: Say the stall is a good place

effects.log: {npc} smiles, a little.

choices.text: Hold the rogue's hand a moment

effects.log: It is thin and warm.

events.text: {npc} dyes clouds for the sunset: a long, hard trade, done at dusk from a skiff with ladles of coloured mist. The order this season is for "a dusk a person can cry at." {He} has tried nine reds. {He} asks if you would hold the ladle while {he} looks for a tenth.
events.arc: The Dyer of Evening Clouds

effects.log: The mist is warm and smells of cinnamon. The tenth red comes up, slowly.
You say, "the colour of a house you left." {npc} goes very still.

choices.text: Say no one cries at sunsets

effects.log: {npc} looks at you with pity.

events.text: The customer, a bereaved immortal, hangs on the quay each evening, watching the dusk, and sobs, and demands a better colour. {npc} is exhausted. {He} cannot give a person a dusk they can cry at; the dusk can only be itself. {He} asks you whether to tell the customer the truth.
events.arc: The Dyer of Evening Clouds

effects.log: {npc} does. The customer weeps harder, and then less.

choices.text: Say dye the sky one more time

effects.log: {npc} does. It is the finest dusk of the age, and does nothing.

choices.text: Say you will sit with the customer

effects.log: You do. It takes an evening.

events.text: The customer, comforted, tells {npc} the dusk is enough. {He} hangs up the ladle for a year and spends it in the garden. When the ladle comes down, the first dusk {he} paints is plain, a quiet gold. A grieving stranger on the quay sighs and smiles.
events.arc: The Dyer of Evening Clouds

choices.text: Watch the plain dusk from the quay

effects.log: It is quiet, and it is right.
{He} is moved. "That is the whole trade," {he} says.

events.text: The finest dusk of the age draws crowds from every isle. The customer cries, and the crowd cries, and {npc} watches from the skiff, appalled. "That was not the sunset," {he} says. "That was a performance." {He} never dyes so grandly again, and the tenth red goes into a cupboard.
events.arc: The Dyer of Evening Clouds

effects.log: {npc} nods. "They hold up better," {he} says.

choices.text: Ask for a vial of the tenth red

effects.log: It glows faintly in the cupboard of your house for centuries.

events.text: {npc} tastes the winds for the Ministry of Weather, and rates them in a notebook: "full," "thin," "peppery," "sour with grief." {He} tastes a new wind at dawn and goes pale. It is, {he} says, a wind from a place that no longer exists. {He} asks you to taste it too, and tell {him} if {he} is mad.
events.arc: The Taster of Winds

effects.log: It tastes of oranges and woodsmoke, and a long ago summer. You cannot say why you feel homesick.

choices.text: Say you do not trust your tongue

effects.log: {npc} nods. "Few do," {he} says.

choices.text: Say the wind is only a wind

effects.log: {npc} writes "unremarkable" with a trembling hand.

events.text: The wind comes every dawn for a week. {npc} traces it, step by step, to a sunken isle at the bottom of the cloud sea. The Ministry will not send a diver. {He} cannot go alone. The wind seems to be growing fainter, as though calling out its last. {He} asks if you will go.
events.arc: The Taster of Winds

choices.text: Go with {npc} to the sunken isle

effects.log: The dive is long and cold. At the bottom, a house, a garden, a door ajar.

choices.text: Go and watch from the rim

effects.log: You hold the rope. {npc} descends alone.
The Ministry sends a brisk refusal.

events.text: In the house on the sunken isle is a kitchen, a table set for two, and a window. The wind enters by the window, finds the table, and stops. {npc} sets down a cup. The wind sighs. On the table, a note: "Come home soon." It has been waiting for a very long time.
events.arc: The Taster of Winds

choices.text: Write a reply on the back

effects.log: The wind carries it up with a cheerful gust.

choices.text: Leave the table as it is

effects.log: You close the door softly.

events.text: {npc} descends alone and returns with the wind in a jar. The Ministry takes the jar for its archive and files it as "Atmospheric, Melancholy." {npc} says the wind is happier in the archive than at the bottom of the sea. {He} does not believe it, and neither do you.
events.arc: The Taster of Winds

choices.text: Visit the jar from time to time

effects.log: It stirs when you come in.

choices.text: Ask the Ministry to release it

effects.log: The Ministry sends a stiff note. A decade later, the jar is quietly uncorked on a windy hill.

events.text: As a servant of the Celestial Ministries you are sent to the Lost-and-Found of the Ministry of Fog, where {npc} has kept an archive of items lost in fog for nine thousand years: umbrellas, shoes, a flute, a lover's ring, one entire pavilion. {He} asks if you can help clear the backlog.
events.arc: The Lost-and-Found of the Ministry of Fog

effects.log: You sort for a week. Every object has a story attached, and a number.

choices.text: Ask what the pavilion is doing there

effects.log: "It was lost in a fog," says {npc}, "and no one has come to claim it."

choices.text: Say the backlog is not your concern

effects.log: {npc} sighs and returns to a shelf of single gloves.

events.text: Among the lost objects you find a letter, addressed to someone who has been dead for centuries, from a friend who is still alive. It has sat in the Lost-and-Found, unopened, for a thousand years. {npc} cannot deliver it. {He} asks whether to give it to the living friend, who might not wish to read it.
events.arc: The Lost-and-Found of the Ministry of Fog

choices.text: Say deliver it, and let them choose

effects.log: {npc} nods and writes the address in a firm hand.

choices.text: Say keep it, as a mercy

effects.log: {npc} files it in a drawer marked "Unresolved."
{npc} refuses, shocked, then pleased you asked.

events.text: The friend reads the letter in the Lost-and-Found, standing up, among umbrellas. It is a reply to a question the friend asked a thousand years ago. The friend reads it three times, smiles, and walks out into the fog. {npc} watches them go. "That," {he} says, "is why we keep the shelves."
events.arc: The Lost-and-Found of the Ministry of Fog

effects.log: The space is left bare, as a mark.

choices.text: Take a lost umbrella as a keepsake

effects.log: It is a good umbrella, and never quite dry.

events.text: The letter stays in its drawer. {npc} does not look at it again for decades. Then, one rainy afternoon, the friend wanders into the Lost-and-Found asking after a lost umbrella, and {npc} hands over the letter, unexpectedly, and says only: "I think this is yours." The friend takes it, puzzled, and reads it on the step.
events.arc: The Lost-and-Found of the Ministry of Fog

effects.log: The rain falls on the shelves. The kettle sings.

choices.text: Ask {npc} why the change of heart

effects.log: "The fog lifted," says {npc}.

events.text: {npc}, a retired marshal of the Celestial Ministries, has taken to gardening and is losing a war to a single gnat. {He} pursues it with a battle plan, a net and a speech. The gnat is unmoved. {He} summons you as a trusted junior officer to advise on the campaign.
events.arc: The Retired Marshal and the Garden Gnat

effects.log: The gnat lives in the lilac and likes a rotting plum. You tell {npc}, who writes it as intelligence.

choices.text: Offer the gnat a plum on a dish

effects.log: {npc} is scandalised. The gnat is delighted.

choices.text: Say the gnat is beneath a marshal

effects.log: {npc} salutes you stiffly and resumes the siege.

events.text: The gnat has been joined by its family. The garden is under siege. {npc} proposes a drastic measure: a smoke from the old war-braziers, which would clear the pests and the flowers both. {He} asks whether the garden should be saved or the principle.
events.arc: The Retired Marshal and the Garden Gnat

choices.text: Say save the garden, sue for peace

effects.log: {npc} is stern. "A marshal does not sue for peace," {he} says. And then: "Yes."

choices.text: Say use the smoke, and win

effects.log: The smoke clears the garden. The garden is dead. {npc} gazes at the grey ground.

choices.text: Say neither, and offer to help with a broom

effects.log: You sweep the garden for a day.

events.text: The peace treaty is a very short document, signed on a petal: the gnats may have the plum tree in return for leaving the lilac alone. {npc} signs it with a ceremonial brush. The next morning the garden is full of butterflies. The old marshal calls them "the guard of honour."
events.arc: The Retired Marshal and the Garden Gnat

effects.log: You drink under the plum tree among the gnats.
It is kept in a glass on the marshal's desk.

events.text: The garden is dead. {npc} stands over the ashes for a week, silent, in full uniform. Then {he} takes a trowel and begins again. It takes years. At the end, there is a plum tree, and a lilac, and, with a pleasant buzz, one gnat.
events.arc: The Retired Marshal and the Garden Gnat

effects.log: You work all spring. The earth is soft and forgiving.
The gnat is called "Honorable Enemy." It buzzes, content.

events.text: The Tern Isle is dying, and its people have gathered at the edge for the old rite: they will carry what is dear to them to the neighbouring isle, and let the Tern Isle go down into the cloud sea. {npc}, the isle's eldest, has refused to leave. {He} asks you to help persuade the rest to go first.
events.arc: The Funeral of an Isle

effects.log: You carry baskets all day. The isle trembles underfoot.

choices.text: Talk with {npc} about the old days

effects.log: {He} has a thousand stories, and tells them all.

choices.text: Say a dying isle is not your problem

effects.log: {npc} says nothing, and turns back to the doorway.

events.text: By the third day only {npc} and a handful remain. The isle sags. The neighbouring isle has sent a boat, and a note: "Come now, or be lost." {npc} stands at the door of a small house, with a hand on the frame. {He} says the house is the oldest thing {he} has and cannot be carried. {He} asks what you would do.
events.arc: The Funeral of an Isle

choices.text: Say take the doorframe, and leave the rest

effects.log: {npc} nods, takes a chisel, and begins to work the frame loose.

choices.text: Say stay, and let the isle take you both

effects.log: {npc} is silent. Then {he} laughs. "Not today," {he} says.
{npc} nods, grateful.

events.text: The doorframe is carried across the water on the last skiff. {npc} sets it in the wall of a new house on the neighbouring isle, and when the door is hung, the old hinges sing. The Tern Isle goes down in the night, a long soft sigh. In the morning {npc} knocks on the frame, and the neighbours gather.
events.arc: The Funeral of an Isle

effects.log: The sound is deep, warm and very old.
The frame fits as though it were made there.

events.text: {npc} stays one more night, and in the morning boards the last skiff alone, with the isle already sinking. You watch it go down from the other deck, a long green shape slipping into the clouds, with a single light in a window. {npc} stands at the rail, bareheaded. The light goes out last.
events.arc: The Funeral of an Isle

effects.log: No one speaks until the clouds close.

choices.text: Hold a lantern for the lost isle

effects.log: You hold it until dawn. {npc} stays beside you.

events.text: {npc} makes a trade of burying dead isles: gently lowering them, in good order, into the cloud sea, with a hymn and a flag. It is an old trade and a quiet one. {He} asks if you would like to see a lowering, because the apprentice has fallen sick, and the hymn needs a second voice.
events.arc: The Undertaker of Dead Isles

choices.text: Agree to sing the second voice

effects.log: The hymn is low and long. The isle goes down slowly.
It is the most solemn thing you have seen.
{npc} sings alone, and well.

events.text: A rival undertaker offers to lower the next dead isle for half the price, with no hymn. The isle's owner is poor and tempted. {npc} says nothing, but does not deny the poor owner a place in the ceremony. The owner looks to you. "Which is better?" the owner asks.
events.arc: The Undertaker of Dead Isles

effects.log: The owner pays {npc}, and is glad of it.

choices.text: Say the cheap lowering is fine

effects.log: The rival lowers the isle in silence. The owner regrets it.
The owner decides, slowly, with tears.

events.text: The hymn is sung, and the isle goes down, and the owner stands on the quay with the flag. A child of the isle, who would not come to the ceremony, comes at the last minute and sings the final line. It is wrong, and perfect. {npc} nods. "The child has the trade," {he} says.
events.arc: The Undertaker of Dead Isles

choices.text: Say the child should be the apprentice

effects.log: {npc} writes the child's name in a small book.

choices.text: Help the owner fold the flag

effects.log: The flag is warm, and smells of rain.

events.text: The rival's lowering is quick and silent. The owner stands on the quay in a strange quiet, and then, haltingly, begins to hum the hymn on their own. {npc} stands at the back, hat in hand. At the end, {he} sets down a small flag at the owner's feet, unpaid. "For the ones who had no hymn," {he} says.
events.arc: The Undertaker of Dead Isles

choices.text: Sing the second voice for the owner

effects.log: Your voice joins theirs. The hymn is finished.
The fee goes into a jar. {He} accepts without a word.

events.text: {npc} has not slept in four hundred years. At first it was a joy, then a habit, then a burden. {He} wanders the Willow Isle at night with a lamp, tapping on shutters, apologising. {He} asks if you would sit up with {him} one night, because the nights are long.
events.arc: The Immortal Who Forgot How to Sleep

effects.log: The night is cold and clear. You discuss everything and nothing.

choices.text: Bring a flask of warm milk

effects.log: {npc} drinks, and says it is the first warm thing in a decade.

choices.text: Say you need your own sleep

effects.log: {npc} nods, and goes on tapping shutters.

events.text: {npc} learns of a cure: a lullaby, sung by a particular tide-singer who lives on the Reed Lake. The singer is old and testy and will not sing for an immortal who has wasted sleep. {He} asks you to plead the case, since {he} is too embarrassed to ask.
events.arc: The Immortal Who Forgot How to Sleep

choices.text: Go and plead with the tide-singer

effects.log: The tide-singer is unimpressed, but tilts an ear.

choices.text: Learn the lullaby yourself and sing it

effects.log: It takes you a month. You are quite bad at it.
It takes {him} a year to try.

events.text: The tide-singer comes and sings, one verse, on the end of {npc}'s bed. The first sleep in four hundred years falls on the sleepless like snow. {He} wakes thirty hours later and says nothing for an hour. Then: "I dreamed. I had forgotten how." {He} weeps with joy.
events.arc: The Immortal Who Forgot How to Sleep

effects.log: The dream-light is faint and gold in the room.
The tide-singer waves it off and goes home.

events.text: Your lullaby is terrible, and it works. {npc} falls asleep in the middle of the second verse, from sheer boredom, and sleeps nine days. When {he} wakes, {he} tells you your singing is the worst in the Heavens and the best medicine. You sing every night for a year.
events.arc: The Immortal Who Forgot How to Sleep

effects.log: It is no better. {npc} sleeps soundly.

choices.text: Teach {npc} to sing it for others

effects.log: The Willow Isle sleeps well for a century.

events.text: At the top of the Quiet Peak, a hermit named {npc} rents out silence by the hour, in a stone room with no door. Cloud-merchants come to sit and think. A sign says: "Paid in advance. No refunds if you speak." {He} gives you a mat and a bell, and says to ring it if you break.
events.arc: The Hermit Who Rented Out Silence

choices.text: Sit for an hour in the silence

effects.log: The silence is enormous. By the end of the hour you hear your own heart.

choices.text: Ask what happens if you speak

effects.log: "Nothing," says {npc}. "But you will not forget it."
{npc} shrugs. "Neither can a cloud," {he} says, "and yet."

events.text: A loud customer, a retired general, has taken the room for a month and tries to talk. Silence rolls off the general like water. {npc} is troubled: the silence of the room is being worn down. {He} asks you to watch the stairs while {he} deals with the matter. The general summons you.
events.arc: The Hermit Who Rented Out Silence

choices.text: Say the room is full, and politely refuse

effects.log: The general fumes, but leaves.

choices.text: Sit with the general in the quiet

effects.log: The general, eventually, shuts up. It takes three days.
{npc} deals with it in a way that leaves no marks.

events.text: The general leaves, quiet, and sends a gift: a single bolt of cloud-silk, with a note that reads, in a stern hand, "Thank you for the rest." {npc} hangs the bolt over the doorway. It stays unspun, a banner of nothing. The room is quiet again.
events.arc: The Hermit Who Rented Out Silence

choices.text: Sit one more hour in the room

effects.log: It is quieter than before.

choices.text: Tell {npc} the story of the silent general

effects.log: {He} laughs, softly, as though in a library.

events.text: You and the general sit three days in the stone room. On the third, the general speaks one sentence, "I have never known what to say," and you say nothing, and it is the right answer. The general leaves in better order than at arrival. {npc} charges for the hour and refuses the extra days.
events.arc: The Hermit Who Rented Out Silence

effects.log: You leave three stones on the mat.

choices.text: Take the room for a month yourself

effects.log: The month is long and sweet.

events.text: {npc} herds clouds on the High Meadow of the Pine Isle, a flock of three hundred, each with a name. This morning the flock is two hundred and ninety-eight. The two missing are the youngest. {He} asks you to help find them before the night wind does.
events.arc: The Cloud-Shepherd Who Lost a Flock

effects.log: You find tracks of mist in the grass, leading toward the cliff.
They drift in agitation, and point in unison.

choices.text: Say clouds go where they like

effects.log: {npc} gives you a look, and goes on alone.

events.text: The two lost clouds are huddled in a hollow on the cliff-side, frightened of the wind, and a stranger is with them: a thin, wild-looking child, no more than three hundred, with a staff of cloud-pine. The child says the clouds are theirs now. {npc} says they are the flock's. Both look at you.
events.arc: The Cloud-Shepherd Who Lost a Flock

choices.text: Say the clouds belong to themselves

effects.log: The child blinks. {npc} chuckles. The clouds stay put.

choices.text: Propose the child join the flock-keeping

effects.log: {npc} grumbles, and agrees, on a trial basis.

choices.text: Say sort it out between you

effects.log: They do, slowly, with tea.

events.text: The clouds decide: they stay with the flock by day, and visit the child by night. {npc} and the child become uneasy allies, and then friends, and then, after twenty years, a pair of old herders, sitting on the meadow grumbling. The flock grows to three hundred and forty. Nobody complains.
events.arc: The Cloud-Shepherd Who Lost a Flock

effects.log: The flock glows pink. The herders wave.

choices.text: Bring a new cloud to the flock

effects.log: It is adopted at once, and named after you.

events.text: The child joins the flock as an apprentice, scruffy, brilliant and loud. {npc} teaches the names, the signs and the winds. In ten years, the apprentice leads the flock to the high pasture alone. {npc} watches from the gate, in a chair, holding a cup of tea. "I did not lose a flock," {he} says. "I gained a herder."
events.arc: The Cloud-Shepherd Who Lost a Flock

effects.log: The tea is hot and sweet.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to tell the flock's story

effects.log: It takes an evening.

events.text: On the Long Bridge a stall sells nothing but mended promises: oaths cracked, vows chipped, a sworn friendship with a hairline split. {npc}, the mender, patches them with gold. A customer arrives with a vow so shattered that it is mostly dust. {He} turns to you. "Can you stay and hold the pieces?"
events.arc: The Mender of Broken Promises

effects.log: They are cold and sharp, and weigh like water.
The customer says: "To go home. I did not."

choices.text: Say a broken vow cannot be mended

effects.log: {npc} nods. "That is why the stall is always busy," {he} says.

events.text: The customer's home no longer exists. The vow cannot be mended as it was. {npc} suggests another way: to bind the pieces with a different promise, a smaller one. The customer is silent. The mender looks to you to name what the new vow should be. It is a heavy request.
events.arc: The Mender of Broken Promises

effects.log: The customer takes the pieces. {npc} sets them with gold.
The customer weeps. {npc} sets the pieces with a brighter gold.

choices.text: Say you cannot choose for them

effects.log: The customer chooses for themselves, after a night.

events.text: The mended vow is a little ring of gold-veined glass. The customer wears it on a string. A year later, the customer comes back and says it has become a home of a sort: a small stall, a lamp, an open door. {npc} grins. "That is the usual result," {he} says.
events.arc: The Mender of Broken Promises

effects.log: It sells tea, plain and hot.

choices.text: Leave a flower at the door

effects.log: The flower is on the sill next morning.

events.text: The vow is set with the gold of remembering, and the customer carries it to the home that is gone. At the quay, they open a small locket, and pour out a pinch of earth from a place that no longer exists, into the sea of clouds. {npc} stands at the rail. "Some promises are kept by not being kept," {he} says.
events.arc: The Mender of Broken Promises

choices.text: Stand with the customer at the rail

effects.log: You say nothing. The earth falls away.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to teach you the gold

effects.log: It is a lifetime's trade. You learn a thimbleful.

events.text: On the Orchard Isle, two neighbours, {npc} and a rival, both claim the last peach of the season: a perfect one, growing on a branch that overhangs a fence. The quarrel has lasted a month. {npc} shows you the branch. "Mine," {he} says. "The root is on my side."
events.arc: The Quarrel Over the Last Peach of the Season

effects.log: The rival insists the fruit is theirs, as the branch leans their way.

choices.text: Suggest cutting the peach in two

effects.log: {npc} is horrified. The rival is intrigued.

choices.text: Say a peach is a peach

effects.log: {npc} spends a day sulking.

events.text: The quarrel spreads: the neighbours' children now refuse to play together, and a cat has taken a side. The Orchard Isle holds a mediation in the orchard-house, and you are asked to chair. The peach, in a bowl, sits on the table, getting riper. The room is tense.
events.arc: The Quarrel Over the Last Peach of the Season

choices.text: Propose a tasting by all three

effects.log: The peach is cut in three. The room is stunned.

choices.text: Propose the peach go to a child

effects.log: {npc} snorts. Then, slowly, nods.
By morning the peach is a little too ripe.

events.text: The peach is cut in three, one for each neighbour and one for you. It is the best peach any of you has ever eaten. The quarrel ends in a long, awkward silence, broken by {npc} saying, in a tiny voice, "I am sorry." The rival says the same. The cat chooses a side: both.
events.arc: The Quarrel Over the Last Peach of the Season

effects.log: The two neighbours dig a hole at the fence. A shoot comes up in a month.

choices.text: Take the pit as a keepsake

effects.log: It sits on your shelf, and hums softly.

events.text: The peach goes to a child, who eats it with a solemnity that melts the room. The neighbours look at each other, ashamed, and then amused. {npc} goes home and plants the pit, which grows, in a year, into a tiny and ridiculous tree. The rival sends a letter of apology on a leaf.
events.arc: The Quarrel Over the Last Peach of the Season

choices.text: Reply in kind on a leaf

effects.log: The exchange of leaves lasts a century.

choices.text: Tell the story at the next feast

effects.log: It becomes the orchard's favourite.

events.text: {npc} sells wind-chimes from a barrow on the market bridge, and cannot hear a note. {He} tunes each chime by eye, and by the way the customers' faces change. {He} asks if you would listen to a new set and say which ring true. It is the first time {he} has asked anyone.
events.arc: The Wind-Chime Peddler Who Could Not Hear

effects.log: Three ring true, and two ring a little sour.
{npc} reads your face and laughs. "Liar," {he} says.

choices.text: Say you do not know music

effects.log: {npc} nods. "Nor do I," {he} says. "That is the point."

events.text: A commission arrives: a chime for a wedding on the Wind Isle, to be rung at the vows. It must be perfect, and {npc} cannot hear it. The couple is demanding. {He} asks you to be the ears. It is a serious request, to be responsible for the sound of another person's happiness.
events.arc: The Wind-Chime Peddler Who Could Not Hear

effects.log: You spend a week at the barrow. {npc} watches your face as you listen.

choices.text: Suggest the couple bring a musician

effects.log: The musician is cheerful and says the chime is fine.

choices.text: Say it is too much to ask

effects.log: {npc} understands, and goes on alone.

events.text: The chime rings at the wedding, a clear and perfect sound. The couple weeps. {npc} stands at the back, hands folded, and watches the faces. When the note rings, {he} knows: the guests' eyes go bright. {He} turns to you. "I heard that," {he} says. "I heard it in all of them."
events.arc: The Wind-Chime Peddler Who Could Not Hear

effects.log: It is the happiest evening of the season.

choices.text: Say nothing and leave a stone

effects.log: On the barrow in the morning, a chime with your name on it.

events.text: The musician says the chime is fine, and the couple, cheerful, accepts it. {npc} is a little hurt, and a little relieved. The chime rings at the wedding in a pleasant, imperfect way, and nobody minds. Afterwards the musician comes to the barrow and buys the sour pair, for an experiment.
events.arc: The Wind-Chime Peddler Who Could Not Hear

choices.text: Ask the musician what they will make

effects.log: It will be called "Imperfect Wedding."
{npc} smiles. "That is high praise, from you," {he} says.

events.text: {npc} is the last who can write the old seal-script, the angular writing of the first slips. No one reads it now but the oldest archivists. {He} sits in a small booth at the foot of the Slip Library, writing names on request, for a stone apiece. {He} offers to write yours in the old style.
events.arc: The Last Calligrapher of the Seal-Script

choices.text: Ask for your name in seal-script

effects.log: It looks like a bird on a branch. You keep it for ever.
The name is a friend's. {npc} writes it with tenderness.

choices.text: Say no one reads it any more

effects.log: {npc} nods. "That is the point of writing it," {he} says.

events.text: {npc} is going blind. The seal-script requires an eye of absolute precision, and the strokes are growing uncertain. {He} will not stop. {He} asks if you will learn the script, to write it when {he} cannot. It is a vast task, for no one's benefit but a dying art.
events.arc: The Last Calligrapher of the Seal-Script

effects.log: {npc} begins to teach you the first twelve strokes.

choices.text: Say the script should be preserved in a book

effects.log: {npc} frowns, then nods. The two of you begin a primer.

choices.text: Say you will think about it

effects.log: {npc} waits, as patient as stone.

events.text: You spend a decade at the booth, learning strokes, and your hand becomes steady. By the time {npc} sets down the brush for good, you can write your own name in seal-script and a thousand others. {He} dies in the booth, in the afternoon, smiling. You write the name on the stone.
events.arc: The Last Calligrapher of the Seal-Script

choices.text: Write {npc}'s name in seal-script on the booth

effects.log: It is the last stroke of the old master, and the first of yours.
You write names on request for a stone apiece, and charge less for friends.

events.text: {npc} and you write the primer together: the twelve strokes, the sixty signs, the thousand names. It is printed on a hundred slips and sent to every isle. A scholar in the far east writes back in seal-script, shakily. {npc} reads it aloud in the booth, with trembling hands.
events.arc: The Last Calligrapher of the Seal-Script

effects.log: Your letter takes a month to write.

choices.text: Sit with {npc} while the old calligrapher reads

effects.log: The booth is full of light.

events.text: A small storm has taken up lodging in the spare room of {npc}'s house on the Pine Isle, paying in rain for the fields. {He} did not rent it; the storm just moved in. It is tidy, but it rumbles at night. {He} is not sure how to bring up the subject. {He} asks you to help.
events.arc: The Immortal Who Rented a Room to a Storm

effects.log: The storm rumbles apologetically. A raindrop lands on your nose.

choices.text: Offer the storm a larger room

effects.log: {npc} is aghast. The storm brightens.

choices.text: Say a storm is a storm

effects.log: {npc} lays out a second blanket, resigned.

events.text: The storm has begun to rain on the neighbours, and the neighbours want it out. A deputation arrives with a petition. {npc} has grown fond of the storm. The storm, for its part, is fond of the house. {He} asks you to represent the household at the neighbours' meeting.
events.arc: The Immortal Who Rented a Room to a Storm

choices.text: Speak for the storm at the meeting

effects.log: The neighbours listen, grumbling. The storm waits outside, politely drizzling.

choices.text: Propose the storm be moved to the hills

effects.log: The neighbours approve. {npc} is silent.

choices.text: Offer to host the storm yourself

effects.log: {npc} brightens, then is sad.

events.text: The neighbours agree, grudgingly: the storm may stay if it keeps to a schedule. It takes the form of a dignified afternoon shower. The fields prosper. {npc} comes to rely on the storm's company, and in a year, the storm is a feature of the isle, a thing visitors ask to see.
events.arc: The Immortal Who Rented a Room to a Storm

choices.text: Come and see the afternoon shower

effects.log: It is neat, brief and surprisingly cheerful.

choices.text: Bring the storm a gift of mist

effects.log: It rumbles with joy.

events.text: The storm goes to the hills with a heavy rumble and a farewell drizzle. {npc} is quiet for a month. Then, on a cold night, a small cloud drifts in through the window and settles on the pillow, damp and affectionate. {He} laughs, and weeps, and puts a blanket over it. The neighbours say nothing.
events.arc: The Immortal Who Rented a Room to a Storm

choices.text: Say nothing and tuck the cloud in

effects.log: The cloud purrs, in thunder.

choices.text: Visit the storm in the hills

effects.log: It rains on you gladly.

events.text: Two tea pavilions stand at the head of the same stair on the Lantern Isle, one above the other, and the owners have quarrelled for centuries over whose guests may use the landing. {npc}, the lower owner, sends you up with a message. {He} says it is only a note about the weather.
events.arc: Two Pavilions That Share a Staircase

choices.text: Carry the note up the stair

effects.log: The upper owner reads it, sniffs, and writes a reply.
It says: "Your tea is thin." You decide to carry it anyway.
{npc} sends the note by a gull.

events.text: The two owners meet on the landing for the first time in a century, at a funeral, and cannot agree on who stands where. Both ask you to settle it. The landing is exactly the width of one person. Mourners are waiting on the stair. The air is stiff. You are looking at the two of them, and at the landing.
events.arc: Two Pavilions That Share a Staircase

choices.text: Say one stands, the other sits on the step

effects.log: The owners glare, but one takes the step, grumbling.

choices.text: Say both stand, shoulder to shoulder

effects.log: It is a tight fit and an uneasy peace.
The owners step aside, red-faced.

events.text: For the first time, the two pavilions share a table at the funeral tea. The talk is dry and awkward and, by the third cup, unbearably funny. In a year, the lower owner has opened a door in the shared wall. In a decade, the two pavilions are one, with two entrances, and a plaque that reads: "The Landing."
events.arc: Two Pavilions That Share a Staircase

choices.text: Sip the first cup at the joined pavilion

effects.log: It is thin. You say nothing.

choices.text: Suggest a new name for the stair

effects.log: The stair is renamed "Both Sides." It sticks.

events.text: The shoulder-to-shoulder arrangement holds for the length of the funeral and no longer. The next week, the quarrel resumes with a new complaint about the width of the stair. {npc} says it was the best funeral anyone attended. The stair has never been so well maintained.
events.arc: Two Pavilions That Share a Staircase

choices.text: Accept that the feud is a landmark

effects.log: The pavilions flourish on rivalry.

choices.text: Drink tea at both pavilions in a day

effects.log: Both owners are insulted and sell you more.

events.text: A debt-ledger stall at the Cloud Market sells little books in which to record who owes whom what. The stall-keeper confides that the best-selling pages are the ones labelled "Forgiven."

choices.text: Buy a book of forgiven pages

effects.log: You never fill it, but you like having it.
"Everyone," says the stall-keeper. "Eventually."

events.text: Two old traders at the Cloud Market have been arguing about the interest on a loan that was repaid two thousand years ago. They have stopped for tea twice. Each insists the other owes them a stone.

choices.text: Settle it with one stone, half each

effects.log: They accept, and the argument ends. They look lost.
The argument is the best entertainment in the market.

events.text: An order comes to the sunset dyers for tomorrow evening: a "quiet orange, suitable for forgiving a friend." The dyer holds the order and says, honestly, that this is the best commission of the century.

effects.log: The orange rises over the cloud sea like a held breath.

choices.text: Order a dusk for a friend of your own

effects.log: The dyer says she will see what she can do.

events.text: A page of the Ministry of Weather's tasting notes has blown into your hands: "Easterly: thin, apologetic. Westerly: full, proud. Northerly: sour with a hint of plum. Southerly: asleep."

effects.log: You taste the winds differently afterwards.
A clerk says it has been missing a week and thanks you gravely.

events.text: At the Ministry of Fog's Lost-and-Found, a long umbrella has stood in the corner for a thousand years. A tag on the handle reads: "Claimed by no one. Still hoping." The clerk sighs each time she passes.

effects.log: It is yours now. It never quite dries.

choices.text: Leave it for the rightful owner

effects.log: You tie a ribbon on the handle. The clerk smiles.

events.text: A retired marshal drinks tea in the Palace garden at the same table every day, with the posture of a man on parade. The younger officials salute as they pass. He salutes back, to everyone, equally.

effects.log: He pours you a cup, and says nothing, kindly.
He tells you, with a gleam, about a battle against a gnat.

events.text: A small flag flies from a stick at the edge of the cloud sea, where an isle once stood. A plaque reads: "Here was the Tern Isle. It was loved." Someone has left a bowl of fresh water beside it.

choices.text: Add a pebble to the cairn

effects.log: It joins a small heap.
The bowl stays full all season.

events.text: A family is leaving their drifting isle for the last time. Their cat, on the porch, refuses to go. The mother says goodbye to it, twice. The cat sits and blinks. It is not clear which of them is more sad.

effects.log: The cat comes with you, unimpressed, and sits on your lap.

choices.text: Help the family carry the last box

effects.log: The family thanks you in a small voice.

events.text: In the small hours on the Willow Isle, an immortal in a long coat walks the streets with a lamp, tapping softly on shutters and whispering "good night." Nobody has ever woken. Everyone has slept better since.

effects.log: The figure pauses, and nods, and goes on.
You walk the whole night. You see the isle in a new way.

events.text: A bench on the Quiet Peak has a sign: "Reserved for no one." Many sit on it. Few speak. A sparrow sits on the arm and watches the clouds. You sit down, and the sparrow does not move.

effects.log: The clouds drift. So do you.
It takes the crumb and sits closer.

events.text: A cloud-shepherd counts the flock at dusk by calling each name. The clouds answer with small puffs. One cloud doesn't, and the shepherd waits patiently, saying its name again, until it drifts in from the hillside, embarrassed.

effects.log: You get most of the names wrong. The clouds forgive you.

choices.text: Watch the late cloud come in

effects.log: It brushes your sleeve on the way.

events.text: A stray cloud has been following you since the market, a small grey one with a hopeful look. When you stop, it stops. When you sit, it settles at your feet. A passing shepherd says it is yours now, if you want it.

effects.log: It sleeps on your windowsill and rains on your plants.

choices.text: Take it to the shepherd's flock

effects.log: The cloud goes happily. You miss it for years.

events.text: On the Long Bridge a sign reads: "Promises mended while you wait." A line of customers stretches back to the lamp. One is holding a vow in two pieces, and has been crying quietly all afternoon.

effects.log: The customer takes it, astonished.
The customer blows their nose, loudly. The line laughs, kindly.

events.text: The Orchard Isle has two neighbours who have not spoken in a decade, divided by a hedge of thousand-year peach. Each leaves the other a pot of jam at midsummer, and neither will admit it.

effects.log: Both are annoyed. Both are pleased.

choices.text: Say nothing and take a jar

effects.log: Each gives you a jar. They taste the same.

events.text: A wind-chime on the market barrow is labelled "tuned by eye." Beneath it, in a small hand: "Please tell me if it sings." You flick it. It sings.

effects.log: The peddler, who cannot hear, grins from ear to ear.
It hangs on your window and sings in your sleep.

events.text: A booth at the foot of the library stairs offers names written in the old seal-script. A sign reads: "Nobody can read it, and that is why it is beautiful." You take a rubbing of the sign.

effects.log: It looks like a flock of birds on a branch.

choices.text: Ask for the booth keeper's name in script

effects.log: It takes a long time. It is beautiful.

events.text: A small thunderhead sits on a doorstep on the Pine Isle, stroked by a child. The child says it is theirs, and its name is Pudding. The thunderhead rumbles, bashfully, and drizzles on the child's boots.

effects.log: It crackles softly. Your hair stands on end.

choices.text: Ask the child how they met

effects.log: The child gives a very detailed and implausible account.

events.text: A sign on the Lantern Isle stair reads: "Two pavilions, one stair. Please do not take sides." Someone has added in chalk: "Go to the lower, the cake is better." Someone else: "Liar."

choices.text: Try the cake at the lower pavilion

effects.log: It is good, and thin on frosting.
It is thin. You do not say so.

events.text: A cloud-cat sleeps on the roof of the Pine Isle post-house each afternoon, in the sun. The postmaster has stopped trying to move it. Letters addressed to the cat arrive weekly, from children on other isles.

choices.text: Add a note of your own

effects.log: In a week the cat has replied, with a paw print and a fish scale.

choices.text: Sit beside the cat in the sun

effects.log: You doze, and wake with a sunburn and a fine mood.

events.text: At dusk on the Lantern Isle the lamplighter pauses at every door and asks, "Anyone home?" Some answer, some don't. At the last door, the answer is always the same: a cough, a thank-you, and a lit lamp.

choices.text: Accompany the lamplighter for a street

effects.log: The streets glow behind you. The lamplighter nods once.

choices.text: Leave a lamp lit on your own step

effects.log: The lamplighter taps the glass as he passes.

events.text: {npc}, a heaven-born child of nine, has noticed that the grandparent who raised them cannot read the jade slips and has hidden it for eight hundred years. The child comes to you in whispers: how does one teach an elder who is proud, without hurting a single feeling? Nobody else has been told.
events.arc: The Heaven-Born Who Taught a Grandparent to Read

choices.text: Suggest starting with a story told aloud

effects.log: The child nods gravely and goes off to plan it.
{npc} is horrified at the thought.

choices.text: Say it is not the child's business

effects.log: {npc} looks at you, hurt, and goes away.

events.text: {npc} reads a slip aloud each evening, pretending to practise. The grandparent listens from the next room, and one night corrects a word. Both go silent. The grandparent steps into the doorway, old and straight, and says, "I would like to learn the signs. Quietly." {npc} looks at you, thrilled and terrified.
events.arc: The Heaven-Born Who Taught a Grandparent to Read

choices.text: Offer a quiet room for lessons

effects.log: The room is small and warm, with a lamp. Lessons begin.

choices.text: Suggest the lessons be a game

effects.log: The grandparent frowns, then laughs, and the lessons become a game.

choices.text: Step back and give them room

effects.log: The child takes it from there.

events.text: In a year, the grandparent reads a slip aloud at the window, haltingly, to the whole isle. It is a poem, an old one, about rain. The listeners pretend not to notice that it has taken eight hundred years. At the end, the child stands on a stool and applauds, alone, and then everyone does.
events.arc: The Heaven-Born Who Taught a Grandparent to Read

effects.log: The grandparent bows, as stiffly as a heron.

choices.text: Bring a book as a present

effects.log: The grandparent reads the first line to you, shyly.

events.text: The lessons are a game of signs drawn in flour and rice, and the grandparent turns out to be a fierce player. Within months the child cannot keep up. The two compete over every slip in the house. At the end of the year, the grandparent has read the whole shelf, and cheats at the next round, laughing.
events.arc: The Heaven-Born Who Taught a Grandparent to Read

effects.log: You lose. It is a close-run thing.
The decision is a draw. Both are furious and delighted.

events.text: Along the Reef Road runs a fence of white posts, mended and repainted by {npc} every year for six hundred years, though no one remembers why it was built. {He} paints one post per day and starts again when the last is done. {He} asks you to hold the pail, because the pail is heavy.
events.arc: The Fence-Painter of the Reef Road

choices.text: Hold the pail for the day

effects.log: The paint is thick and smells of lime. The road goes on.

choices.text: Ask why the fence is there

effects.log: "For the sheep," says {npc}. "There are no sheep. There never were."

choices.text: Say a fence needs no painting

effects.log: {npc} nods, and paints.

events.text: A surveyor from the Ministry of Quays arrives with orders to remove the fence, as it stands on a road that is to be widened. {npc} asks the surveyor to wait until the last post is painted, which will take a year. The surveyor looks at you in desperation. "Who is this person?" the surveyor asks.
events.arc: The Fence-Painter of the Reef Road

choices.text: Say a year is not long, for a fence

effects.log: The surveyor agrees, bewildered. {npc} paints with fresh heart.

choices.text: Say the road can go around

effects.log: The surveyor frowns and redraws the plan.

choices.text: Say you cannot help the surveyor

effects.log: The surveyor leaves, muttering.

events.text: The year ends. The last post is painted, white and gleaming. {npc} stands back and looks at it, and then, to your surprise, begins to cry. "I thought it would never be done," {he} says. The road is widened around the fence, which stands intact, a long white line with no purpose and a great beauty.
events.arc: The Fence-Painter of the Reef Road

choices.text: Stand with {npc} at the last post

effects.log: The sun goes down on it. It is the proudest evening of the road.

choices.text: Offer to paint the first post of the new round

effects.log: You do. It is crooked.

events.text: The road goes around, in a long curve, and the fence stands as the centre of a small green. Children play there, sheep from a mortal-made toy wander across the grass, and {npc} paints the posts on the tenth day of each month, with a crowd. The fence has become a purpose of its own.
events.arc: The Fence-Painter of the Reef Road

choices.text: Sit on the green with a picnic

effects.log: You lie in the grass with a book and a pie.
The surveyor, who stayed on to see it, weeps in an uncharacteristic way.

events.text: The Jade Court's pastry contest has a vacancy among its judges, and {npc}, the steward, has asked a rogue with no faction to fill it: you. {He} says the other judges are tired of one another. The seat will not be named in the Court rolls. It is, {he} says, a quiet honour with a quiet insult tucked in it.
events.arc: The Rogue Asked to Judge the Pastry Contest

effects.log: {npc} hands you a spoon. It is slightly bent.
"You will not be thanked in public," says {npc}, "but you will be fed."
{npc} bows, politely.

events.text: The contest day arrives. A famous baker from the Jade Void wins on reputation, but the best pastry is clearly a small, plain bun by an unknown. The other judges lean toward the baker. The steward watches. {npc} gives you a look that says, quietly: this is why you were asked.
events.arc: The Rogue Asked to Judge the Pastry Contest

effects.log: The other judges gasp. The vote is split, two and two. You are the fifth.
The vote is unanimous. The plain bun is forgotten.
The judges are scandalised. {npc} smiles.

events.text: The plain bun is given the prize. The unknown baker, a stooped immortal from a small isle, weeps on the dais. The famous baker, to everyone's surprise, shakes the winner's hand. The Court records a rogue as a judge for the first time, quietly, in the margin. {npc} says the margin is where the best things are kept.
events.arc: The Rogue Asked to Judge the Pastry Contest

choices.text: Share the plain bun with the winner

effects.log: It is warm and a little burnt, and excellent.
{npc} nods. "Come again next year," {he} says.

events.text: The famous baker wins. The unknown baker leaves in silence, and you never see them again. At the feast afterward {npc} offers you a seat, and does not meet your eye. "I did not ask you to be wise," {he} says. "I asked you to be present." It is some comfort. It is not much.
events.arc: The Rogue Asked to Judge the Pastry Contest

choices.text: Look for the plain baker afterward

effects.log: You find them on a distant isle selling buns to children, and buy six.
{npc} accepts it without comment.

events.text: An elder on the Pine Isle holds a jade slip upside-down and reads it aloud with great confidence. Her grandchild, standing beside her, says nothing, and turns the pages very carefully in the right direction.

effects.log: The elder bows. The grandchild beams.
The grandchild takes it with solemn thanks.

events.text: At the end of the Reef Road stands a single white post, freshly painted, with a small label: "Day one." No one knows who started. A bucket and brush wait beside it, with a note: "Whoever passes."

choices.text: Paint the post a second coat

effects.log: The paint dries quickly in the wind. You feel part of something.

choices.text: Add a note to the bucket

effects.log: You write "Thank you." In a week, someone adds "You're welcome."
